papers.node_id: 100bulrev253!!ARTICLE: ANTICIPATING VENEZUELA'S DEBT CRISIS: HIDDEN HOLDOUTS AND THE PROBLEM OF PRICING COLLECTIVE ACTION CLAUSES
papers.title: ARTICLE: ANTICIPATING VENEZUELA'S DEBT CRISIS: HIDDEN HOLDOUTS AND THE PROBLEM OF PRICING COLLECTIVE ACTION CLAUSES
papers.authors: Robert E. Scott; Stephen J. Choi; Mitu Gulati
papers.abstract:
Venezuela's political and economic difficulties are familiar and well reported in the popular press.What is less understood, however, is the role that Venezuela's ability to restructure its sovereign debt will ultimately play in the country's capacity to overcome the effects of the current crisis. Venezuela's current inability to restructure its debt derives from several sources, including the current regime's efforts to forestall acceleration of the debt as well as the impact of U.S. sanctions on creditors engaging with the current regime.But if and when the current regime is replaced by a more benign government, the question once again will be at the forefront: Can Venezuela reach agreement with its creditors who claim the right to accelerated payment of over $ 140 billion in defaulted loans? Answering that question requires scholars to better understand the impediments to bargaining that prevent individual creditors of sovereign debtors who hold rights of enforcement upon default from rationally agreeing to accept debt reduction in exchange for the promise of payment.
Understanding the impediments to a future Venezuelan government successfully restructuring its massive sovereign debt requires an appreciation of the differences between individual contract rights and collective contract rights. In the typical bilateral debt contract, breach occurs when the debtor fails to make a scheduled payment or takes some action that makes future payment less likely. After breach, the creditor demands full payment and, in the event that is not forthcoming, seeks a judgment in court.In commercial debt contracts, key terms - such as what events trigger a default, when payments can be accelerated, where one can sue, how one can enforce, and what remedies one can request - are governed by specific contractual provisions. The stronger the enforcement rights granted to the creditor under the contract, the greater the recovery the creditor can expect to obtain in the event of default and, therefore, the lower the interest rate the creditor will demand. Moreover, when a debt obligation is sold to a third-party purchaser, different rights of enforcement will command different prices.All things equal, a debt obligation with stronger rights of enforcement will trade at a higher price than one with weaker rights. We refer to this standard view of the relationship between interest rates, market prices, and contractual enforcement rights as the "bilateral model."
As a theoretical matter, the assumption that different contract rights have varying effects and thus trade at different prices works well in bilateral debtor-creditor-third party purchaser relationships, where the incentives and actions ofeach party are readily predictable. But much of commercial lending occurs through multilateral debt obligations where there are many anonymous and dispersed creditors with different characteristics, each of these creditors having participation interests in a single, standardized debt contract. To the extent that the rights in question operate through collective decision-making among anonymous creditors with different interests, making predictions regarding the future price effects of those contract rights is a difficult task. Any single holder of a bond, for example, may wonder whether sufficient other bondholders will act in concert to meet the required threshold to trigger a collective-action contract term (such as changing payment-related terms for the bond). And the task becomes more difficult when most investors are passive and will not choose to enforce collective contractual rights, requiring the single bondholder to assess whether activist creditors will choose to enforce those rights. This is particularly true when the activist creditors have financial incentives to remain hidden to maximize their returns from accumulating a position in the bond.
Our focus is the standardized sovereign bond contract that is characterized by a single debtor and many thousands of dispersed creditors, each of whom may have different interests and capabilities. In prior work, we analyzed the activities of activist creditors acting in sovereign bond markets as contract arbitrageurs.These activist hedge funds specialize in unearthing and then enforcing contract provisions that the market may not have fully priced, paid attention to, or even understood.The rents that these activist creditors capture are a function of the arbitrage services they perform for the market.But what are the consequences if the market does not absorb the pricing efficiencies that arbitrage services typically provide because the arbitrage is hidden from the market's view? In this Article, we explore the case in which activist creditors are able to capture rents while hiding from the market. Addressing the significance of hidden activist arbitrage for market pricing and debt restructuring allows us to take a further step in understanding in what ways and under what circumstances activist creditors influence the value of collective, as contrasted with individual, contract rights.
We advance a theory of how creditors' contractual rights of enforcement are priced by the sovereign debt market - a theory we call the "collective action" model.We distinguish between those contract rights that a creditor receivesdirectly and individually (a "unilateral right") and those that require collective action among a group of parties to the same contract (a "collective action right"). We posit that markets will price differences in unilateral rights when the participants are sophisticated commercial parties. For example, take the unilateral right to sue under the law of the jurisdiction specified in the contract. If German law is more predictably protective of creditors' contract rights than Italian law, then other things equal, creditors will consider debt contracts written under German law to be more valuable than those written under Italian law and thus will pay more to acquire those debt obligations on the market.
In contrast, where a contractual right requires a group of contracting parties to coordinate in order to invoke the right - such as a term that requires a certain percentage of bondholders to agree to change payment-related terms - the pricing of variations in this collective action term will depend not only on the explicit contractual language but also on the range of investors in the market. A debt contract that by its explicit terms is more difficult for a group of contracting parties to modify (e.g., one requiring a 90% vote of the creditors for a modification as compared to one requiring a 75% vote) may nonetheless have a higher likelihood of modification if the parties to the first contract are more concentrated and willing to act collectively.Collective action requires coordination, and coordination requires sufficient access to information to predict the actions of other creditors. Consider, for example, a party who contemplates purchasing a debt obligation that provides for the right to sue the debtor for nonpayment if a stated percentage of all of the creditors agree to declare the debtor in default. The value of the right to enforce the debt is a function of what those other creditors will do. Estimating that value requires the prospective purchaser of the obligation to determine the probability that the requisite number of creditors will join in the default declaration.
But imagine that predicting what the other creditors will do depends on knowing the intentions of a few activist creditors whose identity is unknown and who may have the incentive to block the default declaration (for example, because they sold credit default swaps on that debt).Now the value of the contract right is highly uncertain and may not be capable of determination until these few creditors reveal themselves to the market. A bond requiring 90% of the creditors to agree may not in fact provide greater protection against a change in payment terms compared with a bond requiring only 75% of the creditors to agree if the market is unaware of the precise positions of the activist creditors with the incentives to assemble a holdout block. In short, where the market is uncertain of the composition and the incentives of the parties to debt obligations with collective action terms, explicit differences among contracts in the rights embodied in their collective action terms may not get priced at all.
To test the predictions of this collective action model against the bilateral model, we collect data on Venezuela's sovereign bond offerings as well as information about the creditors who were holding those bonds. Over the past two decades, more than a dozen empirical studies have examined the pricing of "modification" terms, a key set of contract terms in sovereign bond contracts that set the vote thresholds required for modifying the payment terms of a bond (such as principal amounts, interest rates, and dates when payments are due). Such modification terms are known as "collective action clauses" ("CACs").CAC thresholds generally range from a high of 100% (unanimity) to a low of 75% of the principal amount of the bonds.Achieving the necessary voting threshold is a precondition to the defaulting sovereign's ability to bargain for a reduction in its payment obligations. These restructuring efforts can be thwarted, however, if a sufficient number of bondholders obtain the votes to block a modification and elect instead to pursue litigation to recover the principal amount of the debt. This, of course, is the holdout strategy pursued by the activist creditors who seek to capture rents at the expense of more passive creditors (and the citizens of the defaulting sovereign). Given the greater leverage a blocking position affords an activist creditor, the prediction from the bilateral model is straightforward: the higher the vote threshold required for a modification, the stronger the bargaining position of any given creditor upon default. Therefore, bonds with the 100% vote requirement should command a higher price than those with the 85% requirement, and those in turn should be more valued by creditors than bonds with the 75% threshold.
There are two reasons why, in theory, differences among these provisions - whether a sovereign bond's payment terms require a vote of 100%, 85%, or 75% of the creditors for modification - should affect the price of the bond: First, other things equal, because an 85% vote threshold is harder for the sovereign debtor to obtain than a 75% threshold, the sovereign seeking to restructure its debt is motivated to offer holders of the 85% bond a larger payment to obtain their consent. Second, on the flip side, because it is easier for activist creditors holding the 85% bond to organize collectively to block a sovereign's restructuring attempt, they can more easily hold out and, by litigating, coerce the debtor into offering a potentially greater recovery.
Despite the importance of these CAC thresholds, virtually none of a dozen or so prior studies of price effects among different CAC terms find evidence supporting the prediction that the markets will value bonds with the 100% vote requirement more highly than the 75% bonds. Instead, the majority of studies report the price effect of particular CAC terms to be somewhere between negligible and zero.And for those papers that do find price effects, the direction of the price movement is inconsistent and only for subsets of the data: some studies show small positive effects, others show small negative effects, and yet others find results like U-shaped curves.Even though a holdout strategy (a) requires strong contract rights (so a creditor does not get crammed down involuntarily) and (b) provides returns that are as high or higher than if the creditor is unable to hold out, the empirical research consistently fails to show that bonds with stronger collective action contract terms command higher prices than those with weaker terms. In short, the empirical analysis of sovereign bond contracts has failed to map on to the bilateral model of debt pricing.
We build on these prior empirical studies by using a natural experiment thrown up by the Venezuelan debt crisis of 2014-2019 to test the predictions ofthe collective action model against the bilateral model and other explanations for the absence of price effects. The Venezuelan natural experiment addresses the data infirmities that may explain why prior attempts to test the differences between individual and collective contract rights in the context of these modification terms have failed: most of the empirical papers compared bond covenants issued by different sovereigns, leading to questions such as whether the lack of observed differences in pricing was due to variations not captured in the empirical models across sovereigns rather than variations in CAC modification terms. Looking only at variations in contract terms in bonds issued by Venezuela allows us to control for any differences across sovereigns.
The data support the claim that differences in the terms of Venezuelan bonds that require collective action are not priced when the presence of activist creditors with the reputation, ability, and capacity to hold out and function as a collectivizing agent is unknown. As a backdrop, the research on sovereign restructurings shows that these holdout creditors (usually fewer than 5% of the bondholders) have been a consistent feature of sovereign restructurings over the past two decades and that the activist creditors who have successfully held out have, in many instances, received lucrative recoveries.But lacking knowledge of where these activist creditors are building a position, the market is unable to distinguish among bonds with legally relevant differences in collective rights. In contrast, we find that bond terms that either provide unilateral rights to creditors or for which collective rights are supported by the known presence of a collectivizing agent are priced by the market.
There are normative implications to the market's inability to price variations in the strength of creditors' rights of enforcement until the presence of collectivizing agents is known. While activist holdouts may decrease social welfare to the extent that they block value-increasing restructurings, holdouts also arguably increase social welfare to the extent that the threat of costlyholdout litigation leads sovereigns to adopt budgetary policies ex ante that reduce the likelihood of future default. Absent the threat of holdouts, sovereigns who expect low cost restructuring ex post may succumb to moral hazard and undertake excessive spending. In order to reduce this moral-hazard risk, sovereigns may willingly accept stronger enforcement rights in return for lower upfront interest rates. However, where the market does not price variation in enforcement rights at the time sovereign bonds are issued, the sovereign will not have the incentive to adopt optimally stringent enforcement rights even if, in a world where such rights were priced, the sovereign would be motivated to do so.
The Article proceeds as follows: Part I expands on our collective action theory, discards several of the explanations for the failure of prior studies on CACs to find robust price effects, and discusses an alternative explanation for why the literature has failed to show price effects from different CAC terms. Part II sets out the empirical predictions about differences in the pricing of contract terms that are generated by the bilateral and collective action stories, respectively. In Part III, we report results. Part IV then reports the reactions of investment managers to the evidence of collective action impediments to efficient pricing and restructuring. That evidence raises normative questions about the role of contract arbitrageurs in this and other similar markets.In considering these questions, we conclude that firms that specialize in the close reading of contract provisions in order to enforce contract rights aggressively often are able to capture rents at the expense of more passive investors as well as the citizens of the defaulting sovereign state. This practice also impacts social welfare: the absence of a price mechanism undermines the sovereign's incentives to adopt enforcement rights at the time bonds are issued that optimally balance the ex ante benefits of reducing moral hazard against the ex post costs of rent seeking by holdouts.
I. A Collective Action Theory of Pricing Multilateral Contract Terms
We argue that the reported absence of price effects in CAC terms with different voting thresholds is due to the effects of impediments that prevent the bond market from being fully informed on terms that require collective action. While the value of an individual contract right to a bondholder is relatively easy to estimate, the value of a collective right whose exercise depends on the support of other creditors is more uncertain. And that is especially so if it is difficult to determine whether other creditors have the same incentives to join in the collective exercise of the contract right. Litigation is costly, both in terms of direct litigation costs and in terms of indirect reputational costs for the litigating parties. We posit that many institutional investors who purchase sovereign bonds (termed "passive creditors") will not view pursuing a sovereign in court as a viable option because of both the desire to maintain good relationships with sovereigns and the burden of justifying large front-end litigation costs to their investors. Rather, if no other option is available, passive creditors will simplyaccept the restructuring offer of the sovereign. Another option is available, however, if one or more of several institutional investors who have developed expertise as activist creditors are motivated to hold out from restructuring offers and aggressively litigate their position.Then the passive creditors may free ride on the activists' litigation efforts. In this case, the primary value of the CAC contract rights is the option to pursue a holdout strategy. But that option has value to a passive creditor (who, by definition, is reluctant to reject the restructuring offer of the sovereign) only if it can predict which bond offerings activists will choose.
To illustrate, consider the market pricing of a bond with an 85% CAC as against a bond with a 75% CAC and ask whether a passive creditorwould value the former more than the latter. At first cut, because it is harder for the debtor to squeeze the creditors in the 85% bond than the 75% bond, one would expect passive creditors to feel more protected if they are in the 85% bond, where the greater risk of a holdout will more effectively constrain the sovereign's restructuring efforts. That is the basic reason why the market should rationally reflect the preference of most creditors for the 85% bond, thus causing the price of those bonds to rise relative to the less favorable 75% bond.
But for both the bond with an 85% CAC and the bond with a 75% CAC, the passive creditor must assess whether, in fact, a holdout is likely to materialize. To be sure, holding out is easier in theory with the 85% CAC since an activist creditor need only acquire 15% of the outstanding bonds to achieve a blocking position. But in practice the motivations of the other bondholders are critical to determining whether holding out is plausible. The passive creditor must predict whether there are activist creditors among the bondholders for that bond offering who possess the litigation expertise and capital resources to sustain the front-end costs necessary to resist successfully the sovereign's efforts to restructure. Ordinarily, one might think that the CAC itself would provide the basis for such a prediction. Passive creditors could examine the contract terms in different bonds and predict that the bonds with the strongest holdout rights would be those that the activists would target. From this perspective, the bond with the 85% CAC would be a better bet than the bond with the 75% CAC.
The fly in the buttermilk is that the strategy that generates the highest expected payoff for the activist creditor depends on it remaining hidden from the market until after the restructuring deal is done. Activist creditors are able to extract a larger return from holding out if they wait until the debtor first negotiates a significant haircut with the other creditors and only then litigate against both the debtor and the holders of the restructured bonds until a settlement is achieved. Put differently, holding out works best if the population of holdouts is relatively small so that it is in the financial interest of the debtor to pay the holdouts in full in order to settle with the other creditors at the restructured rate. This means that a holdout creditor has an incentive to hide its plans, including which bonds it plans to target, until after the other creditors have settled their claims with the sovereign. If the passive creditors believe that an activist creditor will purchase a blocking position in the 85% bond because it requires a smaller investment, the activist may choose instead to invest in the 75% bond in order to obtain a larger net recovery. And that hidden information likely will prevent the market price from reflecting the true value of the bond that will be selected for litigation by the holdout creditor. In short, because the activists are hidden, there should be little differentiation in bond prices notwithstanding different CAC terms until the holdout creditors are revealed - which typically does not occur until after the restructuring deal is complete and there is no longer any trading on the market.

questions.question: Whether sovereign bond markets price differences in collective enforcement rights (for example, varying vote thresholds in collective-action clauses) when potential activist holdout creditors are hidden or unobservable.
questions.answer: No—when activist holdout creditors are hidden or unobservable, markets do not price differences in collective enforcement rights such as CAC vote thresholds.

questions.question: Whether the presence or visibility of activist creditors who can organize holdouts changes how markets value collective (coordination-dependent) contract rights versus unilateral contract rights.
questions.answer: Yes—when activist creditors (a visible collectivizing agent) are present, markets do price collective, coordination-dependent rights, just as they price unilateral rights.

questions.question: Whether the market's failure to price variation in collective enforcement rights affects sovereigns' ex ante incentives to adopt stronger enforcement terms (i.e., whether this pricing failure increases moral hazard in sovereign borrowing and budgeting).
questions.answer: Yes—the failure to price variation in collective enforcement rights undermines sovereigns’ ex ante incentives to adopt optimally stringent enforcement terms and increases moral-hazard risks.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that the pricing and practical value of collective-action clauses depend on investor composition, repeat players, and whether activist creditors are present or hidden, and Paper B argues that the meaning and usefulness of U.S.-style contract language depend on underlying legal institutions, repeat-player communities, and local contracting practices.

shared_topics.topic: the role of specialized or hidden actors in shaping contracting outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes how activist hedge funds (hidden holdouts) and contract arbitrageurs can determine restructuring outcomes and prevent markets from pricing collective rights, while Paper B highlights how U.S. lawyers and large law firms export documentation practices that shape bargaining dynamics and which actors set contractual norms.

shared_topics.topic: normative and efficiency implications of contract design for incentives, trust, and market welfare
shared_topics.justification: Paper A assesses how CAC design and hidden holdouts affect sovereign incentives, moral hazard, and social welfare in restructurings, and Paper B examines how adoption of complex U.S.-style documentation creates agency costs, an arms race in boilerplate, and potential effects on trust and bargaining efficiency in Latin American transactions.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 1988uilllrev481!!ARTICLE: RECENT REGULATORY PERSPECTIVES ON DEBT-FOR-EQUITY SWAPS AND SECURITIZATION OF THIRD WORLD DEBT © 1988 Center for Transnational Legal Studies
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: RECENT REGULATORY PERSPECTIVES ON DEBT-FOR-EQUITY SWAPS AND SECURITIZATION OF THIRD WORLD DEBT © 1988 Center for Transnational Legal Studies

shared_topics.topic: mechanisms for restructuring sovereign / Third World debt (debt-for-equity swaps, bond modification, securitization)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze concrete tools used to address heavy sovereign indebtedness — Paper A examines regulatory treatment of debt-for-equity swaps and the securitization of bank loans as options for dealing with indebted countries, while Paper B analyzes bond-level restructuring mechanics (collective-action clauses, voting thresholds) and how those mechanisms enable or impede sovereign debt workouts.

shared_topics.topic: transferability of claims and secondary‑market implications of restructuring
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on securitization efforts intended to convert bank loans into more readily transferable instruments in secondary markets, and Paper B studies how the trading, ownership composition, and market pricing of sovereign bonds (including hidden actors) shape the incentives and feasibility of restructurings.

shared_topics.topic: how legal, regulatory, and contractual enforcement rights shape pricing and restructuring outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Both papers engage with the legal/regulatory environment that governs creditor rights — Paper A surveys statutes, accounting standards, and U.S. regulator interpretations affecting novel transactions, while Paper B theorizes and empirically tests how differences in contractual enforcement (unilateral vs collective rights, CAC thresholds) and litigation opportunities affect bond prices and restructuring bargaining power.

shared_topics.topic: the role and incentives of creditors (banks, institutional and activist creditors) in restructuring processes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A addresses how banking institutions are offered a 'menu' of options and the regulatory constraints on banks' participation in restructurings, and Paper B analyzes the strategies and incentives of passive institutional investors versus activist/holdout creditors and how those actors influence pricing, coordination, and the success of restructurings.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 88washlrev1323!!SYMPOSIUM: CONTRACTS IN THE REAL WORLD: ESSAY: CONTRACT AS PATTERN LANGUAGE
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: CONTRACTS IN THE REAL WORLD: ESSAY: CONTRACT AS PATTERN LANGUAGE

shared_topics.topic: how standardized contract clauses (boilerplate, CACs) shape market pricing, liquidity, and tradability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how standardized, modular contract patterns and boilerplate make certain debt instruments 'informationally insensitive' and thus highly tradable and liquid (but also vulnerable), while Paper B empirically studies how standardized sovereign bond clauses—especially collective action clauses—should in theory affect bond prices and liquidity but often do not due to market frictions.

shared_topics.topic: the role of informational opacity and hidden actors in valuation and enforcement of contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that modularity and restricted information transfer can hide information value and contribute to market freezes (e.g., during the financial crisis), and Paper B shows how hidden activist holdout creditors and opacity about their positions prevent markets from pricing collective-action rights correctly.

shared_topics.topic: how contract design choices create incentive effects and normative tradeoffs (moral hazard, social welfare, creditor/debtor incentives)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a normative agenda arguing contract design should be rethought to better serve human needs and to avoid perverse systemic incentives, while Paper B discusses the social-welfare implications of holdouts and how the market's failure to price enforcement rights alters sovereign incentives and moral hazard ex ante.

shared_topics.topic: the systemic consequences of interconnected, interlocking contracts and collective decision provisions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that individual contract patterns interlock into transactions and markets such that local design failures can cascade into systemic crises (e.g., MBS and the shadow banking run), and Paper B examines how the multilateral structure of sovereign bonds and collective-action thresholds (plus holdouts) affect the feasibility of restructurings and can produce macro-level restructuring failures.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 95ambankrlj313!!ARTICLE: The Importance of Being Bound: Bondholders' Vote and Workouts in the U.S. and in Italy
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Importance of Being Bound: Bondholders' Vote and Workouts in the U.S. and in Italy

shared_topics.topic: how bondholder voting thresholds (unanimity vs majority/CACs) affect the feasibility of out‑of‑court restructurings
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes statutory and contractual rules (e.g., §316(b) TIA, Italian indentures) and argues that allowing majority‑binding votes facilitates workouts; Paper B empirically studies variation in CAC vote thresholds (75%, 85%, 100%) and how those thresholds influence the sovereign's ability to obtain creditor consent and thus to restructure debt.

shared_topics.topic: the holdout / collective action problem among dispersed creditors and its impact on restructurings
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames the protection of individual bondholder consent as creating veto power that can block renegotiation and enable holdouts; Paper B develops a theory of activist holdouts (including hidden activists) and shows how holdout behavior can thwart collective restructuring and capture rents.

shared_topics.topic: the tradeoff between creditor protection and debtors' ability to reorganize (normative and policy implications)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A weighs investor protections embodied in the TIA against the issuer's need for midterm modifications to avoid insolvency and proposes policy reforms (majority rule, SEC exemptions); Paper B explores normative consequences of holdouts for social welfare and moral hazard, debating whether stronger enforcement rights (which protect creditors) produce desirable ex ante incentives.

shared_topics.topic: the role of legal/regulatory and contractual design (statute, exemptions, CACs, jurisdiction) in shaping creditor incentives and restructuring outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how statutory interpretation, regulatory exemptions, and indenture terms in different jurisdictions (U.S. and Italy) determine whether core bond terms can be modified out of court; Paper B analyzes how specific contract features (collective action clauses, governing law, enforcement rights) and their observability to the market influence pricing, creditor coordination, and the success of sovereign restructurings.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 1988uilllrev219!!INTERNATIONAL BANKING SYMPOSIUM: FOREWORD 1988 Center for Transnational Legal Studies
compared_to.partner_title: INTERNATIONAL BANKING SYMPOSIUM: FOREWORD 1988 Center for Transnational Legal Studies

shared_topics.topic: sovereign debt restructuring legal mechanisms and stages
shared_topics.justification: Paper A maps and analyzes the legal architecture of sovereign debt restructurings (short-term reschedulings, multiyear restructuring agreements, and later disaggregation/securitization and debt-to-equity conversions) and the documentation that governs them; Paper B examines how contractual design (notably collective-action clauses) affects a sovereign's practical ability to reach restructuring agreements, using Venezuela as a case study.

shared_topics.topic: creditor rights, inter-creditor obligations, and sharing/equality provisions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on contractual devices among commercial creditors—sharing provisions, mandatory prepayment clauses, negative pledges and the principle of equal treatment—that structure creditors' relative positions; Paper B develops a theory distinguishing unilateral versus collective enforcement rights and analyzes how different collective voting thresholds alter creditors' bargaining power and expected recoveries.

shared_topics.topic: holdout creditors, litigation as a strategic tool, and collective-action impediments
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses the surprisingly limited litigation in sovereign restructurings while highlighting doctrinal defences (e.g., act of state) and the implications of creditor litigation for restructuring; Paper B centers on activist ‘holdout’ creditors who use litigation strategically, the incentives for hiding positions, and how these actors create collective-action impediments to consensual restructurings.

shared_topics.topic: secondary-market pricing of sovereign claims and the effects of contractual terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats the disaggregation/securitization of bank claims and the sale of interests into broader secondary markets as a key development affecting debt allocation and creditor exposure; Paper B empirically studies how contract terms—especially CAC thresholds and enforcement rights—are (or are not) reflected in secondary-market prices, showing how informational frictions and hidden activists can prevent pricing differences.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 39harvintllj1!!ARTICLE: ACTS OF STATE AND FOREIGN SOVEREIGN OBLIGATIONS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: ACTS OF STATE AND FOREIGN SOVEREIGN OBLIGATIONS

shared_topics.topic: the enforceability of sovereign contracts in foreign courts and the effect of judicial doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how the act of state doctrine can prevent U.S. courts from adjudicating breaches of sovereign contracts, undermining investors' remedies; Paper B studies how the availability and prospect of successful litigation (holdout suits) shapes creditor strategies and the value of sovereign bonds, implicating courts' willingness to enforce sovereign obligations.

shared_topics.topic: contractual design as a tool to allocate sovereign risk (jurisdictional waivers, guarantees, and collective‑action clauses)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates jurisdictional‑waiver proposals and other contractual devices as means for states to credibly commit and reduce investor risk; Paper B examines how specific bond contract terms—choice of law, forum, and especially collective action clauses—affect creditors' enforcement rights and therefore bargaining power in restructurings.

shared_topics.topic: the impact of legal uncertainty and predictability of enforcement on pricing and investment incentives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that doctrinal uncertainty (ad hoc application of act of state) destroys the ex ante value of sovereign commitments and deters foreign investment or raises required returns; Paper B documents that markets often fail to price differences in collective enforcement rights because uncertainty (including hidden activist behavior) obscures enforceability, which in turn distorts sovereign incentives when issuing debt.

shared_topics.topic: the interaction between private litigation strategies (holdouts/activists) and public foreign‑policy or political constraints
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames judicial abstention doctrines as responses to foreign‑policy concerns that limit private enforcement of sovereign obligations; Paper B analyzes activist holdout litigation—including the strategic choice to remain hidden—and shows how private litigating behavior and external constraints (e.g., sanctions, political regimes) together shape restructuring outcomes and welfare.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 70lawcontempprob115!!ARTICLE: ODIOUS DEBT, ODIOUS CREDIT, ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT, AND DEMOCRATIZATION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: ODIOUS DEBT, ODIOUS CREDIT, ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT, AND DEMOCRATIZATION

shared_topics.topic: legitimacy and repayment of pre-transition sovereign debt (odious debt and successor liability)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly asks whether democracies should inherit and repay debts incurred by prior authoritarian regimes (the odious debt question), and Paper B confronts the related problem after regime replacement by analyzing whether a new Venezuelan government can lawfully and practically restructure or be compelled to pay defaulted loans held by creditors.

shared_topics.topic: role of legal and contractual enforcement mechanisms in sovereign debt outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses international-law doctrines, reputational sanctions, asset seizure, and the lack of sovereign bankruptcy as enforcement tools, while Paper B analyzes contractual enforcement rights (jurisdiction, litigation remedies) and collective-action clauses (CACs) as determinants of creditors' power and restructuring feasibility.

shared_topics.topic: collective action, holdouts, and creditor incentives during restructuring
shared_topics.justification: Paper B develops a collective-action model of CACs showing how holdout creditors and hidden activist arbitrageurs can block or extract rents in restructurings, and Paper A likewise engages with creditor behavior and enforcement (including reputational and litigation risks) that shape whether and how debt is repudiated or restructured after a regime change.

shared_topics.topic: how debt structure and creditor behavior influence a country's economic development and political stability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A ties excessive or illegitimate borrowing under dictatorships to diverted development spending and fragile democratization, while Paper B links a debtor state's ability to restructure (or be held up by creditors) to its capacity to recover economically and stabilize politically after a crisis or government change.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 78stjohnslrev1011!!ARTICLE:TAX MALPRACTICE: AREAS IN WHICH IT OCCURS AND THE MEASURE OF DAMAGES-AN UPDATE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:TAX MALPRACTICE: AREAS IN WHICH IT OCCURS AND THE MEASURE OF DAMAGES-AN UPDATE

shared_topics.topic: measure of legal recoveries and damages for wrongdoing or enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly analyzes the proper measure of damages recoverable in tax malpractice suits, and Paper B studies the recoveries (rents) that holdout/activist creditors obtain via litigation and settlement, treating those recoveries as central to understanding incentives and market pricing.

shared_topics.topic: role, incentives, and accountability of specialist professionals/intermediaries
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines when tax attorneys and accountants can be held financially responsible for flawed advice or malpractice, while Paper B analyzes activist hedge funds and contract-arbitrageurs as specialist actors who strategically enforce rights to capture rents and affect outcomes for passive creditors.

shared_topics.topic: how legal rules and contract design create ex ante incentives and moral hazard
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses how liability rules and IRS enforcement shape advisors' behavior and social consequences (e.g., in tax shelter promotion), and Paper B shows how the (non-)pricing of collective enforcement rights alters sovereigns' and investors' ex ante fiscal and investment incentives, including moral hazard concerns.

shared_topics.topic: empirical or case-based analysis to identify where litigation/enforcement concentrates
shared_topics.justification: Paper A surveys reported tax malpractice cases to identify practice areas (estate planning, late filing, shelters) that spawn suits, and Paper B uses Venezuelan bond data and past restructuring episodes as a natural experiment to detect where collective-action impediments and holdout litigation arise and how markets price them.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 62washlrev397!!ARTICLE: RETHINKING THE ACT OF STATE DOCTRINE: AN ANALYSIS IN TERMS OF JURISDICTION TO PRESCRIBE.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: RETHINKING THE ACT OF STATE DOCTRINE: AN ANALYSIS IN TERMS OF JURISDICTION TO PRESCRIBE.

shared_topics.topic: domestic courts' role in adjudicating and enforcing claims against foreign sovereigns
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes and seeks to redefine the constraints on U.S. courts (the act of state doctrine) when asked to judge the validity or legal consequences of foreign sovereign acts; Paper B studies how private creditors use domestic litigation (and the threat of litigation) to enforce sovereign debt claims and shape restructuring outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: jurisdiction to prescribe / choice of law and forum in disputes involving sovereigns
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes analyzing the act of state doctrine in terms of international law rules on a state's jurisdiction to prescribe which law governs conduct, while Paper B focuses on contractual choice-of-law and forum clauses in sovereign bond contracts and how those legal designations affect enforceability and pricing.

shared_topics.topic: tension between state sovereignty and private creditors' rights in cross-border disputes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A is centrally concerned with reconciling doctrines that protect sovereign acts with private parties' ability to obtain remedies, and Paper B examines the conflict between sovereign debtors seeking collective restructurings and individual (activist) creditors using contractual and judicial rights to block or extract value.

shared_topics.topic: how legal uncertainty or doctrinal ambiguity influences economic behavior and restructuring outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that doctrinal confusion (multiple, inconsistent theories of the act of state) produces arbitrary results and impedes predictable regulation of international transactions, while Paper B documents that uncertainty about collective enforcement (hidden holdouts, unclear likelihood of litigation) prevents markets from pricing differences in collective-action clauses and frustrates efficient sovereign restructurings.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 1989columbuslrev307!!SYMPOSIUM: RETHINKING LEGAL OPINION LETTERS: SAME THOUGHTS ON THE ECONOMICS OF LEGAL OPINIONS
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: RETHINKING LEGAL OPINION LETTERS: SAME THOUGHTS ON THE ECONOMICS OF LEGAL OPINIONS

shared_topics.topic: economic valuation of legal instruments and contractual rights
shared_topics.justification: Paper A asks whether third‑party legal opinions materially add value to commercial transactions and advocates measuring their scope by cost/benefit; Paper B empirically examines whether and how sovereign bond contract terms (especially collective action clauses) are priced by markets, interrogating the economic value of contractual enforcement rights.

shared_topics.topic: information asymmetry and signaling in reliance on legal texts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats the legal opinion as a signaling device that provides reassurance to recipient counsel and induces disclosures, while Paper B shows that hidden actors (activist holdouts) and uncertainty about creditors' incentives prevent markets from correctly pricing collective contract rights, highlighting how asymmetric information shapes reliance and valuation.

shared_topics.topic: standardization of legal forms to reduce transaction costs and uncertainty
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses efforts by bar associations and practitioners to standardize opinion language and formats to lower negotiation costs and avoid traps for unwary lawyers, and Paper B studies standardized sovereign bond contracts (CACs) and how their uniform terms interact with market pricing and negotiating frictions in restructurings.

shared_topics.topic: tradeoffs between ex ante incentives and ex post enforcement costs (cost–benefit of legal design)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames the need for opinions in cost/benefit terms—limiting scope to what business diligence requires—while Paper B analyzes normative tradeoffs between stronger enforcement rights (which can discipline sovereigns ex ante) and the ex post social costs of holdout litigation and rent extraction by activists.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 88nyulrevonline17!!ARTICLE: COMMENT ON MARKET CONDITIONS AND CONTRACT DESIGN: VARIATIONS IN DEBT CONTRACTING +
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: COMMENT ON MARKET CONDITIONS AND CONTRACT DESIGN: VARIATIONS IN DEBT CONTRACTING +

shared_topics.topic: how contract design (covenants, collateral, CACs) affects debt pricing under adverse market conditions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies how variation in collective action clauses (CACs) and other enforcement terms should — in theory — affect sovereign bond prices but finds markets often fail to price CAC strength; Paper B seeks to explain why lenders demand tighter covenants or more collateral as market interest rates rise, linking contract design to pricing and risk premia.

shared_topics.topic: information asymmetries and hidden actors shaping contract choice and market pricing
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes how hidden activist creditors and uncertainty about creditor composition prevent markets from valuing collective enforcement rights; Paper B models adverse selection as a driver of collateral and covenant design that mitigates information problems between borrowers and lenders.

shared_topics.topic: tradeoffs between ex‑ante incentives (moral hazard) and ex‑post enforcement costs in debt contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights normative implications where lack of priced enforcement rights can worsen sovereign moral hazard and alter ex‑ante policy choices, while Paper B explicitly deploys a moral hazard model to explain why collateral (and by implication other enforcement devices) are used to discipline borrowers.

shared_topics.topic: mechanisms for creditor coordination and enforcement (collective action vs. covenant enforcement)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on collective decision thresholds (CAC vote requirements) and the role of activist creditors as collectivizing agents in restructurings, whereas Paper B analyzes how covenant design and collateral operate as contractual governance mechanisms to prevent borrower opportunism and substitute for direct collective creditor action.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: ECONOMIC AND MONETARY UNION IN EUROPE: LEGAL IMPLICATIONS OF THE ARRIVAL OF THE SINGLE CURRENCY

shared_topics.topic: legal treatment and continuity of pre-existing contracts during large-scale monetary or sovereign transitions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how contracts denominated in the ECU or national currencies will be treated, converted, or continued when the euro is introduced and national currencies cease to be legal tender; Paper B analyzes how sovereign debt contracts can be modified or enforced during a sovereign restructuring and how contractual terms (like CACs) affect continuity of payment obligations.

shared_topics.topic: how legal and institutional rules affect pricing and valuation of financial instruments
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses how EMU regulations, fixed conversion rates, and new settlement systems will alter issuance, trading, and pricing of bonds, securities, and derivatives in euro terms; Paper B empirically studies how contract provisions (unilateral vs collective rights, CAC thresholds, jurisdiction) and the presence of activist creditors influence sovereign bond prices.

shared_topics.topic: coordination problems among dispersed market participants and their effects on market outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes the need for coordinated action across Member States, EU institutions, and market intermediaries to implement the single currency and associated market infrastructure; Paper B focuses on coordination (or failure to coordinate) among dispersed bondholders, the role of activist creditors in collectivizing action, and how coordination constraints affect restructurings.

shared_topics.topic: the impact of legal enforcement mechanisms and institutional design on incentives for restructuring and compliance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how EU supervisory structures, legal tender rules, and institutional design (ECB, EMI, convergence criteria) create incentives for Member States and market participants to comply and adapt to EMU; Paper B examines how enforcement rights, litigation risk, jurisdictional rules, and sanctions shape creditors' incentives to hold out or accept restructurings and thereby affect sovereign debt outcomes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 45arizlrev133!!ARTICLE:How to Read a Contract
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:How to Read a Contract

shared_topics.topic: how specific contractual terms determine enforceable rights and shape parties' strategies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how particular bond clauses (e.g., CAC vote thresholds, unilateral vs collective rights) create distinct enforcement powers that enable or constrain holdout and restructuring strategies; Paper B provides a systematic method for reading contract clauses so readers can identify what rights and obligations the text actually creates and how those terms will operate in practice.

shared_topics.topic: information asymmetry and hidden actors affecting contract valuation and enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that market pricing and the exercise of collective rights are distorted when activist creditors remain hidden, creating uncertainty about whether collective actions will materialize; Paper B emphasizes that contract reading requires uncovering implicit or missing information (rules, usages, contingencies) and assessing uncertainty about future events the contract must govern.

shared_topics.topic: how contract design influences incentives, bargaining outcomes, and social welfare
shared_topics.justification: Paper A connects clause design (e.g., CACs, enforcement rights) to incentives for sovereigns and creditors, moral hazard, and welfare consequences of holdouts versus orderly restructurings; Paper B treats contract drafting and the reader's ability to negotiate or revise terms as central to shaping future bargaining positions and protecting parties' interests.

shared_topics.topic: the role of the external legal and normative context in interpreting and valuing contract terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights how governing law and legal enforcement regimes (e.g., jurisdictional differences) affect creditors' expected recoveries and bond prices; Paper B instructs readers to incorporate contract law, regulations, customs, and usages as necessary supplemental text when interpreting what contractual provisions mean and how they will be enforced.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 22fordhamintllj292!!ARTICLE: A PROSPECTIVE ENLARGEMENT OF THE ROLES OF THE BRETTON WOODSFINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS IN INTERNATIONAL PEACE OPERATIONS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A PROSPECTIVE ENLARGEMENT OF THE ROLES OF THE BRETTON WOODSFINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS IN INTERNATIONAL PEACE OPERATIONS

shared_topics.topic: coordination and collective-action problems among dispersed international actors
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents the expanding cast of international participants in peacekeeping, peacemaking, and peace‑building and the resulting need to coordinate mandates, resources, and actions; Paper B analyzes how dispersed bondholders, hidden activist creditors, and collective‑action clauses create coordination failures that shape sovereign debt restructuring outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: institutional and contractual design for managing international crises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues for reforming and enlarging the roles of multilateral institutions (notably Bretton Woods institutions and the U.N.) to better manage post‑Cold War conflicts, while Paper B examines how the design of sovereign bond contracts (CAC thresholds) and market institutions affects renegotiation, pricing, and crisis resolution.

shared_topics.topic: financial capacity, resource allocation, and their impact on crisis recovery
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes the growing financial, technological, and human‑resource demands of contemporary peace operations in low‑income states, and Paper B studies how sovereign debt burdens and creditor behavior determine a country's fiscal capacity and prospects for economic and political recovery after crisis.

shared_topics.topic: normative trade-offs of external enforcement/intervention on sovereign behavior and social welfare
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages with the aims and limits of international peace‑building interventions to consolidate peace and confidence among populations, whereas Paper B explores how creditor enforcement rights and holdout strategies create trade‑offs between ex ante incentives (moral hazard mitigation) and ex post costs (rent‑seeking litigation) for sovereigns and their citizens.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE FACILITATION OF THE BRADY PLAN: EMERGING MARKETS DEBT TRADING FROM 1989 TO 1993

shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents how the growing secondary market in LDC debt materially promoted and facilitated the Brady Plan restructurings in 1989–1993, while Paper B examines how secondary-market features (dispersion of bondholders, trading, and hidden positions) shape the ability of a sovereign to obtain creditor consent and complete restructurings.

shared_topics.topic: pricing and valuation of distressed sovereign debt given contract terms and market information
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes trading in emerging-market debt and the market outcomes for debt exchanges, buy‑backs and swaps that underlie valuation in distressed markets, and Paper B develops and tests a model of how contractual clauses (especially CAC thresholds) and information about creditors affect market prices of sovereign bonds.

shared_topics.topic: the role and strategies of market participants (banks, institutional investors, activist creditors) in shaping restructuring outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on banks' behavior—provisioning, exit from LDC lending, and use of secondary markets to arrange debt-equity swaps and buybacks—while Paper B focuses on activist hedge funds/holdouts and passive institutional creditors and how their strategic choices (including hidden accumulation and litigation) influence restructurings.

shared_topics.topic: how the development of secondary markets changes incentives for creditors and sovereigns (provisioning, moral hazard, contract design)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that secondary-market trading forced banks to recognize loan losses, exit risky lending, and enabled structured debt exchanges, altering creditor incentives; Paper B analyzes how unpriced collective enforcement rights and the threat (or absence) of holdouts create moral‑hazard and contract‑design incentives for sovereigns and creditors.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: SOVEREIGN DEBT EXCHANGES 1988 Center for Transnational Legal Studies

shared_topics.topic: creditor coordination and collective-action problems in sovereign debt restructurings
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines the need to consolidate many creditors into umbrella restructuring packages and the cooperative, consensus-building required to make restructurings work; Paper B analyses how dispersed creditors, vote thresholds, and hidden activist holdouts create collective-action impediments that shape the feasibility and outcome of sovereign restructurings.

shared_topics.topic: legal and contractual design of sovereign debt instruments and their effect on restructuring flexibility
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explores structuring and documenting various debt-exchange transactions (including the legal issues that arise) to restore contractual flexibility, while Paper B focuses on how specific contract terms—especially collective action clauses and enforcement rights—affect bargaining leverage, market pricing, and the ability to modify payment terms.

shared_topics.topic: use of non‑traditional mechanisms and non‑bank actors in sovereign debt resolution
shared_topics.justification: Paper A surveys alternatives to traditional commercial‑bank financing such as debt/equity swaps, debt‑for‑debt, payment‑in‑kind, and debt‑for‑nature transactions as tools to reconfigure sovereign claims; Paper B analyzes the role of activist creditors and hedge‑fund ‘contract arbitrageurs’ as non‑traditional actors whose strategies (e.g., holdouts and litigation) materially influence restructuring outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: distributional and incentive (welfare) consequences of different restructuring strategies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes equitable burden‑sharing among creditors as central to stabilizing debtor/creditor relations, whereas Paper B assesses how holdout strategies and the market's inability to price enforcement rights affect social welfare, sovereign moral hazard, and the ex ante incentives to adopt particular enforcement regimes.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: PARI PASSU CLAUSES AND THE SKEUOMORPH PROBLEM IN CONTRACT LAW

shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames the pari passu clause as a 'skeuomorph' that inexplicably persists in the sophisticated sovereign debt market, and Paper B documents that variation in collective action clauses (CACs) is not reflected in market prices, explaining why legally important but problematic clauses can remain embedded in sovereign bond contracts.

shared_topics.topic: market failure in pricing contractual enforcement rights among sophisticated creditors
shared_topics.justification: Paper A questions the baseline assumption that competitive markets among sophisticated parties will eliminate costly or purposeless contract features, while Paper B empirically shows that markets often fail to price differences in collective enforcement rights (CAC thresholds), contradicting the bilateral-model prediction.

shared_topics.topic: the role of information frictions and hidden actors in undermining efficient contracting and pricing
shared_topics.justification: Paper A raises the puzzle of persistent clauses despite sophisticated actors and surveys possible explanations beyond simple bargaining (including informational and behavioral factors), and Paper B develops and tests a theory where hidden activist creditors and asymmetric information prevent accurate pricing of collective rights and enable holdout strategies.

shared_topics.topic: normative consequences for sovereign debt restructuring and incentives (including moral hazard and contract design)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights that persistent, nonfunctional clauses call into question assumptions about contract design and market-driven correction, and Paper B explores how unpriced collective rights and hidden holdouts affect restructuring outcomes, sovereign incentives, and social welfare (including moral‑hazard concerns).

papers.node_id: 86stjohnslrev953!!ARTICLE: ATTORNEY MALPRACTICE: NEW YORK'S MEASURE OF DAMAGES- BENEFIT-OF-THE-BARGAIN? A ROSE BY ANY OTHER NAME …
papers.title: ARTICLE: ATTORNEY MALPRACTICE: NEW YORK'S MEASURE OF DAMAGES- BENEFIT-OF-THE-BARGAIN? A ROSE BY ANY OTHER NAME …
papers.abstract:
Recently I had occasion to examine the New York measure of damages in tax malpractice situations.During this work I was struck by the realization that with respect to such malpractice causes of action there does not appear to be a clear, well-defined articulation of the applicable measure of damages in New York. This was especially perplexing because in both breach of contract and fraud situations, the measure of damages is well defined. For breach of contract, an injured party may recover "benefit-of-the-bargain" damages,while a defrauded party is entitled to recover "out-of-pocket" damages.Both of these measures of damages are clearly established by the Court of Appeals,and the labels are rather attractive and elegant. In tax malpractice, and in attorney malpractice in general, there simply is no analog.
To the extent there is any attempt to generalize the measure of damages in negligence situations, which includes tax malpractice, the courts state that the injured party is to be made "whole."Unfortunately, this seems to be a goal rather than ameasure of damages. The problem is that there is no fixed definition of what it means to be made "whole." It depends entirely on how "whole" is defined. "To be made whole" has different meanings in different contexts. Thus, to be made whole has been applied with respect to damages from personal injury,breach of contract,negligence or strict products liability,and breach of fiduciary duty by an executorand by an escrow agent,despite the fact that the measure of damages may be different in each situation. The Fourth Department was very perceptive when, with respect to a complaint that alleged causes of action for breach of fiduciary duty, negligence, breach of contract and fraud, it stated: "While the precise measure of damages may vary under each of those theories, there can be no doubt that, under all of them, the "object of compensatory damages' is the same, i.e., to make the plaintiff "whole.' "
While it might be asymmetrical and a bit intellectually troubling that there is no attractive and pithy catch phrase describing the negligence measure of damages, as there is for fraud and breach of contract damages, I do not wish to address the entire negligence area. Negligence seems to be very broad and to include many disparate segments. For instance, it includes personal injuries by automobiles and other means, medical malpractice, damage to property, malpractice by all types of professionals, etc. Many of these areas have developed unique rules to deal with their unique circumstances. I assume the existence of these many different adaptations prevent the broad negligence area from being susceptible to one simple, catchy description. I certainly am unable to suggest one. However, I wish to focus solely on one segment of the negligencearea. It is the thesis of this Article that the traditional measure of damages in New York in all attorney malpractice situations, including tax malpractice, is essentially the same as the breach of contract measure of damages, that is, benefit-of-the-bargain damages. This is based primarily upon the definition of each measure of damages. It is also buttressed by cases that indicate that in attorney malpractice situations the damages recoverable are the same regardless of whether the cause of action is framed in tort, that is, negligence, or breach of contract.
This thesis is probably not very novel. In Solon v. Domino,the Southern District trial judge directly sidestepped addressing this issue: "tabling the legal question whether benefit-of-the-bargain damages are recoverable in a negligence action under New York law."Presumably, this was in response to the plaintiffs' suggestion that benefit-of-the-bargain damages were the appropriate remedy in that tax malpractice situation.
Before proceeding, I wish to emphasize that my thesis is that New York's traditional measure of damages in attorney malpractice cases is essentially the same as the benefit-of-the-bargain measure of damages of contract law. In recent years, courts in New York seem to have strayed from the traditional measure of damages in tax malpractice situations. Instead, they seem to have applied the fraud, out-of-pocket measure of damages.In a recent article,I argued extensively that this deviation is wrong and seems to have occurred inadvertently rather than in a principled manner. Later cases involving negligently rendered incorrect tax advice simply followed the holding in a prior caseinvolving incorrect tax advice withoutfocusing on the fact that the prior case involved only fraud causes of action, which have a much narrower measure of damages than the traditional negligence measure of damages in these situations.
The benefit-of-the-bargain measure of damages for breach of contract seems to be long established and quite well understood. In an early casein which the New York Court of Appeals was contrasting contract damages and fraudulent misrepresentation damages, it described breach of contract damages as follows:
The measure of damages which flows from a breach of contract is the difference between the value of what has been received under the contract and the value of what would have been received if the contract had been performed according to its terms. Damages there are not limited to indemnity for loss suffered through the making of the contract. The injured party is entitled to the benefit of his bargain as written and is entitled to damages for the loss caused by failure to perform the stipulated bargain. That loss may include the profits which he would have derived from performance of the contract.
In a more recent case,the New York Court of Appeals essentially reiterated this earlier formulation:
[A] cause of action for breach of warranty is a contractual remedy[- ]a remedy which seeks to provide the parties with the benefit of their bargain. It is, in essence, a remedy designed to enforce the agreement, express or implied, of the parties and toplace them, should one of the parties fail to perform in accordance with the agreement, in the same position they would have been had the agreement been performed.

questions.question: Whether, in attorney malpractice cases, plaintiffs' recoverable damages should reflect the value of the performance they expected to receive from the attorney (i.e., the lost expected benefit) rather than only their actual out-of-pocket losses.
questions.answer: Yes—the paper’s thesis is that in New York attorney malpractice cases the proper measure is benefit-of-the-bargain damages (the client’s expected benefit), not merely out-of-pocket loss.

questions.question: Whether the measure of damages available to a client varies depending on whether the claim against the attorney is framed as a tort (negligence) or as a contract claim, or whether both formulations should produce the same damage remedy.
questions.answer: They should be the same: the paper cites cases indicating that in attorney malpractice the damages recoverable do not vary whether the claim is framed in negligence (tort) or in contract.

questions.question: Whether courts handling attorney tax-advice errors have shifted from a traditional, broader damage measure toward a narrower out-of-pocket approach, and whether that shift is legally or conceptually justified.
questions.answer: Yes; the abstract says New York courts handling tax-malpractice have shifted toward the fraud-style, narrower out-of-pocket measure, and it contends this deviation is wrong and occurred inadvertently rather than on a principled basis.

matched_themes: What measures of damages should plaintiffs recover in professional malpractice suits arising from tax advice, and what valuation approaches properly reflect lost expected benefits versus out-of-pocket losses?
Can clients recover additional tax liabilities caused by negligent tax advice as compensable damages in malpractice suits, and what measures of damages apply?
Should the measure of damages available to a client against an attorney vary depending on framing as tort (negligence) versus contract, and how should courts determine the appropriate remedy?
When are plaintiffs entitled to recover lost expected benefits versus out-of-pocket losses in attorney malpractice cases?
When courts address damages in tax malpractice cases, what is the appropriate measure and scope of recoverable damages?
Should damage rules designed for intentional misconduct apply to negligence-based malpractice claims in tax advice, or are distinct rules justified?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 70lawcontempprob7!!ARTICLE: RENEGOTIATING THE ODIOUS DEBT DOCTRINE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: RENEGOTIATING THE ODIOUS DEBT DOCTRINE

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal appraisal and critique of purported legal rules
shared_topics.justification: Both papers closely analyze and critique an asserted legal doctrine — Paper A evaluates the purported international-law doctrine of odious-regime debt and rejects it based on state practice and normative flaws, while Paper B scrutinizes New York's de facto measure of damages in attorney (including tax) malpractice and argues the courts have misapplied or muddled the proper doctrine.

shared_topics.topic: diagnosing definitional vagueness and conceptual indeterminacy
shared_topics.justification: Each paper identifies core conceptual ambiguity that undermines application — Paper A shows 'odious debt' and the scope of 'regime' succession are under- and overinclusive, and Paper B shows the phrase 'to be made whole' (and the negligence measure) lacks a fixed definition compared with established 'benefit-of-the-bargain' and 'out-of-pocket' labels.

shared_topics.topic: evaluating doctrine through practice and precedent rather than abstract theory
shared_topics.justification: Both rely on empirical or practice-based inquiry to test doctrinal claims — Paper A surveys state practice and international responses to assess whether an odious-debt rule exists, and Paper B surveys New York case law and judicial decisions to determine which damages measure courts have applied or should apply.

shared_topics.topic: focus on the policy consequences of adopting particular legal rules
shared_topics.justification: Each work ties doctrinal choices to real-world distributional and systemic effects — Paper A emphasizes how accepting an odious-debt rule would affect creditors, successor populations, and global market stability, while Paper B emphasizes how adopting one damages measure over another affects plaintiffs, attorneys, and incentives in malpractice litigation.

shared_topics.topic: proposing reframing or reform to improve doctrinal coherence and outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Both articles move from critique to prescription: Paper A urges reframing succession issues as succession to all commercial obligations and adjusting international decisionmaking, and Paper B urges returning to (or affirming) the benefit-of-the-bargain conception in attorney malpractice to restore doctrinal clarity and correct outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: how legal remedies and measures shape actor incentives and conduct

shared_topics.topic: diagnosis of doctrinal/policy drift and call for corrective reform
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the field's focus on restructuring over lending and urges regulatory reorientation and translation of consumer-protection tools into sovereign debt governance; Paper B argues courts have strayed from the traditional negligence damages rule in malpractice cases and calls for restoring the appropriate measure (benefit-of-the-bargain) to correct that drift.

shared_topics.topic: the use of private-law doctrines or analogies to fill gaps in other legal regimes
