papers.node_id: 83chikentlrev179!!ARTICLE: COMMENTARY: THE TRAJECTORY OF COMPLEX BUSINESS CONTRACTING IN LATIN AMERICA
papers.title: ARTICLE: COMMENTARY: THE TRAJECTORY OF COMPLEX BUSINESS CONTRACTING IN LATIN AMERICA
papers.abstract:
By some accounts, Latin American contract documentation increasingly resembles U.S. contract documentation.This is puzzling, given that the U.S. documentation has developed in a broader institutional context particular to the U.S. The context includes a particular type of legal training, particular types of law firms, particular legal institutions, and so on. Why is this occurring, and what effect will it have on contracting practice in Latin America? This commentary briefly considers these issues; it considers as well some broader implications of international convergence in contracting practices.
Until recently, Latin American contract documentation was quite short, as is typical for civil code countries where the code itself specifies many of the terms for which parties would want to contract. As more transactions in Latin America involve non-Latin American parties, particularly U.S. parties, the contracts are becoming longer and more detailed, and are containing increasing amounts of boilerplate. This is so whether the contracts are governed by U.S. law or by the law of the Latin American country. Indeed, where contracts are governed by the law of a Latin American country, they may cover matters addressed in the applicable civil code. And they may do so in a manner different than the code provision without expressly superseding the code provision - indeed, even without a thought that there are code provisions that are being superseded. In this commentary, I briefly explore a few implications of this development.
I begin with what seems like the easiest inquiry: why might this development have occurred? I reject the idea that U.S.-style documentation is inherently superior, even in the U.S.I argued in two earlier piecesthat U.S.-style documentation, and its increasing use in European transactions, is in significant part a product of agency costs within law firms and between law firms and their clients, as well as path-dependency and a prisoner's dilemma-propelled arms race. There are some functions served efficiently but overall, the process is clearly second-best.
The same sorts of explanations I proposed in those two pieces are applicable here. Once one party comes "armed" with a more complex and comprehensive contract, it is difficult for the other party to say "oh, we don't need all that extra verbiage."The countervailing arguments - this level of detail and intricacy signals distrust, this is a significant increase in paper and money without much (if any) added benefit, the poor trees are being chopped down for no good reason, and that the complexity may lead us to overlook something easy and important - are hard to advance successfully. The other side's client is getting these "protections" - surely our client needs them too.
In Latin America, the same explanation holds with greater force. The U.S. lawyer can get his way using very little of the considerable bargaining power he has available on account of his status as coming from the country of "big deals" and big dealmakers. U.S. deal-making has the reputation of being sophisticated and state-of-the-art. Who wouldn't want to emulate U.S. practices, especially a corporate bar trying to "play in the big leagues?" Furthermore, a not-insignificant number of Latin American lawyers obtain LLM degrees in the United States, and may follow this education with a few years of practice at big U.S. firms.
Indeed, for the many contracts governed by U.S. law, the U.S. parties can successfully argue that U.S.-style documentation is needed - because that language is what the U.S. courts (or U.S. arbitrators) are used to interpreting.This is a view I have critiqued elsewhere - there is a lot to this view, but it's not nearly as powerful or dispositive as its proponents believe it to be - but it does have some power. Thus, the arms race begins and continues. Soon enough, even in purely domestic contracts involving only Latin American parties, the longer U.S.-style contracts become the norm.
My first conclusion is this: notwithstanding the resources and intelligence thrown at sophisticated transactional contracting, it is apparently quite difficult for the documentation and contracting practices of complex business transactions to be first best, either in the U.S. or in Latin America. Indeed, in the U.S., there are ways in which second best is actually pretty good. Because of the broader system in which transactions arise, the documentation serves some important and useful functions: helping firms maintain a hiring process in which they can't tell who will be good, but even not-so-good quality lawyers can be useful and better quality lawyers will become visible as such. It's very hard to tell at junior levels who will be a good lawyer; the documents from previous deals that are used as forms can be modified even by people who don't understand the forms exceedingly well, but those who do will do a better job and will be noticed doing so.Moreover, the U.S. needs the type of documentation it has because interpretive practices and conventions create norms, deviation from which may yield inferences as to what a contract means and as to the effectiveness of a lawyer in her representation of her client. In addition, the U.S. is "mechanically" geared up to have the types of contracts it does. The documents already exist on firms' computer systems, and the people involved are used to working with them. None of these reasons or rationales is present to nearly the same degree, if at all, in Latin America; on the merits, the case for U.S. documentation and practices in Latin America is worse than it is in the U.S.
Many questions arise from the foregoing. In this commentary, I want to raise just a few: How will differences among Latin American countries affect the way contracts for Latin American transactions using U.S. documentation are written? How will contracting practices be affected more broadly? The more that is covered by the contract, the more that is potentially open for negotiation. Will the U.S. norms in which "everything" is negotiated be imported along with the contracts? If so, how will this affect the relationships among transacting parties? Will parties become less trusting,for instance? Or will parties become more trusting, as they can specify more precisely their expectations of one another's conduct?
In this regard, the elaborate specification of what is prohibited in U.S. contracts may have led to an ethos which effectively encourages coming "close to the line." For example, if related party transactions are prohibited and a highly detailed definition of "related party" is included in the contract, some may view this language as sanctioning dealings with a party that doesn't technically meet the description but might, in some common sense manner, be regarded as "related."Will this effect also be imported?
Some broader questions should also be raised. In How Do German Contracts Do As Much With Fewer Words, my co-author and I argued that homogeneous transacting communities consisting of frequent repeat players may be a necessary precondition for shorter, less extensively negotiated contracts.To what extent does the increasing globalization of markets and transactions, and increasing heterogeneity among transacting parties, make U.S.-style contract documentation inevitable, or at least likely to be adopted in any event? One argument made in the U.S. - an argument we criticize in the German Contracts piece - is that because the U.S. potentially involves fifty separate state jurisdictions, more of "the law" that is wanted must be contained in the document.Such an argument may have more plausibility as a transaction document comes to be more of a form for transactions among parties in different countries.
Finally, what determines which types of documentation and transacting practices become dominant? The correlative question is being asked in the sphere of corporate governance, where U.S. and European models sometimes compete, but also sometimes converge;the question has beenfar less explored in the context of transacting practices. Do we have the conditions for true competition among models? My guess is that we do not. If the trajectory is influenced by something other than efficiency, what are the determinants of success? Is more convergence possible, or even desirable? These questions will become more pressing as markets globalize further.

questions.question: Whether and why complex business contract documentation in Latin America is converging toward the longer, more detailed U.S.-style form.
questions.answer: Yes; Latin American contracts are converging toward longer, U.S.-style documentation not because it is inherently superior but due to agency costs, path dependence, a prisoners’ dilemma arms race, the reputational and bargaining power of U.S. lawyers and parties (often educated/practiced in the U.S.), and forum-interpretation arguments that collectively spread these forms even into purely domestic deals.

questions.question: Whether adopting U.S.-style contract documentation in Latin America changes contracting practices and outcomes - for example, the scope of negotiation, transaction costs, parties' trust, and the substantive allocation of risks.
questions.answer: It increases the scope of negotiation because the more the contract covers, the more is potentially open for negotiation, while the abstract leaves effects on trust, transaction costs, and risk allocation as open questions.

questions.question: Whether globalization and increased heterogeneity among transacting parties make comprehensive, U.S.-style contract documentation more likely to become the dominant model across jurisdictions.

papers.node_id: 124pennstlrev353!!ARTICLE: Contract as Swag
papers.title: ARTICLE: Contract as Swag
papers.authors: John F. Coyle; Joseph M. Green
papers.abstract:
In the past, some legal scholars have analogized the contract to a product.Others have compared it to a social artifact.Still others have compared it to a form of technology.Each of these analogies serves a distinct purpose. Reimagining the contract as a product makes it easier to argue that contracts of adhesion should be regulated in the way that other products are regulated. Analogizing the contract to a social artifact makes it possible to develop a deeper understanding of why social actors formparticular kinds of contracts and why social systems generate distinctive contract regimes. And conceptualizing the contract as a form of technology allows researchers to draw upon the existing literature on technological innovation to explain how and why contract language evolves over time.
In this Article, we suggest that the contract may also be usefully analogized to swag. The term "swag" is generally understood to refer to branded merchandise that is given away for free to people who attend or participate in an event. A list of examples might include Westlaw handing out water bottles with its name emblazoned across the side, a law firm giving its associates umbrellas with the firm's name on them, or a law school providing free flash drives decorated with the university's colors and seal. Over the past few decades, we argue, certain contracts have increasingly come to resemble the water bottles, umbrellas, flash drives, and other tchotchkes that are given away by law firms and other providers of legal services. These contracts have, in short, become a form of swag.
Consider the Keep It Simple Security ("KISS"). The KISS is a contract that was developed by a startup incubator - 500 Startups - to facilitate the task of channeling capital from investors to early-stage technology companies.Unlike most contracts, the KISS is not tucked away on a password-protected hard drive at a law firm.It is available for free download from the 500 Startups website.Unlike most contracts, the KISS does not have a boring, descriptive name (like stock purchase agreement). It has a distinctive, memorable name that sets it apart from the mass of other startup financing contracts. The KISS is being given away by 500 Startups for the express purpose of improving its reputation in the startup community in much the same way that Westlaw distributes water bottles with its name on it to improve its brand awareness among lawyers and law students. Significantly, the KISS is not unique. There are a number of other examples of contracts - and individual contractual provisions - being handed out like swag in contemporary practice.
A number of benefits flow from conceptualizing these contracts as a form of swag. Among other things, the analogy helps to explain otherwise inexplicable behavior by lawyer-innovators.It has always been the case that it is difficult, and therefore exceedingly rare, for lawyers to obtain intellectual property rights in the contractual language that they create. This fact has, in turn, led some scholars to argue that lawyers lackmeaningful incentives to innovate and disseminate contractual innovations. "What's the point of creating a new and original contract provision," so the argument goes, "when other firms can simply take that language and incorporate it into their own agreements?" If a contract is reimagined as a form of swag, however, it is easy to see why lawyer-innovators might develop new contracts notwithstanding the lack of intellectual property protection for their creations.These contracts can serve as branding devices that the innovator can use to attract additional clients to her practice.
The contract-as-swag analogy also highlights a distinction that is frequently overlooked in the contractual innovation literature. This is the distinction between thecreationof a particular innovation and the subsequentdisseminationof that innovation to the broader community of contract users.Creators develop new contract language to solve specific problems. Disseminators spread the word about this innovation. The bulk of the scholarship in this area to date has focused on factors that motivate the creation of new innovations rather than their dissemination. The swag analogy serves to remedy this imbalance because it provides insights into how and why some contractual innovations become widely disseminated in the months and years after their creation while others languish in obscurity.
Finally, reimagining the contract as a type of swag illustrates the futility in attempting to develop an all-encompassing theory of contractual innovation.Over the past two decades, a number of scholars have soughtto develop a general theory of contractual innovation modeled on the cycle of product development.Such models, while useful in many respects, cannot account for all the relevant factors underlying the successful introduction of a contractual innovation. In some cases, reputation may play an important role in driving the creation and dissemination of a particular innovation. In other cases, reputation may be completely irrelevant to this inquiry. One final benefit of the contract-as-swag metaphor, therefore, is that it helps to highlight the idiosyncratic character of innovation and to illustrate challenges in trying to develop a single, one-size-fits-all model to explain the process of contractual innovation.
The Article proceeds as follows. Part I surveys the existing legal literature on contract metaphors and discusses the strengths and weaknesses of these analogies.Part II identifies a number of contracts from various areas of the law - including venture capital, corporate law, and arbitration - that bear a strong resemblance to the swag that is so familiar to lawyers and law students. Part III discusses the advantages of conceptualizing these contracts as swag. It shows how this analogy simultaneously explains otherwise inexplicable behavior on the part of lawyer-innovators, supplements the existing literature on the dissemination of contractual innovations, and highlights the challenges in developing a universal model for explaining the process of contractual innovations.

questions.question: Whether some standardized contracts function primarily as branded marketing tools (like promotional 'swag') that incentivize their creation and distribution despite the absence of intellectual property protection, and whether this branding explains lawyer-innovator behavior.
questions.answer: Yes—certain modern contracts are deliberately distributed as branded “swag” (e.g., the KISS) to build reputation and attract clients, which incentivizes their creation and dissemination despite the lack of intellectual property protection and helps explain lawyer‑innovator behavior.

questions.question: How and why certain contractual innovations become widely disseminated while others do not - in particular, what roles reputation, branding, and deliberate dissemination strategies play in the spread of contract language.
questions.answer: Dissemination turns on deliberate swag-like tactics—free public release, memorable branding/naming, and reputation-building—which in some contexts drive wide uptake, though the importance of reputation varies and some innovations still languish.

questions.question: Whether a single, general theory of contractual innovation can account for the varied incentives and dissemination pathways at work, or whether contractual innovation is inherently idiosyncratic and resists one-size-fits-all theorizing.
questions.answer: No; the article argues that contractual innovation is idiosyncratic and resists a one-size-fits-all, product-cycle-style general theory because different factors (including reputation) matter in different cases.

papers.node_id: 85nclrev727!!ARTICLE: CONTRACT, PRIORITY, AND ODIOUS DEBT*
papers.title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT, PRIORITY, AND ODIOUS DEBT*
papers.abstract:
This Article proposes that sovereign nations and their creditors adopt a contractual approach to the seemingly intractable problem of odious debt. Generally speaking, "odious debt" is an obligation incurred in the name of a sovereign nation by a despotic or illegitimate government, the proceeds of which only enrich the despot or fund the repression of his or her subjects. Most writers on the topic agree that such obligations violate principles of justice or reduce social welfare or both; citizens of a sovereign debtor should, ideally, not be bound to repay odious debt incurred by their leaders.Despitethis wide agreement, however, sovereigns generally do not repudiate obligations on the ground that the debt is odious or that it is otherwise inequitable.This is true despite the fact that sovereigns have the ability to thwart enforcement of their obligations if they choose; creditors have no reliable way to reach a sovereign's assets without the sovereign's cooperation.The conventional explanation for this behavior is that sovereigns are restrained from doing so by fear that they will suffer reputational harm or fear that they will be penalized by other countries and international institutions.
The recent transition of regimes in Iraq has unleashed a wave of interest in the possibility of repudiating sovereign debt on equitable grounds. In the wake of the recent war, a variety of commentators, scholars, and policymakers proposed that the new Iraqi regime should repudiate as odious some or all of the debts it inherited from Saddam Hussein's regime.As explained in Part I below, some of these individuals and organizations argued that international law recognizes a doctrine of odious debt.Such a doctrine would provide a defense if a sovereign's creditors attempt to enforce debts that did not provide a benefit to the sovereign's citizens and that were incurred without the citizens' consent. It is not clear, however, whether such a doctrine is in fact part of international law. Furthermore, if it is a viable doctrine in any context, there is serious doubt as to whether it applies in cases of government succession. Given the frailty of this "traditional" odious debt doctrine,various commentators have proposed doctrinal and institutional alternatives.For example, some writers have suggested that sovereigns might challenge enforcement of their obligations in domestic courts pursuant to domestic legal doctrines drawn from private law and corporate law.
Yet another strand of recent commentary and scholarship has considered alternative institutional mechanisms that would enablesovereigns to repudiate odious obligations. For example, a vocal group of writers and advocates proposed creating a tribunal that would have resolved odious debt claims against Iraq's creditors.They proposed that the tribunal be modeled on the U.S.-Iran tribunal and that it employ the doctrine of odious debt noted above.This proposal may now be moot with respect to Iraq, but it provides a general model for a potential odious debt mechanism. Perhaps most ambitiously, Michael Kremer and Seema Jayachandran have proposed an odious debt tribunal or institution that would identify and designate odious regimes, as opposed to odious debts, and do so ex ante.Initially, they proposed that the primary aim of such an institution would be to impose loan embargoes on regimes designated as odious; in a subsequent paper, they have proposed that the institution should aim instead to severely limit lending to these regimes.
This Article represents the first effort to propose and defend a private, contractual approach to the odious debt problem. To adopt a contractual odious debt mechanism, a sovereign would promise its voluntary creditors at the contracting stage that it will not incur odious debt and that it will repudiate or subordinateany of its obligations designated as odious ex post. Incurring odious debt would be an event of default by the sovereign. The sovereign wouldalso promise each creditor that it will inform subsequent creditors of the contractual arrangement and that it will make similar agreements with these creditors. The parties would give a majority or supermajority of the sovereign's creditors authority to designate obligations as odious pursuant to a contractual definition. The sovereign would then be obligated to repudiate debts designated as odious by the creditors. Ideally, the contractual definition of odiousness should be tied to the actual use of the funds obtained by the sovereign. It should also include safe harbors designed to promote effective monitoring by creditors.
Any strategy for discharging odious debt must be carefully circumscribed to assure future lenders that sovereign debtors will not arbitrarily repudiate their obligations. A successful mechanism must distinguish, as clearly and predictably as possible, between debt that the sovereign is expected to repay and odious debt subject to repudiation. If the standard for odiousness is relatively clear and enforcement is predictable, creditors will be able to anticipate the risk of repudiation or subordination on that ground. It will effectively segment the market for sovereign debt, creating a kind of priority scheme, giving priority to non-odious debt.Sovereigns that want to raise funds for legitimate purposes should then be able to incur non-odious debt at lower rates compared to potentially odious debt. Increasing the cost of borrowing potentially odious debt should reduce the amount of odious debt incurred by sovereigns. If the markets for odious and non-odious debt can be segmented in this way, it may enable sovereigns to repudiate odious debt and avoid being punished by market actors or the official sector.
A contractual odious debt arrangement is more likely than other mechanisms to enable repudiation of odious debt while maintaining the stability of the market for sovereign debt.As explained in Part III, there are good reasons to allocate to creditors at least part of the authority to define odious debt, identify particular debts that meet the definition, and enforce the repudiation of those debts. More than any other actors, creditors will internalize the costs and benefits of any odious debt mechanism. They benefit most clearly when their sovereign debtors avoid incurring or repudiate obligations that wouldreduce the value of their own claims. Yet, they will bear direct costs of the mechanism because of the chance that it will be employed against them. They will also bear costs of the mechanism if it destabilizes financial markets or causes other creditors to significantly reduce the credit available to sovereigns in general. If the benefits of the mechanism outweigh these costs, creditors should have an incentive to adopt the scheme.
Sovereign debtors should also have incentives to adopt such a contractual odious debt mechanism. They will benefit from the arrangement because it will make it easier for them to obtain ex post relief from some odious debt. More important, however, it may benefit sovereigns by reducing the cost to them of incurring debt that is clearly not odious. If it makes it easier for sovereigns to credibly commit to borrowing for legitimate purposes, this should reduce their overall cost of borrowing. It follows that the mechanism will probably be most useful for relatively responsible regimes. Bad regimes will almost certainly not contract into the scheme. Still, the availability of an effective contractual mechanism may help countries that overthrow these bad regimes by making it easier for them to repudiate debts incurred by the bad regime and avoid at least some of the negative results of doing so.
To be sure, such a contractual scheme would face significant practical obstacles, especially the logistical challenges of coordinating the mechanism itself.Yet, as other writers have noted in other contexts, a single debtor can coordinate a broad contractual arrangement with its various creditors.A private, contractual odious debt mechanism requires coordination around only one particular issue: whether certain debts incurred by a common sovereign debtor should be repudiated as odious. The fact that market actors may be hesitant to adopt the scheme in the first place presents another obstacle. But market participants, nudged by some official-sector institutions, have increasingly embraced creditor coordination as a potential means to restructure sovereign debt instruments.This development may have helped make market participants more receptive to other contract-based developments.Furthermore, market participants may be increasingly motivated to contract with respect to odious debt as policymakers, advocates, and sovereigns continue to debate employing other, more disruptive approaches. It is worth noting that a contractual odious debt mechanism is not necessarily exclusive of alternative approaches. Finally, if market participants are hesitant to adopt this contractual innovation, the official sector may want to prod them to do so if the contractual scheme would create significant positive externalities.

questions.question: Whether a contractual mechanism between a sovereign and its creditors - under which creditors can designate and trigger repudiation or subordination of obligations incurred by prior illegitimate or despotic governments that enriched rulers or funded repression - can enable a successor sovereign to discharge those obligations while preserving the stability of sovereign debt markets.
questions.answer: Yes: the article argues that a private, contractual odious-debt mechanism—allowing a creditor majority or supermajority to designate and trigger repudiation or subordination of odious obligations—can enable successor sovereigns to repudiate such debts while maintaining the stability of sovereign debt markets.

questions.question: Whether allocating authority to creditors to define, identify, and enforce repudiation of such illegitimate debts will create predictable priority classes in sovereign borrowing and thereby change borrowing costs and incentives for both responsible and irresponsible regimes.
questions.answer: Yes: giving creditors authority to define and identify odious debt under a clear, predictable standard segments the market into priority classes (favoring non-odious debt), lowers rates for clearly non-odious borrowing and raises costs for potentially odious borrowing, encouraging responsible regimes and deterring or excluding bad regimes.

questions.question: Whether sovereigns and private creditors have sufficient incentives to adopt a contract-based scheme for handling debts incurred by prior abusive or illegitimate regimes, given the coordination and monitoring challenges involved.
questions.answer: Yes: the paper contends both creditors and sovereigns should have incentives to adopt the scheme—creditors because they internalize its benefits and costs, and sovereigns because it eases repudiation of odious debts and lowers the cost of legitimate borrowing—despite coordination challenges that are manageable and can be facilitated by growing market coordination practices and official-sector nudges.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 1989columbuslrev307!!SYMPOSIUM: RETHINKING LEGAL OPINION LETTERS: SAME THOUGHTS ON THE ECONOMICS OF LEGAL OPINIONS
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: RETHINKING LEGAL OPINION LETTERS: SAME THOUGHTS ON THE ECONOMICS OF LEGAL OPINIONS

shared_topics.topic: private contractual mechanisms to manage legal risk as an alternative to judicial or public-law remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a contractual odious-debt scheme in which sovereigns and creditors allocate the power to designate and repudiate odious obligations by contract rather than by invoking international-law doctrines or tribunals; Paper B analyzes the function of third‑party legal opinions as contractualized assurances within transactions and treats opinion letters as private-law devices for allocating legal risk instead of suing on representations alone.

shared_topics.topic: cost–benefit and transaction‑cost analysis of legal instruments
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly weighs the market benefits and coordination costs of adopting a contractual odious‑debt mechanism (including effects on borrowing costs and segmentation of debt markets); Paper B argues that the necessity, scope, and standardization of legal opinions should be measured by cost/benefit tradeoffs and by minimizing time and expense in commercial deals.

shared_topics.topic: mechanisms for creditor/counterparty coordination and collective decision‑making
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes majority or supermajority creditor votes and coordination around contractual definitions to identify and repudiate odious debts; Paper B emphasizes standardizing opinion language and reaching professional consensus (e.g., ABA efforts) to avoid bilateral negotiation frictions and reduce the need for ad hoc bargaining between counterparties.

shared_topics.topic: the role of assurances, signaling, and reputation in enabling transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses how reputational concerns and market signals (segmented pricing for odious vs non‑odious debt) influence sovereigns' and creditors' behavior and the credibility of repudiation rules; Paper B treats legal opinions as formal assurances or 'blessings' that signal to recipients and their counsel that a transaction 'works,' relying on reputational effects of law firms and counsel to add transactional confidence.

shared_topics.topic: standardization and clear definitions to improve predictability and market stability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A stresses the need for clear, predictable contractual definitions of 'odiousness' and safe harbors to prevent arbitrary repudiation and preserve sovereign credit markets; Paper B advocates for standardized opinion formats and agreed terminology to reduce negotiation time, lower costs, and make opinions less risky for both counsel and clients.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 85geowashlrev57!!ARTICLE: The Inefficient Evolution of Merger Agreements
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Inefficient Evolution of Merger Agreements

shared_topics.topic: private contractual design as an institutional alternative to public law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes a private, contract-based mechanism to manage and repudiate 'odious' sovereign debt as an alternative to uncertain international-law doctrines or tribunals, while Paper B evaluates how private drafting practices (and potential private-sector standardization) can reshape the legal terms that govern large capital transactions, treating contract design as a primary lever for systemic change.

shared_topics.topic: coordination problems among dispersed market actors and collective-action solutions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how sovereigns and many dispersed creditors must coordinate (e.g., creditor majorities, notification promises) to implement an odious-debt regime, and Paper B documents the lack of coordination in precedent use across law firms and proposes industry-led coordination (e.g., private equity or trade associations) to standardize merger documentation.

shared_topics.topic: path dependence, precedent use, and the evolution of contractual terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A stresses the need for predictable, well-defined contractual standards (and safe harbors) so markets can segment odious versus non-odious debt, while Paper B empirically shows merger agreements evolve through precedent-based, path-dependent edits that produce heterogeneity and hinder predictability.

shared_topics.topic: incentive misalignment of private actors affecting market outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines creditor and sovereign incentives (why some will or will not adopt contractual odious-debt clauses and how costs/benefits are internalized), and Paper B shows how lawyers' billing and drafting incentives produce editorial churning that raises costs and risk for clients, demonstrating how private incentives can frustrate efficient contracting.

shared_topics.topic: information, monitoring, and disclosure mechanisms to improve enforceability and predictability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes creditor monitoring, disclosure to subsequent lenders, and definitional clarity to make repudiation predictable and enforceable, while Paper B recommends tools to reveal prior edits and nonstandard language so drafters can identify and reverse embedded deal-specific terms, thereby improving transparency and legal certainty.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 6jempiricallegalstud818!!ARTICLE: Contractual Complexity and the Cognitive Load of R&D Alliance Contracts
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Contractual Complexity and the Cognitive Load of R&D Alliance Contracts

shared_topics.topic: contract design trade-offs between specificity and transaction costs
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes a detailed contractual mechanism (definitions, creditor voting rules, safe harbors) to enable repudiation of odious debt while limiting market disruption, weighing predictability against the costs of implementation; Paper B empirically studies how adding detail (length, interdependencies) raises cognitive and drafting costs and can create diminishing returns, highlighting the same trade-off between contractual specificity and overall transaction costs.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of decision rights and authority among contracting parties
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on allocating authority to creditors (majority or supermajority) to designate and enforce odiousness, arguing creditors should internalize costs and benefits of that authority; Paper B analyzes how contract structure and complexity convey and allocate control and enforcement rights within R&D alliances and how those allocations affect comprehension and outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: coordination problems among multiple contractual counterparties
shared_topics.justification: Paper A addresses the logistical and collective-action challenges of coordinating many creditors to adopt a common odious-debt clause or voting scheme; Paper B studies interfirm alliance contracts and how parties use contract design (and standard forms) to coordinate expectations and governance across organizational boundaries.

shared_topics.topic: information asymmetries, monitoring, and signaling through contract terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes tying odiousness to the actual use of funds, designing safe harbors to improve monitoring, and using contractual signals to segment markets for odious vs non-odious debt; Paper B discusses how information asymmetries, monitoring dynamics, and the signaling function of contractual complexity affect parties' incentives to write more or less detailed contracts.

shared_topics.topic: interaction between contractual form and legal/institutional interpretation/enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A considers how domestic courts, tribunals, and the official sector might interact with or be bypassed by a private contractual odious-debt regime and the need to make standards predictable for markets; Paper B examines how courts should interpret contracts of varying complexity (literal vs liberal approaches) and how contract form signals the parties' drafting choices to adjudicators.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: DISPUTING BOILERPLATE

shared_topics.topic: contractual clauses as tools to structure enforcement and relief in sovereign debt
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically analyzes how sovereign bond contracts use enforcement-related clauses (forum selection, waivers of immunity) to shape creditors' ability to sue and collect, while Paper B proposes a specific contractual mechanism (events of default, repudiation/subordination clauses) to enable repudiation of odious debt and structure ex post relief.

shared_topics.topic: creditor authority, incentives, and coordination to implement contract-based solutions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights how market practices and creditor-friendly terms reflect creditor interests and affect issuer behavior, and Paper B centers on giving creditors collective authority (and incentives) to define and designate odious debt and the coordination challenges of implementing such creditor-driven arrangements.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates whether forum-selection clauses persist because of stickiness or preference and documents cross-issuer heterogeneity alongside intra-issuer stasis, and Paper B analyzes practical, informational, and market-resistance obstacles to adopting a novel contractual odious-debt mechanism and the potential role of official-sector nudges.

shared_topics.topic: how contract terms allocate enforcement rights, creditor recovery, and market pricing (segmentation/priority)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies sovereign immunity waivers and execution rights that affect creditors' practical recovery, and Paper B shows how a contractual definition of odiousness and a priority/subordination scheme would segment debt markets and alter borrowing costs and creditor recovery expectations.

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM ARTICLE: Tribunalizing Sovereign Debt: Argentina's Experience with Investor-State Dispute Settlement

shared_topics.topic: use of private contractual tools to manage sovereign debt problems

shared_topics.topic: creditor coordination and majority-rule mechanisms for restructuring or repudiation
shared_topics.justification: Both papers examine the role of coordinated creditor decision-making—Paper A treats CACs and creditor fragmentation as central to successful restructurings and the holdout problem, while Paper B designs a creditor-majority/supermajority process to designate and enforce repudiation of odious debts.

shared_topics.topic: trade-offs between legal predictability and sovereign flexibility/political legitimacy in restructuring
shared_topics.justification: Both works weigh the tension between predictable, rule-based enforcement and the need for flexible, politically palatable restructurings—Paper A warns that tribunalization (e.g., ISDS) can undermine flexible settlements, and Paper B insists any repudiation mechanism must be narrowly circumscribed to preserve market confidence and avoid arbitrary repudiations.

shared_topics.topic: institutional design and choice of fora for resolving sovereign debt disputes (arbitral tribunals vs domestic courts vs new institutions)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers engage with which fora should resolve sovereign debt questions—Paper A analyzes the rise of ISDS/ICSID in Argentina and tensions with litigation in national courts, while Paper B evaluates proposals for specialized odious-debt tribunals (and other institutional alternatives) alongside private contractual arrangements.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A CRITIQUE OF THE ODIOUS DEBT DOCTRINE

shared_topics.topic: practical feasibility and implementation mechanisms for addressing odious debt

shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates odious-debt proposals within states' broader strategic tradeoffs (engagement, sanctions, humanitarian goals) and questions why only lending would be regulated, while Paper B considers institutional responses (tribunals, loan-embargo institutions, official-sector nudges) and how those interact with international political actors and policy levers.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The IMF and Regulation of Cross-Border Capital Flows

shared_topics.topic: managing cross-border spillovers from domestic financial policies and debt decisions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on how domestic capital controls, monetary and exchange-rate policies produce international spillovers that require coordination, and Paper B considers how repudiation or restructuring of sovereign debt (and rules governing odious debt) would produce cross-border effects on creditors, markets, and other states that must be managed.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACTS AS TECHNOLOGY

shared_topics.topic: private ordering versus public/international institutions for addressing transnational problems
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts a private, contract‑based fix for odious debt with proposals for tribunals or international doctrinal remedies and discusses when official‑sector nudges might be needed; Paper B assesses the roles of private actors in producing and spreading contractual technology and considers public policy interventions (IP law, clearinghouses, relaxing practice rules) to improve dissemination.

shared_topics.topic: contract design features that manage uncertainty, credibility, and market segmentation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes clear definitions of 'odiousness', safe harbors, predictable enforcement, and a priority scheme to limit arbitrary repudiation and segment markets for odious vs non‑odious debt; Paper B analyzes what makes contractual innovations valuable, how contract features reduce adoption uncertainty, and how design and dissemination affect economic outcomes and diffusion.

shared_topics.topic: logistical and dissemination challenges of multi‑party contractual schemes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A acknowledges the practical coordination/logistical obstacles of implementing a broad contractual odious‑debt mechanism across many creditors and the potential role of market norms or official nudges; Paper B focuses on how contractual innovations become widely used, examining dissemination mechanisms, barriers to adoption, and the organizational sources that can overcome those challenges.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: PUERTO RICO'S ODIOUS DEBT: THE ECONOMIC CRISIS OF COLONIALISM

shared_topics.topic: interplay between domestic law, equitable principles, and international law in resolving debt disputes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts domestic contractual and bankruptcy rules with broader international/equitable frameworks for judging odiousness in a colonial setting, and Paper B contrasts the uncertain international law basis for odious debt with private‑law contractual and tribunal alternatives as means of adjudication and enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: relevance of the debtor's political status or transition (colonialism, illegitimacy, regime change) to whether debt should be repudiated
shared_topics.justification: Paper A foregrounds Puerto Rico's long colonial status as central to assessing whether its debt is odious, while Paper B uses cases of illegitimate or succeeded regimes (e.g., Iraq) to probe how political legitimacy or transition affects the propriety and applicability of odious‑debt relief.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Accord on Fire and Building Safety in Bangladesh: A New Paradigm for Limiting Buyers' Liability in Global Supply Chains? +http://dx.doi/org/10.1093/ajcl/avy030

shared_topics.topic: incentive and market segmentation effects produced by contractually defined categories

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE EFFECT OF BARGAINING POWER ON CONTRACT DESIGN

papers.node_id: 42vandlrev133!!ARTICLE: Contracts as Commodities: The Influence of Secondary Purchasers on the Form of Contracts.
papers.title: ARTICLE: Contracts as Commodities: The Influence of Secondary Purchasers on the Form of Contracts.
papers.abstract:
In 1970 Professor Arthur Leff brought a new vision to a half century of debate about standard form contractsby pointing out that consumercontracts should be seen not primarily as "contracts," but as "things," intangible products, sold to the consumer.As "things," Leff argued, form contracts should be subject to the same kinds of warranty laws as tangible goods.  The debate about form contracts in consumer transactions continues, but, as Leff predicted, the debate largely has ignored his insight concerning the nature of the pieces of paper involved.
In the midst of this debate, there has been little analysis in the legal literature, and none in the economics literature, of why standard form contracts are used.  Most authors merely revisit the reasons listed by Karl Llewellyn in 1939:
Nothing can approach in speed and sanity of readaptation the machinery of standard forms of a trade and for a line of trade, built to meet the particular needs of that trade.  They save trouble in bargaining.  They save time in bargaining.  They infinitely simplify the task of internal administration of a business unit, of keeping tabs on transactions, of knowing where one is at, of arranging orderly expectation, orderly fulfillment, orderly planning.  They ease administration by concentrating the need for discretion and decision in such personnel as can be trusted to be discreet.  This reduces human wear and tear, it cheapens administration, it serves the ultimate consumer.  Standardizing contracts is in this a counterpart of standardizing goods and production processes, as well as a device for adjustment of law to need.
Combined, Leff's insight and Llewellyn's analysis point to anotherpressure for standardization in some kinds of products.  Leff's contractual "things" implicated continuing rights and duties for both sides.  Leff dealt with "things" retailers sold to consumers, but in some industries either party to the initial sale may resell some of its rights and duties to third parties.  For example, a lender first "sells" a mortgage to a home owner and then sells its interest in the mortgage to another financial institution.  When secondary sales are common, the forms are, for many purposes, more akin to frozen pork bellies than to what lawyers consider contracts.They are contracts as commodities.
This Article addresses the effects of secondary purchaserson the standardization of form contracts.  I became interested in this topic while teaching about oil and gas leases in one class and about residential mortgages in two others.  I concluded that secondary purchasers should encourage retailers to standardize their forms across an industry.  To my surprise, I discovered that no writers on form contracts had explored or mentioned the effect, or, in fact, acknowledged the existence of secondary purchasers.  I also discovered a more complicated pattern of form standardization than I had expected.  This Article explores those complications in order to explain how contracts are used in the "real world."
The Article first describes both the theoretical and empirical effects of secondary purchasers on form contracts.  It then discusses the process of standardization, both for tangible products and for several examples of contractual commodities.  After examining several factors that help explain when and why form contracts are standardized, the Article considers changes in policy that might follow from the analysis.

questions.question: Whether and to what extent the existence of secondary purchasers (a market for reselling contractual rights) leads sellers to standardize their form contracts across an industry.
questions.answer: The paper concludes that the existence of secondary purchasers encourages retailers to standardize their form contracts across an industry, although the resulting pattern of standardization is more complicated than expected.

questions.question: How secondary purchasers affect the content, variation, and process of contract standardization - i.e., what economic and institutional factors determine when contracts are treated as commodities and standardized versus when they remain customized.
questions.answer: By making contracts into tradable commodities when secondary sales are common, secondary purchasers create pressure for standardization and shape the standardization process, but the abstract only notes that the determinants are multiple and complex and does not specify them.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE BUTTERFLY EFFECT IN BOILERPLATE CONTRACT INTERPRETATION

shared_topics.topic: the ubiquity and consequences of standard-form/boilerplate language
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how ubiquitous boilerplate language produces interpretive choices whose effects radiate across many identical contracts, and Paper B studies why firms use standardized form contracts (treating them as commodities) and the economic/administrative consequences of that ubiquity.

shared_topics.topic: systemic/external effects from a single interpretive or contractual change
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops the 'butterfly effect' idea that a single court interpretation can alter the meaning of identical boilerplate across countless contracts, while Paper B shows how market processes (especially secondary sales) generate industry-wide standardization so that a single drafting choice or change can have widespread consequences.

shared_topics.topic: the influence of non-parties/third-party actors on contract content and meaning
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights how judicial decisions and precedent—actors outside the original contracting parties—reshape the meaning and practical operation of boilerplate, and Paper B focuses on secondary purchasers and other downstream market actors who shape the form and terms of contracts prior to or after initial sale.

shared_topics.topic: policy and institutional responses to the challenges of standardized contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses implications for judges, legislatures, and scholars about how to handle ambiguous boilerplate given its ripple effects, and Paper B explicitly draws policy implications from its analysis of when and why standard forms emerge and how law or market rules might respond to the influence of secondary markets.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 104minnlrev1839!!ARTICLE: Deal Insurance: Representation and Warranty Insurance in Mergers and Acquisitions
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Deal Insurance: Representation and Warranty Insurance in Mergers and Acquisitions

shared_topics.topic: how third-party market actors (insurers, secondary purchasers) shape contract form and allocation of risk
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how representations and warranty insurance (RWI) allows parties to transfer liability to insurers and how insurers' underwriting practices reshape deal terms; Paper B shows how secondary purchasers who buy contractual interests (e.g., mortgages, leases) create demand for standardized contract forms and thus influence how original sellers draft and allocate rights and risks.

shared_topics.topic: standardization of contract terms driven by transferability and resale markets
shared_topics.justification: Paper B argues that the existence of secondary markets incentivizes firms to produce standardized, 'commodity-like' contract forms; Paper A documents the emergence of standardized RWI policy terms and shows that the availability of insurance can encourage the homogenization of reps and warranty provisions across M&A deals.

shared_topics.topic: warranties/representations as instruments to allocate information and liability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on representations and warranties in M&A as devices to induce disclosure and allocate mispricing risk (and how RWI substitutes for seller liability); Paper B engages with warranties and warranty-law analogies for form contracts and examines how warranty-like promises function when contracts are treated as tradable commodities.

shared_topics.topic: information asymmetries, adverse selection, and moral hazard in contract design and market responses
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly analyzes how information problems in M&A create adverse selection and moral hazard risks and how insurers and deal terms respond; Paper B shows that the need to reduce informational frictions for secondary purchasers (and to signal or assure contract quality) is a key factor driving contract standardization and institutional responses.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 6chijintll333!!ARTICLE: SYMPOSIUM: SOVEREIGN DEBT RESTRUCTURING: The Role of the Official Sector in Sovereign Debt Workouts
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: SYMPOSIUM: SOVEREIGN DEBT RESTRUCTURING: The Role of the Official Sector in Sovereign Debt Workouts

shared_topics.topic: the role of third‑party actors in shaping contractual/claim outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how official sector actors (plaintiff governments, IMF, World Bank) intervene to shape sovereign debt workouts and creditor recoveries, while Paper B examines how secondary purchasers (buyers of contracts/claims) influence the content and form of standard contracts by creating demand for tradable, predictable instruments.

shared_topics.topic: standardization of instruments to facilitate secondary trading or orderly resolution
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses efforts (including proposals like the SDRM) to create standardized procedures and instruments for restructuring sovereign claims to enable orderly, expeditious workouts; Paper B argues that the presence of secondary purchasers drives firms to standardize contract forms so the contracts can be commodified and resold efficiently.

shared_topics.topic: incentives and governance effects on creditors' and debtors' behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A is concerned with designing official‑sector policies that encourage fiscal prudence by debtors and sound credit decisions by lenders, whereas Paper B explores how the prospect of secondary resale changes originators' and purchasers' incentives and thus alters contract terms and allocation of risk.

shared_topics.topic: mechanisms to reduce transaction costs and collective action problems among dispersed creditors
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes the need for mechanisms (official mediation, conditional lending, collective frameworks) to overcome coordination problems among private and bilateral creditors in restructurings; Paper B shows that contract standardization for secondary markets reduces bargaining and administrative costs and helps organize transactions among numerous market participants.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 1989columbuslrev365!!SYMPOSIUM: RETHINKING LEGAL OPINION LETTERS: LEGAL OPINIONS OF NEW YORK COUNSEL IN INTERNATIONAL TRANSACTIONS
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: RETHINKING LEGAL OPINION LETTERS: LEGAL OPINIONS OF NEW YORK COUNSEL IN INTERNATIONAL TRANSACTIONS

shared_topics.topic: third-party-driven standardization of contractual language
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses how international practice (e.g., the IBA Report) and the expectations of foreign recipients shape the wording and scope of New York legal opinions in cross-border financings, while Paper B argues that secondary purchasers in markets (like mortgages or oil/gas interests) create pressure for industry-wide standardized form contracts.

shared_topics.topic: how enforceability and marketability concerns shape contract form in financing contexts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how concerns about enforceability (foreign-law validity, enforceability of foreign judgments, act-of-state issues, and U.S. statutes) affect the content and qualifications of opinion letters for financing agreements, and Paper B shows that the need to make contracts easily marketable and enforceable by downstream buyers is a key driver of standardization in contract terms.

shared_topics.topic: the influence of professional/market norms on what constitutes acceptable contractual assurances
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes accepted lawyerly practice and professional reports (e.g., the IBA Report) that define commonly used opinion language in international deals, while Paper B examines industry practices that converge on particular standardized contract forms because of market incentives from secondary purchasers.

shared_topics.topic: treating contractual rights as transferrable commercial assets and the resulting demand for predictable legal characteristics
shared_topics.justification: Paper B explicitly frames certain contracts as commodities to be resold (e.g., mortgages), arguing that resaleability drives standard terms; Paper A engages the parallel demand for predictable, transferable assurances by considering what opinions New York counsel should give so foreign lenders or purchasers can rely on the legal character and enforceability of the financed asset or agreement.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Contract as Swag

shared_topics.topic: conceptualizing contracts as products/commodities (not just legal promises)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames certain modern contracts as marketable 'swag' and draws on prior analogies of contracts-as-products/technology, while Paper B explicitly builds on Leff's idea of contracts as 'things' or commodities and analyzes the consequences of that reclassification.

shared_topics.topic: factors driving standardization and diffusion of contract forms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A distinguishes creation from dissemination and studies how branded, freely distributed forms (like the KISS) spread through reputation and marketing, whereas Paper B investigates how market mechanisms—particularly secondary purchasers—encourage industry-wide standardization of form contracts.

shared_topics.topic: the influence of market intermediaries and reputational incentives on contract form
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on how actors (e.g., incubators, law firms) use contract templates as branding to attract clients and disseminate innovations, and Paper B analyzes how intermediaries/secondary buyers (e.g., investors, financial institutions) shape which forms retailers adopt and standardize.

shared_topics.topic: implications for regulation and policy given marketized contract forms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses product/branding analogies to rethink incentives, dissemination, and the limits of a universal theory of contractual innovation, while Paper B draws policy conclusions from treating contracts as commodities (including how warranty-like or other regulatory approaches might apply).

compared_to.partner_node_id: 48emorylj547!!ARTICLE:MALPRACTICE AND THE TAX PRACTITIONER: AN ANALYSISOF THE AREAS IN WHICH MALPRACTICE OCCURS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:MALPRACTICE AND THE TAX PRACTITIONER: AN ANALYSISOF THE AREAS IN WHICH MALPRACTICE OCCURS

shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes why businesses use standardized form contracts (and how standardization is amplified by secondary purchasers) to reduce bargaining and administrative costs; Paper B documents that many malpractice claims arise from failures in routine procedural tasks (late filings, missed elections), showing how standardized practices and forms both streamline work and create focal points for liability.

shared_topics.topic: influence of third parties and intermediaries on primary legal relationships and liability allocation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how secondary purchasers of contractual rights transform contracts into tradable commodities and thus affect contract form and enforcement; Paper B examines accountants, associations between accountants and lawyers, and other intermediaries whose involvement blurs professional roles and affects who bears malpractice liability.

shared_topics.topic: use of empirical or case-based analysis to evaluate legal practice and inform policy reforms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A combines theoretical discussion with empirical examples across industries to explain when contracts standardize and to suggest policy changes; Paper B systematically reviews reported tax malpractice cases to identify patterns of malpractice and to draw conclusions about practitioner behavior and damage measures.

shared_topics.topic: allocation and enforcement of continuing rights and duties arising from legal instruments and professional relationships
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that contracts, when treated as commodities, carry continuing rights and duties that survive resale and affect parties down the chain; Paper B focuses on continuing duties of tax practitioners (e.g., filing, making elections) and how breaches of those ongoing obligations lead to malpractice claims and damage assessments.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 1988uilllrev401!!ARTICLE: THE CAPITALIZATION OF SOVEREIGN DEBT: AN INTRODUCTION © 1988 Center for Transnational Legal Studies.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE CAPITALIZATION OF SOVEREIGN DEBT: AN INTRODUCTION © 1988 Center for Transnational Legal Studies.

shared_topics.topic: how assignment or resale of contractual claims changes who bears obligations and how performance can be discharged (including redenomination/redemption in a different currency)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how resale of rights and duties (e.g., mortgages, leases) makes contractual pieces more like tradable commodities and affects continuing rights and duties between parties; Paper B analyzes debt/equity conversions in which purchased sovereign loans are redeemed for local currency, altering who ultimately discharges external obligations and under what terms.

shared_topics.topic: policy and programmatic responses to manage or leverage secondary trading of contracts/claims
shared_topics.justification: Paper A considers policy changes that might follow from recognizing contracts as tradable commodities and the role secondary purchasers play in standardization; Paper B describes debtor-country programs (debt/equity conversion, government approval to redeem in local currency) designed to facilitate secondary transactions and to achieve macroeconomic and investment objectives.

shared_topics.topic: the commodification/marketization of contractual claims and its economic consequences for original contract parties and markets
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames standard form contracts as 'things' or commodities when resale is common and examines resulting economic pressures on form and administration; Paper B treats sovereign loan assets as tradable commodities whose sale at discounts, and subsequent investment uses, have concrete consequences for banks, investors, local firms, and debtor states.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 88nyulrev1!!ARTICLE: THE DYNAMICS OF CONTRACT EVOLUTION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE DYNAMICS OF CONTRACT EVOLUTION

shared_topics.topic: conceptualizing contracts as commodities / mass-produced legal products
shared_topics.justification: Both papers reject the assumption that contracts are bespoke legal texts and instead treat them as standardized, mass-produced goods — Paper A frames form contracts as 'things' or commodities sold and resold, and Paper B emphasizes law firms' template-based production and the commodification that gives rise to boilerplate.

shared_topics.topic: drivers and economics of form-contract standardization (administrative gains, resaleability, transaction costs)
shared_topics.justification: Both studies analyze why parties use standardized forms rather than bespoke drafting — Paper A focuses on economic pressures (speed, administrative ease, and resaleability to secondary purchasers) that encourage cross‑industry standardization, while Paper B highlights production economics (good‑enough templates, lawyer incentives, and economies of scale) that lock in boilerplate.

shared_topics.topic: the role of market actors beyond the original parties in shaping contract terms
shared_topics.justification: Both papers examine how actors other than the immediate transacting parties influence contract content — Paper A highlights secondary purchasers (e.g., mortgage buyers) who create incentives to standardize forms, and Paper B documents how top market participants, investors, and public-sector actors drive adoption and competition over new boilerplate standards.

shared_topics.topic: dynamics and path-dependence of contractual change (industry-wide shifts, triggers, and adoption patterns)
shared_topics.justification: Both engage with how contract terms evolve over time rather than changing deal-by-deal — Paper A studies the process and conditions under which forms standardize across industries, and Paper B empirically traces clustered, path-dependent shifts (slow experimentation, shocks/tipping points, and S-curve adoption) in sovereign bond boilerplate.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 67dukeljonline219!!ARTICLE: BOILING DOWN BOILERPLATE IN M&A AGREEMENTS: A RESPONSE TO CHOI, GULATI, & SCOTT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: BOILING DOWN BOILERPLATE IN M&A AGREEMENTS: A RESPONSE TO CHOI, GULATI, & SCOTT

shared_topics.topic: drivers of contractual standardization (why and when forms standardize)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a theoretical account (and some empirics) showing how market factors—notably secondary purchasers—create pressures toward industry-wide standardization of form contracts; Paper B considers the opposite dynamic by showing how boilerplate is intended to create uniformity in M&A deals but often fails, thereby illuminating the forces that promote or prevent standardization in transactional practice.

shared_topics.topic: effects of reuse/re‑sale/recycling of contract provisions across transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that secondary purchasers and the commodification of contracts (e.g., mortgages, leases) create incentives to produce transferable, standardized forms; Paper B empirically documents how lawyers recycle boilerplate across deals and how such reuse propagates idiosyncratic edits, shaping the transmission and transformation of contractual text.

shared_topics.topic: tension between drafting efficiency/administration and idiosyncratic edits that erode uniformity
shared_topics.justification: Paper A invokes Llewellyn’s efficiency rationale for standard forms (speed, lower admin costs) and analyzes when those efficiencies obtain, while Paper B shows that efficiency motives (rote reuse) combined with ad hoc editorial churning produce ‘drafting drift,’ undermining the very certainty and universality that boilerplate is meant to supply.

shared_topics.topic: empirical and theoretical study of how contract language evolves over generations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A offers theoretical and some empirical discussion of the process by which form contracts standardize (and when they don’t) across industries over time; Paper B provides large‑scale computational empirical evidence tracing micro‑level textual drift and constructing ‘family trees’ of boilerplate to map how contractual provisions evolve across generations of deals.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 1988uilllrev219!!INTERNATIONAL BANKING SYMPOSIUM: FOREWORD 1988 Center for Transnational Legal Studies
compared_to.partner_title: INTERNATIONAL BANKING SYMPOSIUM: FOREWORD 1988 Center for Transnational Legal Studies

shared_topics.topic: the role of standardized contractual clauses in allocating continuing rights and duties among original parties and downstream holders
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that contracts sold into secondary markets carry continuing rights and duties that shape which terms are standardized, while Paper B analyzes specific standardized clauses (sharing provisions, negative pledges, mandatory prepayment provisions) that govern creditor relations and preserve pro rata treatment when debt is restructured or traded.

shared_topics.topic: how secondary trading of contractual interests prompts legal and regulatory change
shared_topics.justification: Paper A considers policy changes that should follow from treating contracts as commodities in light of secondary purchasers, and Paper B describes concrete regulatory, tax, and documentation adaptations (e.g., to permit securitization and debt-to-equity conversions) that were required as creditor interests were restructured and sold into secondary markets.

shared_topics.topic: standardization as a response to transaction costs and large multiparty negotiation problems
shared_topics.justification: Paper A invokes Llewellyn's transaction-cost rationale for widespread use of standard forms to save bargaining time and ease administration, and Paper B recounts how a remarkably uniform approach and standardized documentation were adopted to manage negotiations among hundreds of commercial banks and other stakeholders in sovereign debt restructurings.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 77chikentlrev59!!SYMPOSIUM: THEORY INFORMS BUSINESS PRACTICE:WHY CONTRACTS ARE WRITTEN IN "LEGALESE"
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: THEORY INFORMS BUSINESS PRACTICE:WHY CONTRACTS ARE WRITTEN IN "LEGALESE"

shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze why certain contract texts become standardized across transactions: Paper A emphasizes market forces such as secondary purchasers that create demand for uniform, transferable contractual “things,” while Paper B explains how law-firm production processes, reuse of precedent, and network effects push lawyers to adopt and preserve common forms.

shared_topics.topic: how non-signatory intermediaries shape contract design
shared_topics.justification: Each paper studies how actors other than the original buyer and seller influence contract content — Paper A focuses on secondary purchasers of contractual rights (e.g., mortgage buyers) and their incentives to favor uniform forms, and Paper B shows how intermediaries within the legal production chain (firms, senior lawyers, precedent-holders) determine which clauses persist and how forms evolve.

shared_topics.topic: persistence of suboptimal or cumbersome boilerplate due to path-dependence and network effects
shared_topics.justification: Both works confront why contracts often remain lengthy, redundant, or ambiguous despite imperfections: Paper A documents complex standardization patterns that can lock in particular forms, and Paper B offers an explicit account of path-dependence, switching costs, and learning/production dynamics that cause inefficient features to persist.

shared_topics.topic: trade-offs between administrative efficiency from standardization and substantive imperfections or costs
shared_topics.justification: Each paper weighs the benefits of standardized forms (speed, reduced bargaining costs, easier administration) against their downsides (loss of tailoring, complexity, latent ambiguities), and explores when and why actors accept those trade-offs in practice.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 6chijintll333!!ARTICLE: SYMPOSIUM: SOVEREIGN DEBT RESTRUCTURING: The Role of the Official Sector in Sovereign Debt Workouts
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: SYMPOSIUM: SOVEREIGN DEBT RESTRUCTURING: The Role of the Official Sector in Sovereign Debt Workouts

shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how official-sector actors (Creditor Governments, the IMF, Bretton Woods institutions) intervene to shape outcomes of private claims in sovereign debt workouts, while Paper B analyzes how secondary purchasers (third‑party buyers) exert pressure on original contracting parties to adopt particular standardized contract forms.

shared_topics.topic: impact of transferability/secondary markets on contract design and dispute resolution
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights how integrated financial markets and tradable sovereign claims complicate restructurings and motivate institutional mechanisms (e.g., SDRM) to manage cross‑border distress, and Paper B shows that the existence of secondary purchasers makes contracts behave like commodities, encouraging standardization to facilitate resale.

shared_topics.topic: coordination and collective‑action problems among dispersed creditors and the role of legal/formal mechanisms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on the collective‑action challenge of getting multiple private and bilateral creditors to reach an orderly, expeditious readjustment of claims, and Paper B explores how standard forms and fungibility (driven by secondary markets) alter coordination among market participants and affect how claims are pooled, traded, and enforced.

shared_topics.topic: policy and institutional design tradeoffs between creditor protection, market efficiency, and debtor incentives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A lays out the official sector's policy objectives and tradeoffs (protecting lenders, ensuring recoverability of official funds, avoiding contagion, and preserving incentives), while Paper B draws implications for regulatory or policy changes from the pressures secondary purchasers place on contract form, balancing consumer/protection concerns against efficiency and liquidity in markets.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 107califlrev1119!!ARTICLE: Is There a First-Drafter Advantage in M&A?
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Is There a First-Drafter Advantage in M&A?

shared_topics.topic: whether allocation of drafting responsibility (first-drafter rights) confers advantage in final contract terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how upstream buyers/resellers can drive uniform contract content and thus affect which party's form governs downstream terms, while Paper B empirically tests the 'first-drafter advantage,' showing that who provides the initial draft is associated with more favorable non-price terms for that party in some provisions.

shared_topics.topic: the role of transaction costs and lawyer/agent behavior in determining contract form and content
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes administrative and transaction-cost reasons firms adopt standard forms (saving time, easing administration) and highlights how third‑party resale needs can alter incentives, while Paper B shows that negotiation transaction costs and lawyer agency costs help explain why drafting advantages persist for complex or hard-to-monetize provisions.

shared_topics.topic: empirical investigation of determinants of contract form and final contractual terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A notes the paucity of empirical/economic work on why standard form contracts arise and then sets out theoretical and empirical effects of secondary purchasers on forms, and Paper B constructs a large dataset of merger agreements to empirically identify determinants (auction status, first drafter, bargaining context) of specific deal terms.

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM CONSUMERS IN THE DIGITAL AGE: PERSPECTIVES ON THE INTERSECTION OF LAW, TECHNOLOGICAL INNOVATION, AND CONSUMER PROTECTION:PERSPECTIVES ON ANTITRUST LAW:A Case for Letting a Firm Take Advantage of "Locked-In" Customers

shared_topics.topic: drivers of standardization (contracts or products) and how market structure produces a single prevailing form
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how the existence of secondary purchasers of contractual rights creates incentives for retailers to converge on standardized form contracts, while Paper B analyzes how network effects and market tipping cause consumers and firms to converge on a single product variant, producing industry-wide standardization.

shared_topics.topic: how third parties and downstream markets alter sellers' design and pricing incentives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that secondary purchasers (buyers of contractual interests) influence the original seller's choice of contract terms, and Paper B shows how 'network sponsors', complementary adopters, and downstream user bases lead firms to subsidize or price strategically to build a dominant installed base.

shared_topics.topic: the role of transaction and switching costs in entrenching prevailing forms and limiting consumer choice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes administrative and transaction-cost savings that favor standard form contracts and make deviation costly, while Paper B emphasizes switching costs that reinforce lock-in to dominant technologies and deter entry by superior alternatives.

shared_topics.topic: tradeoffs for regulators between efficiency gains from a dominant standard and potential consumer harms (and appropriate policy responses)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A considers legal and policy changes in response to contracts functioning as commoditized, standardized goods, and Paper B evaluates antitrust remedies (e.g., breakup threats) versus the welfare gains from firms' ability to create networks and lock-in, arguing for careful calibration of enforcement.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Recalibrating Contract Law: Choses in Action, Global Value Chains, and the Enforcement of Obligations Outside of Privity

shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the common‑law device of assigning choses in action so that parties outside the original privity chain can enforce contractual claims; Paper B analyzes how secondary purchasers (buyers of contractual interests like mortgages) make contracts de facto transferable commodities and shape the consequences of resale and assignment.

shared_topics.topic: how evolving commercial practices reshape traditional contract doctrines
