papers.node_id: 121columlrev1405!!ARTICLE: DEALS IN THE TIME OF PANDEMIC
papers.title: ARTICLE: DEALS IN THE TIME OF PANDEMIC
papers.abstract:
On February 20, 2020, Sycamore Partners, a private equity firm specializing in the retail and consumer sectors, announced a deal to buy a 55% stake in Victoria's Secret, the well-known retailer that operates under the Victoria's Secret and PINK brands. Pursuant to the transaction agreement, L Brands, the owners of Victoria's Secret, would create a newly formed subsidiary and transfer certain assets and liabilities related to the Victoria's Secret business to that subsidiary; and then Sycamore would pay L Brands approximately $ 525 million for a 55% equity interest in that new entity.The deal was expected to close in the second quarter of 2020.
The agreement included a "Material Adverse Effect" (MAE) clause, which permitted Sycamore to walk away from the deal if there was a Material Adverse Effect in the Victoria's Secret business. MAE was defined, in part, as any event or circumstance "that has a material adverse effect on the financial condition, business, assets, or results of operations of the Business."However, the agreement also included a list of nine MAE "carveouts," including one stipulating that "the existence, occurrence or continuation of any pandemics . . . or acts of God" shallnotconstitute an MAE and therefore would not give Sycamore the right to walk away.The agreement further included an MAE "carveback," under which a pandemic would again qualify as an MAE, thereby restoring Sycamore's right to walk away "to the extent (and only to the extent) that the Business is materially and disproportionately adversely affected [by the pandemic] . . . as compared to similarly situated businesses in the industry of the Business."The agreement also included a requirement that L Brands would conduct the Victoria's Secret business "in the ordinarycourse consistent with past practice" between February 20 and the closing, unless Sycamore consented in writing.
Of course, shortly thereafter (or, arguably, shortly before), the world fell apart. COVID-19 struck individuals and the global economy with catastrophic force. On March 11, 2020, the World Health Organization declared a global pandemic.As of that date, 114 countries had reported 118,000 total cases of COVID-19, with nearly 4,300 deaths.In the following months, cases would skyrocket, with over 150 million confirmed cases and over three million deaths as of May 4, 2021.
While it was, of course, not the most important implication of COVID-19, these developments raised questions for the Sycamore-L Brands deal, which was still pending. By March 20, L Brands had closed nearly all of its 1,600 Victoria's Secret and PINK brick-and-mortar stores, some under orders from state and local authorities.L Brands also furloughed most of the employees in its Victoria's Secret business, reduced the base compensation for all remaining senior employees by 20%, and failed to pay rent during April 2020 for its retail stores in the United States.
On April 22, Sycamore terminated its deal with L Brands and sought a declaratory judgment in the Delaware Chancery Court that its termination was valid. Interestingly, Sycamore didnotclaim that Victoria's Secret had "materially and disproportionately adversely" suffered from COVID-19 relative to other retailers (so as to avoid the MAE carveout), perhaps because all of retail was in freefall and it would be difficult to argue that Victoria's Secret had suffered more than the retail industry overall. Instead, Sycamore's primary claim was that L Brands violated the covenant requiring it to run Victoria's Secret "in the ordinary course consistent with past practice."
L Brands did not challenge the fact that it was not operating the Victoria's Secret business in the ordinary course consistent with past practice. Matt Levine put it well in Bloomberg News: "I assert that there are zero businesses in the United States right now that are running 'in theordinary course consistent with past practice.'"But L Brands defended its actions, in effect, by asking rhetorically: "What else did you want us to do?" L Brands was stuck between a rock and a hard place: either comply with the ordinary course requirement and watch its business go into the tank, or violate the ordinary course covenant in order to try to save the business, as best as possible.Sycamore responded, in so many words: Your dilemma is not our problem. A contract is a contract, and L Brands violated the ordinary course covenant.
While the Delaware Chancery Court was preparing to resolve these questions, on May 4, the parties agreed to call off their deal. Sycamore walked away without penalty, and L Brands announced that Victoria's Secret would be spun off and trade as a separate public company.L Brands, which had traded as high as $ 100 per share four years earlier, took another 18% hit on its stock price and closed on May 4at $ 9.82 per share.
The Sycamore-L Brands case study illustrates a new deal dynamic that the COVID-19 pandemic has repeatedly exposed since the start of 2020. Practitioners historically have focused on the negotiation of the MAE clause and its carveouts; and, as this Article will show, that clause has been growing rapidly over the past fifteen years. In contrast, the ordinary course covenant has not grown and is rarely negotiated as heavily. Historically, this covenant was meant to be a relatively innocuous provision that protects the buyer against moral hazard and other opportunistic behavior by the seller between signing and closing. But in a rapid and severe downturn, such as COVID-19, the ordinary course covenant can collide with the MAE clause. While the prior academic and practitioner literature has focused on the MAE clause, this Article is the first to examine the interaction between the MAE clause and the ordinary course covenant in mergers and acquisitions (M&A). We construct a new database of 1,300 M&A transactions along with their MAE and ordinary course covenants. We believe it to be the most comprehensive, accurate, and detaileddatabase of such deal terms that currently exists. We document how these deal terms currently appear in M&A transactions, including the sharp rise in "pandemic" carveouts from the MAE clause since COVID-19 (as illustrated by the Sycamore-L Brands agreement). The findings from this database paint a rich and previously undocumented picture of how M&A deals have evolved in their allocation of risk and constraints on the seller over the past fifteen years.
Our empirical findings and recommendations are relevant not just for the next "Act of God" event but also the next (inevitable) downturn in the economy more generally. Specifically, we provide implications of our empirical findings for corporate boards, the Delaware courts, and transactional planners.
For corporate boards, the data presented in this Article highlight why MAE clauses and ordinary course covenants should be a board-level issue, not to be delegated categorically to advisors. Our empirical analysis tells corporate boards specifically where to look in "stress testing" the deal documents. For example, whether the MAE carveouts have a causal requirement can be important for determining the scope of the MAE carveouts, yet this feature of MAE clauses has been completely overlooked by prior academic and practitioner commentators. For the Delaware courts, a key question is how the ordinary course covenant should interact with the MAE clause. Some Delaware judges have suggested that the ordinary course requirement might permit extraordinary behavior when there are unexpected developments. Or, put differently (and in a manner that satisfies the contractual constraint), what is "ordinary course" changes in extraordinary circumstances. While we agree with the underlying intuition that the ordinary course requirement should not be a backdoor reallocation of risk back to the seller (because such allocation of risk is better accomplished through the MAE clause), we disagree that the ordinary course requirement should be so malleable--in effect, a "get out of jail free" card--in extraordinary times. Instead, this Article argues that the ordinary course requirement should be read according to its plain terms, which would not include, for example, unprecedented store closings and layoffs. This reading forces a negotiation between the seller and the buyer about the correct way to mitigate the damage to the company. Basic law and economics analysis shows why this renegotiation is socially optimal compared to unilateral action by the seller. In L Brands, the rock-and-a-hard-place problem would have been solved if L Brands had simply obtained written approval from Sycamore in advance of taking its mitigation actions. By reading the ordinary course requirement according to its plain terms, Delaware courts will force future sellers to negotiate with their buyers rather than try to exploit the old maxim "better to beg for forgiveness than ask for permission."
For transactional planners, our analysis provides guidance for where they should focus their efforts in negotiating MAE clauses and ordinarycourse covenants. On MAE clauses, for example, transactional planners should stipulate the target's industry--or, better yet, enumerate a list of comparable companies--in the merger agreement itself; this is particularly important in view of the proliferation of disproportionality carvebacks from the MAE.And buy-side advisors can generally give the seller more leeway to run the business under the ordinary course requirement in a stock deal rather than a cash deal because the moral hazard problem for the seller is substantially diminished in a stock transaction.These contours of MAE clauses are currently undetectable in the data, yet such structuring could be a significant "win-win" for the parties overall. Finally, to the extent that the Delaware courts read the ordinary course requirement consistently with its plain meaning, as this Article advocates, buy-side and sell-side advisors can work together to clarify how the MAE clauses should interact with that requirement.
This Article has three parts. Part I provides an in-depth discussion of MAEs and ordinary course covenants, with a review of the associated case law and literature. Part II details our findings on MAEs and ordinary course covenants from a database of 1,300 M&A transactions, with particular attention to the sharp rise in "pandemic" carveouts from the MAE clause since COVID-19. Part III examines the implications for corporate boards, the Delaware courts, and transactional planners in light of our findings.

questions.question: Whether and how contractual buyer-termination rights for significant adverse events interact with seller obligations to operate the target business in its ordinary course during systemic shocks (e.g., a pandemic) - in particular, when do ordinary-course restrictions prevent sellers from taking unilateral mitigation steps and thus affect the buyer's ability to terminate?
questions.answer: The paper contends that during systemic shocks the ordinary-course covenant can collide with MAE clauses, and courts should enforce “ordinary course” by its plain terms—meaning unprecedented measures like mass store closures and layoffs are not permitted without buyer consent—so a seller’s unilateral mitigation can breach the covenant and give the buyer termination leverage even when a pandemic is carved out of the MAE.

questions.question: How did the frequency and wording of deal provisions that exempt systemic events (such as pandemics) from buyer-termination rights change after COVID-19, and what empirical patterns exist in how these carveouts and related terms are drafted across transactions?
questions.answer: Based on a 1,300-deal database, the paper documents a sharp post‑COVID increase in explicit “pandemic” carveouts from MAE clauses, a proliferation of disproportionality carvebacks, and highlights important drafting variation such as whether carveouts include a causal requirement.

questions.question: How do different allocations of risk in these clauses affect negotiation incentives and ex ante behavior by buyers, sellers, and corporate boards, and what interpretations or bargaining rules lead to socially (and contractually) optimal outcomes during major downturns?
questions.answer: Strictly reading the ordinary‑course covenant and requiring seller–buyer negotiation (buyer consent) for extraordinary actions allocates risk through MAE rather than ad hoc seller unilateralism, induces socially optimal renegotiation, and—together with board‑level scrutiny of MAE and ordinary‑course terms (including causal requirements, specified industry/comparables, and greater seller leeway in stock deals due to reduced moral hazard)—improves incentives and outcomes in downturns.

shared_topics.topic: empirical analysis of M&A contract terms to inform law and practice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A relies on and references a large empirical study of MAC clauses and surveys MAC litigation to motivate a new interpretive model; Paper B builds a detailed database of 1,300 transactions to document trends (e.g., pandemic carveouts) and to derive implications for boards, courts, and transactional planners.

papers.node_id: 36geojintll299!!ARTICLE: DESIGNING A LEGAL FRAMEWORK TO RESTRUCTURE SOVEREIGN DEBT
papers.title: ARTICLE: DESIGNING A LEGAL FRAMEWORK TO RESTRUCTURE SOVEREIGN DEBT
papers.abstract:
From November 2001 through April 2003, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and its 184 member countries actively considered a fundamental change in the international financial system.The reform envisaged establishing, through an amendment of the IMF's Articles of Agreement, a treaty-based framework to restructure sovereign debt,referred to as the Sovereign Debt Restructuring Mechanism (SDRM). By the end of a period of intensive discussion regarding the design of the SDRM proposal, a relatively detailed blueprint of the proposal had been endorsed by most Executive Directors of the IMF, evidencing broad support among member countries.However, while support for the SDRM proposal was strong, it was not strong enough. An amendment to the IMF's Articles requires the approval of three-fifths of member countries, holding eighty-five percent of the total voting power.A number of emerging-market countries were opposed to the SDRM proposal, and, by April 2003, the United States, which holds 17.14% of IMF voting power, had signaled that it could no longer support the proposal.At that point, the IMF discontinued further work on its development and decided to focus exclusively on more incremental reform measures.
As evidenced by Adam Smith's statement, the notion of establishing some form of insolvency framework for sovereign states is hardly a novel one. The debt crisis that emerged in the 1980s engendered considerable discussion as to whether more forceful official intervention was needed to resolve creditor coordination issues, and, during the 1990s, various legal reform proposals were proposed to addressgrowing discomfort with large IMF financing packages.Indeed, although the SDRM proposal was described as a "bombshell" when it was launched by Anne Krueger, First Deputy Managing Director of the IMF, in November 2001,the concept of establishing some form of statutory framework had in fact been considered within the IMF six years earlier.
What distinguished the SDRM proposal from earlier proposals was the extent to which the mainstream of the official sector embraced it. The willingness of so many senior policy makers to support such a major reform was, in part, attributable to their frustration with the lack of progress on the implementation of market-based solutions. Although the official sector had, since 1996, exhorted emerging-market sovereigns and their creditors to facilitate the restructuring process by including collective action clauses in their international sovereign bonds,there was still very little to show for it--at least with respect to bonds governed by New York law, which represent by far the largest percentage of international bonds issued by emerging-market sovereigns.
The official sector's decision to give serious consideration to the SDRM proposal was also motivated by the tragedy unfolding in Argentina. By the fall of 2001, there was little doubt that Argentina's sovereign debt had become unsustainable and that, accordingly, a restructuringwas inevitable.While it was understood that any major reform would arrive too late to help Argentina, its circumstances highlighted the need to establish a framework that provided strong incentives for a sovereign debtor and its creditors to engage in the restructuring process at an early stage of a financial crisis--thereby limiting both the economic dislocation for the sovereign and the deterioration in the value of creditor claims.Moreover, the magnitude and complex structure of Argentina's indebtedness called into question whether a decentralized contractual framework could adequately address the collective action and creditor coordination problems that arise when a sovereign attempts to reach a restructuring agreement with an atomized creditor community.
Finally, in the absence of a sufficiently robust legal framework that addresses these issues in a predictable manner, there was a concern that the IMF would continue to be under pressure to provide additional financing to countries with unsustainable debt burdens because the alternative path--the restructuring of the sovereign's debt--was perceived as being fraught with difficulty. As noted by Paul O'Neill, then-U.S. Secretary of Treasury, in September 2002, "Today, with no clear process for sovereign debt restructuring in place, when a nation is on the brink of financial collapse, we have two stark and uninviting options--unwarranted lending or sending the nation off a cliff into a catastrophic default."
Whether interest in the SDRM proposal--or some other treaty-basedframework--will re-emerge within the official sector will depend on a number of factors, including the frequency of financial crises and the extent to which alternative, contractual-based frameworks are able to limit their severity. In the immediate term, however, one of the tangible benefits of the SDRM initiative is that market participants and emerging-market sovereigns have finally agreed to include collective action clauses in their debt instruments. It would appear that a credible threat of official intervention prompted this degree of self-regulation.
This Article discusses the underlying rationale for the SDRM proposal, its key features, and the lessons that can be distilled from the vigorous debate that it engendered. Section I discusses the motivations for reform. As will be seen, perceptions vary as to the nature of the weaknesses of the existing system. Not surprisingly, these differences define the contours of any discussion of the design of a new legal framework. Section II analyzes the key issues that arose in the design of the SDRM proposal--many of which will be of relevance to any type of statutory sovereign debt restructuring framework that may be considered in the future. Section III sets forth some general observations as to nature of the resistance to the SDRM proposal and the possible implications of this resistance to any future reform efforts.
The SDRM proposal was developed in the open. At each stage of its evolution, the IMF staff papers outlining the various issues and design options and the IMF Executive Board's views of these papers were published.The financial press followed the SDRM proposal's developmentclosely; many editorial pages gave positive reviews. At the same time, the press observed that the SDRM proposal would continue to face significant political obstacles in attempting such ambitious reform.The feedback from legal and economic scholars, workout practitioners, nongovernmental organizations, and market participants helped shape subsequent versions and sharpened everyone's understanding of the issues, not least that of the IMF's staff.Not surprisingly, the analysis contained in this Article has benefited considerably from this engagement.

questions.question: Whether establishing a treaty-based, statutory framework for restructuring sovereign debt would lead to earlier, more orderly restructurings and reduce reliance on ad hoc official financing
questions.answer: Yes: the proposed treaty-based SDRM was intended to create a predictable process that incentivizes early debtor–creditor engagement, yields more orderly restructurings with less economic dislocation and creditor value loss, and reduces pressure for ad hoc IMF financing.

questions.question: What key design features and trade-offs are necessary in a statutory sovereign-debt restructuring mechanism to solve creditor coordination and collective-action problems
What political, market, and creditor/debtor factors explain resistance to adopting a treaty-based sovereign-debt restructuring framework and how that resistance affects prospects for future reform
questions.answer: Resistance came from opposition by several emerging-market countries and, crucially, the United States withdrawing support (blocking the required supermajority), which led the IMF to abandon the SDRM in 2003 in favor of incremental, contract-based reforms, with prospects for future revival depending on crisis frequency and the effectiveness of contractual alternatives.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 83chikentlrev147!!ARTICLE: DOMESTIC BONDS, CREDIT DERIVATIVES, AND THE NEXT TRANSFORMATION OF SOVEREIGN DEBT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: DOMESTIC BONDS, CREDIT DERIVATIVES, AND THE NEXT TRANSFORMATION OF SOVEREIGN DEBT

shared_topics.topic: collective-action problems in sovereign debt restructurings and the need for a coordination framework
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the SDRM debate as a response to creditor coordination failures in sovereign restructurings and the limits of decentralized contractual solutions; Paper B frames the shift to tradable bonds and later domestic debt as creating collective-action risks that call for contractual or statutory analogues to domestic bankruptcy.

shared_topics.topic: the role of governing law (foreign vs local law) in shaping crisis resolution and legal uncertainty
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes the dominance of New York-law bonds and the difficulty of achieving collective remedies under existing laws, while Paper B directly interrogates how a rise in local-law domestic debt can complicate or increase uncertainty about how sovereign crises are resolved.

shared_topics.topic: how the identity and fragmentation of creditors (foreign vs domestic, atomized vs concentrated) affects restructuring options
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights an atomized creditor community that impedes restructuring and motivated the SDRM, and Paper B examines changes in creditor composition (local vs foreign, new investor types) and how creditor diversity and churning narrow preemptive restructuring space and authorities' options in crisis.

shared_topics.topic: the impact of contractual and financial innovations (collective action clauses, credit derivatives) on sovereign debt management and restructuring outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A credits the SDRM debate with prompting wider adoption of collective action clauses in sovereign bonds as a market-based mitigation of coordination problems, while Paper B maps the rapid growth of credit derivatives and other risk-transfer tools and analyzes how these contractual innovations reshape sovereign risk, litigation, and restructuring dynamics.

shared_topics.topic: implications for crisis governance and the role of official-sector interventions (IMF, policy responses) in managing sovereign insolvency risk
shared_topics.justification: Paper A is centered on the IMF-led SDRM proposal and the political economy of official-sector reform versus lending, arguing for predictable frameworks to limit ad hoc lending; Paper B discusses how the transformation in debt instruments and markets affects governance, risk management, and the set of policy responses available to authorities during sovereign stress.

shared_topics.topic: creditor coordination and collective-action problems when resolving sovereign liabilities
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on creditor coordination failures and promotes collective action clauses and a statutory SDRM to overcome holdout problems; Paper B examines how successor-state scenarios produce coordination challenges among creditors and international actors when apportioning or renegotiating claims.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the political opposition (e.g., vested interests, key member states) that prevented adoption of the SDRM and how politics constrained reform design; Paper B investigates why negotiators and domestic agencies favor non-binding competition chapters, highlighting political, resource, and strategic constraints that shape PTA provisions.

shared_topics.justification: Both engage with how legal design can produce predictable, orderly outcomes—Paper A by evaluating a statutory/treaty-based sovereign debt restructuring mechanism to produce timely restructurings, and Paper B by studying M&A contractual regimes and empirical patterns of deal breakage to understand how law and practice create (or fail to create) deal certainty.

shared_topics.topic: how legal predictability or credible threats change market behavior and self-regulation
shared_topics.justification: Both show that credible legal frameworks or the threat of official intervention alter market practice: Paper A argues that the SDRM debate prompted market adoption of collective action clauses, and Paper B links predictable legal outcomes and empirically observed deal-breakage rates to investor strategies (e.g., merger arbitrage) and counsel practices aimed at securing closings.

papers.node_id: 70lawcontempprob137!!ARTICLE: DEVILRY, COMPLICITY, AND GREED: TRANSITIONAL JUSTICE AND ODIOUS DEBT
papers.title: ARTICLE: DEVILRY, COMPLICITY, AND GREED: TRANSITIONAL JUSTICE AND ODIOUS DEBT
papers.abstract:
As the other contributions to these volumes reveal, issues relating to odious debt and contemporary efforts to expand the odious debt doctrine to cover all debts of odious regimes are maddeningly complex, implicating difficult issues in areas ranging from the international law of state succession to the law of commercial paper - itself a source of biannual trauma for thousands of bar aspirants. Nevertheless, the scope of the debate as it has been developed in the literature is too narrow and, therefore, the questions posed too simple. In particular, any analysis of odious debt must account for issues that inhere to transitions and transitional justice. In this article I make some of these connections and argue that any treatment of odious debts must be consistent with the broader programs of transitional justice in which they are situated. Highest of these are transitional imperatives of truth and justice, which may be compromised in the process of affording successor regimes the opportunity to disavow debts incurred by an odious forebear.
The results of this accounting are not intuitively appealing. In many circumstances, full faith to truth and accountability will require that transitional regimes accept the burden of financial obligations incurred by an odious forebear. Although this is admittedly an unpalatable proposition, the arguments leading to it reinforce assignments of liability to international investors and debtors who supply financial support to odious regimes. Upon a full accounting, then, I argue that the moral discomfort that motivates the odious debt doctrinecan be satisfied by appeal to the international law of state and corporate responsibility and to fundamental tenets of moral, political, and existential responsibility, without compromising transitional commitments to truth and accountability.
Imposing upon international corporations affirmative duties of restitution and repair presents a number of potential concerns. Nevertheless, I conclude that, even though the moral burdens approach to odious debts proposed in this article may tread in "deep moral waters,"investors who proactively engage their human-rights responsibilities through a robust practice of corporate and social responsibility will enjoy an expanded horizon of financial opportunities. More importantly from an investor's point of view, the proposals made here will result in a world less cluttered with mystery and unpredictability than both the world investors now face and the world they would confront were the odious debt doctrine expanded to cover all debts of odious regimes.

questions.question: Whether and under what circumstances successor governments should assume or disavow financial obligations incurred by prior illegitimate or repressive regimes, given transitional imperatives of truth, justice, and accountability.
questions.answer: The paper contends that, consistent with transitional justice’s imperatives of truth and accountability, successor regimes should in many circumstances accept—rather than disavow—debts incurred by odious predecessors, because allowing disavowal risks compromising those imperatives.

questions.question: Whether and to what extent international investors, creditors, and corporations that financed or transacted with prior illegitimate or repressive regimes should bear affirmative duties of restitution and repair, and how imposing those duties affects transitional justice goals and investment predictability.
questions.answer: It argues that international investors, creditors, and corporations that financed odious regimes should bear affirmative duties of restitution and repair (i.e., liability), and that this moral-burdens approach can uphold transitional truth and accountability while creating a less unpredictable investment environment and expanding opportunities for firms that proactively embrace robust human-rights–oriented corporate responsibility.

matched_themes: Under what legal and normative conditions may or should successor governments repudiate, reduce, or assume debts incurred by prior illegitimate, corrupt, or oppressive regimes?
How should predecessor state debts and assets be allocated among successor states when a state dissolves or territorial units secede?
Can domestic or foreign courts refuse to recognize or enforce external state borrowing or guarantees that were contracted in breach of the state's constitutional or budgetary authority?

How should legal and institutional rules balance preserving state discretion over foreign economic policy and regulation with ensuring enforceability of cross-border financial claims and maintaining lender confidence?
How should judges treat foreign sovereign acts that affect intangible property or contractual rights-when should such acts be recognized, enforced, or disregarded by forum courts?
Will exempting successor governments from predecessor debts advance human-rights objectives without inflicting disproportionate harm on creditors, markets, or populations?
Can municipal public debt issued to private investors be contested as illegitimate or unenforceable when borrowing disproportionately benefited creditors and harmed public services?
When and under what conditions should a successor political entity be held responsible for its predecessor's international commercial obligations despite lacking the predecessor's consent?

To what extent can domestic private-law doctrines be used to shield successor governments from enforcement of debts contracted by predecessors under irregular, fraudulent, or non-beneficial circumstances?
Does the prospect of regime change or refusal by a successor government to honor prior debts materially influence creditor behavior and lending to risky or non-democratic governments?

Should international investors, creditors, and corporations that financed or transacted with prior repressive regimes bear affirmative duties of restitution or repair, and how would such duties affect transitional justice and investment predictability?
Should governments repudiate or cancel sovereign debt when debt service substantially impairs their ability to provide public welfare and democratic policymaking?
How should assets and liabilities be allocated and adjudicated when a state disintegrates or undergoes regime change?

Is adjusting or terminating predecessor commercial obligations sufficient to promote the well-being of communities undergoing succession, or are alternative autonomy arrangements and external assistance needed?
Would policy objectives of an existing legal rule be better achieved through alternative doctrines with clearer scope or by legislative reform?
When are legal or policy analogies to private-law relationships between rulers and the ruled (e.g., to justify repudiating prior regimes' obligations) normatively and legally defensible?

Does expanding post-regime relief to cover a wider range of financing transactions (beyond traditional loans) more effectively deter harmful regime financing and reduce associated human-rights, corruption, and environmental harms than relief limited to debt cancellation?
Would formal recognition of an exception permitting repudiation of predecessor-incurred debts materially affect cross-border sovereign lending and capital flows?

Would legally permitting or codifying successor-government exemptions for debts incurred by illegitimate or predatory prior regimes improve successor populations' welfare or deter predatory borrowing, and what are the likely market and political effects of such rules?
Is a post-regime-change state legally and practically obligated to assume external sovereign debt incurred by a prior regime?

papers.node_id: 82templrev1!!ARTICLE: DISPUTING BOILERPLATE
papers.title: ARTICLE: DISPUTING BOILERPLATE
papers.abstract:
Sovereign bond contracts are thought to consist mostly of boilerplate. That is, except for a handful of custom terms, the contracts are assumed to adopt highly standardized provisions that are functionally identical to those used in other bond contracts.The assumption of standardization extends to enforcement-related terms, including terms in which the issuer consents to be sued in the event of a default. Thus, the "standard" choice of forum term is presumed to call for litigation in foreign courts, typically in New York (for New York-law bonds) or England (for English-law bonds).
To describe sovereign bond contracts as "standardized," or "boilerplate," is to invoke significant theoretical baggage. For a variety of reasons, standardized terms may be "sticky."Parties who adopt a standard term may obtain benefits, while those who depart from the standard may incur costs, and these benefits and costs may induce even sophisticated parties to select a standard term over a custom term that matches their unique preferences. Thus, the presumed choice of forum standard may not evidence a preference for litigation over arbitration among participants in the sovereign debt markets. This is because the litigation term is thought to be a sticky default.
The assumptions underlying this "stickiness" explanation, however, are largely untested. Do sovereign bonds really contain standardized dispute resolution terms, and do these terms indeed eschew arbitration for litigation? If so, why attribute these contracting practices to the stickiness of forum selection terms rather than, say, a widely held preference for litigation? This Article explores these questions. In the process, it provides the first systematic empirical look at the manner in which sovereign bond contracts structure the process of enforcing sovereign debt obligations. This analysis reveals a richer and more nuanced picture of how some of the world's most sophisticated contracting parties structure the dispute resolution process, and of the likely impact of standardization on their choices.
Part I begins with an introduction to this unique contracting context, one in which the threat of legal enforcement plays a relatively minor role. Part I also introduces the presumptive standard set of choice of forum and other enforcement-related terms. That standard eschews arbitration in favor of litigation before creditor-friendly courts in New York or England. Part I closesby exploring a common explanation for the widespread use of this presumed standard. This explanation posits that bond contracts choose litigation not because market participants prefer it to arbitration, but because forum selection clauses are sticky.
The foregoing discussion suggests the ambiguity inherent in highly standardized contracts. Do parties simply prefer the standard, or does standardization deter contract innovation and change? Answering these questions requires some prior belief as to the parties' likely preferences, as well as an analysis of the contracts themselves. Part II engages these questions, beginning with an assessment of the merits of arbitration as a means of resolving sovereign debt disputes. I do not purport to offer a definitive resolution. I suggest, however, that few participants in the sovereign debt markets presently have strong reasons to prefer arbitration. That conclusion implies that arbitration clauses may appear infrequently in sovereign bond contracts for reasons having little or nothing to do with contract stickiness.
Part II next reports findings from an analysis of sovereign bond contracts, including at least one issuance from virtually every major (and most minor) issuers of New York-or English-law bonds over the last twenty years. As it turns out, enforcement-related terms vary to a surprising degree across the different issuers in my sample. With respect to choice of forum terms, more than twenty percent of the issuers depart in some way from the presumptive standard, including nearly ten percent whose bonds include arbitration clauses. Different issuers also vary in the degree to which they waive sovereign immunity from suit, from execution, or both. This variance across issuers, however, coexists with intra-issuer contracting stasis. The issuers in my sample may choose nonstandard enforcement terms, but they rarely change their own established contracting practices.
Part III explores the implications of these findings. Contrary to the stickiness explanation, actual contracting practices suggest that market participants generally prefer litigation to arbitration in this context. Most issuers provide for litigation but include broad sovereign immunity waivers in their bond contracts. This practice captures some of the advantages claimed for arbitration, without incurring the potential costs and uncertainty associated with a relatively untested, and unsubsidized, disputing forum. Moreover, when there are unique reasons to prefer arbitration - as when the issuer's courts are unlikely to enforce foreign court judgments - many (though not all) issuers provide for it. And although issuers rarely change their existing dispute resolution terms, they presently have little reason to do so.
Part III closes by briefly situating these findings within the broader body of research into sovereign debt and, more generally, contract innovation and change. At a basic level, the findings serve as a reminder that actual contracting practices are often more diverse than expected. This is especially true across the different issuers in the sample, suggesting that robust models of sovereign debt contracting practices must take into account a more heterogeneous set of terms than has previously been thought to exist. The findings also implicate a larger debate over when and where contract change is likely to occur. Much contractsscholarship focuses on innovation by larger and "high-status" players - those whose economic strength and reputational capital make them ideal "first movers." But the variance in enforcement-related terms tells a different story. In particular, the use of arbitration by relatively minor players in the sovereign debt world calls for greater attention to the forces that drive innovation among less-established and lower-status players.

questions.question: Do sovereign bond contracts typically include standardized dispute-resolution (forum selection) terms that favor litigation over arbitration?
questions.answer: The paper finds that, while the presumed standard favors litigation and most issuers do provide for litigation, dispute-resolution terms are not fully standardized, with over 20% of issuers departing from the standard and nearly 10% using arbitration clauses.

questions.question: Is the widespread use of litigation clauses in sovereign bond contracts explained by the stickiness of boilerplate terms, or by a genuine preference among market participants for litigation?
questions.answer: The prevalence of litigation clauses reflects a genuine market preference for litigation rather than the stickiness of boilerplate terms.

questions.question: How much do enforcement-related terms (forum selection, sovereign immunity waivers, arbitration provisions) vary across issuers, and do issuers change their own dispute-resolution practices over time?
questions.answer: Enforcement-related terms vary to a surprising degree across issuers—over 20% depart from the standard (nearly 10% include arbitration) and issuers differ in the breadth of sovereign immunity waivers—yet within issuers there is contracting stasis, as they rarely change their established dispute-resolution practices.

shared_topics.topic: standardization (boilerplate) versus customized contract drafting
shared_topics.justification: Both papers interrogate the degree to which commercial contracts rely on boilerplate versus bespoke drafting: Paper A contrasts highly modular/standard templates with the mass-customized, hybrid merger agreement, while Paper B empirically evaluates the presumed standardization of sovereign bond enforcement clauses and documents meaningful departures from boilerplate.

shared_topics.topic: empirical analysis of real contract text and variation across deals/issuers
shared_topics.justification: Both articles rely on hand-collected, systematic samples of real contracts to map heterogeneity: Paper A applies network and systems methods to merger agreements to reveal interdependencies, while Paper B surveys sovereign bond indentures across many issuers to show cross-issuer and intra-issuer patterns in enforcement terms.

shared_topics.topic: the role of organizational and market structures (firms, networks, status) in driving contract innovation
shared_topics.justification: Both studies consider how the organization of designers and market position shape contract change—Paper A analyzes law-firm deal teams, network effects, and flexible specialization in producing customized agreements, while Paper B highlights heterogeneity across issuers and innovation emerging from lower-status or niche market players.

papers.node_id: 62harvintllj175!!ARTICLE: Distrust, Disorder, and the New Governance of Sovereign Debt
papers.title: ARTICLE: Distrust, Disorder, and the New Governance of Sovereign Debt
papers.abstract:
The specter of disorder fundamentally defines the international legal system. According to traditional views of international law, sovereign states enter into international agreements and create international institutions to govern their interactions with each other.By doing so, they create conditions for mutually beneficial cooperation by deterring violations of their agreements.The need to formalize and institutionalize cooperation amongautonomous, self-interested state actors drives international regulation in a range of functional areas, including trade, the environment, human rights, and so on.However, the global legal environment is not only confined to bargains between states. International law regulates the conduct of individuals and other nonstate actors in increasingly significant ways.Multinational corporations and other private enterprises exert a particularly strong influence on transnational legal rules and norms, even themselves creating international law.
Within the broad panorama of international law today, the esoteric but enormously important world of sovereign debt finance stands alone in key respects. There is no multilateral institution or treaty system to monitor or enforce commitments between sovereign debtors and their external creditors.Instead, ad hoc, market-based arrangements are the norm. Today, the global sovereign debt market primarily consists of bonds sold in the global capital markets, which are typically re-financed through negotiations between sovereign debtors and their creditors.Reputational sanctions generally hold sovereigns to account with respect to their existing debts,and various contractual innovations introduced in the past couple decades enable sovereigns to restructure their debt in a relatively efficient manner.
However, ineffective coordination and enforcement mechanisms have enabled rogue behavior by opportunistic holdout creditors.Recalcitrant sovereigns have refused to negotiate with creditors, instead making take-it-or-leave-it offers.Judicial unpredictability resulting from novel interpretations of thepari passuclause in bond contractsand invocations of investor-state dispute settlement against sovereigns has further clouded legal enforcement.This lack of predictability has arguably made sovereign debt disputesboth likelier to occur and more costly to resolve.Protracted debtor-creditor standoffs and costly debt crises--such as Argentina and Greece in the past couple decades alone--have spurred calls for new approaches to regulating sovereign debt finance.
This Article argues that international law offers useful lessons for addressing the unique challenges of sovereign debt. The past several decades have seen the emergence of new forms of international financial regulation based on cross-border coordination between government regulators and extensive use of soft law.Pockets of the global financial system have gone a step further by applying a New Governance model of regulation.New Governance incorporates a decentralized range of public and private actors and softer forms of governmental regulation to facilitate or incentivize certain behavior rather than directly mandating it.Sovereign debt has recently embraced New Governance through new initiatives that depart from reform measures based on institutionalized public regulation (i.e., a statutory quasi-insolvency regime, such as the International Monetary Fund's ("IMF") proposed Sovereign Debt Restructuring Mechanism ("SDRM")) and contract-based private law enforcement.These New Governance-inspired approaches constitute a "third way" to sovereign debt restructuring, which this Article collectively refers to as "sovereign debt governance."
But is sovereign debt governance actually effective as a means to address collective action problems in sovereign debt? More precisely, will these New Governance-inspired frameworks enhance the predictability of the restructuring process ex ante and reduce the costs of a restructuring ex post? To address this question, this Article focuses on creditor committees, a key element of sovereign debt governance. Creditor committees consist of a representative group of creditors who are designated to negotiate the terms of adebt restructuring with the sovereign debtor.Committees establish procedures through which key creditors can communicate and coordinate with each other and collectively agree to a restructuring plan.Certain creditor committees, such as the London Club, figured prominently in efforts to facilitate engagement in sovereign debt restructurings when creditors were almost exclusively commercial banks and debt instruments were primarily syndicated bank loans.Since the late 1990s, however, the use of creditor committees in sovereign debt restructurings has waned, reflecting the greater autonomy and fragmentation of the global sovereign debt market.
This Article analyzes creditor committees in the context of sovereign debt governance from three interrelated perspectives: institutional, empirical, and prescriptive. First, we describe New Governance-inspired frameworks advanced in recent years by the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development ("UNCTAD"),the IMF,and the Institute of International Finance ("IIF"), a leading global industry association.Building on our prior research,we show how these frameworks conceptualize debtor-creditor engagement in different ways as a means to incentivize, compel, or constrain the behavior of sovereign debtors and their external private creditors.
Second, this Article empirically examines sovereign debt restructurings based on hand-collected data and secondary sources specifically gathered and organized for this Article.We examine the formation and operation of creditor committees in eighteen sovereign debt restructurings since 1999.Our analysis focuses on the nature and outcomes of the exchanges: the trajectory of creditor behaviors over time, creditor structures and representation, and the procedural dimensions of negotiation and engagement between debtors and creditors. We consider independent variables--such as creditor structure and debtor-creditor engagement--alongside critical restructuringoutcomes, including creditor participation in the exchange and the occurrence of litigation.
Third, drawing on our institutional and empirical analysis, this Article identifies the conditions under which debtor-creditor engagement may be facilitated. In doing so, we scrutinize the objectives and effectiveness of New Governance within the unique legal, political, and economic environments of sovereign debt.
This Article proceeds as follows. Part I describes sovereign debt's unique collective action problems in the context of the New Governance-based approaches that have recently emerged to address them. Part II examines the role of creditor committees in debt restructurings, contrasting their use in sovereign and non-sovereign contexts. Part III presents an empirical analysis of creditor committees to show how they have addressed coordination problems in the current era of sovereign debt restructurings. Drawing on the foregoing analysis, Part IV critically assesses New Governance-based strategies in sovereign debt.
I. Persistent Disorder and the Emergence of Sovereign Debt Governance
The emergence of sovereign debt governance reflects the convergence of two phenomena over the past decade. First, there has been growing concern about the negative consequences of costly, protracted sovereign debt crises arising from structural deficiencies in the restructuring process. Second, there has been growing interest in applying New Governance-based approaches to regulation to the global sovereign debt market.

questions.question: Whether creditor committees, as a New Governance mechanism, increase the predictability of sovereign debt restructurings ex ante and reduce the economic and legal costs of restructuring ex post (e.g., higher creditor participation, less litigation, faster or less costly resolutions).

What creditor- and institutional-level conditions (for example, creditor structure and representation, procedural rules, and the nature of debtor-creditor engagement) make debtor-creditor coordination mechanisms effective at resolving collective action problems in sovereign debt restructurings.

Whether New Governance-style, decentralized public-private regulatory frameworks provide a viable and more effective alternative to purely statutory or purely contract-based approaches for managing and resolving sovereign debt crises.

What institutional or normative responses should manage or limit cross-contract externalities created when a single interpretive decision changes the meaning of boilerplate across many contracts?

shared_topics.topic: how private contracts and market-based arrangements allocate and reallocate risk in the face of systemic shocks
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies how M&A contract terms (MAE carveouts, ordinary-course covenants) allocated pandemic risk between buyers and sellers and how those allocations broke down under COVID-19; Paper B analyzes how sovereign-debt relationships rely on market-based structures and contractual/market mechanisms to allocate risk during financial crises and how those mechanisms perform under stress.

shared_topics.topic: the limits of formal enforcement and the role of courts, reputational sanctions, or regulators in resolving disputes arising from extraordinary events
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines Delaware courts' role in interpreting MAE and ordinary-course clauses and how judicial interpretation can reallocate risk after a shock; Paper B documents judicial unpredictability, the absence of a multilateral enforcement mechanism for sovereign debt, and the role of reputational and regulatory responses in disciplining sovereign behavior.

shared_topics.topic: coordination problems, opportunism, and holdout behavior among dispersed private stakeholders
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on moral hazard and opportunistic interim actions by sellers (and the buyer's protections) between signing and closing; Paper B studies holdout creditors, fragmentation of creditor bodies, and the use (or breakdown) of creditor committees to overcome collective-action problems in restructurings.

shared_topics.topic: the emergence and evaluation of negotiated, soft-law or hybrid governance mechanisms as alternatives to formal statutory regimes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A recommends contractual drafting strategies and negotiated approvals (and discusses how courts should read plain terms) as private-ordering solutions to allocation problems, while Paper B evaluates New Governance initiatives (soft law, creditor committees, IMF/IIF/UNCTAD frameworks) as a 'third way' between statutory insolvency rules and pure contract enforcement.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 39harvintllj1!!ARTICLE: ACTS OF STATE AND FOREIGN SOVEREIGN OBLIGATIONS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: ACTS OF STATE AND FOREIGN SOVEREIGN OBLIGATIONS

shared_topics.topic: predictability and enforceability of sovereign obligations in court
shared_topics.justification: Both papers examine how uncertainty in judicial enforcement undermines reliance on sovereign commitments—Paper A shows judicial unpredictability (e.g., novel pari passu readings and ISDS) increases the costs and frequency of sovereign debt disputes, while Paper B analyzes how the act of state doctrine makes enforcement of sovereign contracts in U.S. courts unpredictable and thus weakens the contracts' value to investors.

shared_topics.topic: limits of contract-based mechanisms to manage sovereign risk
shared_topics.justification: Both articles critically assess contractual solutions for governing relations with sovereigns—Paper A questions whether contract-based restructurings and market-based creditor coordination can solve collective action problems in sovereign debt, and Paper B evaluates whether sovereign contracts actually reduce investment risk given judicial doctrines that may render them unenforceable.

shared_topics.topic: the impact of domestic judicial doctrines on international economic relations
shared_topics.justification: Both works focus on how domestic legal doctrines and court behavior shape cross-border economic outcomes—Paper A emphasizes how domestic court rulings and investor–state arbitration affect sovereign debt restructuring dynamics, and Paper B centers on the U.S. act of state doctrine's role in determining whether courts will adjudicate breaches by foreign sovereigns.

shared_topics.topic: litigation and legal risk as strategic factors in sovereign–creditor/investor interactions
shared_topics.justification: Both papers treat litigation risk as a strategic variable influencing behavior: Paper A analyzes how the threat or occurrence of creditor litigation and holdout strategies alters restructuring negotiations, and Paper B studies how the prospect that courts may refuse to decide (or may decide unpredictably) influences investors' willingness to rely on sovereign commitments.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 88washlrev1323!!SYMPOSIUM: CONTRACTS IN THE REAL WORLD: ESSAY: CONTRACT AS PATTERN LANGUAGE
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: CONTRACTS IN THE REAL WORLD: ESSAY: CONTRACT AS PATTERN LANGUAGE

shared_topics.topic: how contractual design and standardization enable liquid markets while creating systemic risk
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how modular, standardized contract 'patterns' make debt informationally insensitive and tradeable (e.g., asset‑backed securities) but also enable market freezes and shadow‑bank runs; Paper B examines how the structure of sovereign bond markets and market‑based refinancing contribute to protracted crises and systemic disorder in the absence of formal institutions.

shared_topics.topic: collective action and coordination problems among dispersed creditors and counterparties
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that interlocking contract patterns and modularization produce cascading interdependencies and coordination failures across transactions and markets; Paper B empirically studies creditor coordination problems in sovereign restructurings and the use (and limits) of creditor committees to solve collective‑action issues.

shared_topics.topic: the role of private, market‑based governance and 'soft' institutional arrangements versus formal public regulation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses how lawyers, standardized contract clauses, and market practices (private ordering) organize transactions and create markets, for better and worse; Paper B analyzes the emergence of New Governance approaches—creditor committees, soft law, industry frameworks—as a market‑based third way distinct from statutory multilateral mechanisms like an SDRM.

shared_topics.topic: predictability, enforcement, and legal design of contracts as determinants of market outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes how contract language, boilerplate modularity, and automated/routinized drafting affect interpretation, adaptability, and the likelihood of catastrophic failure; Paper B highlights judicial unpredictability (e.g., pari passu interpretations), litigation risks, and whether governance reforms can increase ex ante predictability and reduce restructuring costs.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 82lawcontempprob163!!ARTICLE: CRISIS CONSTRUCTION IN CONTRACT BOILERPLATE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CRISIS CONSTRUCTION IN CONTRACT BOILERPLATE

shared_topics.topic: crisis-driven reinterpretation of legal rules to stabilize financial markets
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents how courts departed from plain-text contract language (permitting sampling instead of loan-by-loan repurchases) in the aftermath of the mortgage crisis to bolster investor confidence and market functioning; Paper B investigates how ad hoc, nonstatutory governance (and novel legal interpretations) has been used to manage sovereign debt crises and reduce disorder in international capital markets.

shared_topics.topic: adequacy and enforcement of standardized contract clauses during systemic crises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the failure of the typical MBS 'sole remedy' repurchase clause to meaningfully resolve mass breaches in a crisis and how courts effectively rewrote enforcement outcomes; Paper B examines how bond contract terms (e.g., pari passu and other boilerplate) and weak enforcement mechanisms contribute to dysfunctional sovereign debt restructurings.

shared_topics.topic: collective-action and coordination problems among dispersed creditors/investors and legal or procedural responses
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows trustees and investors confronting mass loan defects and adopting sampling/damage-aggregation (via judicial allowance) as a way to achieve collective redress, while Paper B empirically studies creditor committees and other governance tools designed to coordinate creditor behavior and overcome holdout problems in sovereign restructurings.

shared_topics.topic: reliance on non-legislative, decentralized, or soft-law mechanisms (judicial discretion, private ordering, New Governance) and the effects on ex ante contracting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights how implicit judicial 'crisis construction' and the resulting precedent influenced parties' decisions to retain boilerplate repurchase provisions, and Paper B analyzes New Governance, soft-law initiatives, and private creditor coordination as alternatives to formal statutory regimes and their impact on contracting and market expectations.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Recalibrating Contract Law: Choses in Action, Global Value Chains, and the Enforcement of Obligations Outside of Privity

shared_topics.justification: Paper A diagnoses how privity and fragmented contracting create coordination failures across global value chains and proposes assignment of choses in action to enable cross-chain enforcement; Paper B analyzes how dispersed sovereign creditors produce holdouts and standoffs and studies creditor committees as devices to coordinate bargaining and reduce collective-action problems.

shared_topics.topic: the inadequacy of traditional legal doctrines or institutions for cross-border enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows the privity doctrine (and traditional contract rules) can block enforcement of obligations along multi-tiered supply chains, while Paper B highlights the absence of a multilateral enforcement or insolvency regime for sovereigns and how unpredictable judicial interpretations undermine debt enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: reliance on private ordering and New Governance (soft-law, hybrid public–private mechanisms) to fill regulatory gaps
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents firms' use of monitoring, certification, indemnities and contractual drafting as ad hoc private-ordering responses and points to assignment as a legal tool to improve outcomes; Paper B situates creditor committees, industry initiatives, and soft-law frameworks within a New Governance approach for sovereign debt restructuring.

shared_topics.topic: contractual and property-law innovations to reallocate enforcement rights and manage holdouts/risk
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on the assignment of choses in action and contract drafting (indemnities, pass-through language) to shift enforcement rights down or across supply chains, and Paper B examines bond-contract innovations, procedural devices, and collective contractual arrangements used to reallocate bargaining power and limit holdout strategies in sovereign restructurings.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: VALUES AND VALUE CREATION IN PUBLIC-PRIVATE TRANSACTIONS

shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how deal lawyers act as intermediaries who translate public-policy goals into private transaction terms in public-private partnerships, while Paper B studies creditor committees and industry actors (e.g., the IIF) as private intermediaries that organize and negotiate with sovereigns to manage debt restructurings.

shared_topics.topic: structuring contracts and arrangements to manage transaction costs, information asymmetries, and collective-action problems
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes lawyers' role in engineering deals to minimize transaction costs and leverage regulatory constraints in public-private partnerships, while Paper B focuses on contractual innovations, creditor committee procedures, and negotiation mechanisms intended to overcome coordination failures and holdout problems in sovereign debt markets.

shared_topics.topic: designing private-ordering to balance economic outcomes with public-policy or collective welfare objectives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that value in public-private deals must incorporate non-economic public-policy goals that lawyers must encode into transactions, and Paper B assesses whether sovereign-debt governance mechanisms (creditor committees, soft-law initiatives) can reconcile creditor interests with the broader public goals of predictable, less costly restructurings and financial stability.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Recalibrating Contract Law: Choses in Action, Global Value Chains, and the Enforcement of Obligations Outside of Privity

shared_topics.topic: private governance mechanisms to manage cross-border enforcement gaps
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze how non-state or hybrid private governance arrangements (creditor committees, industry-led frameworks, monitoring/certification schemes, and contractual devices like assignments) are used to fill enforcement and coordination gaps where multilateral public institutions or statutes are weak or absent.

shared_topics.topic: coordination and collective‑action problems among dispersed transnational actors
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies how fragmented sovereign creditors face collective‑action and holdout problems in restructurings and how committees and CACs respond, while Paper B examines how privity and serial contracting in global value chains create coordination failures that assignment of choses in action can ameliorate.

shared_topics.topic: contractual innovations and legal workarounds as regulatory tools
shared_topics.justification: Both papers focus on the use and limits of private‑law innovations—Paper A on contractual clauses, pari passu litigation, and other restructuring devices under New Governance; Paper B on assignment of choses in action and contract drafting—as deliberate tools to shape rights, obligations, and enforcement across borders.

shared_topics.topic: the limits of traditional legal doctrines/institutions and the search for alternative frameworks
shared_topics.justification: Each article critiques existing legal infrastructures (the absence of a multilateral sovereign‑debt enforcement regime; the privity doctrine in contract law) and evaluates alternative approaches (New Governance and creditor coordination in sovereign debt; property/assignment mechanisms in value chains) to achieve more predictable and effective outcomes.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: TAX LAWYERS AS TAX INSURANCE

shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how tax opinions function as partial indemnities that shift tax risk from clients to transactional tax lawyers (and compares them to third‑party tax insurance), while Paper B examines contractual innovations and creditor committees as market‑based tools that reallocate sovereign credit risk among debtors and diverse creditor groups during restructurings.

shared_topics.topic: the effects of legal uncertainty and judicial/policy unpredictability on market behavior and governance design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes how sweeping tax law changes and uncertainty increase reliance on tax opinions and reshape the market for advice, and Paper B shows how judicial unpredictability and enforcement uncertainty in sovereign debt law drive costly disputes and motivate new governance arrangements.

shared_topics.topic: tradeoffs between private ordering/market solutions and formal public regulation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A raises questions about whether indemnification by lawyers or third‑party insurers should be regulated and contrasts private risk‑shifting with formal insurance regulation, while Paper B contrasts New Governance, industry‑led frameworks, and contract‑based solutions with proposals for institutionalized, public regimes like an IMF SDRM.

shared_topics.topic: the role of reputational sanctions and liability (litigation, malpractice) as enforcement and coordination mechanisms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates tax opinions among reputational intermediaries and malpractice/indemnity as possible enforcement backstops for client reliance, and Paper B discusses reputational sanctions on sovereigns, litigation risks (including holdouts and novel contract interpretations), and how these legal/liability incentives shape creditor and sovereign behavior.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Contract as Swag

shared_topics.topic: contractual innovation and the mechanisms of dissemination
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses contractual innovations in sovereign bond markets (e.g., collective action devices, novel bond clauses) and how those instruments are adopted or fail in restructurings, while Paper B explores why and how new contract forms are created and disseminated (treating some contracts as 'swag') and what drives their uptake across practice communities.

shared_topics.topic: reputational and branding incentives driving legal practice and adoption
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights reputational sanctions on sovereigns and the reputational interests of market actors and industry groups that influence restructuring behavior, and Paper B argues that reputation and branding motives lead lawyer-innovators and organizations to give away standardized contracts to gain market recognition and influence practice.

shared_topics.topic: governance via soft law, market mechanisms, and decentralized coordination rather than formal statutory regimes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames 'New Governance' in sovereign debt as soft-law, decentralized regulatory arrangements and market-based coordination (versus formal SDRM-style statutory restructuring), and Paper B emphasizes informal, nonstatutory diffusion of contractual norms through freely shared templates and community practices rather than top-down regulation.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: WHY NEW STATES ACCEPT OLD OBLIGATIONS

shared_topics.topic: mechanisms for coordination and collective decision-making to resolve creditor/claimant coordination problems
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies creditor committees and other institutionalized or market-based coordination devices to overcome holdout and collective action problems in restructurings; Paper B analyzes how international decision-making, negotiations, and pre-emptive distribution of obligations (e.g., in Kosovo and Iraq) serve as coordination mechanisms among creditors, states, and international actors.

shared_topics.topic: the role of private actors, soft law, and ‘new governance’ or policy-oriented frameworks versus formal public regulation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates New Governance approaches (industry associations, soft law, decentralized public–private coordination) as a ‘third way’ beyond treaties or statutory schemes; Paper B defends and refines a policy-oriented, non-formal legal approach in practice—showing how states, courts, international organizations and private interests produce negotiated outcomes outside hard-law rules.

shared_topics.topic: how judicial decisions and legal unpredictability interact with political and market processes in shaping outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights how litigation risks (e.g., pari passu interpretations, investor–state claims) and judicial unpredictability affect restructurings and creditor behavior; Paper B documents how courts and adjudicative bodies, alongside political choices, have influenced allocation of predecessor obligations after succession (e.g., U.S. court decisions and post‑Iraq/Kosovo processes).

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Law Firm Selection and the Value of Transactional Lawyering

shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how recurring private creditors and creditor committees—repeat players in sovereign debt markets—structure negotiations and influence restructuring outcomes, while Paper B argues that elite law firms, as repeat players in particular types of transactions, shape deal terms and secure better outcomes for clients through accumulated market experience.

shared_topics.topic: how private information and information asymmetries affect bargaining and negotiation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that fragmentation and unequal information among creditors (and judicial unpredictability) exacerbate holdouts and raise restructuring costs, whereas Paper B attributes elite firms' bargaining advantages to their pooled, proprietary knowledge of recent deal terms that mitigates informational gaps in negotiations.

shared_topics.topic: market-based/private governance mechanisms as alternatives or complements to formal regulation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates New Governance approaches (soft law, private-public coordination, creditor committees) as a ‘third way’ between statutory insolvency regimes and pure contract enforcement for sovereign debt, and Paper B documents how private institutions (law firms' knowledge-management practices) effectively govern transactional norms and pricing outside formal regulatory intervention.

shared_topics.topic: how actor structure (concentration versus fragmentation) conditions collective action and negotiation outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically investigates how creditor structure and representation (concentrated committees versus fragmented creditors) affect participation, coordination, and litigation in restructurings, while Paper B links concentration of transactional volume in elite firms to superior bargaining power and persistent market advantage.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: MARKET CONDITIONS AND CONTRACT DESIGN: VARIATIONS IN DEBT CONTRACTING

shared_topics.topic: the limits of private contracting and the interaction between contract design and broader governance institutions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes why standardized boilerplate and private contract design persist or change in response to market and legal incentives, while Paper B studies how sovereign debt relies on market-based, private contracting solutions (and New Governance arrangements) in the absence of a formal multilateral enforcement regime, asking when private mechanisms can effectively govern debt relationships.

shared_topics.topic: coordination, incentive alignment, and collective-action problems among creditors and between creditors and debtors
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on how covenants and collateral are tailored to mitigate adverse selection and moral hazard between a single borrower and lender, whereas Paper B treats collective-action problems among multiple creditors (holdouts, participation) and evaluates mechanisms like creditor committees to coordinate creditor behavior and align incentives in restructurings.

shared_topics.topic: the effect of legal uncertainty and judicial interpretation on contract design and debt outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that judicial interpretation and enforcement of standard terms (boilerplate) create rigidity and affect parties' willingness to customize covenants, while Paper B highlights judicial unpredictability (e.g., pari passu rulings, investor-state claims) as a factor that complicates sovereign debt restructuring and shapes contractual and governance responses.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: WHY NEW STATES ACCEPT OLD OBLIGATIONS

shared_topics.justification: Paper A advocates and evaluates New Governance and soft-law frameworks (UNCTAD, IMF, IIF) as a 'third way' between formal statutory regimes and pure contract enforcement for sovereign debt, while Paper B develops and tests a policy-oriented approach to succession that favors pragmatic, normative guidance and negotiated solutions over the pursuit of authoritative multilateral legal rules.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACTS AS TECHNOLOGY

shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how contractual terms and creditor-committee arrangements function as New Governance tools to coordinate dispersed creditors and resolve sovereign debt restructurings, while Paper B models contractual innovations as a form of technology that can lower production/transaction costs and enable coordination among parties, emphasizing when and why such innovations arise and spread.

shared_topics.topic: the role of private, decentralized institutions and soft-law in governing economic interactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines market-based, New Governance approaches (creditor committees, IIF, UNCTAD proposals) as alternatives to formal multilateral regimes for sovereign debt, and Paper B studies how non-state actors—law firms, trade associations, users, and legal databases—generate and disseminate contract forms and norms that effectively govern private relationships.

shared_topics.topic: mechanisms for dissemination, standardization, and adoption of contractual practices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically investigates how creditor committees and industry practices shape negotiation procedures and participation norms across restructurings, while Paper B focuses explicitly on how contractual innovations become widely used—via trade associations, clearinghouses, databases, or other dissemination mechanisms—and the barriers to adoption.

shared_topics.topic: how legal and regulatory environments affect the creation, predictability, and effectiveness of contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents how judicial unpredictability (e.g., novel pari passu interpretations and investor-state claims) and the absence of formal enforcement institutions shape contract design and restructuring outcomes, and Paper B considers how rules (intellectual property, unauthorized-practice-of-law restrictions, and regulation of legal service providers) influence incentives to innovate and share contractual templates.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: SYMPOSIUM: SOVEREIGN DEBT RESTRUCTURING: The Role of Groups in Norm Transformation: A Dramatic Sketch, in Three Parts

shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues for a narrowly tailored exception or institutional rule to render sovereign contracts reliably enforceable, while Paper B evaluates 'New Governance' approaches (soft law, creditor committees, IMF/UNCTAD proposals) as institutional responses to coordination failures in sovereign debt restructuring.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Abuses of the Act of State Doctrine
