papers.node_id: 83chikentlrev147!!ARTICLE: DOMESTIC BONDS, CREDIT DERIVATIVES, AND THE NEXT TRANSFORMATION OF SOVEREIGN DEBT
papers.title: ARTICLE: DOMESTIC BONDS, CREDIT DERIVATIVES, AND THE NEXT TRANSFORMATION OF SOVEREIGN DEBT
papers.abstract:
Not long ago, rich countries borrowed freely in their own currencies and under their own law. Most had deep and liquid financial markets where both local and foreign residents invested their savings. Unlike poor and middle-income countries, the rich rarely worried about losing access to credit. Conventional wisdom attributed this to some combination of creditworthiness and institutional quality: stable currencies; sound fiscal and monetary policies; trustworthy legal systems; and deep, open, and well-regulated financial markets that encouraged innovation.
The emerging markets - poor and middle-income countries raising money internationally- occupied an exotic corner of the financial universe.Barely two dozen had sustained access to foreign private capital.Those that could borrow abroad had to do so in foreign currency and under foreign law.Domestic credit markets were nonexistent or small, shallow, and closed to foreigners.Emerging economies suffered from frequent shocks and volatile asset prices, which rarely correlated with prices in New York or London. Conventional wisdom attributed this to some combination of low creditworthiness and poor institutional quality.Politics stood perennially in the way of emergence: the legacy of foreign financial exploitation cast a long shadow;domestic pressures drove dubious borrowing and default.
Writing about emerging market debt meant writing about the Big Change: the shift in governments' foreign borrowing from bank loans in the 1970s to tradable bonds in the 1990s.Lawyers and economists expectedthe shift to bring about collective action problems when countries hit financial distress. A cash-strapped sovereign with bonded debt might fail to persuade enough creditors to give it debt relief, leading to protracted economic decline. Such problems called for contractual or statutory analogues to domestic bankruptcy.
Both the loans and the bonds at the center of this literature were denominated in foreign currency, governed by foreign (usually New York or English) law, and presumptively held by foreign residents. But the incident that jump-started the policy response to collective action problems, Mexico's "Tequila" crisis in 1994-95, centered on tesobonos - Mexican-law treasury instruments denominated in pesos and indexed to the U.S. dollar.Some tesobonos were held by foreigners, but most were not. The fact that tesobonos were domestic bonds was completely overshadowed by the fact that they were bonds, and bonds were bad news.
Domestic debt in poor and middle-income countries grew over the next decade; all the while the world debated how to amend New York-andEnglish-law bonds held by foreigners. According to the Bank for International Settlements (BIS), the outstanding stock of domestic bonds in these countries went from one trillion dollars in 1995 to over four trillion dollars in 2006, with public sector borrowing close to three-quarters of the new total.In Mexico, domestic government debt went from just over twenty percent of total debt stock in 1995 to nearly eighty percent in 2007.This rise in domestic debt went hand in hand with innovations in risk management. In the emerging markets, credit derivatives - contracts to transfer credit risk among market participants - grew from zero in the mid-1990s to roughly three hundred billion dollars in 2005, surpassing the market capitalization of the leading bond index at the time, and projected to double annually.
A shift from foreign to domestic borrowing and the rise of new risk transfer tools on such a vast scale portend fundamental change for many countries - reducing vulnerability to currency crises, multiplying debt management options for governments, developing domestic financial markets, and expanding access to credit.For those who see direct links between investor interest and institutional quality, the shift could signal new trust in emerging market institutions, from legal infrastructure to exchange rate regimes. The shift makes the emerging economies look more like "mature" rich ones, with their deep domestic markets and rapid financial innovation.
Yet since there is no single agreed upon definition of "domestic debt," the scope and significance of the shift are unclear.Change is measured byproxy as growth in local-currency,locally-held,locally-issued,or local-lawdebt. To be sure, all of the above grew, but not necessarily in tandem. And the tools designed to manage credit risk in the mainstream markets often cannot do the same in the emerging ones. Assessing change thus requires unpacking its different dimensions to reveal the legal and currency regimes, actors, instruments, and risk-shifting strategies that make up the new financial landscape in the emerging markets.
This symposium contribution examines four such dimensions - governing law, currency of denomination, identity of the creditors, and credit risk transfer - focusing on the implications for emerging market sovereign debt. Government debt is a sensible starting point for studying change because it still dwarfs private debt in poor and middle-income countries. Although domestic corporate issuance is substantial in some parts of the emerging world and rising fast in many more, to the extent there is a story of large-scale transformation, it is most apparent with sovereigns.
Parsing recent sovereign borrowing in this way reveals a partial convergence between emerging and mainstream markets. The two may share investors and use similar financial instruments, but this formal resemblance does not necessarily stand for substantive identity. Instead, investors use similar instruments differently in different markets, which, as some of the examples in the text suggest, can be a new source of risk. The image of "emergence" as a linear march to an ideal of market "maturity" ("development" rebranded) can obscure more than it reveals.
Law scholars played a central role in addressing the shift from bank loans to tradable bonds in the 1990s, but have yet to engage with the rise of domestic debt and credit derivatives in the emerging markets. The goal of this essay is not to offer the definitive analytical framework or policy prescription, but to map the ongoing transformation in a way that highlights gaps between formal and substantive convergence and indicates potential directions for future research.
The next section elaborates on the context for the transformation. Section II then examines four dimensions of change. Starting with governing law, it suggests that, contrary to popular perceptions, the rise of local-law debt may increase uncertainty about crisis resolution. Second, it notes that risk-sharing features often presumed to inhere in local-currency debt are easy to vary by contract, and that such variations were at the center of several recent crises. Third, it argues that the new diversity, mixing, and churning of creditors to emerging market governments may narrow the space for preemptive debt restructuring and may shrink the authorities' options in crisis. Credit risk transfer can exacerbate this effect. In addition, credit derivatives on emerging market sovereign debt have featured disproportionately in recent lawsuits and have helped shape the law governing the broader, multi-trillion dollar derivatives market. This essay concludes with implications for governance, risk management, and research.

questions.question: Does the shift toward domestic-law, local-currency sovereign borrowing and a larger domestic creditor base change the predictability, available mechanisms, and outcomes of sovereign debt restructuring and crisis resolution?
questions.answer: Yes—contrary to popular perceptions, the rise of local-law sovereign debt increases uncertainty about crisis resolution, and the growing diversity, mixing, and churning of creditors narrows the space for preemptive restructurings and shrinks authorities’ options in distress.

questions.question: How do contractual choices about currency denomination and risk-sharing in sovereign debt contracts affect governments' exposure to crises and the likelihood or severity of sovereign default or financial instability?
questions.answer: Contractual choices are pivotal: although shifting to local-currency debt can reduce vulnerability to currency crises, the risk-sharing features often presumed in such debt are easily varied by contract, and these variations were central to several recent crises.

questions.question: How does the growth of credit derivatives and other credit-risk transfer instruments linked to emerging-market sovereign debt affect debt governance, creditor coordination, and litigation or enforcement risks during sovereign distress?
questions.answer: Credit risk transfer and credit derivatives can exacerbate the narrowing of space for preemptive restructuring and reduce authorities’ crisis options, and they have appeared disproportionately in litigation over emerging-market sovereigns, helping shape broader derivatives law.

matched_themes: How did the secondary market for emerging-market and less-developed countries' sovereign debt evolve, and what were its effects on banks, restructurings, and financial globalization?
How have inter-creditor practices, documentation, and management evolved in sovereign debt restructurings in the absence of a formal statutory insolvency framework?

How do credit derivatives and other credit-risk transfer instruments linked to emerging-market sovereign debt affect debt governance, creditor coordination, and litigation or enforcement risks during sovereign distress?
What legal incentives, imperatives, and constraints shape creditor-debtor bargaining and creditor coordination in sovereign or quasi-sovereign restructurings, and how do these affect outcomes?
Does globalization and liberalization of capital markets increase the frequency and severity of sovereign debt crises?

What legal and contractual techniques most effectively enable large-scale sovereign debt restructurings and how do they affect creditor rights, burden-sharing, and orderly negotiation among many creditors?

How do choices about currency denomination and related risk-sharing clauses in sovereign debt contracts affect a government's exposure to crises and the likelihood or severity of sovereign default or financial instability?

Does the standardization and modularization of contract patterns that facilitate tradability and liquidity also increase the likelihood of valuation breakdowns and systemic market failures under stress?
How do contractual language, legal enforcement, and non-legal forces (reputation, ongoing relationships) interact to determine parties' actual obligations and behavior under complex contracts?

How should legal and institutional rules balance preserving state discretion over foreign economic policy and regulation with ensuring enforceability of cross-border financial claims and maintaining lender confidence?
How should the law balance an issuer's need to restructure sovereign debt efficiently against individual bondholders' protection from coercion or unfair impairment?

Can standardized contractual terms in sovereign debt (e.g., currency-of-payment and governing-law clauses) create a common-mode failure that amplifies isolated sovereign distress into systemic financial crises?
How do anonymity and tradability of bond investors shape their incentives in distress, and which contractual or institutional arrangements can mitigate opportunistic behavior?

Does transplanting legal rules and precedents from other jurisdictions into Latin American legal systems produce intended investor protection and economic benefits, or do such norms mutate and yield unintended consequences?

What explains why particular sovereign bond contract terms sometimes change abruptly after legal codifications or perceived legal-environment shifts, even when creditors' substantive enforcement rights remain largely unchanged?
Do sovereign creditors need enforceable duties to one another or external adjudicatory backstops to prevent opportunistic holdouts and side deals during restructurings?
Can creditors in multi-creditor instruments overcome holdout and grab-and-run incentives to achieve coordinated, ratable restructurings without a statutory insolvency backstop?
What are the consequences of sovereign default for restructuring outcomes and for incentives and behavior of international creditors and debtor governments?
How do secondary markets for sovereign debt (emergent purchasers and trading) affect debt restructurings, market liquidity, and form-contract standardization?
To what extent are complex agreements organized as modular subsystems (enabling mass customization) versus thickly interconnected integrated systems, and how does that shape transaction design?

How does the growing share of domestic-law, local-currency sovereign borrowing and a larger domestic creditor base change the predictability, legal mechanisms, and outcomes of sovereign-debt crises and restructurings?
How do secondary markets for sovereign and emerging-market debt affect distribution of costs and benefits between creditors and debtor countries, and did integration increase in the 1990s?

Does the existence of an active secondary market for sovereign debt increase the likelihood of financial globalization and what are the broader macroeconomic consequences (including on crisis incidence) of increased cross-border debt trading?
Should rights and enforcement powers of corporate bond investors be held individually or exercised collectively under representative or majority rules?

How do private standard-setting organizations, form contracts, and transnational documentation practices interact with national legal systems to determine the enforceability, reach, and governance effects of private global legal regimes?
Does maintaining fixed exchange rates while financing fiscal deficits with foreign-currency debt increase sovereign default probability and amplification of post-devaluation debt burdens?
How do social and market forces fail to correct suboptimal allocations of individual versus collective bondholder rights, and what reforms would improve enforcement and market outcomes?
What governance effects do standardized private legal documents and routine documentation work produce-do they replicate, supplement, or supplant state legal authority?
Are proactive resolution approaches (preemptive restructuring frameworks) more effective than reactive strategies at reducing economic harms when governments face rising debt burdens?
How did the growth of secondary markets affect the distribution of costs and benefits between creditors and debtor countries during sovereign debt crises?

Should major legal transplants (e.g., U.S. contract documentation) be expected to produce the same investor-protection effects in other jurisdictions, or do they mutate and yield unintended consequences?

Do standardized contractual features (e.g., CACs, litigation clauses, forum-selection terms) and the anonymity/tradability of bond investors influence market pricing, holdout behavior, and enforcement outcomes in sovereign debt markets?
How do secondary markets for sovereign debt (liquidity, tradability, active buying/selling) affect the feasibility and mechanics of sovereign restructurings?
How do multi-party financial contract disputes and the presence of secondary purchasers affect the process and outcomes of contract standardization and enforcement?
How large and practically significant are downstream effects of standard contract changes-that is, how many contracts and parties are affected and with what consequences?

papers.node_id: 22fordhamintllj1!!ARTICLE: ECONOMIC AND MONETARY UNION IN EUROPE: LEGAL IMPLICATIONS OF THE ARRIVAL OF THE SINGLE CURRENCY
papers.title: ARTICLE: ECONOMIC AND MONETARY UNION IN EUROPE: LEGAL IMPLICATIONS OF THE ARRIVAL OF THE SINGLE CURRENCY
papers.abstract:
On January 1, 1999, Economic and Monetary Union ("EMU") will be achieved among eleven Member States of the European Union (or "EU"). On that day, Europe's single currency, the "euro,"will be introduced. Three years later, after a transitional period designed to permit Europe, and the rest of the world, to accommodate the use of a single currency, the euro will be the sole legal tender in the Member States that participate in EMU. The move to a single currency is a remarkable achievement. It is the result of a series of efforts to coordinate the Member States' economic policies and to pool monetary sovereignty at the European level.
Following the suggestions made in a 1989 report of a specialcommittee chaired by then President Jacques Delors of the Commission of the European Communities ("Commission"),the European Councildecided in June 1989 to introduce EMU in three stages.Stage I of EMU began on July 1, 1990 with the removal of all restrictions on the movement of capital between Member States.For the realization of Stages II and III, the Treaty establishing the European Community("EC Treaty") had to be revised to establish the required institutional structure. It is the amendments to the EC Treaty introduced by the Maastricht Treatythat laid the groundwork for the most important stages - Stages II and III - with the move to a single monetary policy and single currency.As of January 1, 1994, the start of Stage II, Member States undertook to reduce excessive government deficits under close review at the European level.Further, Member States established the European Monetary Institute ("EMI"), the forerunner of the current European Central Bank ("ECB"). As of January 1, 1999, Stage III of EMU will commence with the irrevocable locking of the exchange rates of the currencies of the eleven participating Member States that have met certain convergence requirements laid out in the Maastricht Treaty and have elected to participate in EMU (the "Participating Member States") and with the conduct of the single monetary policy under the responsibility of the ECB.
During a three-year transitional period beginning at the start of Stage III, the euro will exist only in paperless form, pending the production of euro banknotes and coins and their release by January 1, 2002. From the start of Stage III, the Participating Member States' currencies will cease to be independent currencies but will remain legal tender. The currencies will become denominations of the euro, and the conversion rate of each participating national currency will be irrevocably fixed to the euro. At the end of the three-year transitional period, the introduction of the euro will be completed by physical replacement of all participating national currency notes and coins by euro notes and coins. At that time, the participating national currencies will cease to be legal tender.
Financial markets and their participants are preparing the necessary systemic changes to permit a large part of public and private bonds, securities, derivatives, and other financial instruments to be issued, traded, and settled in a euro-denominated form from the start of Stage III. Although the retail sector will be compelled by consumer demand to list simultaneously prices in euros and national currencies during the transitional period, it is expected that large-scale use of the euro at the retail level will commence only by the end of the transitional period. How quickly the business sector will switch over to the new currency depends on the size and nature of the business; for multinational companies, the change is a welcome relief from dealing inmultiple currencies and will be implemented as quickly as possible.
There is currently no Stage IV of EMU under serious discussion, but a logical further step for Member States would entail a move towards a single economic policy, including, among others, a move towards more harmonized fiscal and social policies. Given the controversy surrounding the move to a single monetary policy and single currency, the long and painful discussions about apparent loss of sovereignty for Member States, and the sheer magnitude of the task of initially replacing eleven currencies by a single currency, serious discussions concerning a formal post-Stage III scenario are not expected in the near future. At the end of the day, however, EMU is essentially a political process, involving an increased pooling of sovereignty by Member States, initially at the monetary level, but undoubtedly, with spillovers at the fiscal, financial, and other socio-economic levels.
Part I of this Article presents an overview of EMU, addressing first the Member States that will participate in EMU from the outset and how they were chosen, as well as the new institutions that will guide and support EMU. This Article will then focus on the EU regulations that provide the legal framework for EMU, analyzing issues in the regulations of particular legal interest. This structural discussion will also describe what Participating Members States must achieve to ensure that EMU stays on track and how EU institutions will supervise their performance. Part I closes with a brief look at the international role of the euro. After discussing the structure of EMU, this Article will focus in Part II on what EMU will mean for companies operating in the brave new world of the "euro zone" and, in particular, on the legal issues raised by the introduction of the euro. This Article will look at the implications for the public obligations of companies, and, in particular, concerns about the continuity of contracts denominated in European Currency Unit ("ECU") or in one of the national currencies that will be replaced by the euro. It will then look at how the financial markets - debt, equity, and derivatives - are expected to change and what the change implies for companies seeking to raise financing in these markets. This Article will finally and briefly look at the new systems to be put in place under EMU to facilitate the increased flow of expected transactions.

questions.question: What are the legal and regulatory consequences of adopting a single currency for member states and supranational institutions, including changes to institutional responsibilities, supervision, and the pooling of monetary sovereignty?
questions.answer: Adopting the euro pools monetary sovereignty at the EU level through Maastricht Treaty amendments and EU regulations that created the EMI/ECB and the legal framework for EMU, places the single monetary policy under the ECB, irrevocably fixes exchange rates so national currencies become euro denominations and later cease to be legal tender, and subjects Member States’ performance (including deficit reduction) to EU-level supervision to keep EMU on track.

questions.question: How does the transition to a single currency affect contractual continuity and private-law obligations, particularly for contracts and instruments denominated in replaced national currencies or pre-existing currency units?

How will the introduction of a single currency transform financial markets and corporate financing, and what legal issues will arise for issuance, trading, settlement, and regulation of debt, equity, and derivatives?
questions.answer: From the start of Stage III, financial markets will implement systemic changes so that a large part of bonds, securities, derivatives and other instruments can be issued, traded and settled in euros, companies will adapt their financing to these euro-based markets, and new EMU systems will be introduced to support increased transaction flows.

papers.node_id: 64nyulrev733!!ARTICLE: EURODOLLARS, MULTINATIONAL BANKS, AND NATIONAL LAWS.
papers.title: ARTICLE: EURODOLLARS, MULTINATIONAL BANKS, AND NATIONAL LAWS.
papers.authors: Peter S. Smedresman; Andreas F. Lowenfeld
papers.abstract:
In the good old days -- if there were any -- people put their money in the bank in a given place, and expected to be able to withdraw it in the same place, generally in the currency that was legal tender at that place.  In New York and Chicago banks dealt in dollars, in London banks dealt in pounds sterling, in Paris they dealt in francs, and so on.  Correspondingly, banks lent money, some said created money, in the same currency as that in which they accepted deposits.  There were of course international loans, and governments from time to time interfered with these transactions, sometimes for political, sometimes for economic reasons.Devaluations, freezing of assets, expropriations, and debt moratoriums took place in the pause between the two great wars, and even then the law, designed for a simpler era, failed to keep up.  Three more recent phenomena, each part cause, part effect of the other two, have come together in a way not foreseen by national lawmakers and only dimly andinconsistently understood by courts and commentators.
First,a new medium of exchange and storehouse of value, the Eurodollar, has grown up.  The Eurodollar has some links to the currency issued by the United States Treasury: at any given time U.S. $ 1 = Eur. $ 1.  But the Eurodollar is in many ways independent of the regulatory regime that embraces the national dollar -- reserve requirements, interest ceilings, deposit insurance, and indeed macro-economic policies turning on the supply of national money and credit.Second,the major banks have all become multinational, even when, as in the United States, they have been restrained from expanding within their own country.Third,the revolution in computers and telecommunications has not only made the search for the situs of intangibles more unreal than ever,but in the drive for speed in a high-volume, low-margin market, documentation for deposits (particularly in the "wholesale" market) has all but vanished.  When things go wrong and lawyers and judges are called upon to distribute the losses, the results are bound to be unsatisfying, and explanations about expectations of the participants or intent of the parties are bound to fall flat.
As we shall see, the problem appears in many shapes.  Basically, however, the question turns on the risks and expectations of the two parties to a bank deposit made at a foreign branch of a multinational bank -- the deposit taker, nearly always a bank, and the depositor, which may also be a bank, or may be a corporation or an individual.  Both the home country of a bank (notably the United States) and the host country of the branch may impose restrictions on use or withdrawal of the funds deposited.  Can the depositor reasonably expect the law of the branch to apply if it favors him, and still look to the home office if the law there applicable favors him?  Conversely, can the bank limit its exposure, so that if it follows the law applicable where the deposit is made it will be protected against double liability, and so that it is excused from application of conflicting law of the home country with respect to deposits made at foreign branches? Can the parties determine and allocate the risks by contract and rely on the effectiveness of such contracts?  Looking at the problem from a third side, to what extent are governments limited in the controls they can effectively impose on transnational banking transactions?
We do not claim to have found the Rosetta stone or the unified field theory that can bring together all the claims of depositors against banks at their head office because something went awry at the place where the deposit was made, or claims against branches when something wentwrong at the place of the bank's headquarters.  We are not satisfied, however, with the only rule that emerges from the recent American and English judicial decisions, a surprising number of them, that plaintiffs -- i.e., the depositors -- nearly always win.  We want to see whether the experience of a bank lawyer interested in international law and an international lawyer interested in banking might together develop some suggestions, distinctions, guidelines, or presumptions concerning the relations between multinational banks and their depositors.  We do not here address problems of bank secrecy and disclosure on the one hand,or common efforts to regulate banking practice, including adequate capital bases, on the other.These problems are clearly related to the causes mentioned above, and in some sense also to the task we have set for ourselves.  But one challenge is enough, at least at one time.  We note that all of the cases we discuss were decided in the 1980s.
Section I of this Article provides some basic background on the law of banking, the Euromarket, and the multinational operations of modern banks.  In Section II, we examine recent consideration by European courts of the validity of economic sanctions imposed by the United States and designed to restrain Eurodollar deposits in foreign branches of United States-based banks.  In Section III, we focus on the reverse question: whether the home office of a multinational bank may be liable for a deposit made at a foreign branch notwithstanding economic controls imposed by the country where the foreign branch is located.  The principal cases in both of these sections concern interbank transactions.  Another series of cases, not as important from an overall economic perspective, but raising some of the same issues as the principal cases, involves the closing of branches and the movement of refugees from Cuba and Vietnam.  Weaddress these cases, as well as two cases involving Mexican monetary controls, in Section IV, before offering some tentative suggestions in Section V.

questions.question: When a deposit is made at a foreign branch of a multinational bank, which national law(s) should govern the rights and liabilities of the depositor and the bank when the host-country and home-country rules conflict?

Can banks and depositors allocate legal risks for cross-border deposits by contract (including choice-of-law or limitation-of-liability clauses), and will such contractual arrangements be reliably enforced across jurisdictions?
To what extent can national governments (home or host) effectively impose and enforce controls on cross-border banking transactions and deposits held at foreign branches?

matched_themes: When should domestic courts decline to adjudicate private-law claims that hinge on the validity of a foreign government's acts within its own territory?
What interim legal or policy mechanisms can reduce conflicts caused by extraterritorial enforcement, and are current measures sufficient?

Should international-transaction legal opinions routinely address the enforceability of foreign judgments or remedies in the lawyer's home courts, and how should governing-law conflict-of-laws issues be handled in such opinions?
When should domestic courts defer to a foreign state's determinations about acts within that state's territory, and what limits should govern such deference?

Can the United States lawfully assert extraterritorial jurisdiction to freeze, block, or otherwise control transfers of U.S. dollars or ownership interests in U.S.-dollar accounts held by non-U.S. persons outside the United States?
How should sovereignty be reconceptualized in an era of integrated global commerce and global value chains?
How do conflicting national policies (exchange controls, tax enforcement, capital-attraction measures) interact to affect international banking stability and cross-border lending?

How should counsel determine and state which law governs the valid execution and delivery of cross-border transaction documents, and how should legal opinions account for possible governmental actions affecting contract validity?

How does the legal characterization of 'bank money' (doctrinal, economic, and social aspects) affect which conflict-of-law rules should determine ownership and liability in international banking disputes?

How should legal and institutional rules balance preserving state discretion over foreign economic policy and regulation with ensuring enforceability of cross-border financial claims and maintaining lender confidence?
How should courts allocate competing regulatory authority when both the forum state and a foreign state claim power to regulate the same persons, conduct, or property?
Where should bank-created money (bank liabilities/deposits) be treated as legally located for resolving cross-border disputes over ownership and competing claims?
To what extent can national governments effectively impose and enforce controls on cross-border banking transactions and deposits held at foreign branches?
Which national laws should govern depositor-bank rights and liabilities when deposits are made at a foreign branch and host- and home-country rules conflict?
How should judges treat foreign sovereign acts that affect intangible property or contractual rights-when should such acts be recognized, enforced, or disregarded by forum courts?
What institutional or normative responses should courts, legislatures, or standards bodies adopt to manage cross-contract externalities created by single interpretive decisions?
Do cross-border payment transactions and bank intermediation routinely generate conflicts-of-laws problems that produce uncertainty and litigation risk?
How does judicial abstention from reviewing foreign governments' internal acts affect the enforceability of sovereign contracts in domestic courts?
Can parties reliably allocate legal risks for cross-border deposits and banking operations by contract, and will such contractual allocations be enforced across jurisdictions?
Should a lawyer in one jurisdiction give the traditional opinion that a contract is 'legal, valid, binding and enforceable' when the contract is governed by another jurisdiction's law?
What trade-offs arise between reducing contract customization through standardized 'good-enough' provisions and parties' ability to secure precisely tailored outcomes?
Do courts' efforts to discover and enforce a shared intent for semantically degraded boilerplate create significant social or market costs?
Does narrowly treating foreign governmental acts as determinative change outcomes in international contract disputes involving post-contract foreign laws or decrees?
What speech-act function does entering into a complex business contract serve: creating enforceable promises or setting a framework that enables non-legal governance and cooperation?
What legal and doctrinal reforms would best balance courts' desire for predictability in enforcing sovereign contracts with the need to avoid foreign-relations entanglement?

How do private standard-setting organizations, form contracts, and transnational documentation practices interact with national legal systems to determine the enforceability, reach, and governance effects of private global legal regimes?
What governance effects do standardized private legal documents and routine documentation work produce-do they replicate, supplement, or supplant state legal authority?
Does judicial non-review or abstention of foreign governmental acts vary across jurisdictions, and how does that variation affect litigants and international comity?

Can national governments lawfully assert extraterritorial jurisdiction to freeze, block, or otherwise control transfers of their currency (e.g., U.S. dollar) occurring between non-domestic parties, and what limits should constrain such assertions?
Do cross-border procedural and strategic behaviors-such as litigants preserving uncertainty about court authority-affect forum choice, settlement incentives, and enforcement outcomes?
When do standardized contracts and boilerplate produce social costs by enshrining language that courts enforce differently from parties' intent or that courts reinterpret during crises?

Should major legal transplants (e.g., U.S. contract documentation) be expected to produce the same investor-protection effects in other jurisdictions, or do they mutate and yield unintended consequences?

Should choice-of-law and governing-law issues be framed differently in legal opinions for cross-border transactions, and are some proposed approaches redundant with traditional conflict-of-laws principles?

shared_topics.topic: how national legal frameworks govern multinational economic actors and cross‑border market behavior

shared_topics.topic: regulatory arbitrage and market actors exploiting gaps between jurisdictions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents ways firms can insulate themselves from international competition or evade domestic regulatory pressures (exclusive dealing, distribution foreclosure, lobbying), while Paper B shows how Eurodollar markets and multinational banks seek legal and transactional locations (situs) to escape home‑country controls and exploit differences in national regulation.

shared_topics.topic: the limits of governments' ability to impose controls on transnational economic activity
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights that public‑sector interventions and weak enforcement can produce market distortions and limit the benefits of liberalization, whereas Paper B directly addresses to what extent home and host governments can effectively impose monetary controls, sanctions, or restrictions on cross‑border bank deposits and transactions.

shared_topics.topic: uncertainty from inadequate legal institutions and enforcement capacity affecting investment and market stability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that inadequate resources, administrative capacity, and political support undermine effective competition policy and deter investment; Paper B describes how outdated legal doctrines, inconsistent judicial decisions, and thin documentary records in the Euromarket create uncertainty about depositor rights and liabilities, complicating reliance and risk allocation.

shared_topics.topic: use of law to allocate risks and responsibilities in economic transactions involving large firms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues competition law and competition advocacy provide checks on private and public actors and allocate accountability to prevent anticompetitive conduct, while Paper B analyzes whether contracts or choice‑of‑law rules can reliably allocate deposit/withdrawal risks between depositors and multinational banks and protect parties from conflicting national obligations.

shared_topics.topic: systemic and cross-border contagion risks arising from financial controls or sovereign distress
shared_topics.justification: Both works are concerned with wider systemic effects of localized financial problems — Paper A explicitly lists minimizing contagion from sovereign crises as an objective of official policy, and Paper B highlights how controls on Eurodollar flows, branch closures, or sanctions in one jurisdiction can disrupt interbank markets and create broader international financial spillovers.

shared_topics.topic: the need for institutional or doctrinal frameworks to manage transnational financial disputes
shared_topics.justification: Each paper argues for more coherent mechanisms or rules to handle international financial conflicts — Paper A surveys the official sector’s search (including the SDRM idea) for orderly sovereign debt restructuring frameworks, and Paper B seeks doctrinal guidelines and presumptions to govern disputes between depositors, branches, and home offices in the Euromarket.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes overly broad expansion of odious-debt doctrine for creating unpredictability and proposes grounding obligations in international responsibility and moral duties, while Paper B argues that law has not kept pace with the Euromarket and multinational banking and offers tentative suggestions and presumptions to reduce doctrinal confusion.

shared_topics.topic: responsibilities and duties of private financial actors (banks, investors, corporations) when dealing with politically contentious regimes or cross-border funds

papers.node_id: 49harvintllj109!!ARTICLE: From Odious Debt to Odious Finance: Avoiding the Externalities of a Functional Odious Debt Doctrine
papers.title: ARTICLE: From Odious Debt to Odious Finance: Avoiding the Externalities of a Functional Odious Debt Doctrine
papers.abstract:
A vibrant discourse over sovereign debt forgiveness and cancellation has emerged in recent years as nongovernmental, governmental, and international entities assess the justice of onerous debt levels. Among the facets of this discussion is a newly emerging elucidation of what has been termed the odious debt doctrine.
The odious debt doctrine follows from the normative principle that the debt despots incur should not form a continuing obligation for states emerging from the grips of a despotic government, at least to the extent that thedebt did not benefit the population that existed under the prior regime.This article does not take issue with this normative position.
Rather, this article identifies a key problem with the application of the odious debt doctrine. In particular, it argues that the odious debt doctrine, if implemented alone, would result in unintended consequences because it would create incentives for dictators to search for funds from sources that may harm the economic resources, natural environment, and population at least as much as debt would. Given the odious debt doctrine's moral imperatives and normative goals, it seems unreasonable to develop a functional odious debt doctrine that will give despots cognizable incentives to make yet more use of these (potentially more harmful) methods of financing their regimes.
A more comprehensive view must be taken of the financing mechanisms utilized by despotic governments, such that odious debt is not viewed as so unique as to create doctrines around itself that lead to unanticipated results that might be more detrimental than a world without the odious debt doctrine. This article proposes an odious finance doctrine that considers a variety of financing mechanisms in use by despotic governments and captures other transactions despots use to finance their regimes.
Both the odious debt doctrine and the proposed odious finance doctrine contribute significantly to the burgeoning efforts toward, and popular sensibility regarding, corporate social responsibility and, more broadly, regarding the externalized social and environmental costs of our global economic system. This article argues that the odious finance doctrine will be significantly more beneficial than the odious debt doctrine to close the legal and regulatory gaps with respect to human rights violations, corruption, and environmental harms that are perpetrated or perpetuated in connection with despots.
In establishing an argument for expanding the scope of the odious debt doctrine, the article will proceed as follows: In Part II, the odious debt doctrine--including its historical origins, recent and current wellsprings, and contemporary academic literature on the subject--will be discussed at some length. This Part demonstrates that current academic debates have focused too exclusively on despotic government debt. Part III discusses two international norms governing government succession: the doctrine on the continuation of commercial obligations and the doctrine regarding compensation for expropriation. Under these doctrines the obligations incurred by one regime are binding on its successor. Odious debt--a doctrine of forgiveness--operates as an exception to this general rule, as would the odious finance doctrine proposed herein.
Part IV presents two detailed examples of alternative sources of financing that despotic governments may utilize. Rather than providing an exhaustivecatalogue of the various means by which dictators may raise funds, this Part aims to provoke the reader into thinking about the availability of other sources of funding. Part IV then argues that, in some cases, these alternative sources of financing may be seen as more harmful than loans to the long-term interests of the emerging state. The point of this argument is not to diminish the significant harms that may be bestowed on a successor government and its population by high debt levels. Rather, the goal is to explore the likelihood that some harms wrought by non-debt financing may be worse than those created by debt. Primarily, the article attempts to achieve this goal by way of an exposition of real cases that illustrate this proposition. This exposition does not undermine the utility of the conceptual tools offered by the odious debt doctrine. Rather, it probes whether the concept of odiousness can be applied to transactions other than loans.
Part V provides the contours of an odious finance doctrine, primarily by examining the characteristics of the odious debt doctrine. Central to the application of the doctrine is the categorization of certain debts as "odious" and therefore subject to cancellation. It then asks whether other types of despotic financing might be remedied or deterred by expanding application of the odious debt doctrine to include other transactions despots employ to finance their regimes, thereby giving rise to an odious finance doctrine.
Part VI contextualizes the odious finance doctrine by assessing the limitations on the application of the doctrine and suggesting some practical applications of odious finance that transcend the bounds of odious debt.

questions.question: Does forgiving or canceling obligations incurred by authoritarian regimes create incentives for those regimes to finance themselves through alternative methods that impose greater economic, environmental, or social harm on successor states?
questions.answer: Yes; the paper contends that implementing the odious debt doctrine alone would incentivize dictators to seek alternative financing sources that may harm a successor state’s economy, environment, and population as much as or more than debt.

questions.question: Would expanding post-regime relief to cover a wider range of financing transactions (beyond traditional loans) more effectively deter harmful regime financing and reduce associated human-rights, corruption, and environmental harms than relief limited to debt cancellation?
questions.answer: Yes; the paper argues that an expanded odious finance doctrine covering a broader range of transactions would be significantly more beneficial than debt-only relief in deterring harmful regime financing and in addressing human-rights, corruption, and environmental harms.

matched_themes: Under what legal and normative conditions may or should successor governments repudiate, reduce, or assume debts incurred by prior illegitimate, corrupt, or oppressive regimes?

Does targeting only lending liability (while continuing trade, aid, and engagement) coherently promote democratic reform in authoritarian states without harming welfare?
Will exempting successor governments from predecessor debts advance human-rights objectives without inflicting disproportionate harm on creditors, markets, or populations?

Can a uniform transnational public-policy principle be applied across jurisdictions to resolve disputes over illegitimate sovereign borrowing, rather than leaving outcomes to piecemeal domestic decisions?
Would codifying international rules for repudiation or relief from predecessor-incurred debts be practicable and what would be the effects on cross-border lending and market behavior?

To what extent are many government-to-government transfers documented as loans actually non-debt transfers in substance, and should such transfers bind successor governments as ordinary sovereign debt?
Does forgiving or canceling obligations incurred by authoritarian regimes create incentives for those regimes to finance themselves through alternative methods that impose greater harm on successors?
When and under what conditions should a successor political entity be held responsible for its predecessor's international commercial obligations despite lacking the predecessor's consent?

Should international investors, creditors, and corporations that financed or transacted with prior repressive regimes bear affirmative duties of restitution or repair, and how would such duties affect transitional justice and investment predictability?
How should assets and liabilities be allocated and adjudicated when a state disintegrates or undergoes regime change?

Is adjusting or terminating predecessor commercial obligations sufficient to promote the well-being of communities undergoing succession, or are alternative autonomy arrangements and external assistance needed?
Would policy objectives of an existing legal rule be better achieved through alternative doctrines with clearer scope or by legislative reform?
When are legal or policy analogies to private-law relationships between rulers and the ruled (e.g., to justify repudiating prior regimes' obligations) normatively and legally defensible?
Do successor-state debt doctrines and recognition practices (including diplomatic recognition) influence courts' willingness to validate prior governmental acts in private disputes?

Does expanding post-regime relief to cover a wider range of financing transactions (beyond traditional loans) more effectively deter harmful regime financing and reduce associated human-rights, corruption, and environmental harms than relief limited to debt cancellation?
How should courts and policymakers treat government-to-government transfers that are documented as loans but may be disguised grants or political support (non-debt)?

Would legally permitting or codifying successor-government exemptions for debts incurred by illegitimate or predatory prior regimes improve successor populations' welfare or deter predatory borrowing, and what are the likely market and political effects of such rules?
Is a post-regime-change state legally and practically obligated to assume external sovereign debt incurred by a prior regime?

papers.node_id: 83chikentlrev31!!ARTICLE: INDUSTRIAL AND COMPETITION POLICIES IN MEXICO
papers.title: ARTICLE: INDUSTRIAL AND COMPETITION POLICIES IN MEXICO
papers.abstract:
Thank you very much, Tom, for inviting me to have this exchange of reflections on competition and industrial policies in Mexico; it is a great honor for me to be here. I would like to share with you a few ideas on the development of industrial and competition policies in Mexico, and, of course, the relationship between them.
This is not going to be very different from the elements brought forward by Ambassador Jones- as I said, I can side a lot with his views of what has happened in Mexico over the last few years. Let me focus on the last part of the discussion on competition policy, and on the challenges and problems that we have to tackle in order to bring more efficiency to the Mexican markets.
would like to list the main messages up front. First, I would like to start with a diagnosis of the Mexican industrial policy from the sixties to the eighties, a long period of import-substitution policies in Mexico. I have to say that some of these policies had a positive effect on the economy, but the protection of domestic industries from international competition created important market distortions and inefficiencies. This is something that happens in many markets: if competition principles are taken out of the market, some efficiencies arise, but the benefits are not transferred to the consumers.
Second, I would like to discuss the shift in Mexico, moving towards a more horizontal policy designed not only to promote competition, but also to define a different kind of industrial policy and to sustain it that way.
, and this is the point I was trying to make to Ambassador Jones, despite the reforms, the macroeconomic stabilization, and the subsequent increase of competition and efficiency in the Mexican markets, important inefficiencies and problems still persist. Specially, I would like to focus on a very specific issue: the design of regulation. This is one of the elements that complicate the reform or decision - making processes to control de facto powers of the Mexican economy.
Finally, I would like to note some specific measures that could help to deal with these problems. I will go relatively fast because I think that it will be more interesting to have a good discussion with questions and, I hope, answers as well.

questions.question: Whether Mexico's historical import-substitution industrial policies and protection of domestic industries created persistent market distortions and inefficiencies that reduced consumer welfare.
questions.answer: Yes—the import-substitution era’s protection of domestic industries created significant market distortions and inefficiencies, and when competition principles were removed the benefits were not passed on to consumers.

questions.question: Whether and to what extent the shift toward a more horizontal, competition-oriented industrial policy has increased competition and market efficiency in Mexico.
questions.answer: The shift toward a more horizontal, competition-oriented policy (along with macroeconomic stabilization) increased competition and efficiency in Mexican markets, though important inefficiencies still persist.

questions.question: Whether flaws in the design of regulation explain the persistence of de facto market power and inefficiencies in Mexican markets, and which regulatory reforms would most effectively address those problems.
questions.answer: Yes—flaws in the design of regulation are cited as a key reason why de facto market powers and inefficiencies persist, but the abstract does not specify which regulatory reforms would most effectively address them.

matched_themes: Does competition policy and pro-competitive regulatory reform reduce firms' market power and related rent-seeking and corruption, and did Mexican reforms increase market efficiency?
Under what conditions do pro-competitive regulatory reforms (deregulation, liberalization) produce real competition, and when are explicit competition laws and advocacy also necessary?

papers.title: ARTICLE: INSOLVENCY PRINCIPLES AND THE ODIOUS DEBT DOCTRINE: THE MISSING LINK IN THE DEBATE
papers.abstract:
Politicians in this country, as well as many members of the international human-rights community, view it as fundamentally unfair that the Iraqi people may be saddled with the debts Saddam Hussein's brutal regime incurred. Further, some in the human-rights community generally argue that rich (creditor) countries have a moral duty or obligation to protect citizens of poor (debtor) countries and that richer nations should forgive the debts of poorer nations to help reduce existing inequalities between developed and developing countries. Until recently, arguments that successor governments should not be forced to repay the debts of former leaders or regimes relied almost exclusively on philosophical or humanitarian grounds. This article joins the attempt by scholars in the insolvency community to shift the discussion from the human rights, to the insolvency, arena.
The article does not attempt to outline a framework that should be used to determine whether a debt should be declared odious nor does it propose any specific entity that should have the authority to determine the odiousness of a debt. Instead, the article evaluates the doctrine of odious debts using the insolvency framework found in the United States Bankruptcy Code. Part II of the article provides a brief overview of sovereign lending and notes that entities that lend to, or invest in, sovereigns understand ex ante that many of the typical creditor remedies available upon default (such as repossession of collateral and replacement of managers) simply are not available in the context of sovereign lending. Since sovereigns are atypical debtors, their debt restructurings do not resemble the typical insolvency proceeding or out-of-court workout that involve business debtors.
Part III of the article then briefly describes the odious debt doctrine, discusses instances when it has been invoked to allow a sovereign to repudiate its debts, and briefly discusses the Iraqi debt situation. In considering what obligations a sovereign should have to repay a former regime's debts, the article emphasizes that even sovereigns who refuse to repay their debts cannot be liquidated and political leaders who refuse to repay the sovereign's debts cannot be replaced by lenders (at least not without military assistance). Thus, like consumers and businesses that reorganize in bankruptcy, financially troubled sovereigns will continue to exist notwithstanding their financial crises.
The article concludes by discussing instances where businesses are allowed to repudiate promises made to groups typically favored in our society (employees), are allowed to discharge debts owed to favored (often governmental) creditors, or, are allowed to subordinate certain creditor claims. Since debt restructuring is designed to rehabilitate people and businesses and to allow them to perform their core functions, courts allow debtors to break these promises if forcing debt repayment will prevent a business from rehabilitating itself in bankruptcy. The article argues that sovereign-debt restructurings should focus on the need both to rehabilitate the sovereign's finances and to allow the new leaders to perform the sovereign's principal "business" functions. Since the "business" of a sovereign is principally to provide for the needs of its citizens and to maintain the country's physical infrastructure, and a democratically elected government will be ineffective if it lacks the respect of its citizens or is unable to provide essential health and human welfare services for those citizens, it would be justifiable to forgive odious debts if forcing the sovereign to repay those debts would prevent the sovereign from restructuring itself politically and financially.
Finally, the article notes that an additional benefit to periodical invocation of the odious debt doctrine is that it reminds lenders that the doctrine may at some point gain acceptance in the international financial community. Though the doctrine may not ever be acknowledged by the lending community, creditors (like some involved in the Iraqi debts restructuring) will be forced to bargain during the restructuring in the shadow of the threat that the doctrine might be invoked and this fear may make some commercial lenders exercise more caution in the future when extending credit to regimes.

questions.question: Whether successor governments should be allowed to repudiate or have forgiven the debts incurred by prior regimes when forcing repayment would prevent the state's political and financial rehabilitation and its ability to provide for citizens.
questions.answer: Yes; the article contends it is justifiable to forgive odious debts when forcing repayment would prevent the sovereign from restructuring itself politically and financially and from providing essential services to its citizens.

questions.question: Whether principles and mechanisms used to reorganize and rehabilitate insolvent businesses can appropriately be applied to the resolution and restructuring of sovereign debt.
questions.answer: Yes; the article applies bankruptcy-style rehabilitation principles to sovereign debt, arguing they should guide restructurings even though sovereign workouts do not mirror typical insolvency proceedings.

questions.question: Whether the prospect that a new government might refuse to honor prior regime debts influences creditor behaviour and lending practices toward risky or non-democratic governments.
questions.answer: Yes; the threat that the odious debt doctrine might be invoked compels creditors to bargain under that shadow and may induce more cautious lending to regimes.

matched_themes: Under what legal and normative conditions may or should successor governments repudiate, reduce, or assume debts incurred by prior illegitimate, corrupt, or oppressive regimes?
How should predecessor state debts and assets be allocated among successor states when a state dissolves or territorial units secede?
What legal incentives, imperatives, and constraints shape creditor-debtor bargaining and creditor coordination in sovereign or quasi-sovereign restructurings, and how do these affect outcomes?
How do contractual language, legal enforcement, and non-legal forces (reputation, ongoing relationships) interact to determine parties' actual obligations and behavior under complex contracts?

How should legal and institutional rules balance preserving state discretion over foreign economic policy and regulation with ensuring enforceability of cross-border financial claims and maintaining lender confidence?
How should the law balance an issuer's need to restructure sovereign debt efficiently against individual bondholders' protection from coercion or unfair impairment?

What legal powers and procedural designs (including the ability to extinguish preexisting rights) are necessary in a claims-resolution system to prevent unresolved claims from blocking final status or peace settlements?
Will exempting successor governments from predecessor debts advance human-rights objectives without inflicting disproportionate harm on creditors, markets, or populations?
Can principles and mechanisms from corporate insolvency meaningfully be applied to the resolution and restructuring of sovereign debt?
When and under what conditions should a successor political entity be held responsible for its predecessor's international commercial obligations despite lacking the predecessor's consent?
Does avoiding sovereign default by continuing to service debt produce better or worse renegotiation and welfare outcomes for developing countries?
What are the consequences of sovereign default for restructuring outcomes and for incentives and behavior of international creditors and debtor governments?
Do exceptional legal, political, or institutional protections (sovereign immunities, special statutes) effectively shield sovereigns from creditor litigation and alter restructuring bargaining power?

Can private-law concepts that prioritize substance over form-such as reclassifying or lowering repayment priority of creditors based on conduct-provide a coherent framework for resolving disputed obligations incurred by prior regimes?
Does the prospect of regime change or refusal by a successor government to honor prior debts materially influence creditor behavior and lending to risky or non-democratic governments?

Should international investors, creditors, and corporations that financed or transacted with prior repressive regimes bear affirmative duties of restitution or repair, and how would such duties affect transitional justice and investment predictability?
Should governments repudiate or cancel sovereign debt when debt service substantially impairs their ability to provide public welfare and democratic policymaking?
How should assets and liabilities be allocated and adjudicated when a state disintegrates or undergoes regime change?
How do private-law concepts and analogies between rulers and the ruled historically shape doctrinal limits on state power and inform criteria for rejecting obligations imposed by prior regimes?
Would policy objectives of an existing legal rule be better achieved through alternative doctrines with clearer scope or by legislative reform?
When are legal or policy analogies to private-law relationships between rulers and the ruled (e.g., to justify repudiating prior regimes' obligations) normatively and legally defensible?

Would legally permitting or codifying successor-government exemptions for debts incurred by illegitimate or predatory prior regimes improve successor populations' welfare or deter predatory borrowing, and what are the likely market and political effects of such rules?
Is a post-regime-change state legally and practically obligated to assume external sovereign debt incurred by a prior regime?

papers.node_id: 48amjcompl307!!ARTICLE: International Payments and Conflicts of Laws
papers.title: ARTICLE: International Payments and Conflicts of Laws
papers.abstract:
Since international payments involve contacts with at least two different States and their respective legal systems, it is intuitive that they raise issues of conflicts of laws. Anybody even superficially familiar with private international law would be quick to realize that such issues are bound to be numerous and complicated. Yet it is surprising that, despite the number of international payments made each day around the world and the likelihood of disputes liable to raise conflicts problems, both the case law and the literature on these issues are quite scarce.This could be explained in several ways: either the problems are in practice not relevant; or they are relevant to such an extent intractable that litigants, courts and even conflicts lawyers internationally shy away from them; or they are completely overlooked.
As a conflicts lawyer I cannot accept the first possibility, which would call into question the usefulness of this branch of law, and I obviously have more sympathy for the third one. This justifies the decision to devote an essay to the subject of conflicts of laws in international payments, although I realize that raising the awareness of these problems might simply open a Pandora's box of additional potential for litigation. At the same time the need to keep this paper within reasonable limits provides an excuse for not dealing with any of the matters in depth and thereby having to face up to the conclusion that the issues are indeed intractable and better left unexplored.

questions.question: Do cross-border payment transactions routinely give rise to conflicts-of-laws problems that are numerous, complex, and likely to generate litigation and legal uncertainty?
questions.answer: Yes—because international payments inherently involve multiple legal systems, the paper asserts that conflicts-of-laws issues are numerous and complicated and warns that greater awareness could unleash substantial litigation.

questions.question: Why is there relatively little case law and scholarship on conflicts-of-laws issues in international payments - because the problems are practically irrelevant, because they are too intractable for parties and courts to pursue, or because they have been overlooked?
questions.answer: Because they have been overlooked; the author explicitly rejects irrelevance and does not endorse intractability.

matched_themes: Do cross-border payment transactions and bank intermediation routinely generate conflicts-of-laws problems that produce uncertainty and litigation risk?
Why is conflicts-of-laws litigation around international payments relatively scarce - practical irrelevance, intractability, or academic oversight?

papers.node_id: 1988columbuslrev441!!ARTICLE: INVESTMENT IN FOREIGN EQUITY SECURITIES AND DEBT-EQUITY CONVERSION BY U.S. BANKS, BANK HOLDING COMPANIES, AND FOREIGN BANK HOLDING COMPANIES
papers.title: ARTICLE: INVESTMENT IN FOREIGN EQUITY SECURITIES AND DEBT-EQUITY CONVERSION BY U.S. BANKS, BANK HOLDING COMPANIES, AND FOREIGN BANK HOLDING COMPANIES
papers.abstract:
It is an established policy in the United States to separate commercial banking from other commercial activities.This policy reflects a fear that a bank which engages in a commercial activity may not extend credit to its commercial competitors, and that a bank which controls industrial enterprises would become economically too powerful.  There is also a concern that commercial activities of banks may endanger the safety of deposits: people who are trained as bankers may be bad industrialists; they may extend credit to the bank's commercial affiliates on preferential terms; and, once a commercial affiliate of a bank incurs losses, the bank may be under great pressure to extend unsound credit.  This policy of separation of banking and commerce is carried out by a careful enumeration of the powers of banks in federal and state banking laws,by restrictions on permissible investments,and by the prohibition of certain activities and relationships.Bank holding companies are subject tosimilar restrictions.
In many foreign countries, commercial banks do not operate under similar restraints and are free to invest in commercial enterprises.A tension arises when U.S. banks and bank holding companies engage in activities abroad.  On the one hand, the prohibition against commercial activities creates a severe competitive disadvantage for U.S. banks.  On the other hand, the perceived evil which the policy of separation is supposed to prevent would be permitted to continue if banks were free to engage in commercial activities in foreign countries.  U.S. legislators and regulatory agencies have carefully balanced these competing interests.  The result is a highly complex set of rules.
The limitations on foreign investments imposed by these rules were questioned when the technique of debt-equity conversionpresented U.S. banks with the opportunity to reduce their credit exposure in lesser developed countries by converting debt into equity investments in these countries.  In February, 1988, the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (the "Board") promulgated new regulations designed to facilitate equity investments through debt-equity conversions by banks.It is too early to tell whether these regulations will have the intended effect of encouraging foreign debt-equity conversions by U.S. banks.
This article discusses the rules governing investments by U.S. banks and bank holding companies in foreign equity securities, and in particular analyzes the complex regulations which control debt-equity conversions.

questions.question: How do the regulatory rules governing U.S. banks and bank holding companies limit or permit their investments in foreign equity securities?
questions.answer: They enforce the separation of banking and commerce through enumerated powers, restrictions on permissible investments, and prohibitions on certain activities and relationships, which limit foreign equity investments, while 1988 Federal Reserve regulations were designed to permit and facilitate such investments via debt-equity conversions.

questions.question: Do regulatory changes intended to facilitate debt-equity conversions lead U.S. banks to convert foreign debt into equity to reduce their credit exposure?
questions.answer: It is too early to tell whether the 1988 regulations will have the intended effect of encouraging U.S. banks to convert foreign debt into equity to reduce their credit exposure.

questions.question: What are the policy trade-offs of allowing U.S. banks to engage in commercial investments abroad (balancing depositor safety concerns against competitive disadvantages)?
questions.answer: The policy trade-off is that allowing commercial investments abroad could alleviate the severe competitive disadvantage faced by U.S. banks, but it risks the harms the separation policy seeks to prevent, including threats to deposit safety, preferential lending to affiliates, and excessive economic power.
