papers.node_id: 60wmmarylrev2111!!ARTICLE: TAX LAWYERS AS TAX INSURANCE
papers.title: ARTICLE: TAX LAWYERS AS TAX INSURANCE
papers.abstract:
Transactional tax lawyers, by rendering tax opinions, provide an element of insurance to clients. This insurance is clearly incomplete, but by providing a tax opinion, a lawyer conditionally agrees to indemnify the client for part of the potential loss the client incurs if the favorable tax treatment described in the opinion is successfully challenged. Thus, tax lawyers serve, at least partly, as tax insurers.
This insurance function is missing from the literature about the transactional tax lawyer's role. Ronald J. Gilson's seminal work,Value Creation by Business Lawyers: Legal Skills and Asset Pricing, explains that transactional lawyers add value for clients by being "transaction cost engineers."The voluminous literature that followed Gilson's article provided various other explanations, conceiving transactional lawyers as reputational intermediaries,regulatory cost reducers,enterprise designers,transaction quarterbacks,"risk managers,"aggregators of information about market terms,and more.Considering transactionaltaxlawyers specifically, Victor Fleischer added the role of a "regulatory arbitrageur,"who "tweak[s] a deal structure to achieve better regulatorytreatment [for example, better tax treatment, thereby shifting value from the government to the deal parties] without unduly altering the underlying business arrangements."
The insurance-like aspect of the lawyer-client relationship, however, has been largely overlooked until now. When the insurance aspect of opinions (tax or nontax) is mentioned in the literature, it is most commonly with a brief comment to the effect that "[a] legal opinion is not an insurance policy."These comments, however, are typically made to assert that an opinion does "not guarantee[] that a court will reach any particular result."But insurance need not promise a particular result or provide for 100 percent loss coverage if that result is not achieved. Arrangements can have aspects of insurance without providing a full guarantee of results.Thus, the brief assertions in the literature about opinions not being insurance are too conclusory.
The literature includes rare acknowledgments of the possibility that opinions contain insurance-like features. In the tax area, commentators occasionally mention that tax opinions may serve as "'insurance' against penalties."These commentators typically put the word "insurance" in quotations and imply that tax opinions create a form of government-provided insurance because having an opinion may protect a client from penalties that the client would otherwise owe to the government.These commentators do not, however, seem to contemplate the possibility that the client will recover from thelawyerif penalties are imposed.
Outside the tax area, few commentators acknowledge the possibility of an insurance-like role for opinion-writing lawyers.Of the two commentators who come closest, albeit in a nontax context, to the assertions made in this Article, one briefly--in three sentences--raises and sets aside the possibility that business lawyers could add value for a client by taking on some of the client's riskvia the possibility of a malpractice claim.The other commentator, who provides a slightly longer discussion in two separate articles,approached third-party closing opinion practice primarily through a sociological study rather than through a detailed legal analysis as provided herein.His findings offer a relatively limited account of the insurance role of third-party closing opinions,but he suggested that the insurance-like function of closing opinions may increase in the future.Moreover, he implied that tax opinions, in contrast to third-party closing opinions that were his focus, might be a special case.
The absence of meaningful scholarly attention to the insurance-like function of tax lawyers is surprising because, as this Article demonstrates, the risk shifting from clients to tax opinion-givers can be meaningful and can affect important aspects of the lawyer/ client relationship. Specifically, understanding tax opinions through an insurance lens can affect tax advisers' billing practices, the terms of client engagements, the design of tax opinions, the market for tax advice, and more. Appreciating the tax lawyer's indemnification role is especially important now, after the enactment of the most sweeping tax changes in more than thirty years.The new tax laws bring tremendous uncertainty, which means that clients will be even more dependent on guidance (including opinions) from their tax advisers.Thus, this Article fills the gap in the literature by identifying,exploring, and explaining the consequences of the insurance-like aspect of the transactional tax lawyer's role.
This Article examines only transactionaltaxlawyers, and leaves for future study how the insurance-like paradigm resonates in other transactional practices. It is certainly possible that transactional lawyers in practice areas outside of tax may also serve an insurance-like function when they provide opinions. This Article, however, focuses on the tax context, both because of my expertise and because of features of tax law and tax practice (for example, the centrality of tax opinions to tax practice,the history of professional liability payouts related to tax shelters and tax shelter opinions,and Circular 230's detailed ethical obligations applicable only to tax practice) that may cause the indemnity function of opinions to have particular resonance in the tax context.
To be clear, this Article does not argue that theprimary or predominantfunction of transactional tax lawyers is to provide insurance, nor does this Article assert that tax opinions, or their providers, should beregulatedas insurance (or insurers). Rather, this Article argues that indemnification (in other words, one element of insurance) ispartof the economic relationship between a client and a lawyer who provides a tax opinion, and that the insurance paradigm is an important additional lens through which to understand the role of transactional tax lawyers and the value they provide.
Moreover, this Article acknowledges that the risk shifting accomplished by tax opinions is neither unidirectional nor complete. Tax opinions, by creating penalty-free zones in some cases,can also shift some of the risks and costs of incorrect positions from the taxpayer to the government. And given the barriers to malpractice recoveries and how carefully tax opinions are often written to protect the opinion writer, a taxpayer does retain a significant portion of the risk for taking positions that are successfully challenged.Yet, as this Article demonstrates, tax opinions do shift some portion of that risk from the taxpayer to the opinion writer.
In addition, this Article's claim is descriptive, not normative. Should tax lawyers be required (or allowed) to indemnify their clients for the liability arising from successful challenges to tax positions on which the lawyers opined? Should the law be adjusted to emphasize or deemphasize the tax lawyer's indemnification obligation? Would increasing the extent to which and frequency with which tax advisors indemnify their clients (for example, by lowering the hurdles to malpractice recoveries or increasing the damages that are recoverable)cause advisors to give more conservative advice, thereby increasing tax compliance? Or would doing so hinder compliance by encouraging taxpayers to take riskier positions than they otherwise would because of their ability to recover the costs from their advisors if the positions are wrong?Are tax lawyers effective at managing and distributing risks of client losses or should the large-scale transfer and distribution of tax risks be left to third-party tax insurers? If the latter, does that portend a rise in the market for third-party tax insurers and a decline in tax opinions? These important questions are outside the scope of this Article. They cannot be answered without first examining the extent to which transactional tax lawyers are currently serving an insurance-like role. Only once that baseline is understood can normative questions be engaged effectively. This Article, by identifying that and explaining the extent to which transactional tax lawyers serve an insurance-like function, provides a critical step in understanding and evaluating the risk-shifting dynamic between clients and their tax lawyers.
This Article proceeds as follows. Part I provides background on transactional tax practice in general, tax opinion practice specifically, and tax insurance available from third-party insurers. Part IIdraws an analogy between tax opinions and third-party tax insurance to demonstrate how the former are similar to the latter. Part III examines the extent to which tax opinions reflect traditional indicia of insurance. Part IV discusses evidence, including from malpractice insurance claims data, illustrating how the indemnity function of tax opinions resonates in the reality of tax practice. Part V discusses several implications of understanding the tax lawyer/client relationship through the insurance lens.

questions.question: Whether transactional tax lawyers, by issuing tax opinions, effectively serve as partial insurers who indemnify clients for some losses when the favorable tax treatment in the opinion is successfully challenged
questions.answer: Yes; the Article argues that by issuing tax opinions, transactional tax lawyers provide incomplete but real insurance, conditionally indemnifying clients for part of losses if the opinion’s favorable tax treatment is successfully challenged.

questions.question: To what extent do tax opinions shift risk and financial costs of incorrect tax positions away from taxpayers (and sometimes onto the government) and onto the opinion-giving lawyers
questions.answer: Tax opinions meaningfully but incompletely shift some risk and costs of incorrect positions from taxpayers to opinion-giving lawyers, can also shift some costs to the government by creating penalty-free zones, yet taxpayers retain a significant share due to malpractice barriers and carefully drafted opinions.

questions.question: How does recognition of the insurance-like function of tax opinions affect lawyers' billing practices, engagement terms, the design of opinions, and the broader market for tax advice
questions.answer: The Article asserts that viewing tax opinions through an insurance lens can affect tax advisers’ billing practices, the terms of client engagements, the design of tax opinions, and the overall market for tax advice.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: SYMPOSIUM: SOVEREIGN DEBT RESTRUCTURING: Sovereign Workouts: An IMF Perspective

shared_topics.topic: the demand for legal predictability and its implications under heightened uncertainty

shared_topics.topic: how liability, indemnification, or legal design shapes market behavior and incentives

shared_topics.topic: the role of legal professionals and intermediaries in facilitating transactions and reallocating risk
shared_topics.justification: Paper A portrays transactional tax lawyers as playing an insurance-like intermediary role in transactions by writing opinions that reallocate tax risk, and Paper B highlights the participation of lawyers, workout professionals, and the official sector in designing and implementing sovereign workout processes that redistribute insolvency risks.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: COPYING AND CONTEXT: TYING AS A SOLUTION TO THE LACK OF INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY PROTECTION OF CONTRACT TERMS

shared_topics.topic: statutory versus contractual/regulatory design for allocating liability and priority

shared_topics.topic: credibility and enforceability of commitments as market-stabilizing mechanisms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on the IMF's credibility to withhold or condition financing and how enforceable rules affect crisis outcomes, while Paper B focuses on the practical enforceability and credibility of tax opinions (malpractice recoveries, insurer payouts) and how that affects reliance on and value of those opinions.

shared_topics.topic: the role of intermediaries in reducing transaction costs and coordinating private actors
shared_topics.justification: Paper A reconceptualizes the IMF as a coordinator/intermediary that can authorize priority lending and marshal private creditors to resolve sovereign crises, whereas Paper B treats transactional tax lawyers as intermediaries (reputational and indemnifying) who lower costs and coordinate parties' willingness to accept tax positions.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops the 'standard clause analysis' showing that practitioner‑crafted clauses (e.g., the MAC as a frustration‑analog) are market responses that contract around common‑law defaults, while Paper B shows that transactional tax opinions operate as private instruments (insurance‑like devices) that alter who bears legal risk relative to statutory or default tax liability.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A addresses how drafters and courts should construct and interpret MAC/frustration‑type clauses to handle uncertainty between signing and closing, and Paper B examines how tax opinions and indemnities are used to manage uncertainty created by ambiguous or changing tax rules (especially after major tax reform).

shared_topics.topic: litigation, enforcement, and third‑party/governmental consequences of risk‑shifting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses how invoking MAC clauses can provoke litigation and trigger government intervention (e.g., bailout concerns), and Paper B analyzes malpractice claims, penalty regimes, and how tax opinions can shift enforcement burdens to the government or produce liability disputes between clients and advisers.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: ACTS OF STATE AND FOREIGN SOVEREIGN OBLIGATIONS

shared_topics.justification: Paper A considers how malpractice law, ethical rules (e.g., Circular 230), and courts' treatment of opinions influence advisers' behavior and the market for tax advice, whereas Paper B examines how the act of state doctrine and judicial restraint limit courts' role in adjudicating sovereign contracts and thus shape the incentives of investors and host governments.

shared_topics.topic: tension between private contractual arrangements and public/regulatory/political constraints
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explores how tax law, government penalties, and regulatory obligations interact with lawyers' indemnification through opinions (sometimes shifting risk to the government), while Paper B analyzes how foreign‑policy concerns and the need for 'one voice' constrain judicial enforcement of sovereign commitments, creating a clash between private ordering and public policy considerations.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A surveys doctrinal distinctions (negligence vs fraud vs contract) affecting the scope of recoverable damages in tax malpractice suits, and Paper B complements this by examining empirical and doctrinal impediments to malpractice recoveries (malpractice insurance data, opinion drafting, Circular 230, and other constraints) that limit or shape clients' ability to obtain indemnification from tax advisers.

shared_topics.topic: how liability rules and indemnification affect tax-adviser behavior and the market for tax advice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that courts' choice of damage measure in malpractice litigation has concrete effects on remedies available to clients, while Paper B analyzes how the insurance-like indemnity role of opinions influences billing, engagement terms, opinion design, and whether advisers give more or less conservative advice—both connecting legal standards of liability to practitioner incentives and market outcomes.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The IMF and Regulation of Cross-Border Capital Flows

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A PROSPECTIVE ENLARGEMENT OF THE ROLES OF THE BRETTON WOODSFINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS IN INTERNATIONAL PEACE OPERATIONS

shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how tax opinions shift tax liabilities and penalties (partially) from taxpayers to opinion-giving lawyers and compares that to third‑party tax insurance, while Paper B engages the Bretton Woods institutions' potential financial roles in peace operations — implicating who bears reconstruction and operational costs and how financial burdens are distributed internationally.

papers.node_id: 66amjcompl411!!ARTICLE: The Accord on Fire and Building Safety in Bangladesh: A New Paradigm for Limiting Buyers' Liability in Global Supply Chains? +http://dx.doi/org/10.1093/ajcl/avy030
papers.title: ARTICLE: The Accord on Fire and Building Safety in Bangladesh: A New Paradigm for Limiting Buyers' Liability in Global Supply Chains? +http://dx.doi/org/10.1093/ajcl/avy030
papers.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: FROM NONBINDING TO ENFORCEABLE CORPORATE SOCIAL RESPONSIBILITY
The Accord on Fire and Building Safety in Bangladesh (the Accord)is generally seen as a positive development in ensuring that third-world garment industry workers have access to safe working conditions.A central structural difference between the Accord and most earlier corporate social responsibility (CSR) initiatives is that the Accord takes the form of an enforceable contract that provides direct benefits to workers in Bangladeshi factories.Traditionally, CSR mechanisms tread a fine line between a promise of decent labor conditions, often targeted at first-world consumers, and the nonbinding nature of such mechanisms, at least from the perspective of third-world laborers.The chief competitor of the Accord, the Alliance for Bangladesh Worker Safety (the Alliance), follows the traditional model.
The question of how to organize the governance of a supply chain, via enforceable governance contracts, such as the Accord, or nonbinding governance mechanisms, such as the Alliance, has broad consequences. Production often takes place in global supply chains consistingof chains or networks of contracts.In such structures, contract boundaries traditionally severe liability between actors not in privity. At the same time, buyers may wish to establish control over their entire supply chains, for example by spreading cost management, R&D, or ethical requirements throughout the chain of contracts.In particular, one can ask whether a governance contract, such as the Accord, that establishes privity between supply-chain actors that otherwise would be without privity,is from a supply-chain-governance perspective more effective than nonbinding mechanisms, such as the Alliance, that claim not to interrupt the privity relationships in a chain of contracts.
Scholarship and more general reporting on the Accord seem uniformly positive regarding its enforceable nature.My focus in this Article is this distinction between the positive, empowering image attributed to the enforceable agreement in the case of the Accord and the negative, hollow-words image of compliance mechanisms, such as the Alliance, that do not take the form of an enforceable agreement. I argue that the possibilities for controlling liability allowed by an enforceable governance agreement may outweigh the possibilities for controlling liability allowed by reliance on strict conceptions of privity. From this perspective, the Accord, without prejudice to any positive effects it may have, can be critiqued as providing a new paradigm for controlling the liability of buyers towards their global supply chains. In addition to its possibilities for limiting and controlling liability, the positive image of this new paradigm brings with it a general whitewashing effect towards consumers and regulators. Even more pronounced may be its whitewashing effect towards adjudicators. Courts and arbitral tribunals may be prone to value the sanctity of the four-corners private ordering of transnational contracts, such as the Accord, over locally embedded legal safeguards.
The structure of this Article is as follows. This Introduction is followed in Part I by an overview of the Accord and the Alliance and someof their salient features and critiques. In Part II, focus is on a general critique of governance through contract. This critique is coupled with a historical-comparative look at how law has countered the liability-limiting effects of various kinds of contractual structures in relation to defective products, a development arguably comparable to supply-chain liability or, put another way, production liability. I then extend this critique to discuss its implications for understanding the two paradigms of controlling supply-chain liability represented by the Accord and Alliance. In Part III, I look at current discussions of extending liability in global supply chains. I argue that, from a buyer's perspective, there is a tangible risk for seeing buyers as liable for damages arising out of inadequate control of their supply chains when governance mechanisms similar to the Alliance are used. In Part IV, I argue that if mechanisms such as the Alliance no longer offer adequate certainty for controlling liability, buyers may be pushed towards using direct governance contracts, such as the Accord, to control liability. I ground this argument in a discussion of the possibilities allowed by a direct governance contract for controlling supply-chain liability using the Accord as an example. In the Conclusion, I outline the differences of enforceable and inclusive CSR mechanisms, as represented by the Accord, and the existing paradigm of nonbinding and exclusive CSR mechanisms, as represented by the Alliance, and note the general potential for a paradigm shift in CSR mechanisms. Despite their radically different legal underpinnings, these two paradigms share similar fundamental flaws in their reliance on the benevolence of global buyers. This leads me to raise the question of the adequacy of existing legal safeguards if structures akin to the Accord see increased use for controlling liability.

questions.question: Whether entering into enforceable governance contracts that create direct legal relationships between buyers and suppliers reduces buyers' liability for harms arising in their global supply chains compared with relying on nonbinding corporate social responsibility mechanisms.
questions.answer: Yes—the paper argues that enforceable governance contracts like the Accord provide more effective tools for limiting and controlling buyers’ supply-chain liability than reliance on nonbinding mechanisms such as the Alliance or strict privity.

questions.question: Whether the use of enforceable private governance agreements functions to 'whitewash' buyers' responsibility - that is, to reduce scrutiny by consumers, regulators, and adjudicators - thereby undermining public and legal accountability for supply-chain harms.
questions.answer: Yes—it contends that the positive image of enforceable private governance produces a whitewashing effect that reduces scrutiny by consumers and regulators and, even more, by adjudicators who may privilege the four-corners of such contracts over local legal safeguards.

questions.question: Whether uncertainty about liability under nonbinding governance mechanisms incentivizes buyers to adopt direct enforceable governance contracts as a strategy to control and limit their exposure to supply-chain liability.
questions.answer: Yes—the author argues that uncertainty and tangible liability risks under nonbinding mechanisms like the Alliance push buyers toward adopting direct, enforceable governance contracts (e.g., the Accord) to control and limit their supply-chain liability.

papers.title: ARTICLE: THE ACT OF STATE DOCTRINE IN CONTRACT CASES AS A CONFLICT-OF-LAWS RULE 1988 Center for Transnational Legal Studies
papers.abstract:
Courts have recently begun to apply the act of state doctrine in cases in which a foreign obligor claims that a foreign act of state modifies the contractual obligation owed to a U.S. obligee.Allied Bank International v. Banco Credito Agricola de Cartagois the best known case in this category. For some time courts have encountered a second category of cases involving the performance of contracts.  In these cases a party claims that the foreign act of state modified the contractual obligation of a U.S. obligor owed to a foreign obligee.Alfred Dunhill of London, Inc. v. Republic of Cubamay serve as an example.  In some of these performance of contract cases the courts have held that the foreign act of state modified the contractual obligation; in others, courts have held to the contrary. In all these cases the central question was whether a commercial agreement that had contacts with both the United States and the foreign country was affected by a foreign law or decree promulgated after the contract had been entered into.
Professor Henkin has said that the act of state doctrine is a conflict-of-laws rule.This statement is undoubtedly correct because a rule dealing with the question whether a foreign law or the law of the forum applies to an agreement is a question of conflict of laws.Professor Henkin's statement has been repeated many times by courtsand commentators.Courts and commentators, however, have not analyzed the statement's meaning in connection with contract cases.  The question in these cases is whether and to what extent the act of state doctrine modifies the traditional conflict-of-laws rules applicable to contracts.
This article compares the results that courts have reached by applying or rejecting the act of state doctrine in cases involving performance of contract disputes with the results they would have reached by applying the traditional conflict-of-laws approaches.  The article demonstrates that the results reached in such cases under the act of state doctrine could also have been reached by applying traditional conflict-of-laws rules.  Consequently, the act of state doctrine as applied to contract cases is nothing but a new and fancy dress for old solutions.

questions.question: Whether treating a foreign government's official acts as determinative changes outcomes in international contract disputes about whether a post-contract foreign law or decree alters contractual obligations.
questions.answer: No; applying the act of state doctrine in such disputes does not change outcomes, because the same results could be reached under traditional conflict-of-laws rules.

questions.question: Whether the outcomes produced by that approach could instead be reached by applying traditional conflict-of-laws (choice-of-law) rules, i.e., whether the approach is substantively redundant with existing conflict-of-laws principles.
questions.answer: Yes; the article shows that outcomes reached via the act of state doctrine could also be achieved by traditional conflict-of-laws approaches, rendering it substantively redundant.

matched_themes: When should domestic courts decline to adjudicate private-law claims that hinge on the validity of a foreign government's acts within its own territory?
When should domestic courts defer to a foreign state's determinations about acts within that state's territory, and what limits should govern such deference?
How should courts allocate competing regulatory authority when both the forum state and a foreign state claim power to regulate the same persons, conduct, or property?
How should judges treat foreign sovereign acts that affect intangible property or contractual rights-when should such acts be recognized, enforced, or disregarded by forum courts?
How does judicial abstention from reviewing foreign governments' internal acts affect the enforceability of sovereign contracts in domestic courts?
Does narrowly treating foreign governmental acts as determinative change outcomes in international contract disputes involving post-contract foreign laws or decrees?
What legal and doctrinal reforms would best balance courts' desire for predictability in enforcing sovereign contracts with the need to avoid foreign-relations entanglement?
Do exceptional legal, political, or institutional protections (sovereign immunities, special statutes) effectively shield sovereigns from creditor litigation and alter restructuring bargaining power?
Does judicial non-review or abstention of foreign governmental acts vary across jurisdictions, and how does that variation affect litigants and international comity?
Would policy objectives of an existing legal rule be better achieved through alternative doctrines with clearer scope or by legislative reform?

Should choice-of-law and governing-law issues be framed differently in legal opinions for cross-border transactions, and are some proposed approaches redundant with traditional conflict-of-laws principles?

papers.node_id: 59bclrev71!!ARTICLE: THE ARCHITECTURE OF CONTRACT INNOVATION
papers.title: ARTICLE: THE ARCHITECTURE OF CONTRACT INNOVATION
papers.abstract:
This Article develops a novel theoretical framework and introduces new methods for studying the design of complex contracts. In so doing, it breaks new ground for positive contract scholarship. Complexity has always played an important role in contract research. Contract economics has long recognized that complex decision landscapes, in which contracting parties struggle to appreciate all of the implications of their choices, contribute to contractual incompleteness.Relatively little attention, however, has been paid to complexity within contracts themselves--orinfra-transactionalcomplexity--and how it affects agreement design and enforcement decisions. Legal researchers and social scientists have attempted to address infra-transactional complexity on occasion, but the efforts have been neither entirely satisfactory nor sustained.This Article is a step toward filling that gap in the scholarship.
Evidence suggests that infra-transactional complexity has been increasing dramatically in recent years. Consider, for example, a simple comparison of early twentieth century and early twenty-first century merger agreements. A template agreement for the merger of two publicly held railroad companies taken from a 1930 treatise numbers only three-and-a-half pages and focuses primarily upon delineating the consideration exchanged, transferring liabilities, and executing corporate formalities, such as bylawamendments and shareholder voting.By the twenty-first century, the typical public company merger agreement would be approximately twenty times longer, setting forth a lengthy list of representations and warranties, allocating an array of pre-closing risks, and carefully determining when the agreement may be terminated.Systematic research confirms that anecdote: for instance, a recent analysis of a large sample of merger agreements found that they have grown dramatically more complex over the last two decades.
Infra-transactional complexity matters because it challenges our models of how market participants privately order their exchanges, which in turn has implications for court intervention in contract disputes. The challenge arises from a puzzle that infra-transactional complexity raises. On one hand, increasing the complexity of a contractual system gives transaction designers more options for addressing exchange hazards, allowing them to tinker with different combinations of governance mechanisms from deal to deal. On the other hand, an increase in infra-transactional complexity raises the prospect that change to one term will require adjustments to related terms, raising transaction costs.The costs of complexity also extend to back end enforcement, where courts are often called upon to interpret a provision embedded within a complicated latticework of obligations.
How then do transaction designers manage the costs of changing elements of an agreement without being overwhelmed by the complexity of the contractual system? Current theory suggests that parties may resort to standardizing terms as the costs of complexity increase.If the costs of infra-transactional complexity are so high, then all the better to standardize the contract and thereby rationalize the web of interconnections between provisions once and for all. Such an approach allows, for example, a law firm junior associate to design a sovereign bond indenture in three and a half minutes.Indeed, use of boilerplate contract terms may be exactly what explains how deal lawyers cope with the mergers and acquisitions (M&A) market's highly compressed timelines--examples ranging from Pritzker's infamous negotiation of the Trans Union deal in approximately one weekto Facebook's more recent one-billion-dollar acquisition of Instagram over a long weekend.
Curiously, however, the M&A market displays limited standardization despite high levels of infra-transactional complexity.Instead of significantly standardizing agreements as in the market for sovereign debt, M&Aattorneys design hybrid agreements by starting with standardized templates and then materially altering the language to fit the specific circumstances of a deal, mixing bespoke and boilerplate terms.Merger agreements exhibit "constrained variation," in which transaction designers recombine elements from a common menu of governance mechanisms to produce contracts that are neither entirely unique nor carbon copies of earlier precedent.Such agreements are the transactional equivalent of mass customizable products, achieving economies of both scale and scope.
The mass customization of merger agreements only deepens the puzzle of how deal lawyers handle infra-transactional complexity. If transaction designers are not fully standardizing merger agreements, how are they then not falling victim to the challenge of coordinating changes across a series of customized contractual provisions? How does contractual mass customization work?
Answering that question requires supplementing our theory of how parties privately order exchange. Understanding how the costs of infratransactional complexity are managed requires further analysis of theprocessby which contracts are designed. The literature on contract economics typically abstracts away from the contract design process--assuming that contract terms map onto parties' preferences, subject to the limits of human foresight and differentials in bargaining power.Recent legal scholarship on the standardization of contract terms has taken an important step toward unpacking the contract design process, but that research's primary emphasis has been upon understanding how network effects shape and even inhibit design changes.This emphasis has led to theories of contractual evolution reminiscent of punctuated equilibrium models of institutional change.There is not yet a theory that explains the middle ground, where significant customization occurs at scale.
This Article addresses that middle ground by introducing a more comprehensive theoretical framework of how contracts are designed. That framework includes two paradigmatic approaches that transaction designers might pursue in order to manage infra-transactional complexity. First, as has already been recognized by some scholars, designers may use a "modularity" strategy to manage the costs of infra-transactional complexity.Modular designs manage complexity by isolating discrete sub-systems from one another.So long as all sub-systems comply with a standard interface rule, they can be adjusted independently and asynchronously of one another, thus reducing the costs of change within the system.The second approach, which has largely been overlooked in legal literature, is "flexible specialization," whereby thick connections between sub-systems are maintained and the costs of changing those interlocking components are managed by fostering organizational routines that allow transaction designers to quickly coordinate adjustments across the integrated system.Those routines reduce the costs of change by making information transparent throughout the system, reducing barriers to communication, and learning among the designers tasked with maintaining the system.
Whether modular design or flexible specialization is used has important implications for doctrine, policy, and research.Therefore, this Article undertakes a preliminary empirical study of the process of contract innovation in the M&A market. Whereas recent scholarship has persuasively argued that the broad collection of contracts memorializing an M&A transaction are "unbundled" according to a modular logic,this study focuses squarely on the merger agreement at the heart of the deal, asking whether that contract andthe multi-lawyer team that designs it exhibit evidence of modularity or flexible specialization. The available evidence suggests that flexible specialization plays a significant role in the design of complex merger agreements, and, in turn, that the application of modular design to these complex contracts has its limits.
This Article uses methods from systems engineering and network analysis to study the structure of both merger agreements and the law firms that designed them for evidence supporting either the modularity thesis or flexible specialization thesis. This Article is the first to employ such methods, and it is important to underscore the preliminary nature of the results reported here. The methods introduced here complement a small but growing body of research using natural language processing techniques to study contract design, and an important project for subsequent work is to combine both approaches to achieve more detailed and rigorous analyses.
, a sample of merger agreements, hand-collected from public company Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) filings, is analyzed for evidence of modular subdivisions.The results of that analysis reveal contracts with thickly interconnected sub-systems, providing limited evidence that merger agreements are purely modular, and support for the argument that flexible specialization plays a role in agreement design. Second, the law firms that designed the sampled merger agreements are analyzed for evidence of modular or integrated structure. A sample of M&A deal teams, hand-collected from the publicly available press releases of three major New York law firms, is examined, resulting in little evidence of discernable modules within the three firms. Rather, it appears that deal teams repeatedly recombine in unique configurations from deal to deal, promoting the dissemination of design-relevant information throughout the firm and, in turn, the tacit routines that foster rapid learning among the transactional lawyers. Taken together, those preliminary results suggest that flexible specialization is an important part ofdeal lawyers' strategy for achieving the mass customization of merger agreements.
The vision of private ordering that emerges from the analysis emphasizes the role that the network of deal lawyers plays. Path dependencies appear to be moderated by fluid organizational routines, which simultaneously interrogate prior practice as they provide stability for the innovation process. The preliminary results here should not, of course, be construed to suggest that modularity plays no role in the design of complex agreements. Additional research, ranging from more rigorous quantitative analyses to detailed ethnographic studies, beyond the preliminary analysis here is required to determine whether modularity plays a more nuanced role, perhaps at different stages of the design process. It is quite possible that subsequent research will find that a sophisticated combination of flexible specialization and modularity is often employed. Thus, the results here make a subtler and, ultimately, more intriguing point: flexible specialization should be considered one important factor among many to be considered in the diverse production system that designs complex commercial transactions.
Complex markets with contract design regimes that include a flexible specialization strategy demand infrastructure as dynamic as they are. In that respect, this Article underscores recent calls for a contingent approach to contract enforcement, with the appropriate interpretive regime determined by the underlying characteristics of a given transaction.This study adds an important dimension to that argument by demonstrating that the integrated nature of complex agreements is a variable that may restrict or amplify, in unexpected ways, the scope of court intervention in a contract dispute.
, the preliminary results suggesting that the M&A market includes a logic of flexible specialization challenge deterministic accounts of the legal industry's transformation and highlight the overlooked trade-offs that disruption of the market for contract design services presents. This issue is important because many markets are currently undergoing a period of significant change. For the past generation, the organization of production has been changing, as an economic landscape dominated by vertically-integrated companies engaged in arm's-length supply relationships has given way to hand-in-glove collaborative contracting arrangements.If thestory of contract institutions during 19th and 20th century industrialization is one of scaling a universal set of governance institutions across a new national market,then one of the stories of contract in the 21st century economy is the dramatic scaling of governance institutionswithinexchange relationships between leaner companies inhabiting innovation networks.That revolution in economic organization is accompanied by new technological developments that present the possibility of new forms of market infrastructure. For instance, the advent of blockchain technology as a potential (if largely untested) disruptive technology for "smart contracting" emphasizes the need to understand the design and evolution of contract institutions by presenting the possibility of parties using an entirely different platform from traditional legal infrastructure for creating and enforcing agreements.
, and finally, in order to improve our models of contractual innovation, this Article demonstrates the need for more detailed theoretical and empirical research on the interaction effects between governance mechanisms in an agreement.That work would, for example, explore how interdependencies affect the evolution of a given provision or set of provisions over time, providing a finely-grained mapping of contractual innovation and moving beyond the single-governance mechanisms studies that currentlydominate the literature.The empirical methods outlined here for mapping the network topology of complex agreements provide a foundation for that subsequent work.
This Article proceeds as follows. Part I explains the motivation behind this study, outlining the existing literature on contract design and demonstrating the need for new approaches to analyze complex contracts.Part II outlines the empirical methods employed here and tests the hypotheses that complex contracts are either modular or integrated systems by applying those methods to a sample of merger agreements.The results of those tests suggest that merger agreements and the organizations that design them are integrated, rather than modular, systems. Part III discusses the implications of those preliminary results for (1) doctrines of contract interpretation, (2) industrial policy with respect to the market for corporate control, and (3) next steps in the positive study of contract design.

questions.question: Do transaction designers manage infra-transactional complexity in complex contracts by using modular designs or by using flexible specialization?
questions.answer: They manage it through flexible specialization, with modular design showing clear limits.

questions.question: Are complex merger agreements themselves organized as modular subsystems or as thickly interconnected (integrated) systems?
questions.answer: They are thickly interconnected, integrated systems rather than purely modular subdivisions.

questions.question: Do the law firms and deal teams that design complex agreements exhibit modular organizational structure or integrated, flexible-specialization routines that enable mass customization?
questions.answer: They exhibit integrated, flexible-specialization routines, with deal teams recombining rather than operating in discernible modules.

Does standardizing the form and language of legal opinions and contract documents reduce negotiation time, transaction costs, and inefficient or overly broad opinion requests?
Do recurring, modular 'contract patterns' systematically structure how attorneys draft agreements and how those agreements interlock and scale into complex transactions and markets?

Why and by what mechanisms are contractual innovations and standardized clauses created, disseminated, and adopted across legal markets?

How can institutional and interpersonal contexts (adjudication fora, reputational networks, repeat dealings, and professional practices) substitute for formal intellectual-property protection and affect incentives for contractual innovation?

Why are complex commercial contracts frequently long, redundant, and written in dense legalese - is this primarily due to reliance on prior-transaction forms, form-based production processes, editorial churning, branding incentives, or other causes?

Should empirical contract research prioritize testing existing theories or seek new interdisciplinary explanations for real-world contracting puzzles?
Do courts' efforts to discover and enforce a shared intent for semantically degraded boilerplate create significant social or market costs?
What speech-act function does entering into a complex business contract serve: creating enforceable promises or setting a framework that enables non-legal governance and cooperation?

What factors explain the persistence or 'stickiness' of particular disclosure and boilerplate practices-do market norms and network effects keep standard language unchanged despite substantive shifts?

Can pattern-language approaches, standardized clause libraries, XML-style structured contract languages, or other 'standard-clause' methods measurably improve contract intelligibility, reduce drafting errors, and serve as effective default rules without unduly rigidifying contracting?
Do elite contract drafters largely copy boilerplate blindly or actively tailor language over time, and how does editorial churning affect clause evolution?
To what extent are complex agreements organized as modular subsystems (enabling mass customization) versus thickly interconnected integrated systems, and how does that shape transaction design?
Why do persistent, costly, or apparently nonfunctional boilerplate clauses persist in sophisticated contracts?
Are complex merger agreements modular subsystems or tightly integrated systems, and how does that structure affect drafting and interpretation?
Why do some inefficient or nonfunctional contract features persist in markets despite competition - is path dependence, network effects, or branding responsible?
Does drafting public merger agreements come from common standardized templates or evolve across generations of precedents, and how significant is cross-deal textual heterogeneity?

Do elite contract drafters and sophisticated market participants tend to copy boilerplate verbatim, self-consciously adapt it, or actively lead innovations, and who drives adoption of new standard terms across markets?
Do organizational approaches to studying private contracts better explain their public, social, and political effects than transaction-cost/opportunism-focused models?
Can a single general theory of contractual innovation account for diverse incentives and dissemination pathways, or is contractual innovation inherently idiosyncratic?

Do legal, institutional, and normative features (statutory backstops, professional practices, standardized forms, repeat-dealing norms) reduce the need for bespoke contract customization and thereby lower transaction costs?

How do transaction designers manage infra-transactional complexity in large contracts - by modular designs or by flexible specialization - and what are the implications for drafting, negotiation, and enforcement?

Do law firms and transactional deal teams organize contract production as modular, standardized subsystems that enable mass customization, or as integrated, flexible-specialization routines, and how do these organizational forms affect drafting quality, diffusion, and persistence of boilerplate?
How do standardized forms, firm templates, intermediaries, and market participants drive convergence or heterogeneity in transactional documentation across deals and jurisdictions?
Do market learning and network externalities cause firms to converge on standardized contract terms rather than customize or innovate them?
Who creates contractual innovations, why do they create them, and to what extent do elite law firms capture informational advantages that deliver incremental value to clients?
Is drafting complex contracts as flexible stage-setting (for future accommodation) superior to exhaustive literal specification given limits of knowledge and language?
Do contract drafters typically copy boilerplate blindly across deals or actively tailor and evolve terms, and what organizational routines explain their behavior?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 67dukelj1!!ARTICLE: THE BLACK HOLE PROBLEM IN COMMERCIAL BOILERPLATE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE BLACK HOLE PROBLEM IN COMMERCIAL BOILERPLATE

shared_topics.topic: interpretation problems posed by standardized boilerplate terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how repetitiously used boilerplate (e.g., pari passu) can lose shared meaning and create a judicial 'black hole' that frustrates interpretation, while Paper B situates boilerplate within a broader tradeoff between standardization and customization and examines how such standardized terms complicate interpretation within dense contractual systems.

shared_topics.topic: infra-transactional complexity (complexity within contracts) and its effects on drafting and enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper B develops a framework for infra-transactional complexity and shows how dense interdependencies in merger agreements raise costs for design and judicial enforcement; Paper A documents a related phenomenon where complexity-through-repetition and encrustation of boilerplate undermines communicative clarity and increases litigation costs for courts and markets.

shared_topics.topic: the contract design process, private ordering, and barriers to revising problematic terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies coordination and agency costs that prevent market actors from revising black-hole boilerplate after an adverse judicial reading, and Paper B analyzes how transaction designers (law firms and deal teams) organize—via modularity or flexible specialization—to manage complexity and implement design changes across deals.

shared_topics.topic: implications for contract doctrine and tailored judicial approaches
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues for rethinking contract doctrine because searching for lost shared intent in black-hole boilerplate imposes social costs, while Paper B advocates a contingent approach to contract enforcement that aligns interpretive regimes with underlying contract architecture (modular vs integrated).

shared_topics.topic: use of empirical and text/network methods to study contractual form and evolution
shared_topics.justification: Paper A assembles a dataset of pari passu clauses and conducts interviews to trace how boilerplate evolved and resisted revision, and Paper B introduces systems-engineering and network-analysis methods (and calls for combining NLP) to map interdependencies within merger agreements and the organizations that design them.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 82templrev1!!ARTICLE: DISPUTING BOILERPLATE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: DISPUTING BOILERPLATE

shared_topics.topic: standardization (boilerplate) versus customized contract drafting
shared_topics.justification: Both papers interrogate the degree to which commercial contracts rely on boilerplate versus bespoke drafting: Paper A contrasts highly modular/standard templates with the mass-customized, hybrid merger agreement, while Paper B empirically evaluates the presumed standardization of sovereign bond enforcement clauses and documents meaningful departures from boilerplate.

shared_topics.topic: why standard terms persist (stickiness, preference, or organizational choice)
shared_topics.justification: Both works question standard-explanations for frozen contract language—Paper B tests the 'stickiness' hypothesis versus genuine preference for litigation or arbitration, and Paper A examines whether standardization is a rational response to infra-transactional complexity or whether alternative organizational strategies (like flexible specialization) explain persistence.

shared_topics.topic: empirical analysis of real contract text and variation across deals/issuers
shared_topics.justification: Both articles rely on hand-collected, systematic samples of real contracts to map heterogeneity: Paper A applies network and systems methods to merger agreements to reveal interdependencies, while Paper B surveys sovereign bond indentures across many issuers to show cross-issuer and intra-issuer patterns in enforcement terms.

shared_topics.topic: implications of contract design for enforcement and judicial interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Both papers link contract structure to downstream enforcement issues: Paper B focuses on how forum, arbitration, and sovereign-immunity clauses shape dispute resolution, and Paper A argues that infra-transactional complexity and interdependent provisions affect courts' interpretive burdens and the appropriate doctrines for intervention.

shared_topics.topic: the role of organizational and market structures (firms, networks, status) in driving contract innovation
shared_topics.justification: Both studies consider how the organization of designers and market position shape contract change—Paper A analyzes law-firm deal teams, network effects, and flexible specialization in producing customized agreements, while Paper B highlights heterogeneity across issuers and innovation emerging from lower-status or niche market players.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A SHORT HISTORY OF THE CHOICE-OF-LAW CLAUSE

shared_topics.topic: diffusion and historical evolution of standardized clause language (e.g., choice-of-law and deal provisions)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces the historical emergence, drafting changes, and slow diffusion of the choice-of-law clause across centuries of form books and court cases, while Paper B documents how modern deal provisions in merger agreements have grown and evolved in complexity and form, treating clause-level change as an object of empirical study.

shared_topics.topic: how contract drafters' practices and organizational routines shape contract design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A questions assumptions of rational, unitary drafters by showing puzzling additions and omissions in choice-of-law clauses, and Paper B analyzes how multi-lawyer deal teams and firm routines (flexible specialization) drive the mass customization of contracts.

shared_topics.topic: the tradeoff between standardization (boilerplate) and customization in managing infra-transactional complexity
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how standardized choice-of-law templates responded (slowly) to doctrinal shifts, and Paper B theorizes and empirically studies the tension between boilerplate standardization and bespoke recombination (constrained variation) as ways to cope with contract complexity.

shared_topics.topic: the relationship between contract form/complexity and judicial interpretation or enforcement regimes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on how courts, legislatures, and restatements have interpreted and enforced choice-of-law clauses (shaping drafting), while Paper B links contract integration and complexity to limits on court intervention and argues for contingent interpretive regimes based on contract architecture.

shared_topics.topic: empirical, text-based study of real-world contracts using hand-collected corpora and novel methods
shared_topics.justification: Paper A builds a hand-collected historical dataset of thousands of choice-of-law clauses and surveys form books to study drafting practice, and Paper B hand-collects merger agreements and deal-team data and introduces network and systems-analysis methods to map contract structure and innovation.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 77chikentlrev59!!SYMPOSIUM: THEORY INFORMS BUSINESS PRACTICE:WHY CONTRACTS ARE WRITTEN IN "LEGALESE"
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: THEORY INFORMS BUSINESS PRACTICE:WHY CONTRACTS ARE WRITTEN IN "LEGALESE"

shared_topics.topic: the use and persistence of contract forms/boilerplate in drafting complex deals
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how lawyers reuse and iteratively modify prior contracts (the “form”), showing why boilerplate proliferates and persists despite redundancy and ambiguity; Paper B documents that M&A lawyers likewise begin with templates and then materially alter them, treating boilerplate as the baseline for customization.

shared_topics.topic: the organizational production process of contract design within law firms (division of labor, junior/senior roles, and routines)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A models the drafting process as a production system that offloads work to junior associates and embeds learning through reuse of forms; Paper B empirically studies deal teams and argues that law-firm routines and recombining deal teams (flexible specialization) are central to how contracts are actually designed.

shared_topics.topic: path-dependence and network effects versus efficiency in explaining contractual outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames contract imperfections as potentially path-dependent or network-driven rather than purely efficient choices, and analyzes switching costs; Paper B engages the same tension by examining how network effects and path dependencies in precedent interact with routines that enable ongoing innovation in contract design.

shared_topics.topic: managing infra-transactional complexity and the resulting trade-offs in contract quality and interpretability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents how accumulated contingency clauses, redundancy, and ad hoc band-aids create cumbersome, sometimes ambiguous agreements as a byproduct of the drafting process; Paper B explicitly theorizes infra-transactional complexity, its costs for modification and enforcement, and studies how that complexity shapes contract architecture.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between standardization and mass-customization (modularity vs bespoke tailoring) as a strategy to cope with time and transaction costs
shared_topics.justification: Paper A describes why lawyers defer to standard forms to save time yet produce second-best, customized fixes under deadline pressure; Paper B analyzes why merger agreements show constrained variation (mass customization), testing whether designers adopt modular templates or coordinate changes via flexible specialization to balance economies of scale and deal-specific tailoring.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 94iowalrev937!!ARTICLE: VALUES AND VALUE CREATION IN PUBLIC-PRIVATE TRANSACTIONS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: VALUES AND VALUE CREATION IN PUBLIC-PRIVATE TRANSACTIONS

shared_topics.topic: the role of deal lawyers as value-creating transaction engineers
shared_topics.justification: Both papers treat transactional lawyers as active creators of deal value rather than mere drafters: Paper A analyzes how law firms and deal teams produce novel contractual architectures that enable tailored exchanges, while Paper B theorizes lawyers as transactional engineers who structure deals to create economic and programmatic value (including 'regulatory translation').

shared_topics.topic: managing contractual complexity (modularity vs coordinated routines)
shared_topics.justification: Both engage substantively with how parties cope with complex multi-term agreements: Paper A develops a theoretical distinction between modularity and flexible specialization as strategies for managing infra-transactional complexity, and Paper B examines how lawyers confront and structure the complex, often conflicting objectives (economic and public-policy) inherent in public-private transactions.

shared_topics.topic: customization versus standardization of contracts
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze the tension between boilerplate standardization and bespoke drafting: Paper A documents 'constrained variation' and mass customization in M&A agreements and the firm routines that support it, while Paper B emphasizes tailoring deal structures to particular public-policy goals and argues that lawyers actively reshape transaction forms to produce different kinds of value.

shared_topics.topic: the influence of public/institutional environments on private contract design and enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Both works consider how external institutional actors and infrastructures affect contracting choices: Paper A links contract architecture to implications for court interpretation and broader market infrastructure (including technological platforms), and Paper B foregrounds the regulatory/state context—positions on the public–private spectrum—and shows how that context reshapes lawyers' structuring choices through regulatory translation.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 53vandjtransnatll1023!!ARTICLE: Deal Breakage in Domestic and Cross-Border Mergers and Acquisitions: New Data and Avenues for Research
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Deal Breakage in Domestic and Cross-Border Mergers and Acquisitions: New Data and Avenues for Research

shared_topics.topic: role of deal lawyers, law firms, and organizational routines in structuring transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically studies how multi-lawyer teams design merger agreements and argues that flexible specialization and firm routines enable mass customization of contracts; Paper B foregrounds the practical role of M&A counsel in delivering deal certainty and frames lawyer behavior and drafting choices as central to whether transactions survive to closing, motivating the need for granular deal outcome data.

shared_topics.topic: empirical methods and datasets for studying M&A contracts and outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A introduces systems-engineering and network-analysis methods applied to hand-collected merger agreements and law‑firm deal teams to map interdependencies among provisions, while Paper B constructs a comprehensive, classified dataset of large definitive M&A deals (1996–2018) designed to support systematic empirical analysis of deal breakage and other outcomes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 39harvintllj1!!ARTICLE: ACTS OF STATE AND FOREIGN SOVEREIGN OBLIGATIONS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: ACTS OF STATE AND FOREIGN SOVEREIGN OBLIGATIONS

shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that predictable enforceability of sovereign contracts is essential to reduce political risk and attract foreign investment, and shows how the act of state doctrine undermines that predictability; Paper B shows that courts' interpretive regimes and uncertainty about enforcement of embedded provisions matter for how parties design complex contracts and manage transactional risk.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes doctrinal limits (the act of state rule) and advocates a narrowly tailored waiver exception to allow judicial adjudication of sovereign contracts, while Paper B argues for a contingent approach to contract enforcement—adapting judicial interpretation to the underlying characteristics of complex agreements—and emphasizes that doctrinal choices affect private contracting outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: private ordering and contract design as tools to allocate and internalize transaction‑specific risks
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats sovereign contractual commitments and guarantees as private‑ordering devices by which host governments assume political risk for investors, whereas Paper B studies how transaction designers (via modularity, standardization, or flexible specialization) structure agreements to allocate risks and cope with infra‑transactional complexity.

shared_topics.topic: need for institutional or legal reform and infrastructure to support modern contracting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes doctrinal reform (a waiver exception) to make sovereign contracts reliably enforceable in U.S. courts, and Paper B calls for doctrinal, empirical, and infrastructural innovations (including alternative platforms and new enforcement regimes) to accommodate the design and enforcement of increasingly complex contracts.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: INDUSTRIAL AND COMPETITION POLICIES IN MEXICO

shared_topics.topic: how governance architecture influences market efficiency and distribution of benefits
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that import‑substitution and protectionist industrial policies produced market distortions that prevented efficiency gains from reaching consumers, while Paper B shows that contract architecture (standardization, modularity, or flexible specialization) affects transaction costs, enforcement, and thus the efficiency of commercial exchanges and the allocation of gains from deals.

shared_topics.topic: the role of complexity and coordination costs in designing market governance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights that poorly designed regulation complicates reform and decision‑making, creating barriers to controlling market power, and Paper B centers on 'infra‑transactional' complexity — showing how interdependencies among contract terms raise coordination costs and constrain how agreements can be changed or enforced.

shared_topics.topic: implications of design choices for enforcement and institutional intervention
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that regulatory design determines how effectively authorities can intervene to promote competition, and Paper B links contract integration/modularity to the appropriate interpretive and enforcement regimes (including courts and alternative infrastructures), arguing that design features constrain or enable enforcement options.

shared_topics.justification: Both papers emphasize human cognitive limits as a constraint on contract design: Paper B develops the notion of cognitive load and links complexity to misunderstanding and mistakes, and Paper A highlights how infra-transactional interdependencies challenge designers' ability to anticipate effects and thus shape choices about how to structure and coordinate provisions.

shared_topics.justification: Both articles consider how complexity should affect courts and policy: Paper A argues that integrated, complex agreements call for contingent interpretive regimes and may limit or expand court intervention, while Paper B explores whether courts should adopt literal versus liberal interpretive techniques depending on the contract's complexity and the contracting environment.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights cross‑border conflicts (e.g., differing segregation rules and bankruptcy regimes) that complicate the legal resolution of customer property claims, while Paper B explores how contract complexity and new platforms (including calls for contingent interpretive doctrines and blockchain/smart contracting) affect courts' ability to interpret and enforce agreements—both examine limits of existing enforcement regimes when faced with complex, multi‑jurisdictional transactions.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on market infrastructure (clearinghouses, depositories, regulators and private acquirers like ING) and their role in restoring liquidity and containing systemic risk after a default, while Paper B examines the institutional infrastructure of contract production (law firm routines, templates, and design processes) and how that architecture shapes transactional resilience and market functioning—both analyze how institutional design choices influence systemic stability and the conduct of markets.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Mozambican Illegal Debts: Testing the Odious Debt Doctrine

shared_topics.justification: Paper A links the structure and secrecy of the Mozambican borrowing to market reactions (donor suspension, currency collapse, downgrade) and subsequent debt-restructuring litigation, while Paper B shows that contractual architecture and production of agreements (modularity vs flexible specialization) shape transaction costs, enforcement practices, and the institutional infrastructure needed for markets to function and adapt.

papers.node_id: 67dukelj1!!ARTICLE: THE BLACK HOLE PROBLEM IN COMMERCIAL BOILERPLATE
papers.title: ARTICLE: THE BLACK HOLE PROBLEM IN COMMERCIAL BOILERPLATE
papers.authors: Stephen J. Choi; Mitu Gulati; Robert E. Scott
papers.abstract:
A question that courts face whenever they are asked to interpret a standard provision in a commercial contract is how to determine what the parties understood that provision to mean when they contracted. The interpretive goal in contract cases is to recover and then enforce the parties' apparent intentions, as they existed at the time of contracting. This goal implies that courts will attempt to interpret even ambiguous terms in a manner consistent with the ex ante intentions of the contracting parties in so far as a court can recover those intentions from the contract or the surrounding context.But standardized terms in boilerplate contracts between sophisticated parties are vulnerable to misinterpretation. At the limit, a boilerplate term that is reused for decades and without reflection merely because it is part of a standard-form package of terms, can be emptied of any recoverable meaning: this creates a contractual black hole.More commonly, terms that havelost much meaning still may provoke litigation over essentially meaningless variations in the boilerplate language. In this latter case of contractual grey holes,courts may be functionally incapable of devising a plausible meaning that was attached to the linguistic variations at the time the contract was drafted. Thus, regardless of whether a boilerplate term has lost all or only almost all meaning, courts will face an interpretation conundrum that we collectively term the "black hole" problem.
The dilemma that courts sometimes face when interpreting boilerplate is an inherent cost of the reliance on standardized contract terms in commercial contracts. Boilerplate terms are ubiquitous in commercial contracting because they offer the efficiency advantages of standardization. Those advantages include the development of a uniform system of communication that is independent of any particular contractual context.Thus, parties in heterogeneous environments whowish to communicate a shared intent can embody that intent in a fixed and reliable formulation whose meaning does not vary with the nature of the contract or its context.Unfortunately, the very elements of fixed and unchanging meaning that make boilerplate terms attractive are the same elements that can lead to the process of repetition without reflection that contributes to the erosion of that meaning over time.
In addition to the ordinary risks of obsolescence, the repetitious use of boilerplate has two pernicious effects that can undermine the utility of some boilerplate terms. The first effect is "rote usage": some standardized terms may get used by rote so consistently that they lose a shared meaning and become a ritualized legal incantation."Encrustation" is a second cost of too much repetition: the intelligibility of language deteriorates significantly as legal jargon is added to standard formulations, leading to linguistic variations of the same clause.This process further weakens the communicative properties of boilerplate terms, reducing even more their reliability as signals of what the parties really meant.In combination, terms that develop linguistic variations and thereafter are repeated by rote, even after the original meaning has been largely lost, can become contractual black holes.
Contractual black holes present a heightened risk that courts may be persuaded to adopt an interpretation of the term at issue that is antithetical to the functioning of a market that relies on the standard contract to regulate the rights and duties of the participating parties. The market may have disregarded the term before a court gives the black hole a contemporary interpretation. Nonetheless, the market may have an understanding of what the term does not mean, oftenbecause of the high cost to market participants of an aberrant interpretation. Unfortunately, correcting the courts' interpretation in such a case can be a slow and difficult process, even when the judicial error imposes high costs. This resistance to revision is a function of what we will call the "evidentiary vacuum" that results when a term loses its original meaning and lacks an evidentiary record of its contemporary meaning. Here the chance of a court issuing an aberrant interpretation is heightened as compared with a boilerplate term with a well-known meaning.
These conditions appear to describe the case of the pari passu clause, a boilerplate formulation common to sovereign debt contracts for nearly 200 years whose contemporary meaning was hopelessly unclear.The recent history of judicial interpretation of this clause began in Brussels in a case against the Republic of Peru in September 2000, in which a court issued the first interpretation of the clause in at least a half century.The same interpretation of pari passu was affirmed by a federal court in New York in a case against the Republic of Argentina in December 2011,and affirmed again on appeal in that same case in October 2012and August 2013.In each of these cases, the courts endorsed an interpretation of a particular variation of pari passu that required holdout creditors to be paid in full as a condition to the sovereigns paying consenting creditors under a restructuring agreement. Even though this interpretation effectively undermined efforts by sovereigns to restructure their bonds, and even though the courts' interpretation was widely vilified in the market, meaningful revisions to the language of the boilerplate term did not even begin to appear until late 2014.
The extent of rote usage and encrustation in commonly used boilerplate remains an open question because the issue is only nowbeginning to be examined by legal and economic scholars.But preliminary evidence from other markets where standard form contracts are ubiquitous suggests that the pari passu saga is representative of a larger phenomenon, extending beyond sovereign bond contracts to other contexts where boilerplate is commonly used, including insurance and merger and acquisition agreements.To the extent this problem exists more broadly, it argues for a shift in contract doctrine away from the futile and ultimately costly effort to discover a shared meaning that no longer exists.In this Article, we explore whether courts, or other state actors, might better deal with contractual black holes in boilerplate contracts. Our purpose is to begin the scholarly focus on the effects of this phenomenon by using the pari passu story as a prototypical exemplar. We use both qualitative and quantitative data to support the claim that courts searching for shared intent in the case of black holes in standardized contracting can result in substantial social costs.
The Article proceeds as follows. In Part I, we focus on identifying the causes and effects of black holes in standard form commercialboilerplate. We show how both agency and coordination costs peculiar to the inertia that results from black holes can undermine the standard assumption that commercial parties will promptly revise an unanticipated interpretation that generates market inefficiencies. Part II frames the inquiry: Does the celebrated dispute over the meaning of the pari passu clause provide evidence that the current means of revising black holes impose large and uncompensated social costs? In Part III, we evaluate a dataset on pari passu clauses assembled from over 1500 sovereign and quasi-sovereign issuances in the period from June 1, 2011 to May 30, 2016, together with interviews with the participants in the market. Part IV discusses the implications of the finding that, at least in certain markets, commercial actors face extraordinary difficulties in repairing black hole boilerplate following what the market perceives as an aberrant judicial interpretation of the term's contemporary meaning. These difficulties present a collective action problem whose solution can be daunting owing to the combination of coordination and agency costs that may impair the efficiency of standardized commercial contracting in large-scale markets.

questions.question: Whether standardized contractual boilerplate commonly loses its shared, recoverable meaning through repetition and linguistic variation, producing clauses that courts cannot plausibly interpret (i.e., contractual "black holes").
questions.answer: The paper argues that repetition without reflection (rote usage) and encrustation in standardized boilerplate can erode or even empty clauses of shared, recoverable meaning, creating black/grey holes that courts cannot plausibly interpret.

questions.question: Whether courts' efforts to discover and enforce a shared intent for such semantically degraded boilerplate generate significant social and market costs or inefficiencies.
questions.answer: Yes—courts’ attempts to recover and enforce a shared intent for degraded boilerplate can yield aberrant interpretations that undermine market functioning, generate substantial social costs, and are hard to correct due to an evidentiary vacuum.

questions.question: Whether market participants can effectively revise or repair degraded boilerplate after an adverse or unexpected judicial interpretation, or whether coordination and agency problems prevent timely, collective correction.
questions.answer: The paper finds that coordination and agency costs create collective action problems that impede timely, collective correction, making it difficult for market participants to revise degraded boilerplate after adverse judicial interpretations, as illustrated by the delayed revisions to pari passu clauses.
