papers.node_id: 82lawcontempprobi!!ARTICLE: THE BUTTERFLY EFFECT IN BOILERPLATE CONTRACT INTERPRETATION
papers.title: ARTICLE: THE BUTTERFLY EFFECT IN BOILERPLATE CONTRACT INTERPRETATION
papers.abstract:
Legal disputes relating to contract interpretation are frequently conceptualized as one-and-done affairs. A court will adopt what it considers to be a reasonable interpretation of the contract, rule in favor of one of the parties, and decide the case. Neither the judge nor the litigants tend to think overmuch about how the decision will affect other contract users going forward. In cases where the language being interpreted is contract boilerplate, however, past interpretive decisions will inevitably affect future ones. Just as a butterfly flapping its wings in Tokyo can change the weather in London, so too can a judicial decision interpreting boilerplate language alter the meaning of identical language in thousands of other contracts. To speak of the "butterfly effect" in contract interpretation, therefore, is to describe the effect that a single interpretive decision can have on the interests of far-flung parties not involved in the litigation at hand.
This special issue ofLaw and Contemporary Problemsis devoted to exploring the butterfly effect in boilerplate contract interpretation.This short essay introducing the volume has two objectives. First, it provides a general introduction to the butterfly effect and explains, conceptually, why it is useful to think about boilerplate contract interpretation through this particular lens. Second, it provides summaries of the other articles in the special issue, each of which sheds important light on the workings of the butterfly effect. These contributions, it is hoped, will prove useful to future scholars, judges, and   legislatures grappling with the interpretive challenges posed by ambiguous contract boilerplate.

questions.question: Whether and how a judicial interpretation of boilerplate contract language creates spillover effects on the meaning and enforcement of identical boilerplate across many other contracts (the "butterfly effect").
questions.answer: Yes; when courts interpret boilerplate, past decisions inevitably influence future interpretations, so a single ruling can alter the meaning of identical language in thousands of other contracts and affect parties not before the court.

questions.question: How large and practically significant those downstream effects are - e.g., how many contracts and parties are affected and with what consequences for rights, duties, and transactions.
questions.answer: The effect can be large, potentially changing the meaning of identical boilerplate in thousands of contracts and impacting the interests of far-flung nonparties, though the abstract provides no further quantification or specific consequences.

questions.question: What institutional or normative responses (by courts, legislatures, and scholars) are appropriate to manage, limit, or harness such cross-contract externalities from single interpretive decisions.
questions.answer: The essay recommends conceptualizing boilerplate interpretation through the butterfly-effect lens and offers summaries to assist scholars, judges, and legislatures in grappling with these challenges, but it does not propose specific institutional or normative reforms.

papers.node_id: 1988uilllrev401!!ARTICLE: THE CAPITALIZATION OF SOVEREIGN DEBT: AN INTRODUCTION © 1988 Center for Transnational Legal Studies.
papers.title: ARTICLE: THE CAPITALIZATION OF SOVEREIGN DEBT: AN INTRODUCTION © 1988 Center for Transnational Legal Studies.
papers.abstract:
A sovereign debt crisis results when the inflow of foreign exchange into the debtor countryis insufficient to cover the country's payments in foreign currencyover a prolonged period.  A "liquidity crisis" of this kind ends when the balance between the inflow of foreign currency and the country's payments in foreign exchange is restored by means such as reducing or rescheduling external debt service payments, scaling back of imports, stimulating exports and tourism, or resuming foreign borrowing. The debtor country's immediate difficulty, however, results from the need to purchase imports and make external debt service payments in scarce foreign exchange.  Were these obligations capable of being discharged inlocalcurrency, this particular constraint would disappear.
Unfortunately, foreign exporters and creditors typically have little desire to accept the debtor country's local currency in payment for their goods, services or credits, unless that currency can be freely converted outside the debtor country.  The makings of a mutually advantageous transaction may be present, however, if third parties who have a use for local currencycan be persuaded to purchase the debtor's foreign currency denominated obligations from the current holders and redeem these obligations for their equivalent value in local currency.  For such transactions to occur on any scale, an active secondary market in the trading of the external debt obligations of borrowers located in the debtor country must exist and, in many cases, the debtor government must also approve the discharge of such obligations with local currency.
Several debtor countries have instituted programs designed to encouragetransactions in which the country's external debt obligations are redeemed in local currency for specified purposes.Such debt/equity conversion programsare a response to several factors that were not present at the outset of the global debt crisis six years ago.  During this intervening period, the positions of the various parties caught up in a sovereign debt crisis have evolved along the following lines:
(i) The foreign commercial bank creditors of many sovereign borrowers no longer have any realistic hope that their credits will be repaid in the foreseeable future.  Instead, some banks see a dismal prospect of repeated reschedulings, periodic new money requests based on the level of existing credit exposure, and eroding margins. In the face of these unpleasantries, some banks are prepared to sell their sovereign loan assets for cash, even though this may involve accepting a discount from the face value of the loan.(ii) A frequent result of a national debt crisis is the debtor government's need to finance its own deficit from domestic credit markets. This can push local interest rates to prohibitively high levels and can leave local companies without their customary sources of financing for domestic operations.(iii) Foreign investors, who will have shown some reluctance to commit additional resources during the early years of the crisis, may be prepared to capitalize subsidiaries or commence new operations if the debtor country's financial prospects begin to improve or if there is a sufficient incentive for them to do so.(iv) The debtor government will probably want to stimulate foreign investment, particularly in priority sectors such as export production, after enduring several years of a contracting or, at best, a stagnant economy.  As long as the shadow of the country's debt problem remains visible, however, some of these investors may be chary of committing additional resources without a special inducement of some kind.(v) In any event, the debtor government will wish to reduce the level of its external debt stock and thereby alleviate to some degree its debt service burdens.
The recent conjunction of these factors in a number of debtor countries has given rise to debt/equity conversion programs.  In the garden-varietyconversion transaction, a foreign investor purchases the sovereign loan asset of a commercial bank at a discount, redeems the credit for its value in local currency, and invests the proceeds in a local enterprise, which may be a subsidiary of the foreign investor.  Thus, after the conversion transaction,
(a) the foreign investor will have obtained the local currency necessary to capitalize the local company at a highly favorable effective exchange rate -- a rate reflecting the discount the investor received when it purchased the loan from the bank;(b) the local company will have received an infusion of new capital without resorting to local borrowing;(c) the commercial bank will have received cash in hand for a loan whose ultimate repayment by the borrower was not expected to take place, if at all, until the indefinite future; and(d) the debtor country will have simultaneously (i) reduced its aggregate stock of external debt, (ii) encouraged foreign investment in a domestic industry and (iii) possibly removed a cantankerous lender from its creditor group.

questions.question: Whether debt/equity conversion programs-where foreign investors buy sovereign loan assets at a discount, redeem them for local currency, and invest the proceeds domestically-reduce a debtor country's external debt stock and stimulate foreign investment.
questions.answer: Yes—after a debt/equity conversion the debtor country simultaneously reduces its aggregate external debt stock and encourages foreign investment in domestic industry.

questions.question: Whether active secondary markets for external sovereign debt and creditor willingness to sell loans at discounts can alleviate a debtor country's foreign exchange (liquidity) constraints by enabling redemption of obligations in local currency.
questions.answer: Yes—if an active secondary market exists and creditors are willing to sell at discounts (with government approval where needed), third parties can buy the debt and redeem it in local currency, thereby removing the foreign-exchange constraint.

questions.question: Whether debt/equity conversion transactions produce mutually beneficial outcomes for the key parties (commercial banks, foreign investors, and the debtor government) compared with continued debt rescheduling or holdout creditor positions.
questions.answer: Yes—these conversions are described as mutually advantageous, giving investors local currency at a favorable effective rate, providing banks cash for loans unlikely to be repaid soon, and yielding the debtor country reduced external debt, more foreign investment, and possibly the removal of a cantankerous lender.

papers.node_id: 57harvintllj151!!ARTICLE: The Challenge of Legitimacy in Sovereign Debt Restructuring
papers.title: ARTICLE: The Challenge of Legitimacy in Sovereign Debt Restructuring
papers.abstract:
Something of a scholarly cottage industry exists to assess the legitimacy of major international organizations once they have been established, including by focusing on the degree to which these powerful actors are sufficientlyparticipatory, accountable, and respectful of fundamental values. This academic writing resonates with similar concerns voiced by civil society groups and the broader public, and the attention to these questions is unsurprising given that these institutions have become a focal point for popular discussion in recent decades. The international economic organizations, which now govern a significant swathe of transnational economic life, have been among the foremost targets in this commentary. Recent writing investigates the legitimacy of the World Trade Organization ("WTO"), the World Bank, the International Monetary Fund ("IMF" or "the Fund"), and the constellation of institutions and practices that make up the investor-state arbitration system.
Notably absent from this list is any dedicated transnational institution or mechanism for addressing sovereign debt issues--the myriad troubles that arise when sovereign state borrowers find themselves unable to pay their creditors, many of whom may be located overseas. This institutional omission hardly results from an absence of contemporary problems in the global debt arena, as anyone having even a cursory familiarity with international financial issues is well aware. Nor does it result from a historical failure to imagine the utility of such a mechanism on the part of key architects of the post-World War II economic system. Harry Dexter White, special adviser to the U.S. Treasury on international financial issues at the time, envisaged a dedicated commission that "could approach the problem [of sovereign debt] with a great deal more objectivity than could be true of a bondholders' committee … . It could in its recommendations take a broader point of view."Ultimately, a mechanism designed to deliberately incorporate this broader point of view, presumably addressing the reasonable concerns of both creditorsand debtors, never made it into the modern international economic order.
The resulting gap in the international financial architecture has produced deeply problematic outcomes. Commentators have found the "non-system" of sovereign debt sorely lacking--fragmented, inconsistent, and providing insufficient relief to reboot economic growth.Recent developments in sovereign debt litigation, including the extended and rancorous stalemate surrounding Argentina's 2001 debt default and subsequent restructuring, not to mention the specter of Greek exit from the Euro due to debt problems, have only deepened the widespread dissatisfaction with the current approach. As a result, key actors have called for serious consideration of a more coherent and comprehensive mechanism for debt workouts. The IMF recently undertook a major review of sovereign debt restructuring,and in October 2014 the United Nations General Assembly voted in favor of working toward a permanent restructuring system.This policy effort has joined and built upon significant academic attention to diagnosing the current problems and also proposing potential solutions.Although progress is hardly guaranteed, and previous efforts have come to naught, this work proceeds apace, and there is no indication that the need for more rationalized sovereign debt restructuring will subside anytime soon.
Given all this activity, it is surprising that the published writing thus far has lacked a specific focus on the question of legitimacy--even more so in light of the fact that this question is virtually guaranteed to frame ex post commentary on any institutionalized debt workout mechanism ("DWM") that does emerge. This Article seeks to bridge that gap by arguing that serious attention should be paid to the question of legitimacy in advance of negotiating and establishing a possible sovereign debt restructuring institution,and by considering more concretely what such attentiveness might mean in practice. Explicitly addressing these concerns early on may make such an institution more successful, both by helping to attract support ex ante (that is, in the initial development of any treaty, ad hoc, or soft law restructuring mechanism) and also by encouraging states and their creditors to actually use a DWM ex post. Such attention to legitimacy is especially important in the international arena, given the absence of a clear global enforcement mechanism and in light of the historical resistance of some states and other institutional actors to the development of a DWM.
But why would it matter on the ground whether a debt workout framework is considered legitimate? What might perceptions of legitimacy do for any given sovereign debt restructuring? A restructuring can be a fairly traumatic economic, social, and political event in the life of a country. While it should ideally offer financial relief in the form of extended payment schedules or a debt write-down, the process also can entail a fiscal consolidation that results in cuts to government programs and other austerity measures. Setting aside for now the question of when such measures can become counterproductive, these policies often have significant domestic distributional ramifications, and the resulting anger may erupt in economically and politically disruptive ways.While entirely understandable, this second-order disruption can add to and extend the distress and sacrifice already generated by the restructuring itself.
How does legitimacy play into this dynamic? Perhaps the unique feature of institutions or rules that are considered legitimate is their ability to encourage voluntary compliance--to command a higher degree of support or acquiescence than might otherwise exist in the absence of coercion or self-interest.A DWM perceived to be more legitimate could thus encourage a greater willingness on the part of domestic groups to engage in consensual restructuring processes and then implement the resulting agreements with relative equanimity, thereby minimizing the second-order disruptions that can accompany a restructuring. Of course, this is hardly to deny that the anger arising out of debt restructuring is frequently justified, and that it can direct attention to important imbalances of power both domestically and internationally. But if a consensual debt workout frequently is the right choice, which I assume for the purposes of this Article, then we should establish mechanisms to achieve restructuring in a smooth, efficient, and minimally disruptive manner. Ideally, any anger that remains would materialize not as destructive expressions of dissatisfaction with a DWM or a narrow restructuring outcome. Rather, it would be more productively channeledinto holding internal political elites accountable or perhaps into longer-term efforts to alter the structures and rules of global economic and political life. And, of course, this instrumental value of legitimacy only supports the inherent value of institutions that enable individuals and groups to comply with agreements as a result of considered choice rather than perceived duress or coercion.
All that said, a number of tensions and difficulties immediately emerge with an explicit focus on legitimacy, particularly given that the concept means different things to different people. Applying such a conceptually slippery term to the complex world of sovereign debt is no easy task. How do we define legitimacy, and what are the appropriate sources for such a definition? Which elements might enhance or diminish perceptions of the legitimacy of a DWM? To what degree do these factors fit together seamlessly, and how might they be in tension? Ultimately, what is reasonable to expect from something so politically fraught as sovereign debt restructuring? These are among the questions that this Article seeks to address.
Part I of this Article begins the discussion by introducing the multifaceted concept of legitimacy itself, laying out different schools of thought on the characteristics of a legitimate institutional order and developing a preliminary list of features applicable to the DWM context. Part II considers the institutional and historical background of debt restructuring in light of these themes to better understand the political and economic context of current discussions of a possible DWM. Part III lays out how two cognate domestic and transnational institutions attempt to meet standards associated with ideas of legitimacy, focusing on domestic insolvency laws and on investment treaty arbitration rules. Finally, Part IV of this Article offers preliminary recommendations for how a future DWM might attempt to satisfy calls for legitimacy, and briefly assesses existing proposals in light of these themes. This last section also highlights several political obstacles to incorporating the institutional features most associated with legitimacy, which stakeholders must consider and address in any negotiations. In foregrounding these concerns, this Article draws attention in advance to issues and controversies that will likely be relevant for the foreseeable future: any DWM will take some time to develop and, once established, will no doubt be subject to criticism (and perhaps modification) throughout its lifespan.

questions.question: How should legitimacy be conceptualized and operationalized when designing a sovereign debt restructuring mechanism?
questions.answer: Legitimacy should be treated as a multifaceted concept synthesized from multiple schools of thought and translated into a preliminary list of concrete design features to be incorporated early in negotiating a DWM so as to attract support and encourage its use.

questions.question: What institutional features increase perceptions of legitimacy for a sovereign debt restructuring mechanism?

Does greater perceived legitimacy of a sovereign debt restructuring mechanism increase voluntary compliance, encourage its use, and reduce the social and political disruptions that accompany restructurings?
questions.answer: Yes—because institutions perceived as legitimate elicit more voluntary compliance, a more legitimate DWM would likely attract greater ex ante support, be used more readily ex post, and reduce second-order social and political disruptions by fostering consensual participation and calmer implementation.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how specific contract 'patterns' (e.g., sticky clauses in sovereign bonds and securitizations) interlock to make contracts hard to value or restructure and can precipitate market freezes; Paper B examines how the existing structure of sovereign bond contracts and litigation history (e.g., Argentina) produces fragmented restructurings and motivates calls for a more coherent debt-workout mechanism.

shared_topics.topic: legitimacy, consent, and equity as design criteria for contractual and institutional arrangements
shared_topics.justification: Paper A raises normative concerns about consent, equity, and human-centered drafting when contracts (especially standardized or automated ones) bind individuals or markets; Paper B centers the argument that perceptions of legitimacy—fairness, participation, and accountability—are crucial for voluntary compliance with sovereign debt restructurings and for minimizing political and social disruption.

shared_topics.topic: how standardization/modularity and fragmentation of rules affect market functioning and crisis vulnerability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that modular, standardized contract patterns can create informationally insensitive, highly liquid instruments that nevertheless become impossible to value and cause cascading failures; Paper B documents how a fragmented, inconsistent 'non-system' for sovereign debt (lack of standard procedures or unified rules) undermines efficient restructurings and contributes to economic instability.

shared_topics.topic: the need for institutional (design) solutions and the political obstacles to reforming sovereign-debt governance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses a pattern-language lens to argue for rethinking contract design to prevent systemic breakdowns and to make contracting more adaptive; Paper B provides a detailed normative and institutional analysis of designing a debt-workout mechanism and identifies political barriers and trade-offs that any such institutional reform would face.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 83chikentlrev67!!ARTICLE: THE INVESTMENT CLIMATE, COMPETITION POLICY, AND ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT IN LATIN AMERICA
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE INVESTMENT CLIMATE, COMPETITION POLICY, AND ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT IN LATIN AMERICA

shared_topics.topic: political legitimacy and support for economic institutions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that effective competition law-policy depends on political support (noting incumbent firms' influence, lobbying, and government-business capture) and that weak political backing undermines enforcement; Paper B centers the legitimacy of a sovereign debt workout mechanism as decisive for its adoption, perceived fairness, and voluntary compliance by states and domestic constituencies.

shared_topics.topic: administrative capacity and enforcement constraints on institutional effectiveness
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents how inadequate resources and administrative capacity limit implementation and enforcement of competition laws in Latin America; Paper B highlights the lack of a clear enforcement mechanism and practical political obstacles that would constrain any centralized debt restructuring institution's ability to produce reliable outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: interaction between domestic institutions and international economic integration
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how trade liberalization, foreign investment, and international competition interact with domestic market structures (e.g., nontradables, distribution channels, cartels) to shape whether liberalization produces competitive outcomes; Paper B examines how international creditor–debtor relations and global institutional choices (IMF, UN initiatives, or absence of a DWM) influence domestic debt outcomes and the scope for orderly, cooperative restructurings.

shared_topics.topic: distributional and social consequences of economic policy and institutional decisions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A links competition policy to broad-based participation, poverty reduction, and mitigation of rent-seeking, arguing that market structure affects distributional outcomes; Paper B discusses how sovereign debt restructurings and attendant austerity measures have significant domestic distributional impacts and argues that perceived institutional legitimacy can shape social acceptance and the political fallout of those policies.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 70lawcontempprob53!!ARTICLE: INSOLVENCY PRINCIPLES AND THE ODIOUS DEBT DOCTRINE: THE MISSING LINK IN THE DEBATE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: INSOLVENCY PRINCIPLES AND THE ODIOUS DEBT DOCTRINE: THE MISSING LINK IN THE DEBATE

shared_topics.topic: normative legitimacy of debt relief mechanisms and debt forgiveness
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how perceptions of legitimacy (participation, accountability, fairness) shape the acceptability and effectiveness of a formal debt workout mechanism (DWM), while Paper B engages the normative case for relieving (odious) sovereign debts—arguing forgiveness can be justified to rehabilitate a state and protect citizens—thus both address why and on what grounds debt relief is considered legitimate.

shared_topics.topic: using domestic insolvency principles as models for sovereign debt resolution
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly examines domestic insolvency laws as a cognate institutional model to inform the design and legitimacy of a DWM, and Paper B evaluates the odious debt doctrine through the lens of the U.S. Bankruptcy Code, so both deploy insolvency frameworks to analyze and prescribe approaches to sovereign debt restructuring.

shared_topics.topic: domestic political and social consequences of sovereign restructurings
shared_topics.justification: Paper A foregrounds the distributional, political, and social 'second‑order' disruptions (public anger, loss of support for elites, service cuts) that restructurings can trigger and argues legitimacy can mitigate these effects; Paper B similarly assesses how forcing repayment (including of odious debts) can undermine a government's ability to provide services and to politically and financially rehabilitate, linking restructuring outcomes to domestic welfare and stability.

shared_topics.topic: creditor incentives, bargaining dynamics, and the external constraints on restructuring outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses the need to attract creditor support and how institutional design affects creditors' willingness to participate in consensual workouts, while Paper B examines how the limited creditor remedies in sovereign lending and the potential invocation of doctrines like odious debt shape creditor behavior and bargaining leverage during restructurings.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 1988uilllrev493!!ARTICLE: THE EFFECT OF THE SOVEREIGN DEBT RESTRUCTURING PROCESS ON INTER-CREDITOR RELATIONSHIPS 1988 Center for Transnational Legal Studies.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE EFFECT OF THE SOVEREIGN DEBT RESTRUCTURING PROCESS ON INTER-CREDITOR RELATIONSHIPS 1988 Center for Transnational Legal Studies.

shared_topics.topic: collective creditor coordination and collective-action dynamics in sovereign debt restructurings

shared_topics.topic: absence of a formal statutory/international restructuring framework and reliance on consensus or soft-law solutions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that inter-creditor norms and restructuring practices evolved without statutory or regulatory bankruptcy-like rules and instead through creditor consensus. Paper B foregrounds the institutional gap in the international financial architecture, critiques the current 'non-system', and debates how a treaty, ad hoc, or soft-law DWM might be designed (and legitimated) to fill that vacuum.

shared_topics.topic: use and expansion of contractual or institutional mechanisms to govern inter-creditor relations and secure participation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents how restructuring agreements repurpose and expand contractual provisions (originally tailored to individual loans) to regulate behavior and status across all commercial bank lenders in a debtor country. Paper B evaluates how alternative institutional or legal tools (drawing on domestic insolvency and arbitration models) might be structured to perform similar governance functions and how those designs fare with respect to legitimacy.

shared_topics.topic: balancing creditor treatment with domestic political and distributive consequences to secure compliance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on assuring equal treatment among creditors as a prerequisite for bank participation in restructurings. Paper B examines how perceptions of legitimacy—and fair, accepted procedures—matter for domestic acceptance of restructuring terms, arguing that legitimate processes can reduce politically and socially disruptive backlash and improve voluntary compliance.

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM ARTICLE: Tribunalizing Sovereign Debt: Argentina's Experience with Investor-State Dispute Settlement

shared_topics.topic: legitimacy and governance of a sovereign debt workout mechanism (DWM)

shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses Argentina's Abaclat and related ICSID cases to show how creditors have invoked BITs to adjudicate bondholder claims and the legal imagination driving that strategy; Paper B treats investment treaty arbitration as a cognate institutional model, assessing its rules and legitimacy as relevant comparators when thinking about debt workout institutions.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A lays out the debate between institutional reformers (SDRM-like mechanisms) and contractualists (collective action clauses, exit consents), analyzing strengths and limits of CACs in practice; Paper B surveys prior reform proposals and evaluates how different institutional designs interact with legitimacy concerns, implicitly weighing contractual fixes against formal institutional mechanisms.

shared_topics.topic: holdout creditors, creditor coordination problems, and enforcement challenges (litigotiation and forum-shopping)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents the fragmentation caused by holdouts, the shift toward 'litigotiation' across multiple jurisdictions, and the difficulties of enforcing judgments against sovereigns; Paper B discusses the fragmentation and inconsistent outcomes in the current 'non-system', highlights Argentina's protracted holdout litigation as symptomatic, and links these coordination and enforcement failures to the rationale for a DWM.

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: FINAL STATUS FOR KOSOVO: UNTYING THE GORDIAN KNOT:III. ARTICLE: RESOLVING CLAIMS WHEN COUNTRIES DISINTEGRATE: THE CHALLENGE OF KOSOVO

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: ACTS OF STATE AND FOREIGN SOVEREIGN OBLIGATIONS

shared_topics.topic: the intermediary role of legal professionals or institutions in allocating risk, providing validation, and shaping bargaining dynamics
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on international institutions and proposed mechanisms (DWM, IMF, arbitration) as intermediaries that structure creditor/debtor interactions and assign legitimacy, while Paper B analyzes how lawyers and their opinion letters operate as intermediaries that allocate legal risk, validate transactions, and influence counterparties' bargaining positions.

papers.title: ARTICLE: THE COLOR OF BRAZIL: LAW, ETHNIC FRAGMENTATION, AND ECONOMIC GROWTH
papers.abstract:
It is widely accepted in economics literature that ethnically contested societies are prone to political instability, which in turn is an established impediment to economic growth and development.Many developing countries have begun to recognize the importance of a properly functioning legal framework for economic development. Legal responses to ethnic discrimination or other forms of social differentiation come mostly in the form of antidiscrimination laws. As many developing countries invest in stronger legal frameworks, antidiscrimination laws have become a pervasive tool in efforts to mitigate socioeconomic inequalities in the labor market and in society in general.
Antidiscrimination laws are designed to correct labor market distortions on the basis of somewhat settled distinctions such as race, gender, age, and sexual orientation.However, in many developing countries where the basis of discrimination is primarily based on ethnic orientation, understanding its various manifestations is critical to proposing laws that can effectively ameliorate ethnic bias in society and promote economic growth and development. Most empirical studies that have examined the link betweenethnicity and growth have relied on the Ethno-linguistic Fractionalization Index (ELF).I have discussed elsewhere the limits of ELF, primarily its undue reliance on language as a measure of ethnic fractionalization.I proposed a more robust measure, called the Social Diversity Index (SDI) that more fully captures the complexity of ethnicity.In this article, I examine the application of SDI in a legal context where antidiscrimination laws have been enacted to ameliorate the destabilizing effects of fractionalization. Using Brazil as a case study, I suggest ways in which legal remedies may be more effectively designed to contain effects of heterogeneity, especially its impact on economic growth potential.
There are a number of reasons for choosing Brazil in this study. Besides having the largest economy and being the most populous country in Latin America, Brazil has a unique history of cultural and racial migration, which has created a racially diverse society. Despite this racial diversity, marked inequalities continue to prevail along racial lines, especially in education, as well as in the labor market and other sectors of the economy.Brazil has one of the highest levels of income inequality in the world.This complex relationship between social identity and the economic performance of Brazil continues to generate research initiatives and is the focus of this paper.
In Part I of this paper, I discuss race, color and economic growth in Brazil. In Part II, I examine policy considerations for legal responses to ethnic fragmentation in Brazil, and in Part III, I offer my conclusions.

questions.question: Whether ethnic fractionalization in Brazil, measured with a more comprehensive index of social diversity, reduces economic growth potential.
questions.answer: Ethnic heterogeneity in Brazil, more fully captured by the Social Diversity Index than by ELF, is presented as having destabilizing effects that reduce economic growth potential.

questions.question: Whether antidiscrimination laws and other legal remedies can meaningfully mitigate socioeconomic inequalities tied to race/color and thereby lessen the negative economic impact of ethnic heterogeneity in Brazil.
questions.answer: The paper contends that antidiscrimination laws and related legal remedies can mitigate racial socioeconomic inequalities and ameliorate the destabilizing effects of heterogeneity, thereby lessening its negative impact on growth when properly designed.

questions.question: How legal remedies should be designed to more effectively contain the destabilizing effects of social/ethnic fragmentation on political stability and economic development in Brazil.
questions.answer: Legal remedies should be grounded in a nuanced understanding of ethnicity's diverse manifestations, as captured by the Social Diversity Index, and tailored to correct labor market and broader societal inequalities to contain the destabilizing effects of fragmentation on development.

matched_themes: Can antidiscrimination laws and legal remedies meaningfully mitigate socioeconomic inequalities tied to race and thereby lessen the negative economic impact of ethnic heterogeneity in contexts such as Brazil?

papers.node_id: 56dukelj1201!!ARTICLE: THE DILEMMA OF ODIOUS DEBTS
papers.title: ARTICLE: THE DILEMMA OF ODIOUS DEBTS
papers.authors: Lee C. Buchheit; G. Mitu Gulati; Robert B. Thompson
papers.abstract:
"If we were all responsible for the misdeeds of the governments that represent us, thought Isabel, then the moral burden would be just too great."
Public international law requires that states and governments inherit ("succeed to") the debts incurred by their predecessors, however ill-advised those borrowings may have been. There are situations in which applying this rule of law strictly can lead to a morally reprehensible result. Example: forcing future generations of citizens to repay money borrowed in the state's name by, and then stolen by, a former dictator.
Among the purported exceptions to the general rule of state succession are what have been labeled "odious debts," defined in the early twentieth century as debts incurred by a despotic regime that do not benefit the people bound to repay the loans. The absconding dictator is the classic example.
The removal of Iraq's Saddam Hussein in 2003 sparked a resurgence of interest in this subject. By enshrining a doctrine of odious debts as a recognized exception to the rule of state succession, some modern commentators have argued, a successor government would be able legally to repudiate the loans incurred by a malodorous prior regime. This, they contend, would have two benefits: it would avoid the morally repugnant consequence of forcing an innocent population to repay debts incurred in their name but not for their benefit, and it would simultaneously force prospective lenders to an odious regime to rethink the wisdom of advancing funds on so fragile a legal foundation.
In this recent debate, the adjective "odious" has quietly migrated away from its traditional place as modifying the word "debts" (as in "odious debts"), so that it now modifies the word "regime" (as in "debts of an odious regime"). This is a major shift. If this new version of the odious debt doctrine is to be workable, someone must assume the task of painting a scarlet letter "O" on a great many regimes around the world. Who will make this assessment of odiousness and on what criteria? The stakes are high. An unworkable or vague doctrine could significantly reduce cross-border capital flows to sovereign borrowers generally.
We are skeptical that this definitional challenge can be met. Rather than jettison the initiative as quixotic, however, we investigate how far principles of private (domestic) law could be used to shield a successor government from the legal enforcement of a debt incurred by a prior regime under irregular circumstances. A wholesale repudiation of all contracts signed by an infamous predecessor may be more emotionally and politically satisfying for a successor government, but establishing defenses to the legal enforcement of certain of those claims based on well-recognized principles of domestic law may be the more prudent path. Such defenses exist under United States law (and presumably elsewhere) and could be used to address many, although admittedly not all, cases of allegedly odious debts.

questions.question: Whether successor governments can lawfully refuse to repay sovereign debts incurred by prior regimes that did not benefit (or were diverted from) the population.
questions.answer: While public international law generally requires succession to sovereign debts, the paper contends that successors can lawfully resist enforcement of many such debts by using domestic private-law defenses, though not all debts would be covered.

questions.question: To what extent principles of domestic private law can be used to shield a successor government from legal enforcement of debts contracted by a predecessor under irregular, fraudulent, or non-beneficial circumstances.
questions.answer: Well-recognized domestic (private) law defenses, available under U.S. law and presumably elsewhere, could shield successor governments from enforcement in many, but not all, cases of allegedly odious or irregular debts.

questions.question: Whether formal recognition of an exception permitting repudiation of such predecessor-incurred debts would materially affect cross-border sovereign lending and capital flows.
questions.answer: Yes; the paper warns that an unworkable or vague odious-debt exception could significantly reduce cross-border capital flows to sovereign borrowers.

Do declarations of constitutional nullity over state loans and guarantees render those agreements unenforceable and produce restitution rights for private parties under domestic law?
How should judges treat foreign sovereign acts that affect intangible property or contractual rights-when should such acts be recognized, enforced, or disregarded by forum courts?
Will exempting successor governments from predecessor debts advance human-rights objectives without inflicting disproportionate harm on creditors, markets, or populations?

What institutional or normative responses should courts, legislatures, or standards bodies adopt to manage cross-contract externalities created by single interpretive decisions?
Can municipal public debt issued to private investors be contested as illegitimate or unenforceable when borrowing disproportionately benefited creditors and harmed public services?
Would codifying international rules for repudiation or relief from predecessor-incurred debts be practicable and what would be the effects on cross-border lending and market behavior?
How do social movements, civil society advocacy, and legal strategies influence sovereign debt restructuring outcomes and the adoption of debt cancellation policies?

What institutional processes (bright-line rules versus negotiated, case-by-case adjustments) best resolve disputes over successor commercial obligations to balance financial stability and citizens' recovery rights?
When and under what conditions should a successor political entity be held responsible for its predecessor's international commercial obligations despite lacking the predecessor's consent?

To what extent can domestic private-law doctrines be used to shield successor governments from enforcement of debts contracted by predecessors under irregular, fraudulent, or non-beneficial circumstances?
What legal and doctrinal reforms would best balance courts' desire for predictability in enforcing sovereign contracts with the need to avoid foreign-relations entanglement?
Is a mandatory bankruptcy-style majority-action framework necessary to secure efficient sovereign debt restructurings, or can voluntary contractual solutions achieve the same goals?

How do contractual amendment and informal amendment strategies compare with sweeping legal or institutional reforms as practical ways to resolve sovereign workouts without undermining investor confidence?
Do exceptional legal, political, or institutional protections (sovereign immunities, special statutes) effectively shield sovereigns from creditor litigation and alter restructuring bargaining power?

Can private-law concepts that prioritize substance over form-such as reclassifying or lowering repayment priority of creditors based on conduct-provide a coherent framework for resolving disputed obligations incurred by prior regimes?
Does the prospect of regime change or refusal by a successor government to honor prior debts materially influence creditor behavior and lending to risky or non-democratic governments?
Should governments repudiate or cancel sovereign debt when debt service substantially impairs their ability to provide public welfare and democratic policymaking?
How should assets and liabilities be allocated and adjudicated when a state disintegrates or undergoes regime change?
How do private-law concepts and analogies between rulers and the ruled historically shape doctrinal limits on state power and inform criteria for rejecting obligations imposed by prior regimes?
Would policy objectives of an existing legal rule be better achieved through alternative doctrines with clearer scope or by legislative reform?
When are legal or policy analogies to private-law relationships between rulers and the ruled (e.g., to justify repudiating prior regimes' obligations) normatively and legally defensible?
Do successor-state debt doctrines and recognition practices (including diplomatic recognition) influence courts' willingness to validate prior governmental acts in private disputes?
Would formal recognition of an exception permitting repudiation of predecessor-incurred debts materially affect cross-border sovereign lending and capital flows?

Would legally permitting or codifying successor-government exemptions for debts incurred by illegitimate or predatory prior regimes improve successor populations' welfare or deter predatory borrowing, and what are the likely market and political effects of such rules?
Is a post-regime-change state legally and practically obligated to assume external sovereign debt incurred by a prior regime?

papers.node_id: 88nyulrev1!!ARTICLE: THE DYNAMICS OF CONTRACT EVOLUTION
papers.title: ARTICLE: THE DYNAMICS OF CONTRACT EVOLUTION
papers.authors: Stephen J. Choi; Mitu Gulati; Eric A. Posner
papers.abstract:
The literature on the evolution or production of contracts is sparse. Scholars frequently assume that parties draft bespoke contracts that serve the needs of specific transactions.But this assumption does not reflect the reality of the contract production process.
Contracts are more like commodities than custom-made items. They are mass-produced by law firms, which typically serve large numbers of clients with divergent interests.Like any other mass producer seeking to serve a broad client base, law firms sell products that help serve the needs of clients. The client typically wishes to consummatea deal - not to produce the perfect contract.The economics of the production process then results in a method where lawyers produce "good enough" contracts, and where the majority of these contracts are modifications of existing templates, including older contracts or forms that have been developed by trade associations.
Barak Richman explains that "the paradigmatic question each attorney asks regarding a new legal product is, 'Has this worked before?' not 'How can we make this work best?' or even 'What is it that we are making?'"Contract drafters are more like inventors than authors: They take existing products and try to improve them so that they can meet the clients' needs at hand. As a result, contract production is path-dependent, giving rise to the phenomenon of boilerplate.Boilerplate has an odd dual quality: It is thought to be necessary (which is why it is left in the contract), but parties often do not know why it is important. Judicial opinions reflect this confusion, with many courts expressing skepticism about boilerplate even while they frequently enforce it.
Boilerplate is sticky but not static. We know that boilerplate and form contracts generally change over time. But we know little about how these contracts change. In a prior article, we examined the evolution of sovereign debt contracts over a roughly fifty-year period.We found that changes did not occur on a deal-to-deal basis as assumed by the conventional model. Rather, contracts generally changed on an industry-wide basis, in response to major events, such as global financial crises.Individualized change also tended to show up in response to shocks or significant events, but the events in question were significantfor particular actors and not the market as a whole. In the case of sovereign debtors, individual defaults, rather than regional or global crises, provide the spark to alter boilerplate and form contracts.
In this article, we extend our prior research to analyze the internal dynamics of these periods of clustered change and assess how boilerplate terms shift to a new standard. The industry we use in our analysis is the sovereign bond market for foreign-law governed bonds. These bonds are typically purchased by cross-border investors and are largely governed by either the laws of New York or England. The parties in this market - such as states, banks, mutual funds, pension funds, and hedge funds - tend to be sophisticated. Regulation is sparse; after all, the key actors are the states themselves. The basic economic problem in the transaction has remained the same over centuries: States borrow money from foreign investors, but it is hard to force the states to pay the money back if the states decide they would rather not. States nonetheless have an economic incentive to give investors some confidence in getting repaid in order to convince the investors to lend to the states in the first place. The stability of this basic economic transaction over time is important because it enables us to test our evolutionary model over a long period of time.
We focus on a particular shift in the boilerplate sovereign bond contract for those issuances governed under New York law: the shift toward collective action clauses (or "CACs") from unanimity action clauses (or "UACs") governing changes to payment-related terms. The shift to CACs was a watershed event in the history of sovereign bond covenants.It significantly increased the ability of bondholders and issuers to engage in debt restructurings.Our interest is not onlywith how and when New York-law governed contracts shifted from UACs to CACs for payment terms but also the process of change for a number of other CAC-related terms, including the vote threshold for non-payment terms as well as disenfranchisement, mandatory meeting, and aggregation clauses (we define these later). Together, particular combinations of these terms form the model that applies in any particular sovereign bond contract. In discussing the evolution of this model, we will occasionally describe innovations as major and minor. Consistent with the policy debates over CACs, we label the shift away from the requirement of unanimous approval from all bondholders to alter payment terms as the major shift and the changes in other terms as minor shifts.
Shocks to the sovereign debt market, in the form of Mexico's crisis in 1995, the Asian financial crisis in 1997-1998, and Argentina's default in 2001, represented triggers for the changes in the contract model. We report on the types of contract innovations that took place with the start of these shocks and the market participants associated with these changes. Importantly, a shift towards the CAC model as the new standard did not occur overnight. Instead, there was a period of time after Mexico's crisis in 1995 through Argentina's default in 2001 during which the use of CACs was infrequent and only associated with more marginal market participants.
After this initial period, a tipping point occurred - driven by the cumulative effect of the default shocks as well as vocal public sector pressure - at which point top market participants changed from supporting the old standard to competing actively with one another to generate the new standard. At this tipping point, the usage of the old standard dropped rapidly and the incidence of the new CACs increased dramatically - giving an X pattern at the point where their usage percentages in the market crossed. Our study shows that once this tipping point - the X point - is reached, subsequent CAC innovations, largely involving CAC-related terms such as the aggregationclause, are driven by the top market participants competing to control the new CAC standard. This competition eventually led to a new standard - Mexico's version of the CAC first used in 2003 - and a gradual slowing of growth in the adoption of the CAC model in the market as CACs saturated the market. This slow initial experimentation, then rapid acceleration of adoption, followed lastly by a slower growth rate of market adoption as the CAC became dominant, roughly takes the shape of an S curve.
In Part I, we survey the literature on contract innovation. We draw from this literature to set up our hypotheses regarding the process of boilerplate contract evolution. We also describe our sovereign bond dataset, including the key CAC clauses, and the shocks to the sovereign bond market during the time period of our dataset that we use in our empirical tests. These shocks primarily affected issuers using New York-law governed bonds, and that was the market segment from which the impetus for innovation arose. Part II presents evidence from the New York-law governed portion of our sovereign bond dataset on the process of contract change. Part III extends our analysis to the parallel contractual change that occurred in the CACs within the English-law governed sovereign bond market. We use differences in how contract innovation occurred in this separate market to illuminate what distinguishes the initial stages of contract innovation from later stages of new contract standardization. In particular, the presence of external calls for change (in our case, from the public sector) is an important factor in determining when top market participants shift from defending the existing standard to competing in order to generate the new standard.

questions.question: Whether sovereign bond contracts governing cross-border debt shifted from requiring unanimous bondholder approval for payment-related changes to permitting majority-based (collective) approval, and what drove that shift.
questions.answer: Yes—New York-law governed sovereign bond contracts shifted from unanimity action clauses to collective action clauses for payment-related changes, a move triggered by crises such as Mexico (1995), the Asian crisis (1997–98), and Argentina (2001) and pushed past a tipping point by the cumulative impact of these defaults plus vocal public-sector pressure, after which top market participants raced to establish the new CAC standard (culminating in Mexico’s 2003 version).

questions.question: Whether market shocks (e.g., sovereign defaults or financial crises) and cumulative events produce clustered, industry-wide changes in standard contract boilerplate-creating a tipping point that yields rapid adoption (an S-curve) rather than incremental deal-by-deal change.
questions.answer: Yes—the paper finds that market shocks generate clustered, industry-wide shifts in boilerplate that reach a tipping point and then diffuse along an S-curve (slow early experimentation, rapid acceleration, then saturation), rather than incremental deal-by-deal change.

questions.question: How the identity and behavior of market participants (marginal vs. top participants) and external pressures (such as public-sector calls for reform) influence who initiates innovations in boilerplate terms and who ultimately standardizes the new terms.
questions.answer: Initial CAC innovations were associated with more marginal market participants, but as cumulative shocks combined with public-sector calls for change, top market participants switched from defending the old standard to competing to define and refine the new CAC standard, ultimately converging on Mexico’s 2003 version.

How do collective action clauses (CACs), bond amendment provisions, and creditor voting thresholds shape creditor coordination, holdout incentives, and market pricing?
Do elite contract drafters largely copy boilerplate blindly or actively tailor language over time, and how does editorial churning affect clause evolution?
To what extent are complex agreements organized as modular subsystems (enabling mass customization) versus thickly interconnected integrated systems, and how does that shape transaction design?
Why do persistent, costly, or apparently nonfunctional boilerplate clauses persist in sophisticated contracts?

What creditor- and institutional-level conditions (creditor structure, representation, procedural rules, debtor engagement) make multicreditor coordination mechanisms effective at resolving collective-action problems?

Which contractual and documentary designs (e.g., debt-for-equity, debt-for-nature, PIKs, exchange mechanics) most effectively restore contractual flexibility and reconcile debtor-creditor relationships in multiparty sovereign restructurings?
Why do some inefficient or nonfunctional contract features persist in markets despite competition - is path dependence, network effects, or branding responsible?
Should rights and enforcement powers of corporate bond investors be held individually or exercised collectively under representative or majority rules?

How do private standard-setting organizations, form contracts, and transnational documentation practices interact with national legal systems to determine the enforceability, reach, and governance effects of private global legal regimes?

Do elite contract drafters and sophisticated market participants tend to copy boilerplate verbatim, self-consciously adapt it, or actively lead innovations, and who drives adoption of new standard terms across markets?
How do social and market forces fail to correct suboptimal allocations of individual versus collective bondholder rights, and what reforms would improve enforcement and market outcomes?
Do organizational approaches to studying private contracts better explain their public, social, and political effects than transaction-cost/opportunism-focused models?
What governance effects do standardized private legal documents and routine documentation work produce-do they replicate, supplement, or supplant state legal authority?
Can a single general theory of contractual innovation account for diverse incentives and dissemination pathways, or is contractual innovation inherently idiosyncratic?

Do legal, institutional, and normative features (statutory backstops, professional practices, standardized forms, repeat-dealing norms) reduce the need for bespoke contract customization and thereby lower transaction costs?
Does replacing prohibitions on collective clauses or enforcing defaults change contracting behavior and foster market innovation in bond contract terms?

What measures and institutional designs are needed to convert borderline-unsustainable government debt into sustainable financing for sovereigns and subnational entities given modern creditor diversity and collateralization?
To what extent did public-sector actors influence contractual and market shifts through non-coercive means (advocacy, informational cueing) versus private-market learning and network effects?
Do market norms, network effects, or legal stickiness explain persistence of dated disclosure or opinion practices despite material changes in contract substance?
Do lawyers' origin myths and origin stories about contract terms match historical evidence, and why are such myths propagated?
How do standardized forms, firm templates, intermediaries, and market participants drive convergence or heterogeneity in transactional documentation across deals and jurisdictions?

Should major legal transplants (e.g., U.S. contract documentation) be expected to produce the same investor-protection effects in other jurisdictions, or do they mutate and yield unintended consequences?
Should a country's collective private-law rules vest enforcement rights in individual bondholders or in representative/majority decision mechanisms, and what are the tradeoffs?
Do market learning and network externalities cause firms to converge on standardized contract terms rather than customize or innovate them?

Who initiates innovations in boilerplate clauses, how do marginal versus leading market participants and external pressures influence who standardizes new terms, and does editorial churning cause rapid 'speciation' of document lineages?
How does relative bargaining power influence the design of nonprice contract terms such as warranties, covenants, termination rights, and indemnities?
How do multi-party financial contract disputes and the presence of secondary purchasers affect the process and outcomes of contract standardization and enforcement?
Do contract drafters typically copy boilerplate blindly across deals or actively tailor and evolve terms, and what organizational routines explain their behavior?
How large and practically significant are downstream effects of standard contract changes-that is, how many contracts and parties are affected and with what consequences?
How do creditor coordination mechanisms (creditor committees, collective action clauses, creditor-coordination platforms) affect restructuring predictability, participation, litigation, and costs?

papers.node_id: 50wmmarylrev2007!!ARTICLE: THE ECONOMICS OF DEAL RISK: ALLOCATING RISK THROUGH MAC CLAUSES IN BUSINESS COMBINATION AGREEMENTS
papers.title: ARTICLE: THE ECONOMICS OF DEAL RISK: ALLOCATING RISK THROUGH MAC CLAUSES IN BUSINESS COMBINATION AGREEMENTS
papers.abstract: In the acquisition of any large business, various corporate and regulatory reasons require that there be an interim period between the date on which the parties enter into a merger agreement (the signing) and the date on which the purchase price is paid and the ownership of the business is transferred (the closing).Between signing and closing, the business or financial condition of the company being acquired may deteriorate. Merger agreements typically address this problem through complex and highly-negotiated "material adverse change" or "MAC" clauses,which provide that, if a party has suffered a MAC within the meaning of the agreement, the counterparty can costlessly cancel the deal. Parties to merger agreements have often disagreed about whether one of them has suffered a MAC, and so MAC clauses have resulted in litigation in which tremendous sums of money, sometimes tens of billions of dollars, are at stake.

questions.question: Who should bear the risk that a target firm's business or financial condition materially deteriorates between signing and closing of an acquisition, and how should contracting parties design cancellation-for-adverse-change clauses to allocate that risk efficiently?
questions.answer: Merger agreements typically allocate this interim-deterioration risk through MAC clauses that let the counterparty cancel the deal costlessly if a material adverse change occurs.

questions.question: How do cancellation-for-adverse-change clauses affect parties' incentives - including pricing, negotiation, disclosure, management of the business during the interim, and the likelihood and cost of litigation - and what are the resulting economic trade-offs?
questions.answer: MAC clauses have often led to disagreements that result in litigation with tremendous sums of money at stake.

matched_themes: Who should bear the risk that a target firm's business or financial condition materially deteriorates between signing and closing, and how should cancellation-for-adverse-change clauses be designed to allocate that risk efficiently?
What is the proper meaning and scope of a buyer's termination right tied to post-signing deterioration in a seller's condition, and how should such clauses be triggered and limited?
What speech-act function does entering into a complex business contract serve: creating enforceable promises or setting a framework that enables non-legal governance and cooperation?
When does an adverse change justify closing-stage termination in an M&A transaction and what standards should courts apply to assess such claims?
How do buyers' termination rights tied to post-signing deterioration (MAC/adverse-change clauses) function in practice, and how do they interact with ordinary-course obligations and systemic shocks?
How do M&A deal documents allocate interim risk for target-business deterioration, and what design of adverse-change or MAC (material adverse change) clauses is economically optimal?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 42harvintllj355!!ARTICLE: State Succession to Debts and Assets: The Modern Law and Policy
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: State Succession to Debts and Assets: The Modern Law and Policy

shared_topics.topic: allocation of financial risk/liability during transitional periods
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how merger parties use Material Adverse Change (MAC) clauses to allocate the risk that a target's business deteriorates between signing and closing, while Paper B studies how successor and creditor states allocate a predecessor state's debts and assets during state dissolution—both focus on who bears financial losses arising in an interim or transition period.

shared_topics.topic: mechanisms for dispute resolution and enforcement in high-stakes allocations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents how contested MAC determinations frequently lead to expensive litigation and outlines enforcement consequences for deal parties, while Paper B surveys arbitration commissions, creditor interventions, and international negotiation processes used to resolve successor-state debt and asset disputes—both consider how institutional dispute-resolution and enforcement regimes affect outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: normative principles guiding allocation (efficiency, equity, and creditor protection)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A takes an economic perspective on how MAC clauses allocate risk efficiently between buyer and seller, and Paper B interrogates the principle of equitable allocation, pacta sunt servanda, and creditor protections in dividing state debts and assets—both examine competing normative criteria (efficiency, fairness, and creditor interests) that justify particular allocation rules.

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: CONTRACTS IN THE REAL WORLD: ESSAY: CONTRACT AS PATTERN LANGUAGE
