papers.node_id: 98valrev1665!!ARTICLE: THE EFFECT OF BARGAINING POWER ON CONTRACT DESIGN
papers.title: ARTICLE: THE EFFECT OF BARGAINING POWER ON CONTRACT DESIGN
papers.authors: Albert H. Choi; George G. Triantis
papers.abstract:
WHEN two parties enter into a contract, their relative bargaining power affects the terms of their deal. While the allocation of bargaining power clearly determines price, it is an open question whether and how it also affects nonprice terms (what we are alternatively referring to as "contract design"). It is common for practitioners and industry observers to attribute seemingly one-sided nonprice terms to unequal bargaining power and to explain changes in nonprice terms over time as a result of shifts in such power. Consider the following examples of such observations:
(1) Disclaimers of warranties and limitations on damages in a sales contract are due to the power of the monopolist.
(2) Broad termination rights are included in a merger or acquisition agreement when the acquirer has the power to dictate the terms of the agreement to the target company.
(3) The purchase order forms of a large corporation, facing many potential suppliers, insist that all litigation will be held in the courts of the purchaser's state.
The objective of this Article is to begin a systematic analysis of how bargaining power might determine the agreement to such apparently one-sided terms. An important normative question is whether the efforts of the stronger party to appropriate a larger share of the surplus through these terms compromise the size of the surplus. Would a more equal sharing of bargaining power be more likely to lead to efficient (surplus-maximizing) contract provisions?
In legal scholarship, the issues of one-sided contract terms bear on the antitrust regulation of monopolies, as well as the policing of contracts under the doctrine of unconscionability. Early legal scholarship maintained that monopolists often used contracts of adhesion that contained one-sided terms.Law-and-economics scholars argued in response that bargaining power affects price, but not other terms.The basic argumentcan be found in an early work by now-Judge Richard Posner, who argued that a profit-maximizing monopolist would offer product quality that efficiently meets buyer preferences, that is, improving quality until the incremental cost of further improvement outweighs the incremental value to the buyer.Thus, a monopolist producer of cars should find it in its self-interest to offer any warranty for which the buyer is willing to pay more than the cost to the producer, just as if it were a seller in a competitive market. The difference between a monopoly and a perfectly competitive market, then, should be the market price, not the warranty terms offered. The argument that a monopolist extracts its rent through price rather than quality continues to be the conventional wisdom among the leading scholars in law-and-economics.
Empirical literature on the relationship between bargaining power and nonprice terms, such as warranties, is thin but mixed.Recently, in a study of terms in end user licensing agreements ("EULAs"), Professor Marotta-Wurgler found little evidence to support the hypothesis that market concentration causes terms to be more seller-friendly than they would be in competitive markets.The study suggests, therefore, that market power alone should not be sufficient to trigger the scrutiny of a court under the doctrine of unconscionability.In contrast, Professors Ben-Shahar and White examined auto-manufacturer supply contracts and found variations in nonprice terms, such as warranty and termination provisions, that seemed correlated with bargaining power.While reading and search costs may be a confounding factor in consumer standard-form contracts, such as the EULAs in Marotta-Wurgler's study, Ben-Shahar and White's sample is pertinent to our analysis because it contains business-to-business contracts where this factor is less likely to be an issue. In light of the conventional wisdom in law-and-economics, Ben-Shahar and White remarked that "given the enormous stakes, we expected that economic power would be used to dictate low prices, not selfish boilerplate."They speculated that the variation and the potential inefficiency were due to internal agency conflicts within the parties, but conceded that they did not "offer a satisfactory explanation for the variance of terms across the different [original equipment manufacturer("OEM")] contracts, or for the conjecture that some of these terms are inefficient."
The puzzle that Ben-Shahar and White raise is echoed repeatedly by practitioners and commentators in the business and legal press, who invoke bargaining power to explain both static and dynamic observations of contracting patterns. One static observation is that business entities that dominate their industries tend to adopt different contractual allocations of similar risks depending on whether they are buyers or sellers. When they are buyers or licensees, they demand extensive warranties and indemnification promises from their counterparts; when they are sellers or licensors, they disclaim, limit remedies, and demand indemnification from their customers. A dynamic observation is that contract terms such as covenants in loan and debt agreements, or material adverse change ("MAC") clauses in mergers and acquisitions agreements, fluctuate over time between "buyer-friendly" and "seller-friendly" versions as market conditions change.
The set of questions addressing when and why bargaining or market power is a determinant of nonprice terms remains unexplored and worthy of investigation. The conventional law-and-economics theory offers a starting point for this analysis by offering two irrelevance propositions: (1) bargaining power affects the price but not the nonprice terms of a contract (the strong-form version); and (2) the allocation of bargaining power may lead to different nonprice terms but does not change the likelihood that the parties will agree to efficient terms (the weak-form version).Each of these propositions depends on a set of implicit assumptions, including perfect information and zero transactions costs. We relax these assumptions in this Article to bridge theory and practice, by providing a theoretical framework to understand when and how bargaining power determines contract design. To focus on bargaining power, we assume that each party can read and understand all provisions in their contract and set aside important effects that stem from lack of sophistication or bounded rationality.
The strong-form irrelevance proposition treats a price term as purely distributional: it allocates the surplus and has no effect on size. However, variations in price terms can change the optimal nonprice terms when there is a change in price. We give two instances of this phenomenon. First, a different price alters one (or both) party's rate of substitution between price and nonprice terms. For example, a business executive who is richly paid may be willing to sacrifice a greater amount in salary for an official title than one who is less well paid. Second, a higher or lower price determines the severity of the adverse-selection or moral-hazard problems. For example, we would expect a loan agreement to have tighter and more extensive covenants to address these problems when the market rate of interest is high than when it is low, all else equal.
Turning to the weak-form proposition, we outline four ways in which the shift in the bargaining power might lead to a deviation from efficient contract design. First, the pursuit of advantage in negotiations exacerbates the inclination of negotiators to engage in value-claiming rather than value-creating strategies. Second, the party with greater bargaining power has better incentives to invest effort and resources in innovating and developing contractual opportunities to create value. Third, business contracting often occurs in a two-stage process: the price and other important terms are decided by the business principals, and the design "details" are delegated to their respective lawyers. The exercise of bargaining power in the second stage, after price has been determined, may distort the agreement on nonprice terms. Fourth, in negotiations characterized by information asymmetry, unequal bargaining power might encourageexcessive signaling or screening activity in the design of nonprice terms.
Each of these effects warrants more detailed treatment and we analyze only one of them in this Article. We examine the impact of unequal bargaining power when markets have buyers with heterogeneous valuations of alternative contract terms and these values are not observable by the seller(s).Building on insights from the economics of industrial organization, we demonstrate theoretically that one-sided bargaining power can lead to the inefficient use of nonprice terms to screen or signal (depending on whether the power lies with the seller or the buyer, respectively). We show that a monopolist or otherwise dominant seller may screen by offering suboptimal contract quality to the buyer who values quality less. At the other extreme, when the buyer has all the bargaining power, similar to the case of perfect competition, the buyer who values the nonprice term less will seek to avoid subsidizing other buyer types by agreeing to suboptimal nonprice terms, to signal her type to the sellers.
To illustrate, consider a market for automobiles in which sellers can agree to either limited or extended warranties and in which buyers have different valuations of the warranty provisions because they are either careful or careless drivers. The seller cannot observe which drivers are careful or careless. Suppose that both groups of buyers would pay more for the extended warranty than it would cost the seller to provide, and the extended warranty is therefore efficient. A monopolist would seek to maximize its share of the surplus in each sale by offering both extended and limited warranties at prices that would induce the careful driver to purchase a limited warranty. Similar inefficient separation would occur in a perfectly competitive market. If sellers offered the extended warranty to all buyers at a single price, careful drivers would subsidize the careless drivers. The careful drivers, then, would have an incentive to choose the limited warranty so as to signal their type to the market andreceive a price reduction that exceeds the value of the foregone warranty.
The problem of extreme allocations of bargaining power in either direction stems, in part, from the fact that one party has the power to dictate the terms of trade. The party with this power is willing, in many circumstances, to sacrifice some of the aggregate surplus in order to capture a larger share of the surplus. Therefore, a more "even" sharing of the surplus may address these inefficiencies in contract design. The circumstances that would balance bargaining power in this manner, however, are not obvious. After all, competitive markets essentially allocate all the power to the buyers without leaving any surplus for the sellers. We suggest three ways of representing more "even" sharing of bargaining power. In the first, some competition is introduced by allowing another seller (an entrant) to compete with an existing seller (an incumbent). In the second, the power of commitment is reduced by letting the contracting parties renegotiate the original contract. In the third, the seller's power to dictate the terms is curtailed by allowing the buyer to dictate the terms with some delay. In each of these cases, we demonstrate the key result that the conditions mitigate or eliminate the inefficiencies of screening and signaling through nonprice terms.
The Article is organized as follows. Part I investigates various meanings for unequal bargaining power. Part II states the weak and strong forms of the bargaining power irrelevance propositions, and then outlines various paths by which bargaining power might determine contract design. Part III reviews related literature in industrial organization concerning how monopoly and perfect competition can distort the quality of goods provided. Part IV provides a more detailed analysis of the effect of unequal bargaining power on contract design when parties are asymmetricallyinformed as to the value and cost of a given nonprice term. Part V shows that more even bargaining power can attenuate inefficient screening and signaling through nonprice terms. Despite the inefficiencies caused by unequal bargaining power, we suggest briefly in Part VI that legal institutions are unlikely to be able to mitigate these problems by constraining the parties' freedom of contract. We conclude with a comment as to possible directions for future research.

questions.question: Whether and how the relative bargaining power of contracting parties affects the design of nonprice contract terms (for example, warranties, termination rights, and indemnities).
questions.answer: Yes; relative bargaining power affects nonprice contract design by changing the price (which shifts parties’ trade-offs and the severity of adverse selection and moral hazard) and, under asymmetric information, by enabling the use of nonprice terms for screening or signaling.

questions.question: Whether unequal bargaining power leads parties to adopt inefficient, surplus-reducing nonprice contract terms-particularly under information asymmetry where screening or signaling can occur.
questions.answer: Yes; with unobservable heterogeneity, one-sided bargaining power leads to inefficient, surplus-reducing nonprice terms—dominant sellers screen by offering suboptimal quality, and buyers with all the power induce suboptimal terms to signal their type.

questions.question: Whether making bargaining power more balanced (for example, by adding competition, allowing renegotiation, or enabling delayed buyer-driven terms) mitigates or eliminates inefficiencies in nonprice contract design.
questions.answer: Yes; making power more balanced—by introducing competition, allowing renegotiation, or permitting delayed buyer-dictated terms—mitigates or eliminates the screening/signaling inefficiencies in nonprice term design.

matched_themes: Do parties adopt changes in standard boilerplate primarily for direct contractual effects or to achieve indirect goals such as signaling, reputation, or coordination?

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: DEVILRY, COMPLICITY, AND GREED: TRANSITIONAL JUSTICE AND ODIOUS DEBT

shared_topics.topic: allocation of costs, risks, and liability between powerful actors and weaker successors/counterparties
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes who must bear financial obligations when an ‘odious’ regime’s debts are challenged, arguing for assigning liability to international investors in some cases while recognizing successor states may shoulder burdens for transitional justice; Paper B analyzes how dominant parties use bargaining power to shift risk and capture surplus through nonprice contract terms, producing one-sided allocations of costs between powerful firms and weaker counterparties.

shared_topics.topic: the adequacy and role of legal doctrines and institutions to constrain or reassign harms created by economic actors
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates the odious debt doctrine and proposes relying on international state and corporate responsibility norms (and duties of restitution) to address investor complicity, while Paper B examines doctrines like unconscionability and antitrust and asks whether courts or legal rules can or should correct inefficient, power-driven contract design.

shared_topics.topic: tension between normative goals of justice/accountability and economic efficiency or predictability in legal responses
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights trade‑offs between transitional imperatives of truth and accountability and the economic consequences of disavowing debts (sometimes requiring successor states to accept obligations), whereas Paper B studies when unequal bargaining power leads parties to adopt inefficient nonprice terms and whether more equal power-sharing (or legal intervention) would improve surplus and predictability.

shared_topics.topic: the significance of actors' knowledge, intent, or information asymmetries for assigning legal consequences or shaping contractual design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A attributes moral and legal responsibility to international investors who knowingly or recklessly supported odious regimes and links truth‑seeking to revealing complicity, while Paper B models how asymmetric information and unobserved valuations drive screening/signaling through contract terms and how bargaining leverage interacts with informational problems to produce suboptimal outcomes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 6chijintll311!!ARTICLE: SYMPOSIUM: SOVEREIGN DEBT RESTRUCTURING: From Rogue Creditors to Rogue Debtors: Implications of Argentina's Default
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: SYMPOSIUM: SOVEREIGN DEBT RESTRUCTURING: From Rogue Creditors to Rogue Debtors: Implications of Argentina's Default

shared_topics.topic: commitment failures and renegotiation in long‑term agreements
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents how the Argentine government's inability to credibly maintain its exchange‑rate and debt commitments precipitated a run, capital controls and eventual sovereign debt restructuring; Paper B analyzes how the power to commit (and the option to renegotiate) alters contract design and can mitigate or exacerbate inefficiencies in negotiated agreements.

shared_topics.topic: how market structure and relative bargaining power shape nonprice terms of agreements
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights the imbalance between sovereign borrowers and global creditors that governs the terms and outcomes of cross‑border lending and restructuring, while Paper B develops a theoretical framework showing how dominant versus weak parties use bargaining power to dictate nonprice contract terms (warranties, covenants, termination rights) and how competition shifts those allocations.

shared_topics.topic: credibility, signaling, and asymmetric information as drivers of inefficient outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes erosion of regime credibility and market perceptions (leading to runs and currency collapse) as central to the crisis, and Paper B shows how asymmetric information about counterpart types leads to inefficient screening/signaling via nonprice contract terms under unequal bargaining power.

shared_topics.topic: limits of legal institutions and enforcement in correcting contractual imbalances across jurisdictions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A implies that cross‑border finance and sovereign status constrain remedies and enforcement (manifest in freezes, controls, and costly restructurings), and Paper B argues legal constraints are often ill‑suited to eliminate inefficiencies from unequal bargaining power or to police one‑sided contract terms.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 42vandjtransnatll15!!Article: The Kosovo Crisis: A Dostoievskian Dialogue on International Law, Statecraft, and Soulcraft
compared_to.partner_title: Article: The Kosovo Crisis: A Dostoievskian Dialogue on International Law, Statecraft, and Soulcraft

shared_topics.topic: how relative power shapes the content of legal agreements and institutional decisions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how unequal bargaining power between contracting parties alters nonprice contractual design (warranties, termination rights, forum selection) and can change surplus allocation and efficiency; Paper B examines how great-power politics (Russia vs. the West) influenced the construction, interpretation, and application of international-legal instruments (UN resolutions, ICJ/ICTY, recognition of secession) to produce different legal outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: the strategic use of legal rules and institutions to capture advantage
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows how a dominant seller or buyer can design contractual terms to appropriate a larger share of surplus (even at some efficiency cost), while Paper B documents Russia’s deliberate use of UN fora, advisory opinions, and legal arguments to advance geopolitical aims and contest Western actions—both treating law as a tool of state or party strategy rather than a neutral constraint.

shared_topics.topic: the limits of legal remedies and institutional reform to correct power imbalances
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues legal constraints on contracting (e.g., unconscionability doctrines) are unlikely to fully correct inefficiencies produced by bargaining power and suggests institutional or market adjustments instead; Paper B explores how reliance on existing international-law institutions and doctrinal debate may fail to reconcile great-power disagreements and may be inadequate to settle the Kosovo dispute or prevent politicization of international organs.

shared_topics.topic: legal language and contractual/institutional terms as mechanisms for signaling or screening under informational and strategic asymmetries
shared_topics.justification: Paper A models how nonprice contract terms can be used to screen or signal buyer types under asymmetric information (leading to inefficient separation), and Paper B shows states using differing legal narratives, forum choice, and doctrinal arguments to signal legitimacy, intent, and to screen for sympathetic international audiences or venues.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 6chijintll219!!ARTICLE: SYMPOSIUM: SOVEREIGN DEBT RESTRUCTURING: Sovereign Exchange Offers in 2010
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: SYMPOSIUM: SOVEREIGN DEBT RESTRUCTURING: Sovereign Exchange Offers in 2010

shared_topics.topic: how the distribution of bargaining power shapes non‑price contract terms and economic efficiency
shared_topics.justification: Paper A builds a theoretical framework showing how unequal bargaining power leads parties to choose inefficient nonprice provisions (warranties, covenants) through screening, signaling, or value‑claiming; Paper B examines how sovereigns' relative negotiating leverage versus dispersed bondholders (and mechanisms that shift that leverage) determines the terms and success of exchange offers and restructurings, affecting repayment profiles and overall restructuring efficiency.

shared_topics.topic: the impact of collective decision rules and commitment power (unanimity vs majority/CACs) on the ability to amend contracts and resolve holdouts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how reducing a party's ability to unilaterally dictate terms (introducing competition, renegotiation, or delayed buyer dictation) can mitigate inefficiencies, while Paper B focuses on the move from unanimity to collective action clauses and how majority amendment rules and exchange offers change creditors' ability to restructure debt and overcome holdout problems.

shared_topics.topic: strategic bargaining behavior (value‑claiming, holdouts, signaling/screening) and its consequences for restructuring or contract performance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A identifies ways negotiators pursue value‑claiming over value‑creating and models how asymmetric information produces signaling or screening via nonprice terms; Paper B addresses creditor strategic behavior in exchange offers and restructurings (including holdouts, participation incentives, and coordination problems) that shape outcomes of sovereign debt adjustments.

shared_topics.topic: the role of legal and institutional design in shaping contractual outcomes and remedial options
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses doctrines (unconscionability, antitrust) and argues legal constraints are imperfect tools for correcting bargaining‑power induced inefficiencies in contract design, while Paper B evaluates how governing law (New York law), contract clauses (CACs), and proposals for sovereign bankruptcy affect the mechanics and prospects of debt restructurings.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 119yalelj848!!Article: Strategic Vagueness in Contract Design: The Case of Corporate Acquisitions
compared_to.partner_title: Article: Strategic Vagueness in Contract Design: The Case of Corporate Acquisitions

shared_topics.topic: nonprice contract terms as screening and signaling devices under asymmetric information
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze how clauses other than price (warranties, covenants, MAC/termination clauses) are used to elicit private information or separate types: Paper A models how unequal bargaining power produces inefficient screening/signaling via nonprice terms (e.g., warranties), while Paper B shows that vague MAC clauses (and litigation) can function as deliberate screens/signals in acquisition agreements.

shared_topics.topic: the effect of transaction, verification, and litigation/ enforcement costs on contract-form (vague vs precise) and clause design
shared_topics.justification: Both engage with front‑end and back‑end costs in choosing contract detail: Paper A relaxes the zero transaction‑cost assumption and links information/transaction costs and delegation/renegotiation to nonprice design, and Paper B develops a detailed account of how verification and litigation costs (and their ratio to stakes) make vague standards sometimes preferable to precise proxies.

shared_topics.topic: efficiency consequences of strategic contract design and the influence of bargaining power
shared_topics.justification: Both assess whether contract design maximizes surplus or instead sacrifices aggregate efficiency to reallocate surplus: Paper A asks when unequal bargaining power leads parties to adopt inefficient nonprice terms and identifies mechanisms (value‑claiming, delegated bargaining, signaling), while Paper B evaluates whether strategically vague clauses improve or harm ex ante investment, contracting and trade efficiency.

shared_topics.topic: the role of legal enforcement, courts, and contractual dispute‑resolution mechanisms in shaping drafting choices
shared_topics.justification: Both papers consider how the legal system and enforcement tools feed back into drafting: Paper A discusses doctrinal limits and the (limited) ability of legal institutions to correct inefficiencies from bargaining power, and Paper B analyzes how courts' informational limits, litigation stakes, liquidated damages, and dispute‑resolution design influence whether parties choose vague versus precise clauses.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 80chikentlrev119!!SYMPOSIUM: FINAL STATUS FOR KOSOVO: UNTYING THE GORDIAN KNOT:III. ARTICLE: RESOLVING CLAIMS WHEN COUNTRIES DISINTEGRATE: THE CHALLENGE OF KOSOVO
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: FINAL STATUS FOR KOSOVO: UNTYING THE GORDIAN KNOT:III. ARTICLE: RESOLVING CLAIMS WHEN COUNTRIES DISINTEGRATE: THE CHALLENGE OF KOSOVO

shared_topics.topic: institutional design of dispute- and claims-resolution mechanisms to manage allocational conflicts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how legal and contracting institutions (courts, renegotiation, competition, delegation to lawyers) affect the use of nonprice contractual terms and can mitigate inefficient outcomes from unequal bargaining power; Paper B surveys institutional options (tribunals, claims-resolution systems, private international law rules) for resolving competing claims arising from state disintegration and designs mechanisms to clear or allocate those claims.

shared_topics.topic: how shifts in relative power or authority change allocations of rights and contract/claim terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies how changes in bargaining power (e.g., monopoly vs. competition, buyer vs. seller dominance) lead to different nonprice contract terms and dynamic flips between buyer- and seller-friendly clauses; Paper B examines how the breakup or displacement of state authority (e.g., Kosovo) changes who is entitled to assets or bound by debts and how those reallocations depend on shifting political and legal power.

shared_topics.topic: the limits of legal doctrines and institutions to constrain opportunistic capture of surplus or claims by powerful parties
shared_topics.justification: Paper A questions whether doctrines like unconscionability or antitrust can or should police one-sided nonprice terms and argues legal institutions may be ill-suited to fully correct inefficiencies created by unequal bargaining power; Paper B discusses the necessity and limits of claims-resolution systems and extinguishment powers to prevent powerful claimants from appropriating state assets or evading liabilities in the absence of clear legal frameworks.

shared_topics.topic: choice-of-forum/choice-of-law and cross-jurisdictional rules as instruments of allocation and leverage
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses examples (forum-selection clauses, litigation in purchaser's state) to show how powerful parties impose procedural/choice-of-law terms to capture advantage in contracts; Paper B centrally addresses private international law, applicable substantive law, and enforcement mechanisms for claims that cross national jurisdictions after state breakup.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 49vandjtransnatll1045!!ARTICLE: A New Model of Sovereignty in the Contemporary Era of Integrated Global Commerce: What Anthropology Contributes to the Shortcomings of Legal Scholarship
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A New Model of Sovereignty in the Contemporary Era of Integrated Global Commerce: What Anthropology Contributes to the Shortcomings of Legal Scholarship

shared_topics.topic: how asymmetrical power shapes legal arrangements (state sovereignty and private contracts)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that contemporary sovereignty is fundamentally about how states strategically manage their interface with the global market under asymmetric economic pressures, while Paper B analyzes how unequal bargaining power leads parties to design one-sided nonprice contract terms to capture surplus.

shared_topics.topic: the influence of market structure and economic interdependence on legal form and content
shared_topics.justification: Paper A locates the transformation of sovereignty in globalization and global value chains that bind jurisdictions and legal regimes, and Paper B shows how market concentration, competition, and price regimes alter the optimal design of contract terms.

shared_topics.topic: the insufficiency of traditional legal theories/models when economic realities change
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contends that conventional legal definitions of sovereignty (and many disciplinary approaches) are outdated for the integrated global economy, and Paper B questions law-and-economics irrelevance propositions that assume perfect information and zero transaction costs, arguing they fail to predict real-world contract design.

shared_topics.topic: distributional consequences of legal design and the normative stakes of legal choice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that sovereignty discourse conceals power relations with real social and political consequences (including for Indigenous peoples), while Paper B focuses on how contract terms reallocate surplus between parties and can create inefficiencies and equity concerns that implicate antitrust and unconscionability doctrines.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 69sclrev597!!ARTICLE: WHEN TO PRAISE THE MACHINE: THE PROMISE AND PERILS OF AUTOMATED TRANSACTIONAL DRAFTING
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: WHEN TO PRAISE THE MACHINE: THE PROMISE AND PERILS OF AUTOMATED TRANSACTIONAL DRAFTING

shared_topics.topic: delegation to lawyers and two-stage contracting (business principals set deal economics; lawyers draft nonprice details)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A models contracting as a two-stage process in which principals decide price and business terms while lawyers draft the detailed nonprice provisions, showing how bargaining power exercised in the drafting stage can distort outcomes; Paper B studies transactional drafting practice and how attorneys (and their automation tools) actually produce those detailed provisions, raising concerns about how delegation and drafting workflows affect contract content.

shared_topics.topic: how process, tools, or market power change the efficiency and quality of nonprice contract terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that unequal bargaining power and strategic incentives can lead to inefficient allocation of warranties, covenants, and other nonprice terms (reducing aggregate surplus); Paper B examines how document automation and AI can both reduce drafting errors and also introduce new risks that may improve or worsen the substantive quality and reliability of transactional provisions.

shared_topics.topic: management of information problems in contracting — screening, signaling, and due diligence
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how asymmetric information about parties' valuations leads to screening/signaling encoded in nonprice terms (and how bargaining power amplifies this); Paper B addresses how automation and AI change how transactional lawyers collect, process, and present information (due diligence, clause selection), altering the practical handling of informational asymmetries and the risk of misplaced reliance on computerized outputs.

shared_topics.topic: the role of legal rules, institutional constraints, and professional norms in policing or mitigating problematic contract terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages with doctrines such as unconscionability and asks whether legal intervention can or should correct inefficient, one‑sided nonprice terms created by bargaining power; Paper B focuses on ethical obligations, competence, and professional standards for attorneys using automation, considering whether professional norms or regulation should govern technology use to prevent harmful contracting outcomes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 67dukeljonline219!!ARTICLE: BOILING DOWN BOILERPLATE IN M&A AGREEMENTS: A RESPONSE TO CHOI, GULATI, & SCOTT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: BOILING DOWN BOILERPLATE IN M&A AGREEMENTS: A RESPONSE TO CHOI, GULATI, & SCOTT

shared_topics.topic: determinants of nonprice (boilerplate) contract terms in M&A transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically analyzes why boilerplate provisions in merger agreements change across deals (attributing variation to editorial churning and precedent copying), while Paper B investigates how relative bargaining power drives the inclusion and shape of nonprice terms (e.g., termination rights, warranties, MAC clauses) in similar transactional settings.

shared_topics.topic: role of lawyers, drafting practices, and two-stage delegation in shaping contract clauses
shared_topics.justification: Paper A attributes textual drift to lawyers' rote reuse, idiosyncratic edits, and 'encrustation' during drafting, and Paper B explicitly models contracting as a two-stage process where principals set business terms and lawyers later draft details—showing how that delegation can distort nonprice terms when bargaining power is unequal.

shared_topics.topic: efficiency implications of how contract terms are created and evolve
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights how accumulation of cosmetic edits undermines legal certainty and the functional meaning of boilerplate (a potential inefficiency), while Paper B analyzes when bargaining-power-driven nonprice terms lead to surplus-reducing (inefficient) screening, signaling, or value-claiming in contract design.

shared_topics.topic: temporal dynamics and cross-deal variation of contractual clauses
shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces micro– and macro–level textual 'drift' and 'speciation' of boilerplate across generations of merger agreements using longitudinal text analysis, and Paper B documents and theorizes why nonprice clauses (like covenants or MACs) fluctuate over time with market conditions and shifts in bargaining power.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 83fordhamlrev3293!!ARTICLE: TRANSNATIONAL ENFORCEMENT DISCOVERY
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: TRANSNATIONAL ENFORCEMENT DISCOVERY

shared_topics.topic: the appropriate role of courts in shaping or policing privately negotiated outcomes (contract terms vs enforcement discovery)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines whether and how courts and legal doctrines (e.g., unconscionability, antitrust) can or should constrain one-sided nonprice contract terms created by disparate bargaining power; Paper B analyzes when courts should permit or limit post‑judgment enforcement discovery and cross‑border asset searches, i.e., judicial involvement in making private entitlements practically enforceable.

shared_topics.topic: information asymmetry as a justification for legal tools that alter private bargains (screening/signaling vs discovery for asset location)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows how asymmetric information about buyer types leads parties with bargaining power to use nonprice terms to screen or signal, producing inefficiency; Paper B treats enforcement discovery as a legal mechanism to overcome informational gaps about a debtor's assets and thus enable satisfaction of judgments, and asks how discovery standards should differ from merits discovery because of that informational role.

shared_topics.topic: when pursuit of private advantage by a powerful party undermines broader systemic goals (surplus/efficiency vs comity and fair enforcement)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how dominant parties may sacrifice aggregate surplus to capture a larger share through contract design, harming efficiency; Paper B studies how aggressive extraterritorial discovery or seizure by judgment creditors can conflict with foreign sovereignty, execution rules, and the objectives of a coherent transnational enforcement system.

shared_topics.topic: limits of transplanting doctrinal rules from one context to another without modification
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the application of law‑and‑economics ‘irrelevance’ propositions that assume perfect information and zero transaction costs, arguing context matters for contract terms; Paper B argues that pretrial discovery doctrines cannot be simply imported into the post‑judgment/enforcement context and proposes new, tailored standards for enforcement discovery.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 21fordhamintllj1152!!ARTICLE: THE TRANSFORMATIVE POTENTIAL OF A SECONDARY MARKET: EMERGING MARKETS DEBT TRADING FROM 1983 TO 1989
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE TRANSFORMATIVE POTENTIAL OF A SECONDARY MARKET: EMERGING MARKETS DEBT TRADING FROM 1983 TO 1989

shared_topics.topic: how secondary markets and trading in distressed sovereign debt facilitate debt restructuring and portfolio adjustment
shared_topics.justification: Paper A chronicles how the nascent secondary market for emerging‑market sovereign debt created the instruments and liquidity used for debt‑equity swaps, buybacks, and portfolio reallocation that eased the 1980s debt crisis; Paper B analyzes how contractual design (including covenants and renegotiation) in loan and debt agreements affects the feasibility and efficiency of restructuring and how market features can alter those outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: the impact of market structure and relative bargaining power on nonprice contract terms in debt and loan contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper B develops a theory of how unequal bargaining power leads to one‑sided or inefficient nonprice terms (warranties, covenants, MAC clauses) and how competition/renegotiation can mitigate that; Paper A documents a changing market environment (banks swapping loans, emergence of brokers and a secondary market) that altered creditors' and debtors' options and thus the practical allocation of contractual rights and obligations in sovereign debt dealings.

shared_topics.topic: the temporal evolution of contractual forms and market institutions in response to crises and changing conditions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A provides a periodized history (1983–1989) of how the secondary market and associated practices evolved during the Latin American debt crisis; Paper B studies dynamic observations of contract terms fluctuating over time with market conditions and explains mechanisms (entry, renegotiation, shifting power) that drive such changes.

shared_topics.topic: the role of intermediaries and delegation in shaping transaction outcomes and contract design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights the emergence of brokerages and interbank swapping as intermediaries that enabled trades and restructurings in emerging‑market debt; Paper B analyzes how delegation (e.g., principals setting price while lawyers draft nonprice details) and agency conflicts can distort contract design and produce inefficient allocations of risk.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 6chijintll287!!ARTICLE: SYMPOSIUM: SOVEREIGN DEBT RESTRUCTURING: The Role of the IMF in Sovereign Debt Restructuring
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: SYMPOSIUM: SOVEREIGN DEBT RESTRUCTURING: The Role of the IMF in Sovereign Debt Restructuring

shared_topics.topic: how asymmetries of power produce inefficient or unintended terms in agreements
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that the IMF's political power and governance structure can produce outcomes in sovereign debt restructurings that reformers did not intend, while Paper B analyzes how unequal bargaining power (monopolists, dominant buyers/sellers) leads parties to adopt suboptimal nonprice contract terms through screening, signaling, or value-claiming.

shared_topics.topic: the limits of technocratic or formalistic proposals when institutional politics are ignored
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that proposals to give the IMF a larger technical role in debt restructuring founder if they ignore the Fund's inherently political decisionmaking, and Paper B critiques law-and-economics 'irrelevance' results that rely on perfect-information/zero-transaction-cost assumptions, showing those technocratic conclusions can fail under realistic institutional constraints.

shared_topics.topic: the role of institutional design and governance rules in shaping negotiated outcomes and reform feasibility
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on how IMF governance and institutional features constrain and alter sovereign-debt-restructuring reforms, and Paper B examines how institutional interventions (introducing competition, allowing renegotiation, or delaying term-setting) can rebalance bargaining power and mitigate inefficient contract design.

shared_topics.topic: multi-stage, multi-actor negotiation processes and delegation that distort intended agreements
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes how accommodating multiple national political and legal systems and political actors alters international arrangements' outcomes, while Paper B studies two-stage contracting (business principals set price, lawyers draft details) and multi-actor market interactions that produce distortions in nonprice terms.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 119yalelj848!!Article: Strategic Vagueness in Contract Design: The Case of Corporate Acquisitions
compared_to.partner_title: Article: Strategic Vagueness in Contract Design: The Case of Corporate Acquisitions

shared_topics.topic: design and allocation of non‑price contract terms (e.g., MACs, warranties, termination rights, indemnities)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze how parties draft and negotiate non-price terms—Paper A studies MAC clauses and other excuse/termination provisions in acquisition agreements, while Paper B studies warranties, termination rights, forum-selection and similar nonprice clauses across industries—to show how these terms allocate risk and shape transactional outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: use of contract terms as screening and signaling devices under asymmetric information
shared_topics.justification: Both papers treat nonprice provisions as instruments to reveal private information or separate types—Paper A shows how vague standards plus the prospect of litigation can screen sellers and signal quality in acquisitions, and Paper B models how sellers and buyers use warranties or contract designs to screen or signal buyer/seller types, potentially producing inefficient separation.

shared_topics.topic: the role of transaction, verification, and enforcement costs (including litigation and renegotiation) in producing incomplete or vague contracts
shared_topics.justification: Both works emphasize that front‑end drafting costs, back‑end verification/enforcement costs, and the costs or prospects of renegotiation shape whether parties prefer precise proxies or vague standards—Paper A develops a detailed argument that litigation costs can justify vagueness in MACs, while Paper B relaxes zero‑transaction‑cost assumptions and examines how such frictions and institutional constraints affect the equilibrium design of nonprice terms and the possibility of renegotiation.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 45ohiostlj883!!ARTICLE: The Extra-Territorial Application of United States Antitrust Laws: A Proposal for An Interim Solution. The authors gratefully acknowledge the assistance of David A. Cohen.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Extra-Territorial Application of United States Antitrust Laws: A Proposal for An Interim Solution. The authors gratefully acknowledge the assistance of David A. Cohen.

shared_topics.topic: when and how market/bargaining power should influence legal or regulatory scrutiny of private transactions (e.g., unconscionability, antitrust enforcement)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly asks whether and when a party's bargaining or market power should change scrutiny of nonprice contract terms (invoking unconscionability and antitrust concerns), and Paper B analyzes the consequences of aggressive application of U.S. antitrust law abroad—both engage the problem of how legal rules should respond to parties with unequal market or jurisdictional power.

shared_topics.topic: the limits of legal institutions and doctrines to resolve harms created by power imbalances
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that courts and legal constraints are unlikely to fully remedy inefficiencies in contract design caused by unequal bargaining power, while Paper B catalogues how judicial limiting doctrines, executive-branch efforts, and negotiated understandings have failed to resolve the political and legal conflicts created by extraterritorial antitrust enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: policy and institutional mechanisms to rebalance or mitigate the effects of asymmetric power
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies institutional fixes (introducing competition, enabling renegotiation, delaying term-setting) that can reduce inefficient outcomes from unequal bargaining power, and Paper B considers negotiated bilateral understandings, international norm‑building, and executive diplomacy as mechanisms to moderate the disruptive effects of expansive antitrust jurisdiction.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 65tullrev1323!!ARTICLE: WHEN THE BORROWER AND THE BANKER ARE AT ODDS: THE INTERACTION OF JUDGE AND ARBITRATOR IN TRANS-BORDER FINANCE.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: WHEN THE BORROWER AND THE BANKER ARE AT ODDS: THE INTERACTION OF JUDGE AND ARBITRATOR IN TRANS-BORDER FINANCE.

shared_topics.topic: effect of relative bargaining power on nonprice contract terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a theoretical framework showing how unequal bargaining power alters nonprice terms (warranties, termination rights, indemnities) and can induce inefficient screening/signaling; Paper B documents the same phenomenon in international finance where banks and borrowers use contract terms (forum selection, summary procedures) strategically depending on their leverage.

shared_topics.topic: use of dispute-resolution and forum-selection clauses as strategic, nonprice contractual devices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A cites forum clauses as an example of one-sided nonprice terms tied to market power, while Paper B is devoted to how lenders and borrowers draft arbitration versus court clauses to capture advantage, improve enforceability, or avoid debtor defenses.

shared_topics.topic: the influence of legal institutions and enforceability on contract design and economic outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses whether legal doctrines (e.g., unconscionability, antitrust) and the limits of legal intervention affect inefficient contract terms created by bargaining asymmetries, and Paper B analyzes how international legal rules (New York Convention, FSIA, national summary procedures, IMF rules) shape parties' choices of contractual dispute-resolution mechanisms and the reliability of credit arrangements.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 70lawcontempprob165!!ARTICLE: SOVEREIGNS, TRUSTEES, GUARDIANS: PRIVATE-LAW CONCEPTS AND THE LIMITS OF LEGITIMATE STATE POWER
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: SOVEREIGNS, TRUSTEES, GUARDIANS: PRIVATE-LAW CONCEPTS AND THE LIMITS OF LEGITIMATE STATE POWER

shared_topics.topic: use of private-law concepts (agency, trust, wardship) to delimit authority and obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A invokes agency conflicts within contracting parties to explain why negotiators and lawyers distort nonprice terms, modeling parties as principals/agents whose incentives affect contract design; Paper B places agency, trust, and wardship at the center of a theory that governments act as agents or trustees of their peoples and thus that some state acts (e.g., odious debt) may be beyond their legitimate authority.

shared_topics.topic: how asymmetric power affects who bears legal obligations and the efficiency or legitimacy of those obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how unequal bargaining power leads dominant parties to appropriate surplus and to inefficient screening or signaling via nonprice contract terms; Paper B investigates how unequal international/domestic power (imperial, trustee, or sovereign relationships) changes whether obligations bind populations and whether those obligations are legitimate or disownable.

shared_topics.topic: reexamination of dominant doctrinal presumptions through historical or economic critique
shared_topics.justification: Paper A challenges the law‑and‑economics irrelevance propositions (that market power affects price but not contract design) by relaxing idealized assumptions and using economic models to show when doctrine fails; Paper B revisits legal and intellectual history to show that modern Westphalian presumptions obscure earlier private‑law concepts that shaped limits on state power, calling for doctrinal reinterpretation.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 1988uilllrev481!!ARTICLE: RECENT REGULATORY PERSPECTIVES ON DEBT-FOR-EQUITY SWAPS AND SECURITIZATION OF THIRD WORLD DEBT © 1988 Center for Transnational Legal Studies
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: RECENT REGULATORY PERSPECTIVES ON DEBT-FOR-EQUITY SWAPS AND SECURITIZATION OF THIRD WORLD DEBT © 1988 Center for Transnational Legal Studies

shared_topics.topic: regulatory influence on contract design where bargaining asymmetries exist

papers.title: ARTICLE: THE EFFECT OF THE SOVEREIGN DEBT RESTRUCTURING PROCESS ON INTER-CREDITOR RELATIONSHIPS 1988 Center for Transnational Legal Studies.
papers.abstract:
Fairy tales customarily begin with the preamble "Once upon a time." Advocates, when commencing arguments before judicial tribunals, traditionally preface their remarks with the phrase "May it please the court"; and communications announcing the commencement of a major sovereign debt restructuring are invariably add "To the International Banking Community."
The ability of sovereign borrowers to begin their communications in this way may well be one of the major innovations brought about by the global debt crisis that commenced in 1982.  Implicit in this form of address is the premise that all commercial bank lenders to a debtor country can and will be treated as a single group in implementing the restructuring program irrespective of location or individual credit position.  At the outset of the debt crisis, nothing in the law or practice of international finance required this result, and a great deal suggested it would be very unlikely to occur.
For example, the hundreds or thousands of credits that purport to be covered by a restructuring request will have been separately negotiated between borrowers (both public and private sector) and individual banks or, in some cases, "syndicates" of banks lending pursuant to a single loan agreement.  These banks, located in countries all over the world, are subject to differing regulatory and disclosure regimes, and have distinct lending and credit review policies and widely divergent practices in important areas such as loan loss reserve provisioning. Moreover, the documentation for these individual credits ranges fromsingle-line telexes to hundred-page syndicated loan agreements.  Finally, and perhaps most importantly, at the time the banks extended the loans they regarded each other as intense competitors.  The prerogative of individual bank action and enterprise was jealously guarded.  It is of great significance, therefore, that sovereign borrowers can in one stroke cut across these many and varied creditor relationships with a single telex containing the now ominous salutation: "To the International Banking Community."
The thesis of this article is that the sovereign debt restructuring process has forced the international banking community into a rather uneasy confederation.  The enormity and complexity of sovereign debt problems preclude individual banks from negotiating adjustments to their own credit exposure in isolation from fellow lenders.  Unanimous participation by the banking community in these affairs, however, was thought achievable only if very strict assurances could be given that all similarly situated lenders would be treated equally.  The banking community pursued the goal of equal treatment by incorporating into restructuring agreements certain contractual provisions that, in their original form, were designed to regulate the behavior and status of various lenders to a particular borrower.  In the restructuring context, however, these provisions are significantly expanded in an effort to replate the behavior and status ofallcommercial bank lenders to all borrowers in a debtor country.
This article will focus on certain aspects of the way in which inter-creditor relationships were conceived, documented, and managed both before and after the beginning of the current debt restructuring era.  It is worth bearing in mind from the outset, however, that patterns of accepted inter-creditor behavior in these circumstances have evolved without any statutory or regulatory guidelines for reorganizing the financial affairs of a sovereign borrower comparable to domestic bankruptcy or insolvency laws.What has happened, therefore, has happened only through a consensus among the participants, without the benefit of any outside policy-making authority or enforcement mechanism.

questions.question: Whether and how the sovereign debt restructuring process alters the relationships and collective behavior among commercial bank creditors of a debtor country.
questions.answer: The sovereign debt restructuring process forces previously competitive, disparate banks into an uneasy, consensus-driven collective that is treated and acts as a single group, curtailing individual negotiations in favor of coordinated participation and equal treatment.

questions.question: Whether contractual provisions in loan and restructuring agreements are used to secure equal treatment and coordinated participation among disparate lenders during sovereign restructurings.
questions.answer: Yes; to secure equal treatment and coordinated participation, banks incorporated and significantly expanded contractual provisions in restructuring agreements to regulate the behavior and status of all similarly situated lenders across the debtor country.

questions.question: How inter-creditor practices, documentation, and management have evolved in sovereign debt restructurings in the absence of a formal statutory insolvency framework.
questions.answer: Without a statutory insolvency framework, inter-creditor practices, documentation, and management evolved through participant consensus, using expanded contractual mechanisms to standardize and govern relationships and conduct.

papers.node_id: 45ohiostlj883!!ARTICLE: The Extra-Territorial Application of United States Antitrust Laws: A Proposal for An Interim Solution. The authors gratefully acknowledge the assistance of David A. Cohen.
papers.title: ARTICLE: The Extra-Territorial Application of United States Antitrust Laws: A Proposal for An Interim Solution. The authors gratefully acknowledge the assistance of David A. Cohen.
papers.authors: Thomas W. Dunfee; Aryeh S. Friedman
papers.abstract:
The extra-territorialapplication of the U.S. antitrust lawsto foreign parties during a period of increasing international trade has resulted in an escalation of legal confrontations between the U.S. and foreign nations.The furor surrounding recent attempts to apply U.S. antitrust laws extra-territorially in In re Uranium Antitrust Litigation (Westinghouse),International Association of Machinists v. The Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC),and Laker Airways Ltd. v. Sabena Belgian World Airlines (Laker)and the recent reintroduction of clawback legislationin the Canadianand Australianparliaments are prime examples.  Treble damage suits initiated by private plaintiffs asserting claims under U.S. competition law exacerbate the problem; unlike the government, individuals are not required to evaluate the impacts on foreign policy of a lawsuit.
U.S. courts have adopted limiting doctrinesdesigned to avoid the assertion of prescriptive jurisdictionin the most sensitive private cases, seeking to reduce the likelihood of divisive confrontation.  The executive branch of the U.S. government has responded by participating in international attempts to articulate universal norms of economic regulation.  The executive branch has also negotiated several bilateral understandings with trading partners, providing for notification and consultation.These limited responses have failed to resolve U.S. conflicts with other nations.  Confrontations now occur with even greater frequency and intensity in a variety of procedural and legal contexts.The underlying problem seems impervious to resolution.
The intractability of the problem is rooted in the basic nature of extra-territorial antitrust litigation.  The following characteristics of U.S. antitrust litigation have a particular impact upon foreign defendants and nations:

questions.question: Whether applying a country's competition laws to conduct or parties located abroad increases the frequency and severity of legal and diplomatic conflicts with foreign governments.
questions.answer: Yes—the abstract states that extraterritorial application of U.S. antitrust laws has escalated legal confrontations with foreign nations, with conflicts occurring with greater frequency and intensity.

questions.question: Whether permitting private plaintiffs to pursue multiplied monetary remedies in domestic competition suits against foreign defendants exacerbates international tensions or undermines foreign-policy interests.
questions.answer: Yes—private treble-damages suits exacerbate the problem because, unlike the government, private plaintiffs need not consider foreign-policy impacts.

questions.question: What interim legal or policy mechanisms (for example, procedural limits, notification/consultation arrangements, or executive negotiation) can feasibly reduce conflicts caused by extraterritorial enforcement, and are current measures sufficient?
questions.answer: Courts’ limiting doctrines to avoid asserting prescriptive jurisdiction in sensitive private cases, executive participation in international norm-setting, and bilateral notification/consultation arrangements are identified, but the abstract says these limited responses have failed to resolve the conflicts and are thus insufficient.

matched_themes: When should domestic courts decline to adjudicate private-law claims that hinge on the validity of a foreign government's acts within its own territory?
What interim legal or policy mechanisms can reduce conflicts caused by extraterritorial enforcement, and are current measures sufficient?
When should domestic courts defer to a foreign state's determinations about acts within that state's territory, and what limits should govern such deference?
How should courts allocate competing regulatory authority when both the forum state and a foreign state claim power to regulate the same persons, conduct, or property?
Does applying a country's competition laws extraterritorially increase the incidence and severity of legal and diplomatic conflicts with foreign governments?
What institutional or normative responses should courts, legislatures, or standards bodies adopt to manage cross-contract externalities created by single interpretive decisions?
Do multiplied monetary remedies in domestic competition suits against foreign defendants exacerbate international tensions or undermine foreign-policy interests?

papers.node_id: 21fordhamintllj1802!!ARTICLE: THE FACILITATION OF THE BRADY PLAN: EMERGING MARKETS DEBT TRADING FROM 1989 TO 1993
papers.title: ARTICLE: THE FACILITATION OF THE BRADY PLAN: EMERGING MARKETS DEBT TRADING FROM 1989 TO 1993
papers.abstract:
The modern secondary market in the debt of less developed countries ("LDCs"), now known as the emerging market, grew out of the debt crisis of 1982. The first six years of the market's development were considered in an earlier Article,which analyzed the evolution of the market in the following periods: (i) Birth: 1982 to May 1985; (ii) Infancy: May 1985 to May 1987; and (iii) Childhood: May 1987 to March 1989. The Article concluded that the market's principal effects were to force a degree of realism upon a bank's loan loss provisions, to provide an exit from LDC lending for certain banks, and to facilitate a range of debt exchanges including debt-equity swaps and debt buy-backs.
This Article completes the analysis of the first decade of the market's operation by considering two further periods: (iv) Adolescence: March 1989 to October 1991; and (v) Young Adulthood: October 1991 to December 1993.The primary importance of the market in these periods, as will be discovered, lies in its promotion and faciliation of the Brady Plan.

questions.question: Did the development of the secondary market for less developed country (LDC) debt from 1989-1993 promote and facilitate the implementation of large-scale sovereign debt restructuring plans (e.g., the Brady Plan)?
questions.answer: Yes—the market's primary importance in 1989–1993 was its promotion and facilitation of the Brady Plan.

questions.question: How did activity in the LDC debt secondary market during 1989-1993 affect banks' management of their LDC exposures-including loan-loss provisioning, decisions to exit LDC lending, and the use of debt-exchange mechanisms such as debt-equity swaps and buy-backs?

matched_themes: How did the secondary market for emerging-market and less-developed countries' sovereign debt evolve, and what were its effects on banks, restructurings, and financial globalization?

What legal and contractual techniques most effectively enable large-scale sovereign debt restructurings and how do they affect creditor rights, burden-sharing, and orderly negotiation among many creditors?
Would official intervention in sovereign restructurings strengthen or weaken international capital markets' functioning and asset quality for sovereign debt?
Under what conditions do voluntary debt-exchange programs encourage creditor participation and facilitate sovereign borrowers' return to competitive financial markets?
How does official-sector involvement (governments, IMF, multilateral lenders) affect incentives, spillovers, and the performance of sovereign debt workouts?
Can creditors in multi-creditor instruments overcome holdout and grab-and-run incentives to achieve coordinated, ratable restructurings without a statutory insolvency backstop?
How did the secondary market for less-developed countries' sovereign debt emerge and evolve during the 1980s, and what role did it play in debt restructuring mechanisms?
What are the consequences of sovereign default for restructuring outcomes and for incentives and behavior of international creditors and debtor governments?
How do secondary markets for sovereign debt (emergent purchasers and trading) affect debt restructurings, market liquidity, and form-contract standardization?
Do official-sector interventions in restructurings improve orderly outcomes and creditor recoveries, or do they weaken international capital-market functioning?
What legal, tax, accounting, and banking regulatory issues arise when banks convert cross-border loan exposures into equity or otherwise restructure foreign claims?

What measures and institutional designs are needed to convert borderline-unsustainable government debt into sustainable financing for sovereigns and subnational entities given modern creditor diversity and collateralization?
How do secondary markets for sovereign debt (liquidity, tradability, active buying/selling) affect the feasibility and mechanics of sovereign restructurings?
How did activity in low- and middle-income country (LDC/emerging-market) debt secondary markets in the late 1980s and 1990s affect banks' management of exposures and use of restructuring tools?

Do market-based restructuring techniques (ad hoc creditor groups, debt/equity swaps, debt-for-nature, debt-equity conversion) meaningfully restore contractual flexibility, reduce external debt stocks, and stimulate domestic investment?

papers.node_id: 82scallrev481!!ARTICLE: THE FAILURE OF PRIVATE EQUITY
papers.title: ARTICLE: THE FAILURE OF PRIVATE EQUITY
papers.abstract:
The fall of 2007 heralded a tumultuous time in the U.S. capital markets. The implosion of the subprime mortgage market disrupted the economy and caused the credit markets to dry up and become increasingly illiquid.Almost overnight, credit became both more expensive and more difficult to obtain as financial institutions became unwilling to extend financing.The credit securitization market was particularly affected, leaving many financial institutions with pending and existing loans that they could only securitize and sell, if at all, at a large loss.Faced with these potentially large losses, financial institutions began to balk at funding preagreed private equity acquisitions.This sudden, unexpected turn of events and the general revaluation and decline in stock prices it wrought led private equity firms to reassess their pending acquisitions - acquisitions which had been agreed to in more stable times.The private equity firms'reevaluations were often unkind. Throughout the fall and into 2008, private equity firms repeatedly attempted to terminate their contractual obligations to acquire companies.
Many private equity firms successfully relied on the negotiated language in their contracts either to terminate their pending acquisitions or to agree on a settlement with the same effect.In many instances, litigation ensued before such dispositions. The litigation surrounding these terminations and the heightened scrutiny directed on the terms of private equity agreements opened a revealing window into the practices of parties and attorneys who had negotiated and structured private equity transactions. Under the public glare, many apparent contractual drafting errors in the private equity structure came to light. Moreover, the intricate structures of these transactions appeared to be fundamentally flawed or otherwise the product of suboptimal structuring and contracting.Observers particularly criticized acquirees for agreeing to optional takeover structures: the inclusion of reverse termination fee provisions that permitted private equity firms to terminate an acquisition for any reason by paying a flat fee of approximately 3 percent of the transaction value.A blame game unfolded and fault for these failures was alternatively pinned on financial institutions, investment bankers, private equity firms, acquiree boards, and acquiree attorneys.
This Article examines the structure of these private equity transactions and the role of lawyers, particularly those representing acquirees, in their negotiation and documentation. It seeks to understand the forces driving the evolution of the private equity structure, the rationale for the structure, and its contractual terms. I look to answer these questions through an examination of litigation transcripts, interviews with industry participants, information from a database of 193 private equity contracts, and otherpublic records.
This Article ultimately seeks to explain and understand the reasons for the collapse of these private equity deals. The principal failure of the private equity industry in the period leading up to August 2007 was the failure of financial institutions to properly price their loans and financial instruments.This allowed private equity firms to acquire a vast portfolio of companies at low interest rates and flexible credit terms, with minimal money invested.This pricing failure is part of a broader credit failure that has caused the current financial crisis.
The focus of this Article is not on that aspect of the private equity industry, but rather it is on the serial collapse of private equity acquisitions after August 2007. These deals failed because private equity firms and financial institutions attempted to terminate contractual commitments made in better economic times. Given the new economic environment and loss incentives, these private equity firms and financial institutions leveraged any advantageous contractual clause or ambiguity to escape their contractual obligations. It was in these extraordinary measures to escape their commitments that the so-called "flaws" in the private equity structure became apparent.
This Article is about this alleged failure of private equity: whether these flaws existed and, if so, why lawyers - particularly lawyers for acquirees - negotiated them and allowed them to exist. Here, the claimed errors and failures in the private equity structure that this Article highlights and seeks to examine and explain are of a two-fold variety: (1) first-order mistakes such as contractual drafting errors made by private equity lawyers, and (2) second-order errors resulting from lawyers negotiating a fundamentally flawed private equity structure.
The first-order failures were rather apparent in the disputes of 2007 and 2008, but the existence of second-order failures is uncertain. Here, some have asserted that the structure of private equity itself was not fundamentally flawed, but rather it was a result of arms-lengthbargaining.In other words, many lawyers have argued that, until August 2007, the structure of private equity was simply the best deal available. This only partly explains the rationale for the structure of private equity, however, because notions of transactional "optimality" in the private equity structure are relative. The structure of private equity results from "good enough" structuring decisions made by transactional attorneys who are disincentivized to innovate.I find that the private equity attorney, as a transaction-cost engineer, structures the private equity contract by heeding contractual terms and law, contractually created forces, and nonlegal factors such as reputation.The attorney measures the weight of each of these and adjusts contractual terms and transaction structure in response. These extracontractual forces, however, incentivize private equity lawyers to avoid innovating. Change in the private equity structure is thus intermittent, caused by exogenous forces, and results in piecemeal revisions premised on the preexisting structure. The structure of private equity cannot be characterized as an efficient one due to the structure's strong path dependency.
Moreover, the private equity legal universe is small and self-contained. From January 1, 2004, through August 1, 2007, the same twenty-two law firms represented either an acquiree or a private equity acquirer in 91 percent of all private equity transactions.Given that these law firms repeatedly represent private equity firms but only represent acquirees on a one-off basis, these law firms may not be fully incentivized to negotiate innovative, beneficial provisions for acquirees. While this agency cost may not have been the determining factor in the failure of the private equity structure, it likely contributed to the forces working againstinnovation in the private equity structure.Reliance on extracontractual legal forces additionally allowed attorneys to hide this possible bias.
The findings of this Article contribute to a larger debate about what business lawyers actually do and how they add value to transactions. This debate is framed by Ronald Gilson's seminal 1984 article, Value Creation by Business Lawyers: Legal Skills and Asset Pricing.In that article, Gilson postulated that business lawyers create value in transactions, net of legal fees, by negotiating "a transactional structure which reduces transaction costs and therefore results in more accurate asset pricing."Since that time, little has been written on this issue.This story of private equity and its attorneys is an attempt to add to this literature by describing the good and the bad of transactional lawyering, and the agency and other costs that are associated with it. Lawyers may add value as Gilson theorizes, but they may also increase transaction costs and fail to realize their full value potential.
In this regard, this Article is a wider case study of how business lawyers negotiate contracts, how contracts function in a particular industry, how path dependency can exist even in sophisticated environments, and how extralegal norms and conventions can fail. Here, this Article aims to fill an increasingly noted gap in the contracts and "dealmaking" literature.There has been much theoretical discourse but little research into how business clients and their attorneys negotiate and agree to complex contracts in either continuing or discrete relationships.
In looking at this question, I find that the private equity bargain is a rich, textured environment. The terms of the contractual relationshipsbetween the private equity firm and the acquired company are partly analogous to an iceberg: they form only the publicly available view of a much deeper understanding between the parties. In the private sphere, parties to private equity contracts and their lawyers utilize norms, conventions, and outside constraints to fill contractual gaps, to override explicit contractual terms, and to achieve a negotiated solution beyond the four corners of the contract. In this world, negotiating attorneys have their own discourse on contract language, particularly with respect to open terms, which often differs from the judicial interpretations of the terms they utilize.
The private equity contract, thus, is merely the starting point for analyzing the negotiated understanding of the parties. In the private equity structure, though, the contract still has a very real and valid purpose. It outlines the relationship of the parties and documents their agreement to the extent feasible, creating a bonded relationship to affect future conduct. This is a world where parties and their attorneys do not necessarily leave terms ambiguous for future litigation or negotiating purposes.Rather, the contract functions as a fulcrum for further private bonding, interpretation, negotiation, and agreement after execution of the acquisition agreement.
In the private equity structure, however, contract terms do play an important, flexible role throughout the relationship. Flipping the iceberg on its head, the contract is not the endpoint; rather, it is the foundation and starting point for an understanding among the parties. The contract mattersfrom the beginning in the private equity structure. The picture painted has much to offer in terms of further understanding and judicial interpretation of complex contracts - a topic I will explore in a companion paper to this one.It is also a world that Lisa Bernstein and Stewart Macaulay, who have written extensively on social norms and their role in establishing extralegal business relationships, would not find surprising.
Part II of this Article examines the historical evolution of the private equity contract and structure. Part III details the very public failure of these contracts. Part IV focuses on the structure of private equity and its alleged failures as well as the negotiation process for these transactions and the drafting errors made by lawyers documenting this structure. Part V details the path dependency of the private equity structure and the role of attorneys, particularly those for acquirees, in perpetuating the structure. Part VI concludes with a discussion of the response of market participants to the failures of private equity and its implication for the future structure of these transactions.

questions.question: Whether the contractual structure and drafting practices used in private equity acquisition agreements materially contributed to the widespread termination of deals during the 2007-2008 credit crisis.
questions.answer: Yes—the negotiated structure and drafting (including reverse termination fees and exploitable ambiguities) provided mechanisms that private equity buyers and lenders used to terminate or settle out of signed deals during 2007–2008.

questions.question: Whether lawyers for acquirees systematically negotiated suboptimal or ambiguous terms-because of path dependency, agency incentives, or concentrated market practice-that increased the likelihood of post-signing deal collapse.
questions.answer: Yes—because of path dependency and agency incentives within a highly concentrated repeat-player legal market, acquiree-side lawyers tended to accept non-innovative structures and made drafting errors, contributing to vulnerabilities (though not necessarily as the determining cause) that facilitated post-signing deal failures.

questions.question: Whether extralegal norms, reputational considerations, and a small, repeat-player legal market caused private equity contracts to operate as flexible, negotiated frameworks (rather than precise enforceable instruments), affecting parties' ability to enforce or exit acquisitions in times of financial distress.
questions.answer: Yes—the private equity contracting environment relied on extralegal norms, reputational forces, and a small repeat-player bar so that contracts functioned as flexible starting points for ongoing negotiation and interpretation, and in the crisis parties leveraged contractual terms and ambiguities to escape obligations.
