papers.node_id: 48emorylj547!!ARTICLE:MALPRACTICE AND THE TAX PRACTITIONER: AN ANALYSISOF THE AREAS IN WHICH MALPRACTICE OCCURS
papers.title: ARTICLE:MALPRACTICE AND THE TAX PRACTITIONER: AN ANALYSISOF THE AREAS IN WHICH MALPRACTICE OCCURS
papers.abstract:
As an attorney for approximately twenty-five years, I have been cognizant of the apparent increase in litigiousness of modern society,and of the concomitant increase in malpractice suits against professionals, both lawyers as well as non-lawyers.As a teacher of tax law, I am especially interested in how this trend impacts the tax lawyer, as well as other tax practitioners.What I am especially interested in is determining which areas of tax law and tax practice have generated the most malpractice claims so that practitioners may embark into such areas forewarned. Unfortunately, most of the existing literature focuses on various aspects of the elements of the malpractice cause of action or defenses thereto.Accordingly, I have undertaken this study primarily to analyze the reported tax malpractice cases from the vantage of substantive tax law to attempt to determine whether certain areas of tax law or aspects of tax practice seem to generate more malpractice claims than others. As a secondary inquiry, where the court addresses the measure of damages, or where otherwise appropriate, the discussion will focus on the proper measure of damages recoverable on account of the malpractice.
This study focuses solely on the reported cases. It examines instances of claimed malpractice involving federal income, estate, and gift taxes. It doesnot focus on any other federal taxes such as employment or excise taxes, nor on state or local taxes. While it is believed that most of the reported cases have been reviewed, I acknowledge the possibility that some may have avoided detection. This is possible especially in light of the esoteric venues in which some of the tax malpractice cases reside. For instance, tax malpractice situations have been discovered in insurance coverage litigation,an executor's fee-setting proceeding,and in several Tax Court cases in which the issue was the taxability of recoveries received in settlement of tax malpractice claims.
Originally, the focus of this study was to be limited solely to tax attorneys. However, it quickly became obvious that the focus should be enlarged to also include accountants. The dividing line between the work of the tax attorney and the accountant, at best, has always been murky and the subject of attention from both professions.Today, that line is becoming still more blurred. Recently, although ultimately one firm was vindicated, two of the "big five" accounting firms have been investigated for engaging in the unlicensed practice of law by virtue of their tax practices within Texas.Congress, in the Internal Revenue Service Restructuring and Reform Act of 1998,extended the traditional attorney-client privilege to accountants (as well as other tax practitioners). Additionally, overseas the big five accounting firms extensively associate and amalgamate with attorneys, including tax attorneys.At present, there is even at least one domestic instance of the "association" of a big five accounting firm with a law firm renowned for its tax practice.Many of the reported cases involve accountants. In most situations the defendantpractitioner could just as easily be from either profession. Finally, the interchangeability of the two professions is so great that a number of courts simply state that the malpractice standards are the same for both professions.
At the inception of this study, the author's worst fear was that due to the complexity of the tax law there would be instances of malpractice under virtually every section of the Internal Revenue Code, regardless of how innocuous the section appears. Again, at the inception of this undertaking, the author's most fervent hope was that an analysis of the reported cases would yield a clear indication of those specific areas of the tax law where errors leading to claims of malpractice were especially rampant so that the reader could be alerted to the special danger lurking there. As will be developed in the course of the ensuing discussion, neither the author's worst fear nor his most fervent hope turned out correct. While there are many instances of alleged and proven malpractice, they definitely do not include every, or even nearly every, section of the Internal Revenue Code. On the other hand, while tax shelter investing and the estate and gift tax area seem to have more reported cases than other areas, there also does not appear to be any one or several Internal Revenue Code sections or specific areas of tax practice that appear much more prone to malpractice litigation than other sections or areas. Indeed, a significant portion of the reported tax malpractice cases are not so much "tax malpractice" as they are general malpractice occurring in a tax context. For instance, this is certainly the situation with all the cases involving late-filing and non-filing of tax returns.Also, many of the errors are not due to complexity but, rather, to the practitioner ignoring or overlooking some simple, clearly mandated requirement such as making an election or obtaining consent before doing something.
Before presenting the results of the study in Part II, Part I will very briefly review the elements of the cause of action for malpractice. Concluding observations then follow.

questions.question: Which substantive areas of tax law and aspects of tax practice generate the most malpractice claims against tax practitioners (attorneys and accountants)?
questions.answer: The study finds that while tax shelter investing and the estate and gift tax area seem to have more reported malpractice cases than other areas, there is no clear set of Internal Revenue Code sections or specific practice areas that are markedly more prone to malpractice litigation.

questions.question: When courts address damages in tax malpractice cases, what is the appropriate measure and scope of recoverable damages?

Are malpractice claims in the tax context primarily caused by the inherent complexity of tax rules or more often by basic practitioner errors and general malpractice (e.g., missed elections, late or non-filing, oversight)?
questions.answer: They are more often caused by general practitioner errors—e.g., late or non-filing and overlooking simple, clearly mandated requirements such as making a required election or obtaining consent—rather than by the inherent complexity of tax rules.

papers.node_id: 77nyulrev1040!!ARTICLE:RETHINKING CORPORATE BONDS: THE TRADE-OFF BETWEEN INDIVIDUAL AND COLLECTIVE RIGHTS
papers.title: ARTICLE:RETHINKING CORPORATE BONDS: THE TRADE-OFF BETWEEN INDIVIDUAL AND COLLECTIVE RIGHTS
papers.abstract:
Together with stocks, bonds are the most commonly issued corporate securities.Bondholders and stockholders obtain rights from common legal sources: a contract (the "indenture") for bonds; corporate law and the certificate of incorporation for stocks. Among holders of bonds and stocks of the same issue, these rights are generally identical and thus, in a relevant sense, shared by all. Therefore, a degree of interdependence exists among bondholders as well as among stockholders. Any system for the modification and enforcement ofthese shared rights necessarily involves a tradeoff between individual rights, held separately by each holder, and collective rights, held only by a specified group of holders or by some representative.
For stocks, this system of individual and collective rights is largely set by law. Corporate statutes provide for a board of directors that is elected by shareholders and that represents shareholders' economic interests in the company.The board is empowered to manage the company,though it must obtain shareholder approval for charter amendments and certain extraordinary transactions.When shareholder approval is required, consent by the requisite majority of shareholders, with some narrow exceptions,binds all shareholders of the company. Thus, shareholder rights are predominantly collective, exercised either by the collective representative (the board) or by a majority of shareholders.Still, some shareholder rights - enforcement rights being the most significant - are held individually. Hence, if the board of directors violates its duties to shareholders,an individual shareholder may bring a suit against the directors to enforce her rights.
By contrast, the system of rights for bonds is largely specified in a contract, the bond indenture.While that system has superficial similaritiesto the system for stocks, the system for bonds differs in fundamental respects. Just like stockholders, bondholders have a collective representative, the "indenture trustee," who is meant to represent their economic interests.However, the structure of the indenture trusteeship diverges in important ways from the structure of the board of directors, not least in that bondholders do not elect the trustee.Just as for stockholders, consent by holders of a majority of outstanding bonds is required to amend the indenture.Nonetheless, unlike a stockholder, a bondholder faces substantial barriers to bringing a suit against the company if her rights are violated. Many claims can be brought only by the trustee or by a large group of holders, and then only after they comply with certain other requirements.
This overview raises a fundamental question about the structure of bondholder rights: Whatever the substantive content of these rights, to what extent should any particular right be vested individually or collectively? After a brief summary of bondholder rights in Part I, Part II presents a framework for analyzing this question. This framework will take account of the theoretical advantages and disadvantages of vesting rights individually and collectively as well as of institutional features that bear on the practical significance of these advantages and disadvantages for the U.S. corporate bond market.
Part III argues that the structure of individual and collective bondholder rights established by the typical bond indenture is flawed. The resulting system is inconsistent, unworkable, illogical, and imprudent. The system is inconsistent in that individual bondholders have veto power over the amendment of certain rights yet lack the power to enforce these rights if they are violated. The system is unworkable in that neither bondholders nor the trustee may be able to assert certain bondholder rights. The system is illogical in that violations of certain rights which affect only individual bondholders, rather than all bondholders as a group, are nevertheless not enforceable individually. Finally, the system is imprudent in that significant enforcement powers are given to the trustee - who has limited incentives to enforce bondholderrights - and substantial limits are placed on enforcement by bondholders themselves. Part III also discusses several reasons that may account for the failure of market forces to correct these defects.
Part IV makes specific recommendations on how to revise the present system of individual and collective rights. Some of these recommendations entail changes in the interpretations courts have accorded to the relevant indenture provisions. Others entail changes in these provisions themselves. The Appendix contains a sample set of provisions that could be inserted in an actual indenture to correct the identified defects.

questions.question: To what extent should the rights of corporate bond investors (including enforcement rights) be vested in individual bondholders versus exercised collectively through a representative or majority decision rule?
questions.answer: The paper contends that typical indentures misallocate rights by overrelying on collective/trustee control and unduly restricting individual enforcement, and it advocates revising interpretations and contract terms to create a coherent mix that permits individual enforcement—especially for rights affecting individual holders—and aligns enforcement powers with amendment/veto rights.

questions.question: Does concentrating enforcement authority in collective representatives while restricting individual enforcement produce inconsistent, ineffective, or misaligned enforcement outcomes for bond investors?
questions.answer: Yes; vesting substantial enforcement authority in the trustee while curtailing individual bondholder suits creates an inconsistent, unworkable, illogical, and imprudent system that misaligns enforcement with investor interests and sometimes leaves rights effectively unenforceable.

questions.question: Why do market forces fail to correct suboptimal allocations of individual versus collective bondholder rights, and what contractual or interpretive reforms would improve enforcement and market outcomes?
questions.answer: The paper states that there are several reasons market forces have not corrected these defects (not specified in the abstract) and recommends reforms through revised judicial interpretations and amendments to indenture provisions, including sample clauses, to realign individual and collective enforcement.

papers.node_id: 51emorylj1317!!ARTICLE:SOVEREIGN BONDS AND THE COLLECTIVE WILL+
papers.title: ARTICLE:SOVEREIGN BONDS AND THE COLLECTIVE WILL+
papers.authors: Lee C. Buchheit; G. Mitu Gulati
papers.abstract:
Multicreditor debt instruments such as bonds and syndicated bank loans are uncommon legal arrangements. In most contracts, the parties know each other's identity beforehand, and they make a conscious decision to enter into a legal relationship. In a multicreditor debt instrument, the borrower's identity is of course known by each investor, but what the investors don't know - what they often never know - is the identity of each other. Bond investors are like the patrons in a theater audience: each one has decided to see a particular play on a particular night, but none has any idea who she will be seeing it with. If you wish to carry the analogy further, the tradable nature of bonds means that fellow patrons are constantly leaving and entering the theater throughout the performance.
Now this promiscuous grouping of investors in a bond issue is not troubling as long as you believe that the only important relationship here is that between the debtor and each separate investor. Look at a bond issue close enough, this theory contends, and you will see that it breaks down atomically into hundreds or thousands of bilateral contracts between the bond issuer and each investor; the appearance of an investor group or syndicate is just that, an appearance, with few practical or legal implications. This view assumes, of course, that all bondholders are the passive recipients of payments from the issuer and that the behavior of any one bondholder is a matter of indifference to the other bondholders.
And so it may be, but only until things go wrong. It is when the bond issuer runs into financial difficulties that the actions of any one bondholder can dramatically affect the interests of all the other lenders. For example, if each holder has the unfettered discretion to accelerate its bonds following an event of default, to commence a lawsuit and attach the borrower's assets, to force a foreclosure on collateral or to push the borrower into bankruptcy, the other bondholders may then find that their own options in dealing with the situation are dangerously curtailed. The ruthful bondholders, however large their majority, are thus at the mercy of their most ruthless colleagues. Visible financial strains on the bond issuer will thus bring out a sauve qui peut response from some bondholders. Grabbing a borrower's assets ahead of one's fellow bondholders may reveal an underdeveloped fraternal instinct, but it probably makes good business sense; there usually is little left for the hindmost creditor.
By the late nineteenth century, many bond issuers and investors had come to believe that bondholder cooperation in a distressed situation was highly desirable. In those days, bankruptcy generally meant liquidation and liquidation often meant recoveries by the creditors (particularly the unsecured creditors) of only a small portion of what they were owed. Allowing a single bondholder to force a liquidation of the debtor or, very nearly as bad, giving such a holder the leverage to compel other investors to buy him out on preferential terms in order to forestall liquidation, was therefore something that many bondholders felt should be avoided.
The problem had several interrelated aspects. How could the "grab and run" instinct of each bondholder be kept in check long enough to permit a coordinated workout to the ratable benefit of all creditors? How could the majority of bondholders ensure that their collective judgment about the terms of such a workout would be binding on all bondholders? Finally, how could the majority neutralize the ability of dissident creditors to force a preferential buyout of their claims as the price of not putting the debtor into liquidation?

questions.question: How can creditors in multicreditor debt instruments overcome individual holdout and grab-and-run incentives to achieve coordinated restructurings or workouts that are ratably fair to all lenders?
questions.answer: By promoting bondholder cooperation in distress and using mechanisms that restrain individual enforcement, make majority workout decisions binding on all holders, and neutralize dissidents’ ability to demand preferential buyouts, creditors can coordinate ratable restructurings.

questions.question: How do the anonymity and tradability of bond investors shape their incentives in distress, and what contractual or institutional arrangements can mitigate opportunistic behavior that would force liquidation or extract preferential treatment?
questions.answer: Because anonymous, tradable bondholders can in distress race to accelerate, sue, seize assets, or force bankruptcy (or leverage threats to extract buyouts), mitigation requires cooperative arrangements that curb unilateral action, bind minorities to majority-decided workout terms, and prevent single holders from forcing liquidation or preferential treatment.

papers.node_id: 85cornelllrev956!!ARTICLE:SOVEREIGN DEBT RESTRUCTURING: A BANKRUPTCY REORGANIZATION APPROACH
papers.title: ARTICLE:SOVEREIGN DEBT RESTRUCTURING: A BANKRUPTCY REORGANIZATION APPROACH
papers.abstract: The "pressures and problems that have led to corporate bankruptcy law also operate in the case of a sovereign borrower in financial distress."Yet legal scholars have never systematically examined sovereign debt restructuring in light of bankruptcy reorganization law principles,which are designed to solve such fundamental problems as the ability of holdout creditors to undermine collective action toward a negotiated settlement. Moreover, absent the bankruptcy reorganization incentives that encourage free market liquidity, multilateral governmental institutions such as the International Monetary Fund (IMF) must act by default as lenders of last resort. This not only forces taxpayers to subsidize foreign governments and their creditors, but also creates problems such as moral hazard: countries anticipating an IMF bailout might have less reason to take a prudent economic course, and lenders expecting protection from the consequences of default might have a greater tendency to take unwarranted financial risks. This Article proposes that an international convention for sovereign debt restructuring based on three fundamental principles of bankruptcy reorganization law could address these problems, without requiring supervision by an international bankruptcy court. The convention also would permit the IMF, through a mechanism of back-to-back nonrecourse lending, to continue its current practice of imposing conditionality on funding without triggering the problems presently associated with IMF lending.

questions.question: Whether an international legal framework for sovereign debt restructuring, modeled on corporate bankruptcy reorganization principles, would reduce holdout creditor problems and enable more orderly collective renegotiation of sovereign debts.
questions.answer: Yes—the paper argues that an international convention grounded in bankruptcy reorganization principles would address holdout creditor problems and support collective action toward negotiated settlements without needing an international bankruptcy court.

questions.question: Whether adopting such a framework would allow multilateral lenders to provide conditional emergency financing without producing taxpayer-subsidies and the moral hazard currently associated with last-resort sovereign bailouts.
questions.answer: Yes—it contends that such a framework would let the IMF provide conditional financing via back-to-back nonrecourse lending without triggering the taxpayer subsidies and moral hazard now associated with last-resort bailouts.

papers.node_id: 78stjohnslrev1011!!ARTICLE:TAX MALPRACTICE: AREAS IN WHICH IT OCCURS AND THE MEASURE OF DAMAGES-AN UPDATE
papers.title: ARTICLE:TAX MALPRACTICE: AREAS IN WHICH IT OCCURS AND THE MEASURE OF DAMAGES-AN UPDATE
papers.abstract:
About five years ago, I published an article exploring the areas in which reported tax malpractice cases arose.
As a secondary inquiry, that article, hereinafter referred to as Malpractice I, also focused on the measure of damages awarded in such cases. The result of that study indicated that many of those cases involved general malpractice in a tax context, as opposed to "tax malpractice." Many of the errors involved missing time deadlines, such as late-filing and non-filing of tax returns. Other errors included "ignoring or overlooking some simple, clearly mandated requirement such as making an election or obtaining consent" when necessary.Apart from a large number of tax shelter-related cases, which arose from the tax shelter frenzy of the late 1970s and early 1980s, and cases in the estate planning/estate and gift tax area, Malpractice I was unable to identify or predict any area or areas of tax practice more likely than others to spawn tax malpractice litigation.Malpractice I did allay my worst fear that due to the complexity of the tax law there would be innumerable instances of tax malpractice involving virtually every section of the Internal Revenue Code (I.R.C.).
In the years since the publication of Malpractice I, I have received a number of calls and e-mails from practitioners inquiring as to whether, in the course of my research, I had encountered a situation "on all fours" with the one they were working on. One of these inquiries even led me to explore whether issuing an incorrect federal information return, such as a W-2 form or a form 1099, could be the basis of a tort recovery similar to recoveries for tax malpractice.These inquiries convinced me of the continuing importance of this area. As if further encouragement were needed, the recent Internal Revenue Service (IRS) crackdown on attorneys and accountants involved in the sale of overly aggressive and likely flawed tax sheltersfollowing in the footsteps of a number of financial scandals - such as Enron, which had accounting and tax machinations at its core-emphasized the importance to society of a developed and principled body of law governing when and to what extent professional advisors might be held financially responsible for their advice.
Primarily, this Article will analyze the tax malpractice cases that have been reported since Malpractice I was published from the vantage of substantive tax law to attempt to ascertain whether certain areas of tax law or certain aspects of tax practice seem to generate more malpractice claims than others. As a secondary inquiry, the Article will discuss the proper measure of damages recoverable on account of such malpractice.
This Article focuses solely on reported cases. It examines instances of claimed malpractice involving federal income, estate, gift, and generation skipping taxes. It does not focus on other federal taxes such as employment taxes. While state and local taxes are not intended to be focused upon separately, this Article discusses several cases that involve allegations of wrong advice in connection with state sales taxand state personal property tax.While I have attempted to locate and review all of the reported cases, I acknowledge the possibility, or more accurately, the likelihood, that I missed some,especially since tax malpractice situations continue to sometimes lurk in esoteric venues. For instance, I will discuss an interpleader action where the court allocated the proceeds from a tax malpractice settlement,and an action to set aside a divorce settlement that refers to a previous tax malpractice litigation arising from the same divorce.
Both tax attorneys and accountants are focused on in this study. While, from a purely theoretical standpoint, it might be desirable toanalyze these professions separately, the pragmatic truth is that the dividing line between the work of the tax attorney and the accountant, at best, has always been murky.It is not possible to separate out the two professions. The dividing line may have become murkier when Congress, in 1998, extended the traditional attorney-client privilege to accountants, as well as to other tax practitioners.There are instances where attorneys and accountants share the role of defendant.In many situations, the defendant-practitioner could just as easily be from one profession as from the other. Given the interchangeability of these two professions in the malpractice area, many courts simply hold both professions to the same malpractice standards.
The results of this update are roughly consistent with the results of Malpractice I. The area that seems to generate the most cases, as it did before, is estate planning, or more specifically, the estate and gift tax cases discussed in Part II.D.2. These cases generally involve planning the transmission of property to one's heirs at the least possible tax cost.
The tax shelter area, which generated a relatively large number of cases in Malpractice I, was pretty quiet during recent years. However, with the IRS's current aggressive pursuit of investors in tax shelters,a wave of malpractice suits against the accountants and attorneys involved in facilitating or even promoting these unsuccessful shelters seems to be just over the horizon, perhaps to come into full view in five to ten or fifteen years ("Malpractice III" or even "Malpractice IV"?).Beyond the estate planning area, more cases have arisen in the very broad general negligenceareas, including late filing, non-filing and negligent preparation, than in any other specific area. As before, only a relatively small number of cases address the issue of what types of damages are recoverable, and much work remains to be done in this area.
Before presenting the results of this study in Part II, Part I will briefly review some elementary background principles, such as the elements of the malpractice cause of action and the measure of damages. Concluding observations will follow.

questions.question: Which areas or types of tax practice are more likely to generate professional malpractice claims against tax advisors?
questions.answer: Malpractice claims most frequently arise in estate planning—particularly estate and gift tax matters—with additional concentrations in broad general negligence such as late filing, non-filing, and negligent preparation, while tax-shelter cases have been quiet recently but may surge in the future.

questions.question: What types and measures of damages can plaintiffs recover in professional malpractice suits arising from tax advice?
questions.answer: Only a relatively small number of cases address what types of damages are recoverable, and the proper measure of damages remains underdeveloped, with no specific measures detailed in the abstract.

papers.node_id: 84washulrev1627!!F. HODGE O'NEAL CORPORATE AND SECURITIES LAW SYMPOSIUM: PUBLIC SYMBOL IN PRIVATE CONTRACT: A CASE STUDY
papers.title: F. HODGE O'NEAL CORPORATE AND SECURITIES LAW SYMPOSIUM: PUBLIC SYMBOL IN PRIVATE CONTRACT: A CASE STUDY
papers.abstract:
In June 1997 a developing country defied convention. It issued New York law bonds that let 75 percent of the bondholders change key financial terms.Until then, standard form New York law contracts required unanimous consent. But no one seemed to notice the innovation, and just about no one followed suit.
In February 2003 another developing country issued New York law bonds with a 75 percent amendment threshold.This time, the world ofinternational finance erupted in applause and criticism. Major press outlets, finance ministers, and senior executives publicly pondered the shift.Other countries adopted similar provisions under the rubric of "Collective Action Clauses" or "CACs." Academic study of sovereign debt contracts took on new importance. This article is part of an effort to understand what happened and what it means.
Standard - or "boilerplate" - terms in complex financial contracts rarely change.The prevalent theoretical explanation of boilerplate attributes its existence to learning and network effects and associated "switching costs."This body of theory suggests that market participants attach value to contract terms either because they have been used in the past and are well known (learning effects), or are widely used now and/or are expected to be widely used in the future (network effects).As a result, firms might adopt terms that are suboptimal on their own merits just because they are well understood or widely used. Switching may be costly for a single firm because it takes time and effort to produce a new term that works and to educate the target audience about its meaning. There is no guarantee that investors, analysts, and judges will interpret a new term in a way that is favorable to its original proponent or, as the example in our opening paragraphs illustrates, that others will adopt the term in the foreseeable future.
Boilerplate change is poorly understood because it happens rarely, slowly, and quietly. Contract terms do not normally feature on the editorial pages of The Wall Street Journal, The Economist, or The Financial Times, or in dozens of academic studies across law, economics, and political science. Against this background, the dramatic and public shift in sovereign bond documentation beginning in 2003 offers a rare perspective on the contracting process and boilerplate change.
The CAC episode is unusual in another respect. World leaders generally do not know what boilerplate is, much less advocate for it incommuniques reserved for big-picture concerns such as global economic imbalances. Yet for nearly a decade CACs had a guaranteed spot in summit statements alongside financial stability and currency regimes.Moreover, boilerplate theory does not usually contemplate a leading role for the public sector in promoting optimal private contract terms.But in the case of Collective Action Clauses, governments not party to the contracts got credit for driving the shift.Judging from recent policy initiatives, the apparent success of the CAC campaign may have spawned a new model of framing economic policy proposals in terms of private contract reform. The latest public-sector effort to promote GDP-indexed bonds cites the CAC experience as an inspiration, and even adopts some of the organizational features of the earlier initiative, such as the expert contract drafting group.
For all its value as precedent, the public sector's role in the CAC episode remains unexplored. Proponents in the Bush II administration called the shift "market-based" even as market commentary attributed it to government pressure.On the other hand, neither the United States nor any other G-7 government appears to have issued direct threats or bribes - the traditional instruments of "hard power."Financial industry regulators refused to mandate CACs or otherwise promote their inclusion; instead, pressure came in the form of exhortations by economic policy officials.Did the "soft power"of G-7 ideas convince developing countries of the inherent virtues of CACs? No emerging market official would tell us thathe participated in the CAC shift because the clauses could alter the course of a crisis. Even after moving to CACs, borrowers expressed skepticism about the extent of the holdout problem CACs would solve. Alternatively, scholars have suggested that G-7 governments engaged in informational "cueing" to help overcome network effects, a form of "soft" regulation.Here too, no early mover admitted acting in expectation of a market-wide shift; few thought the G-7 capable of delivering such a shift and all worried that their country would pay a penalty for innovating.
A final lingering puzzle of the CAC episode is just how few private or public sector participants in it express strong feelings about the clauses as such. We spoke with dozens of actors whose websites and speeches proclaim the seminal importance of the CAC shift (usually as they claim paternity), yet in our interviews a scant few described the change itself as important in addressing the problems of sovereign debt restructuring or financial crises in the emerging markets. Many were unsure of how the new clauses would work in a crisis; most said they were probably good; none said they were clearly bad. More participants volunteered strong feelings about the process that led to the shift - praising cooperation, grumbling about wasted time and official meddling. Was this another instance of wasted lawyering or runaway process?
If true in part, this description is incomplete and not entirely fair. Most participants suggested that their efforts on CACs had less to do with the clauses' literal purpose (facilitating future contract modification) than with their relative utility in advancing other goals, such as demonstrating commitment to a new crisis management strategy, currying political favor, or establishing reputations in the market. Some were successful in achieving these goals; others failed. Their collaboration produced a revealing study in the uses of contract form and ways of governance.
We depart from earlier quantitative and analytical studies of sovereign debt contractsin favor of an interview-based approach. We have collected over 100 accounts of the CAC shift from market participants,officials, and others who took part in it, and have supplemented these with our own observations from the daily work of law firms and government offices, conferences and negotiations, press accounts, official documents, and of course the debt contracts themselves.
Below we first review the sovereign debt context in the early 2000s, the contract provisions at the center of the study, and the process that led to the shift in 2003. Second, we recount alternative explanations for the shift that have been published to date. We then describe the findings from our interviews and conclude with implications for contract change, the uses of contract, and governance.

questions.question: Why did sovereign borrowers and creditors shift from unanimous-consent amendment provisions to supermajority (e.g., 75%) collective amendment clauses in sovereign bond contracts beginning in 2003?
questions.answer: According to participants’ accounts, the move to supermajority CACs in 2003 was driven less by the clauses’ direct restructuring utility and more by their value as a public symbol to signal a new crisis-management strategy, gain political favor, and build market reputations.

questions.question: To what extent did public-sector actors influence that shift through non-coercive means (e.g., advocacy, informational cueing or 'soft power') versus the change arising from private-market dynamics like learning and network effects?
questions.answer: While G‑7 officials promoted CACs through exhortation rather than coercion and were publicly credited with spurring the change, interviewees generally did not attribute their decisions to such soft power or to expectations of network-driven tipping, implying only limited direct influence from non‑coercive public action relative to other strategic motives.

questions.question: Do contracting parties adopt changes in standard boilerplate clauses primarily for their direct contractual effects, or instead to achieve indirect goals such as signaling policy commitment, building reputation, or facilitating coordination among stakeholders?
questions.answer: Parties adopted the boilerplate change chiefly to achieve indirect goals—signaling policy commitment, currying political favor, and enhancing reputation—rather than for the clauses’ literal, direct contractual effects.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents how the developing secondary market in LDC debt (the emerging‑market market) promoted and facilitated the Brady Plan debt exchanges in 1989–1993; Paper B studies how changes in sovereign bond documentation (CACs) arose in the international bond market as a mechanism intended to affect future restructurings and market behavior.

shared_topics.topic: contractual innovation as a tool for managing sovereign debt crises (new instruments and clauses)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on debt exchanges, Brady bonds, debt‑equity swaps and buy‑backs as novel contractual/instrument responses to the debt crisis; Paper B examines the introduction and significance of Collective Action Clauses as a new contractual term intended to alter how sovereign debt can be modified in crises.

shared_topics.topic: the influence of public policy and government initiatives on private sovereign‑debt contract forms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the market’s role in promoting the Brady Plan—a policy‑driven restructuring framework that reshaped private debt contracts—and Paper B interrogates the G‑7/U.S. policy campaign and other public actors' 'soft power' role in promoting CAC adoption in private bond contracts.

shared_topics.topic: how market structure, participant incentives, and network/boilerplate effects affect the adoption and diffusion of contract changes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes stages of the emerging‑market trading market and how market dynamics led banks and investors to accept Brady Plan exchanges; Paper B studies why boilerplate terms are sticky, how switching costs and network effects shaped CAC uptake, and the incentives and signaling reasons that drove (or inhibited) adoption.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 6jempiricallegalstud818!!ARTICLE: Contractual Complexity and the Cognitive Load of R&D Alliance Contracts
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Contractual Complexity and the Cognitive Load of R&D Alliance Contracts

shared_topics.topic: factors driving the design and evolution of contract language (costs, reputation, trust, and network effects)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how drafting costs, information asymmetries, monitoring, trust, and reputation shape whether parties produce simple or complex R&D alliance contracts, while Paper B investigates switching costs, learning and network effects, and reputational/political incentives that explain why market participants adopt or resist new sovereign bond boilerplate like CACs.

shared_topics.topic: contracts as signals or tools for broader governance and strategic ends rather than just literal allocations of rights
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues contractual complexity serves a signaling function about the parties' costs and practices and can affect interpretation and enforcement, and Paper B shows that adoption of CACs and other boilerplate was often used instrumentally to signal policy commitments, market credibility, or political alignment rather than solely to change legal mechanics.

shared_topics.topic: the role of external actors and institutions in shaping contract form and interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A considers how courts, lawyers, and policymakers should account for contractual complexity in enforcement and rule design, and Paper B documents how governments, international policy actors, and regulators played a central (often ‘soft power’) role in promoting or framing changes to private contract terms like CACs.

shared_topics.topic: the dynamics and empirical study of contract change and measurement of contract content
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops and tests objective and subjective measures of contractual complexity (length, kilobytes, cognitive load) and examines how clauses accumulate, while Paper B studies the rare, slow process of boilerplate change through interviews and documentary evidence to explain how and why specific contract terms (CACs) shifted in market practice.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: PARI PASSU CLAUSES AND THE SKEUOMORPH PROBLEM IN CONTRACT LAW

shared_topics.topic: persistence of seemingly nonfunctional boilerplate clauses in sovereign debt contracts
shared_topics.justification: Both papers investigate why clauses that appear costly or purposeless continue to appear in sovereign bond documentation: Paper A treats the pari passu clause as a puzzling, persistent provision, while Paper B studies why standard terms (like amendment thresholds) are sticky and how change in sovereign bond boilerplate is rare and surprising.

shared_topics.topic: conceptualizing contract terms as product attributes or skeuomorphs that diffuse and persist
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly frames contract clauses as product features and labels pari passu a skeuomorph adapted from earlier practice, and Paper B likewise treats contract terms as 'boilerplate' attributes whose adoption and diffusion follow dynamics similar to other product or standard features.

shared_topics.topic: mechanisms explaining boilerplate inertia — learning, network effects, switching costs, and cognitive/reputational influences
shared_topics.justification: Both engage with explanations for why suboptimal clauses persist: Paper B emphasizes learning/network effects and switching costs as theoretical drivers of boilerplate stability, while Paper A surveys reputational pressures, cognitive biases, and historical adaptation as complementary reasons such phenomena endure.

shared_topics.topic: how contract clauses affect sovereign debt restructuring and the role of external (public or reputational) actors in promoting or impeding contract change
shared_topics.justification: Each paper links clause form to restructuring outcomes and to influences beyond bilateral bargaining: Paper A highlights the mischief pari passu causes in sovereign debt contexts, and Paper B analyzes CACs as a reform affecting restructuring dynamics and investigates how public-sector actors and ‘soft power’ interventions helped (or were perceived to help) shift private contract terms.

shared_topics.topic: use of New York law as the governing law in international financial transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes when and how New York counsel should give opinions about agreements that are governed by foreign law or by New York law in cross-border deals; Paper B studies the widespread use of New York law in sovereign bond contracts and the implications of issuing developing‑country debt under New York law.

shared_topics.topic: the role and formulation of standard/boilerplate contract clauses in cross-border deals
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on the legal effect and conflict‑of‑laws implications of clauses like governing‑law and execution/choice provisions when international counsel gives opinions; Paper B examines the adoption and change of boilerplate (notably Collective Action Clauses) in sovereign debt documentation and why standard terms persist or shift.

shared_topics.topic: how domestic/state action or domestic statutes affect private international contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A considers the impact of U.S. statutes (e.g., presidential authorities), the act‑of‑state doctrine, and other state‑law interventions on the content and qualifications of New York legal opinions; Paper B investigates the influence of public actors (G‑7 exhortations, government 'soft power') and policy campaigns on private contract form and market practice.

shared_topics.topic: cross‑border enforceability and mechanisms for resolving transnational disputes or restructurings
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses enforceability issues including recognition of foreign judgments, which law governs execution/delivery, and limitations on enforceability arising from foreign or U.S. public law; Paper B addresses how contractual devices (CACs) and contract design aim to affect sovereign debt restructuring outcomes, holdouts, and the practical enforceability of collective remedies across jurisdictions.

shared_topics.topic: mechanisms for managing sovereign or systemic financial crises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on capital‑flow management, macroprudential tools, and policy sequencing to preserve domestic and global financial stability, and Paper B studies the adoption of Collective Action Clauses as a contractual mechanism aimed at facilitating sovereign debt restructuring and reducing holdout risks in crises.

shared_topics.topic: international coordination and market‑wide change
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes the need for multilateral coordination and the IMF's multilateral surveillance to address spillovers of domestic policies on global capital flows, and Paper B examines how cross‑border informational campaigns and coordinated signals by public actors helped produce a market‑wide shift in sovereign bond contract terms.

shared_topics.topic: interaction between legal frameworks and financial policy (constraints and channels)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights the fragmented web of bilateral, regional, and multilateral legal obligations that constrain states' ability to manage capital flows, whereas Paper B analyzes how private contract boilerplate (and its reform) functions as a legal channel through which policy goals and crisis management practices are implemented and promoted by public actors.

compared_to.partner_title: INTERNATIONAL BANKING SYMPOSIUM: FOREWORD 1988 Center for Transnational Legal Studies

shared_topics.topic: contractual mechanisms for creditor coordination and preventing holdouts in sovereign debt restructurings
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the standard documentation developed during the 1980s debt crisis (sharing provisions, mandatory prepayment, negative pledges and pari passu treatment) as tools to ensure pro rata treatment and block early exit by creditors; Paper B studies Collective Action Clauses (majority-amendment thresholds) as a later contractual innovation aimed at resolving holdout problems and facilitating coordinated restructurings.

shared_topics.topic: standardization and change in sovereign-debt boilerplate/documentation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A describes the emergence of a remarkably uniform set of rescheduling documents and later modifications (securitization, debt-to-equity exchanges) that altered longstanding document terms, while Paper B investigates the rare, publicized episode of boilerplate change when CACs were adopted and the dynamics that enabled (or impeded) such a shift.

shared_topics.topic: the role of public-sector and international institutions in shaping private debt contracts and restructurings
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes the involvement of the IMF, official creditors, regulators and national law (tax and banking regulation) in structuring debt workouts and enabling instruments like debt-to-equity programs, and Paper B examines how G-7 governments, policy officials and summit politics used soft power, exhortation and informational cueing to promote CAC adoption in private sovereign bond contracts.

shared_topics.topic: legal enforceability, dispute risk, and doctrinal issues surrounding sovereign debt instruments
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights the relative paucity of litigation, the significance of doctrines like act of state, and conflicts-of-law questions arising from rescheduling documentation and extraterritorial discovery, while Paper B interrogates uncertainties about how newly adopted clauses (CACs) would operate in crisis, how judges and market actors would interpret novel boilerplate, and the legal risks attendees feared or disregarded.

shared_topics.topic: design of contractual clauses to manage cross-border creditor–debtor relations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes lenders' and borrowers' choice between court forum-selection and arbitration clauses in international loan agreements and how those clauses affect enforceability and remedies; Paper B studies the adoption of Collective Action Clauses (CACs) in sovereign bond documentation as a discrete instance of changing boilerplate terms intended to alter how cross-border financial contracts operate in crises.

shared_topics.topic: enforcement and restructuring of sovereign or transnational debt (holdouts, recognition, sovereign defenses)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on enforceability differences between judicial judgments and arbitral awards, and how sovereign immunity, act-of-state doctrines, and exchange controls complicate enforcement and rescheduling; Paper B examines CACs as a contractual mechanism to mitigate holdout problems and facilitate sovereign debt restructuring and collective decisionmaking.

shared_topics.topic: the influence of public law and policy on private financial contract terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses statutory and international instruments (e.g., amendments to FSIA/Arbitration Act, IMF Articles, New York Convention effects) that change the calculus of including arbitration or forum clauses in loans; Paper B documents how governments, summit statements and G‑7 ‘soft power’ campaigns shaped market adoption of CACs and how public-sector initiatives can induce private boilerplate change.

shared_topics.topic: creditor coordination, bargaining leverage, and renegotiation dynamics in international finance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A addresses how borrower size, sovereign status, and debtor leverage affect lenders' bargaining options and the choice of forum in rescheduling negotiations; Paper B investigates how changing the amendment threshold in bond terms (CACs) alters collective creditor decisionmaking, bargaining dynamics, and the incentives for holdouts during sovereign restructurings.
