papers.node_id: 1988uilllrev219!!INTERNATIONAL BANKING SYMPOSIUM: FOREWORD 1988 Center for Transnational Legal Studies
papers.title: INTERNATIONAL BANKING SYMPOSIUM: FOREWORD 1988 Center for Transnational Legal Studies
papers.authors: Ralph Reisner; Michael Gruson; Roger W. Thomas
papers.abstract:
This symposium is the outgrowth of various programs and activities of the University of Illinois College of Law which it has conducted in the field of international banking since the midseventies.  One set of activities in this area began in 1975 when the College of Law was commissioned by the Organization of American States and later the Inter-American Development Bank to conduct a series of annual seminars pertaining to legal developments in the field of international finance and particularly as these related to Latin America.  As might be expected, after 1982 these programs began to focus on the legal issues surrounding the debt crisis. In July 1983 the College of Law independently sponsored a conference at the Rockefeller Foundation in Bellagio, Italy, attended by leading financial law experts, to explore the legal consequences that would attend a default by the sovereign debtors.  The papers presented at this conference were later published as a symposium of theUniversity of Illinois Law Review.This conference, as well as later conferences conducted under the auspices of the Inter-American Development Bank on related topics,would not have been possible without the generous and unstinting time commitment of many of the lawyers, bankers, and government officials who were directly involved in the various rescheduling negotiations.
Another set of activities and programs have focused on the regulation of foreign banking.  For instance, in November 1979 the College ofLaw sponsored a colloquium in Chicago, Illinois to analyze and assess the newly enacted International Banking Act of 1978.  The papers presented at this conference by national authorities in the field of banking regulation were subsequently published as a symposium of theUniversity of Illinois Law Forum.
Two areas of immediate concern to the international financial community are treated in this symposium.  One pertains to the regulation of foreign banks in the United States, the other focuses on emerging legal issues related to the sovereign debt crisis.  While both of these topics have been the subject of earlier analysis in this review,intervening developments in both of these areas of concern make the present reexamination particularly timely.
This year marks the tenth anniversary of the enactment of the International Banking Act of 1978 (IBA)which provided the first comprehensive regulation of the activities of foreign banking in the United States.  Much has taken place in these ten years.  The Federal Reserve Board has promulgated regulation Kcarrying out the directions of the IBA.  Congress has amended section 2(h) of the Bank Holding Company Act of 1956,and several provisions of the IBA were tested in the courts. The tight legal restrictions on U.S. banks (e.g., the Glass-Stegall Act and limitations on interstate banking) that were intended to safeguard the public interest have, in the view of some, become heavy leg irons that prevent U.S. banks from competing on an equal basis with nonbank financial institutions.  These same legal restrictions apply to foreign banks in the United States.  Because Congress has been unable to arrive at a consensus on how to structure the financial sector in the United States, the regulatory agencies, the courts, and the state legislatures have become the battleground for changes of banking regulations.  In general, foreign banks with a banking presence in the United States have also benefited from these changes.
A primary concern of Congress in enacting the IBA was to achieve "parity of treatment between foreign and domestic banks in like circumstances."The lead article by Messrs. Carr and More, which includes a timely assessment of how foreign banks have fared since the enactment of the IBA ten years ago, suggests that this congressional purpose has been substantially realized.  In terms of this symposium, the Carr/More contribution provides a comprehensive assessment of the regulatory structure, both federal and state, which governs the manner and form inwhich foreign banks do business in the United States.  Aside from its analysis of how foreign banks may be structured for their U.S. operations the article also serves as a useful introduction to the subject of foreign bank regulation in general.
The IBA must also be evaluated in light of broader changes that have taken place in the international banking landscape.  European banks will soon have a common European banking market and they will be able to freely branch and provide services in that market.  Access to the various banking markets has become a central issue.  From the U.S. standpoint, regulatory barriers in Japan serve to limit U.S. banks' access to that market; European banks complain that they cannot operate as global banks when entering the United States.  In the past, principles such as "national treatment" or reciprocity have been used as a yardstick to gauge the appropriateness of national regulatory policyvis a visthe foreign banking sector.  Given the increasingly global nature of banking and the rendering of financial services, strict adherence to these traditional concepts may not be sufficient to establish the preconditions of a true international banking system.  Mr. Michael Orr's article,Reciprocity and Regulation of Entry, contains a very timely reflection on some of these problems.
In practical terms, the rules governing foreign acquisitions of U.S. banks will, in effect, determine the actual scope of foreign banking in the United States.  Current U.S. policies in this regard are, thus, a crucial part of the entire regulatory matrix.  The article by Mr. Tortoriello provides a comprehensive examination of federal and state banking laws governing the acquisition of a U.S. bank or a bank holding company by foreign bank entities.
Although not directly a matter of bank regulation, the operation of foreign banks in the U.S. is fundamentally affected by tax considerations. The Tax Reform Act of 1988,changed the rules of the game with respect to the tax treatment of U.S. branches of foreign banks.  The article by Messrs. Groff and Hoch analyzes not only this recent statutory development, but also the overall tax structure governing the operation of foreign bank entities.
The six articles comprising the second part of this symposium deal with the sovereign debt crisis.  Unlike the earlier treatment of this subjectthe issues dealt with here pertain exclusively to developments in recent years.  The legal management of the debt crisis has, in fact, undergone essentially three stages since its onset in the fall of 1982.  The special character of the first stage resulted from the fact that unlike earlier debt crises the external indebtedness of the debtor countries was owed principally to commercial banks rather than to governments. Thus, the crises had to be dealt with in conventional contract andremedies law terms.  At the same time, there was the need to develop a format or structure for the conduct of the negotiations between the debtors and their several hundred bank creditors.  In many ways, devising such a decision-making structure was a new problem that the international banking, regulatory, and legal communities addressed reasonably well considering very few precedents were available in the early years of the crisis.  In effect, a remarkably uniform approach was adopted in virtually all of the countries involved in this crisis, notwithstanding the variations on the theme that met the special characteristics of the countries concerned.  To cope with the process, a de facto framework was developed that involved the International Monetary Fund (IMF), the official creditors of the countries, and the commercial bank creditors of the countries. Each party contributed to the building of this framework which, in turn, permitted the indebtedness of the countries at large, and particularly that of the commercial bank, to be restructured.  During this initial phase the countries in effect catalogued and consolidated their debt and restructured only those maturities coming due in the relatively near future.
The second phase, which was applied to only some of the countries, was characterized by the use ofmultiyearrestructuring agreements. These agreements encompassed not only immediate maturities, but also those in the medium term and were structured to take into account the country's debt service capacity over an extended period of time (in some cases as long as twenty years).  In line with this approach, the agreements would generally involve the use of grace periods during the initial restructuring years, a reduction of pricing, and a lengthening of the amortization period.  Frequently, these multiyear restructuring agreements were coupled with "new money" facilities designed to stimulate some measure of growth and development which would, in turn, enhance the capacity of the debtor country to meet subsequent years' debt service obligations.  As a result of the first and second phase, there was put in place for every single country a very complex and extensive set of documentation that established the rules of the game with respect to the debt concerned.  The documents set forth not only the point in time when the debt will be repaid and the interest rate that will accrue in the meantime, but also the important aspects of how the parties interrelate with one another in respect to their claims against the countries concerned.  The most prominent feature of this standard documentation is that each commercial bank agreed not to be repaid according to the terms of the original indebtedness and that when repayment took place, each would essentially be treated equally.  They agreed that they would all remain in this relationship until they all got out.  The most important features of the documents from this point of view are the mandatory prepayment provisions, the negative pledges, and the sharing provision.  Together they provide that no bank is to have a preferred position, that no bank is to get out of its loans before every other bank gets out of its loans, and that if any bank is paid in advance of any other bank, the country becomesobligated to make sure that every other bank is paid a pro rata share of the amount owed to it.  Two of the articles in this symposium deal with this multiyear restructuring phase.  The one by Lee Buchheit provides a comprehensive overview and analysis of the alternative techniques that are available for the longer term restructuring of sovereign debt.  The other by Buchheit and Reisner focuses on the effect of the debt restructuring process on the rights and duties of the creditors inter se.
A third phase which began in about 1985 is characterized by initiatives designed in a sense to disaggregate the debt.  Under these new arrangements the commercial bank debt is dissembled into different credit forms which, in turn, permits the sale of interests in the original debt obligations to investors in a broader secondary market.  Various approaches have been used or proposed to achieve such a disaggregation of the commercial bank debt.  One proposed solution which has, however, not gained broad acceptance within the banking community, is the "securitization" of existing LDC loan debt in a manner that would permit the sale of interest in these debt obligations to investors in a broader secondary market.  A variant on this theme is the purchase of the commercial bank debt by the debtor country in exchange for securities which the creditor banks may then be able to distribute in a secondary market. This, in effect, was the approach contemplated by the Mexican Floating Rate Bond program of January 18, 1988.
A more promising approach which has gained wide acceptance among both the creditors and the debtor countries are the debt-to-equity conversion programs.  Under these programs, portions of a country's stock of external debt is redeemed in its local currency equivalent with a view to having these funds utilized to fund equity investments in the debtor country.  From the perspective of the debtor country, such debt-to-equity programs serve to reduce its external indebtedness.  From the standpoint of the banks, these programs can serve either to reduce immediately a bank's credit exposure in a particular debtor country or to create an equity interest which can be marketed at some time in the future to individual investors.  These initiatives, which have already achieved some measure of success in the case of Chile, Mexico, and Brazil, required extensive modification of the regulatory framework both in the U.S. and the participating debtor countries.  Implementation of these programs has also required complex modifications in the terms contained in the documentation negotiated in earlier reschedulings.  The major thrust of these changes has been to introduce some measure of flexibility into the principle of equality of treatment and burden sharing among creditors that had been a feature of all prior agreements.
Three articles in this symposium address developments in this more recent phase.  One by Lee Buchheit provides an introduction into thesubject of the capitalization of sovereign debt.  The article by Messrs. Chamberlin, Weltchek, and Gruson provides a comprehensive analysis of the mechanics of debt-to-equity exchanges.  The regulatory structure controlling the participation of U.S. banks in the securitization of debt and debt-to-equity exchange programs is presented with great clarity in the article by Ms. Ricki Rhodarmer Tigert.
The debt crisis has spawned extraordinarily little litigation.  In part this is, undoubtedly, due to the general realization of all concerned that it was not to anyone's advantage to trigger endless and fruitless litigation over the external debt of the countries concerned.  Also, various loan documentation provisions such as the sharing clauses served to reinforce the perception that those initiating litigation against the debtor stood to gain very little.  At the same time it is noteworthy that only one case,Allied Bank International v. Banco Credito Agricola de Cartago,has raised an issue of major doctrinal significance.  The decision inAlliedultimately rejected the application of the act of state doctrine under the facts of that case.  Nevertheless, the decision left open the possibility that the doctrine might be available as a defense when application of the doctrine has the support of the executive branch.The concluding article by Michael Gruson, which examines the act of state doctrine in light of conflicts-of-law principles, brings needed clarity to this vital area of the law.
This issue also contains a student note that addresses extraterritorial discovery and the problems U.S. courts face when ordering production of documents protected by foreign bank secrecy laws.  The authors wish to thank the 1988-89 Board of Editors andLaw Reviewmembers for their substantial contribution to this issue.

questions.question: To what extent do U.S. regulatory, judicial, and state-level developments produce parity between foreign and domestic banks, and how do those developments affect foreign banks' market access, organizational form, and competitive position in the United States?
questions.answer: The foreword reports that, under the IBA and subsequent regulatory, judicial, and state-level changes, Congress’s goal of parity has been substantially realized, foreign banks with a U.S. presence have generally benefited despite being bound by the same restrictive rules as U.S. banks, and federal/state regimes—especially entry and acquisition rules—govern their market access, permissible structures, and competitive footing.

questions.question: What legal and contractual techniques most effectively enable large-scale sovereign debt restructurings (including short- and multi-year arrangements), and how do those techniques affect creditor rights, burden-sharing, and the orderly negotiation among many commercial creditors?
questions.answer: Large-scale restructurings were enabled first by a de facto IMF–official–commercial creditor framework grounded in contract and remedies law to consolidate and reschedule near-term maturities, and then by multiyear agreements (with grace periods, reduced pricing, longer amortization, and “new money”) implemented through standardized documentation featuring mandatory prepayment, negative pledge, and sharing clauses that enforce equal treatment, pro rata burden-sharing, and orderly collective creditor behavior.

questions.question: How feasible are market-based approaches to disaggregating sovereign bank debt (such as converting claims into tradable instruments or equity), and what legal, regulatory, tax, and cross-border litigation or enforcement issues determine whether and how those approaches can be implemented?
questions.answer: Market-based disaggregation has been mixed—securitization has not gained broad acceptance while debt-to-equity conversions have achieved wide uptake and some success (e.g., Chile, Mexico, Brazil)—and implementation depends on extensive changes to U.S. and debtor-country regulatory frameworks and to prior restructuring documentation (to introduce flexibility into equality/burden-sharing), is governed by U.S. rules on bank participation, and occurs against a backdrop of limited litigation with unresolved act-of-state and extraterritorial discovery issues.

matched_themes: How did the secondary market for emerging-market and less-developed countries' sovereign debt evolve, and what were its effects on banks, restructurings, and financial globalization?
How have inter-creditor practices, documentation, and management evolved in sovereign debt restructurings in the absence of a formal statutory insolvency framework?
When should domestic courts decline to adjudicate private-law claims that hinge on the validity of a foreign government's acts within its own territory?
What legal, tax, accounting, and regulatory issues arise from different types of voluntary sovereign debt exchanges, and how do these issues influence program design and implementation?
Which tactical renegotiation changes to how sovereign debt owed to commercial banks is restructured are feasible under existing political, legal, and regulatory constraints?
When should domestic courts defer to a foreign state's determinations about acts within that state's territory, and what limits should govern such deference?
What legal incentives, imperatives, and constraints shape creditor-debtor bargaining and creditor coordination in sovereign or quasi-sovereign restructurings, and how do these affect outcomes?

What legal and contractual techniques most effectively enable large-scale sovereign debt restructurings and how do they affect creditor rights, burden-sharing, and orderly negotiation among many creditors?
What design features and trade-offs are necessary in a statutory or treaty-based sovereign-debt restructuring mechanism to solve creditor coordination and collective-action problems?
Do debt-for-equity or debt/equity conversion programs reduce external debt stocks and stimulate domestic investment in debtor countries?
How do contractual language, legal enforcement, and non-legal forces (reputation, ongoing relationships) interact to determine parties' actual obligations and behavior under complex contracts?

How should legal and institutional rules balance preserving state discretion over foreign economic policy and regulation with ensuring enforceability of cross-border financial claims and maintaining lender confidence?
Who creates contractual innovations, why, and what incentives and constraints shape the supply of such innovations?
How should the law balance an issuer's need to restructure sovereign debt efficiently against individual bondholders' protection from coercion or unfair impairment?
How should courts allocate competing regulatory authority when both the forum state and a foreign state claim power to regulate the same persons, conduct, or property?
Do regulatory changes intended to facilitate debt-equity conversions lead banks to convert foreign debt into equity as a credit-risk management strategy?
Do market shocks and cumulative events produce clustered, industry-wide changes in standard contract boilerplate-creating tipping points that yield rapid adoption rather than incremental change?
Do creditor committees and collective representative enforcement architectures increase predictability and reduce economic and legal costs of sovereign debt restructurings?
To what extent can national governments effectively impose and enforce controls on cross-border banking transactions and deposits held at foreign branches?
How should judges treat foreign sovereign acts that affect intangible property or contractual rights-when should such acts be recognized, enforced, or disregarded by forum courts?

Do proactive resolution strategies-preemptive negotiation or restructuring-prevent borderline unsustainable sovereign or subnational debt from becoming fully unsustainable and preserve public services?
Which legal designs or interim mechanisms best enable binding majority-approved workouts across jurisdictions while limiting investor harm?
Do recurring, modular 'contract patterns' systematically structure how attorneys draft agreements and how those agreements interlock and scale into complex transactions and markets?
How does a forum state's recognition of a foreign government affect its courts' willingness to accept or validate that government's prior acts in private disputes?

To what extent do U.S. regulatory, judicial, and state-level developments produce parity between foreign and domestic banks, and how do these developments affect foreign banks' market access and organizational form?
What are the policy trade-offs of permitting U.S. banks to make commercial investments abroad, balancing depositor safety against competitive concerns?
How do business lawyers add value in complex transactions-do they act primarily as transaction-cost engineers who structure deals, allocate risk, and influence asset pricing?
Do sovereign creditors need enforceable duties to one another or external adjudicatory backstops to prevent opportunistic holdouts and side deals during restructurings?
Can creditors in multi-creditor instruments overcome holdout and grab-and-run incentives to achieve coordinated, ratable restructurings without a statutory insolvency backstop?

Can active secondary markets and creditor willingness to sell at discounts relieve a debtor country's foreign-exchange liquidity constraints by enabling redemption of external obligations in local currency?
How does judicial abstention from reviewing foreign governments' internal acts affect the enforceability of sovereign contracts in domestic courts?
How did the secondary market for less-developed countries' sovereign debt emerge and evolve during the 1980s, and what role did it play in debt restructuring mechanisms?
How do changes in market conditions and relative bargaining power cause systematic shifts in the nonprice terms of debt contracts (covenants and collateral requirements)?
How do contractual provisions in loan and restructuring agreements secure equal treatment and coordinated participation among disparate lenders during sovereign restructurings?
Do standardized private legal documents and documentation personnel in transnational finance produce governance effects that replicate or supplant state legal authority?
What trade-offs arise between reducing contract customization through standardized 'good-enough' provisions and parties' ability to secure precisely tailored outcomes?
What are the consequences of sovereign default for restructuring outcomes and for incentives and behavior of international creditors and debtor governments?
How should regulatory and accounting frameworks treat securitization of loans to heavily indebted countries, and what are the implications for banking organizations?
Does narrowly treating foreign governmental acts as determinative change outcomes in international contract disputes involving post-contract foreign laws or decrees?
What speech-act function does entering into a complex business contract serve: creating enforceable promises or setting a framework that enables non-legal governance and cooperation?
Do groups of market participants (committees, task forces, networks, trade associations) overcome coordination problems to facilitate efficient change in entrenched contractual or social norms?
How do secondary markets for sovereign debt (emergent purchasers and trading) affect debt restructurings, market liquidity, and form-contract standardization?
To what extent are complex agreements organized as modular subsystems (enabling mass customization) versus thickly interconnected integrated systems, and how does that shape transaction design?
Should courts abolish or restrict judicial abstention rules that allow declining to decide cases involving foreign sovereign actors?
Do official-sector interventions in restructurings improve orderly outcomes and creditor recoveries, or do they weaken international capital-market functioning?
Under what conditions do pro-competitive regulatory reforms (deregulation, liberalization) produce real competition, and when are explicit competition laws and advocacy also necessary?
What legal, tax, accounting, and banking regulatory issues arise when banks convert cross-border loan exposures into equity or otherwise restructure foreign claims?

What creditor- and institutional-level conditions (creditor structure, representation, procedural rules, debtor engagement) make multicreditor coordination mechanisms effective at resolving collective-action problems?
How do U.S. banking and bank holding company rules limit or permit investments in foreign equity securities and how does regulatory parity between domestic and foreign banks affect market access?
Do exceptional legal, political, or institutional protections (sovereign immunities, special statutes) effectively shield sovereigns from creditor litigation and alter restructuring bargaining power?

Which contractual and documentary designs (e.g., debt-for-equity, debt-for-nature, PIKs, exchange mechanics) most effectively restore contractual flexibility and reconcile debtor-creditor relationships in multiparty sovereign restructurings?
Should rights and enforcement powers of corporate bond investors be held individually or exercised collectively under representative or majority rules?

How do private standard-setting organizations, form contracts, and transnational documentation practices interact with national legal systems to determine the enforceability, reach, and governance effects of private global legal regimes?
How do social and market forces fail to correct suboptimal allocations of individual versus collective bondholder rights, and what reforms would improve enforcement and market outcomes?
What governance effects do standardized private legal documents and routine documentation work produce-do they replicate, supplement, or supplant state legal authority?

Do legal, institutional, and normative features (statutory backstops, professional practices, standardized forms, repeat-dealing norms) reduce the need for bespoke contract customization and thereby lower transaction costs?
Does judicial non-review or abstention of foreign governmental acts vary across jurisdictions, and how does that variation affect litigants and international comity?
How does the sovereign debt restructuring process alter relationships and collective behavior among commercial bank creditors of a debtor country?

What measures and institutional designs are needed to convert borderline-unsustainable government debt into sustainable financing for sovereigns and subnational entities given modern creditor diversity and collateralization?

Are market-based disaggregation approaches (converting sovereign claims into tradable instruments or equity) feasible, and what legal, regulatory, tax, and enforcement issues determine their implementation?
Do debt-for-equity or debt-conversion transactions produce mutually beneficial outcomes for banks, foreign investors, and debtor governments compared with alternative restructuring methods?

Does application of abstention doctrines (e.g., political question, act-of-state) produce harmful effects, including judicial evasion, doctrinal confusion, undue deference to the executive, and stunted international-law development?
Should a country's collective private-law rules vest enforcement rights in individual bondholders or in representative/majority decision mechanisms, and what are the tradeoffs?
Do market learning and network externalities cause firms to converge on standardized contract terms rather than customize or innovate them?

Do standardized contractual features (e.g., CACs, litigation clauses, forum-selection terms) and the anonymity/tradability of bond investors influence market pricing, holdout behavior, and enforcement outcomes in sovereign debt markets?
Why is conflicts-of-laws litigation around international payments relatively scarce - practical irrelevance, intractability, or academic oversight?
Is drafting complex contracts as flexible stage-setting (for future accommodation) superior to exhaustive literal specification given limits of knowledge and language?
How do secondary markets for sovereign debt (liquidity, tradability, active buying/selling) affect the feasibility and mechanics of sovereign restructurings?
How do multi-party financial contract disputes and the presence of secondary purchasers affect the process and outcomes of contract standardization and enforcement?
How large and practically significant are downstream effects of standard contract changes-that is, how many contracts and parties are affected and with what consequences?
How do creditor coordination mechanisms (creditor committees, collective action clauses, creditor-coordination platforms) affect restructuring predictability, participation, litigation, and costs?
How did activity in low- and middle-income country (LDC/emerging-market) debt secondary markets in the late 1980s and 1990s affect banks' management of exposures and use of restructuring tools?

Do market-based restructuring techniques (ad hoc creditor groups, debt/equity swaps, debt-for-nature, debt-equity conversion) meaningfully restore contractual flexibility, reduce external debt stocks, and stimulate domestic investment?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 88nyulrev1!!ARTICLE: THE DYNAMICS OF CONTRACT EVOLUTION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE DYNAMICS OF CONTRACT EVOLUTION

shared_topics.topic: standardization and evolution of sovereign debt contract terms (boilerplate and standard documentation)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically analyzes how boilerplate sovereign bond clauses (notably CACs and related terms) evolve into market standards through template reproduction and law‑firm production; Paper B documents the emergence of near‑uniform restructuring documentation (sharing clauses, negative pledges, mandatory prepayment provisions) developed during 1980s sovereign debt restructurings.

shared_topics.topic: creditor collective action and voting/aggregation mechanisms in restructurings
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on the shift from unanimity action clauses to collective action clauses and the design of vote thresholds, aggregation, disenfranchisement and meeting clauses; Paper B examines the de facto decision‑making structures among hundreds of commercial bank creditors and contractual mechanisms for equal treatment and coordinated restructuring outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: financial crises as triggers for contractual and market change in sovereign debt
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows how discrete shocks (Mexico 1995, Asian crisis, Argentina 2001) precipitated experimentation and then rapid adoption of new bond clauses (CACs); Paper B situates the 1982 debt crisis and subsequent phases as the catalyst for new restructuring formats (multiyear agreements, securitization/debt‑to‑equity) and attendant documentation innovations.

shared_topics.topic: role of public institutions, market elites, and law firms in producing contractual standards
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights law firms’ mass‑production of templates and the tipping‑point role of top market participants plus public‑sector pressure in creating a new CAC standard; Paper B describes how the IMF, official creditors, regulators, banks, and legal practitioners jointly designed the institutional and contractual framework used to manage the sovereign debt crisis.

shared_topics.topic: governing law, enforcement, and cross‑border legal obstacles affecting sovereign debt
shared_topics.justification: Paper A compares New York‑law and English‑law governed bonds and reports judicial attitudes toward boilerplate enforcement; Paper B addresses cross‑border legal issues such as the act of state doctrine, extraterritorial discovery, and how national regulatory and court doctrines affect enforcement, creditor remedies, and participation in restructurings.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 57vandlrev1!!ARTICLE: Sovereign Debt Reform and the Best Interest of Creditors
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Sovereign Debt Reform and the Best Interest of Creditors

shared_topics.topic: sovereign debt restructuring processes and legal frameworks
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the legal mechanics of sovereign 'compositions' versus proposed sovereign bankruptcy regimes (including how contract terms like UACs/CACs shape restructurings), while Paper B chronicles the practical phases and legal structures used in 1980s sovereign restructurings (rescheduling, multiyear restructurings and their documentation), situating both works in the study of how restructurings are legally organized.

shared_topics.topic: creditor coordination problems and intercreditor rights/duties
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on collective-action problems (holdouts, free‑riding) created by unanimous action clauses and the need for intercreditor good‑faith obligations, and Paper B treats sharing clauses, mandatory prepayment, equality of treatment and analyzes the rights and duties of creditors inter se in actual restructurings—both engage substantively with how creditor coordination is governed and contested.

shared_topics.topic: the role of the IMF and official‑sector actors in restructuring outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates how IMF lending and bailout policy affect creditor incentives and the debate over market versus mandated solutions, while Paper B documents the IMF’s central place in the de facto negotiation framework of the debt crisis and how official creditors shaped rescheduling practices—both examine how official actors influence restructuring incentives and institutional design.

shared_topics.topic: contractual documentation and boilerplate clauses governing sovereign debt
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates long‑standing boilerplate clauses (UACs, CACs) and the implications of governing law (e.g., New York contract law) for restructurings, and Paper B gives detailed attention to the standard documentation features used in practice (sharing provisions, negative pledges, mandatory prepayment) and the legal changes required for debt conversion/securitization—both analyze how specific contract terms determine restructuring possibilities.

shared_topics.topic: reform proposals and market innovations for resolving sovereign indebtedness
shared_topics.justification: Paper A assesses proposals for introducing majority‑action regimes or a minimal sovereign bankruptcy and the feasibility of market transitions from UACs to CACs, while Paper B evaluates practical innovations used or proposed during the crisis (debt‑to‑equity conversions, securitization, disaggregation of bank debt) and their regulatory/legal implications—both engage with options for reforming how sovereign debt problems are resolved.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 1988uilllrev481!!ARTICLE: RECENT REGULATORY PERSPECTIVES ON DEBT-FOR-EQUITY SWAPS AND SECURITIZATION OF THIRD WORLD DEBT © 1988 Center for Transnational Legal Studies
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: RECENT REGULATORY PERSPECTIVES ON DEBT-FOR-EQUITY SWAPS AND SECURITIZATION OF THIRD WORLD DEBT © 1988 Center for Transnational Legal Studies

shared_topics.topic: debt-for-equity (debt-to-equity) swaps as a sovereign-debt restructuring tool and their regulatory treatment
shared_topics.justification: Both papers examine debt-for-equity conversions as a method to reduce external indebtedness — Paper A surveys the emergence, mechanics, and regulatory changes required for debt-to-equity programs in countries like Chile, Mexico, and Brazil, while Paper B analyzes recent Federal Reserve regulations that permit U.S. banking organizations to undertake loan-for-equity exchanges and the attendant legal/regulatory issues.

shared_topics.topic: securitization/disaggregation of commercial sovereign debt to create transferable instruments
shared_topics.justification: Both papers engage the idea of securitizing or otherwise disaggregating bank-held LDC debt to enable secondary-market transfers — Paper A describes securitization proposals (including Mexico's floating-rate bond program) and their limited uptake, while Paper B focuses on the major Mexican debt-exchange effort and how regulators and accounting staffs have treated the securitization-like conversion of bank loans into marketable bonds.

shared_topics.topic: regulatory and accounting implications for U.S. banks participating in debt-restructuring transactions
shared_topics.justification: Both works analyze how U.S. banking regulation and accounting rules affect bank participation in debt restructurings — Paper A discusses the necessary regulatory framework changes and an article on U.S. regulatory control over bank participation in securitizations and debt-to-equity exchanges, and Paper B details Federal Reserve rules plus interagency (SEC/OCC/FDIC) interpretations of regulatory and accounting issues arising from such transactions.

shared_topics.topic: needed legal/documentation modifications and creditor-equality principles in restructuring agreements
shared_topics.justification: Both papers address how traditional loan documentation (sharing clauses, negative pledges, prepayment provisions) and the principle of equal treatment among creditors must be modified to implement newer restructuring techniques — Paper A analyzes how multiyear restructurings and debt-to-equity programs required complex contractual and regulatory adjustments, while Paper B considers the legal/regulatory consequences of converting loans into different instruments (e.g., Mexican debt-for-bond exchanges) and the documentation changes that implicate regulators and accountants.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 61adminlrev463!!ARTICLE: REGULATION BY DEAL: THE GOVERNMENT'S RESPONSE TO THE FINANCIAL CRISIS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: REGULATION BY DEAL: THE GOVERNMENT'S RESPONSE TO THE FINANCIAL CRISIS

shared_topics.topic: how legal and statutory constraints shape governmental responses to financial distress
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how statutes, regulations, and doctrines (e.g., IBA, Bank Holding Company Act, act-of-state doctrine) limited and channeled the options available to regulators and creditors during bank operations and sovereign-debt crises; Paper B traces how existing statutory and administrative authority (and its limits) shaped the Treasury and Federal Reserve’s deal-driven bailout strategies and required rapid reinterpretation or new congressional authorization (EESA).

shared_topics.topic: legal and transactional mechanisms for restructuring distressed claims and institutions (securitization, asset purchases, debt-to-equity, forced sales)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines multiyear sovereign-debt restructurings, securitization proposals, and debt-to-equity conversions as legal/transactional tools to manage LDC indebtedness; Paper B analyzes the government’s use of asset-purchase programs, equity stakes, forced sales/mergers, and other transaction structures as instruments to resolve distressed financial institutions and troubled assets.

shared_topics.topic: cross-border and international dimensions of banking regulation and crisis spillovers
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on foreign banks’ access to the U.S. market, reciprocity, and how international banking arrangements affect regulation and restructuring of sovereign debt; Paper B addresses the global nature of the financial system, cross-border liquidity interventions, and how U.S. regulatory choices (bailouts, market interventions) had international market implications.

shared_topics.topic: the evolution and reform of banking regulatory frameworks in response to crises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A reassesses the International Banking Act and subsequent federal/state regulatory changes a decade after enactment and considers reforms prompted by the sovereign-debt crisis; Paper B evaluates how regulatory gaps and failures exposed by the 2007–09 crisis prompted new statutory authority, reinterpretations of agency power, and debates about longer-term regulatory reform.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 70lawcontempprob115!!ARTICLE: ODIOUS DEBT, ODIOUS CREDIT, ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT, AND DEMOCRATIZATION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: ODIOUS DEBT, ODIOUS CREDIT, ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT, AND DEMOCRATIZATION

shared_topics.topic: whether successor governments are bound to repay predecessor's sovereign debts (legitimacy of odious debt)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes legal consequences of sovereign default and the restructuring agreements that bind debtor states and their creditors, while Paper B questions the moral and legal obligation of new democratic governments to honor debts incurred by corrupt or dictatorial predecessors (the odious debt problem).

shared_topics.topic: legal doctrines and enforcement mechanisms governing sovereign-debt disputes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines doctrines and litigation risks (e.g., act of state, conflicts-of-law, sharing clauses, creditor remedies) that shape creditors' and debtors' rights, and Paper B discusses international-law norms, reputational sanctions, and the practical enforcement pressures (including asset seizure) that compel repayment.

shared_topics.topic: resolving sovereign debt crises through ad hoc multilateral frameworks in the absence of sovereign bankruptcy
shared_topics.justification: Paper A describes the de facto negotiation architecture (IMF, official creditors, commercial banks) and restructuring techniques (rescheduling, multiyear agreements, debt-to-equity, securitization), while Paper B highlights the lack of a sovereign bankruptcy mechanism and the resulting reliance on reputational and ad hoc solutions for resolving unsustainable debts.

shared_topics.topic: how debt burdens and restructuring choices affect economic development and political stability (including democratization)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses restructuring tools and ‘new money’ facilities aimed at restoring growth and debt service capacity in debtor countries, and Paper B emphasizes how odious or excessive debt service can drain resources, undermine public services, and destabilize or derail nascent democratic transitions.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 79chikentlrev889!!SYMPOSIUM:"LAW &": PHILOSOPHICAL, PSYCHOLOGICAL, LINGUISTIC, AND BIOLOGICAL PERSPECTIVES ON LEGAL SCHOLARSHIOP:I. LAW AND LANGUAGE:HOW DO GERMAN CONTRACTS DO AS MUCH WITH FEWER WORDS?
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM:"LAW &": PHILOSOPHICAL, PSYCHOLOGICAL, LINGUISTIC, AND BIOLOGICAL PERSPECTIVES ON LEGAL SCHOLARSHIOP:I. LAW AND LANGUAGE:HOW DO GERMAN CONTRACTS DO AS MUCH WITH FEWER WORDS?

shared_topics.topic: law as a coordination and focal mechanism in commercial transactions (beyond mere breach remedies)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes how international banking law, IMF frameworks, and standardized debt documentation function to coordinate sovereign-debtor and creditor behavior beyond simple enforcement (e.g., sharing clauses, negative pledges), while Paper B analyzes how German law and legal norms operate expressively and as focal points that shape contracting practices and reduce the need for bespoke enforcement-oriented provisions.

shared_topics.topic: standardization of contract forms and documentation to lower transaction costs
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents the emergence and centrality of complex, standardized multilateral loan and restructuring documents (e.g., multiyear agreements, mandatory prepayment/share provisions, securitization/debt‑to‑equity instruments) used across many creditors, and Paper B explains how German contracting relies on trade association and firm forms and standardized solutions to achieve similar commercial outcomes with far fewer words.

shared_topics.topic: transnational pressures and globalization reshaping domestic contracting and regulation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats how European integration, cross‑border banking, and foreign‑bank access to U.S. markets (and resulting regulatory adjustments) affect domestic banking law and documentation, and Paper B discusses how Anglo‑American firms and cross‑border transactional practice (and European integration) are changing traditional German contracting norms toward more customized, Anglo style documents.

shared_topics.topic: mechanisms for multi‑party coordination to constrain opportunism among numerous stakeholders
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes institutional and contractual mechanisms (IMF involvement, creditor committees, sharing clauses, collective restructuring techniques) designed to prevent individual creditors from gaining advantage and to limit litigation, whereas Paper B theorizes how norms, default rules, and standardized provisions reduce the ‘arms race’ of bespoke anti‑opportunism drafting among contracting parties.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 93tullrev1!!ARTICLE: Recalibrating Contract Law: Choses in Action, Global Value Chains, and the Enforcement of Obligations Outside of Privity
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Recalibrating Contract Law: Choses in Action, Global Value Chains, and the Enforcement of Obligations Outside of Privity

shared_topics.topic: legal mechanisms for enforcing obligations across multi‑party international networks
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how assignment of choses in action can let an upstream firm sue a distant supplier outside traditional privity in global value chains; Paper B analyzes how complex loan documentation (sharing clauses, negative pledges, mandatory prepayment) and restructuring agreements create enforceable rules among hundreds of cross‑border creditors.

shared_topics.topic: contractual and institutional innovations to coordinate dispersed actors and allocate risk
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on contractual workarounds (indemnities, chain drafting) and proposes use of assignment to reallocate remedies along supply chains; Paper B describes contractual and market innovations (multiyear restructurings, securitization, debt‑to‑equity conversions) and institutional arrangements (IMF, creditor coordination) used to manage sovereign default risk among many creditors.

shared_topics.topic: jurisdictional and extraterritorial limits on remedies and governance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights how privity and cross‑border supplier relationships limit a firm's legal control over overseas factories and standards enforcement; Paper B addresses extraterritorial problems in international banking and sovereign debt (act of state doctrine, extraterritorial discovery, regulation of foreign banks, and cross‑border tax/regulatory constraints).

shared_topics.topic: the interplay of private ordering and public regulation in transnational commerce
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses firms' private monitoring, certification, and contractual drafting as responses to legal gaps in governing labor/environmental standards in supply chains; Paper B documents the complementary and sometimes competing roles of legislation, regulators, and international institutions (IBA, Fed regulations, IMF) alongside private creditor arrangements in shaping cross‑border banking and debt solutions.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 60wmmarylrev2111!!ARTICLE: TAX LAWYERS AS TAX INSURANCE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: TAX LAWYERS AS TAX INSURANCE

shared_topics.topic: legal mechanisms for allocating and shifting financial risk (contracts, clauses, and indemnities)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes contractual devices and restructurings—sharing clauses, mandatory prepayment provisions, debt-to-equity swaps, and securitizations—that reallocate sovereign-creditor risk; Paper B analyzes tax opinions and indemnification (and their similarity to insurance) as a mechanism by which transactional tax lawyers shift portions of clients' tax risk onto advisers.

shared_topics.topic: how regulatory and statutory change shapes financial/legal market practices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how the International Banking Act, Federal Reserve regulation K, the Tax Reform Act of 1988, and other regulatory changes reshaped foreign-bank operations and debt-restructuring options; Paper B treats recent sweeping tax-law changes and Circular 230 obligations as drivers of increased uncertainty that alter demand for tax opinions, indemnities, and the market for tax-risk allocation.

shared_topics.topic: private ordering and industry practices as substitutes or complements to public law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes de facto frameworks created by banks, the IMF, and creditors (e.g., multiyear restructurings and collective creditor agreements) that governed sovereign-debt resolution outside litigation; Paper B treats tax-opinion practice, contractual engagement terms, and the market for malpractice/insurance as private-ordering mechanisms that structure tax risk allocation and compliance behavior.

shared_topics.topic: litigation risk, liability doctrines, and their effects on behaviour
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses the relative paucity of litigation in the sovereign-debt crisis, doctrines such as act of state, and how sharing/contractual arrangements discouraged suits; Paper B studies malpractice recoveries, barriers to suing advisers, and how litigation exposure and indemnity prospects influence adviser behavior and client choices.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 42harvintllj355!!ARTICLE: State Succession to Debts and Assets: The Modern Law and Policy
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: State Succession to Debts and Assets: The Modern Law and Policy

shared_topics.topic: mechanisms for allocating sovereign debt burdens among creditors and debtors
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes contractual mechanics of sovereign debt restructurings (sharing clauses, mandatory prepayment provisions, multiyear restructurings, debt‑to‑equity swaps and securitization) that determine how repayment burdens are shared among commercial banks, while Paper B studies how debts and assets of predecessor states are allocated among successor states (and between successor states and creditors), including principles for dividing identifiable and unidentifiable debt.

shared_topics.topic: the role of creditor coordination and creditor states in shaping restructuring outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes the de facto framework that brought together commercial banks, the IMF, and official creditors to coordinate rescheduling and burden‑sharing, and Paper B examines how creditor states (and institutional creditor bodies) actively participated in and sometimes imposed allocations of successor‑state debt, influencing negotiation outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: legal instruments, doctrines and institutional fora used to restructure or reassign sovereign obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on private and regulatory documentation and doctrines affecting restructurings (loan documentation, negative pledges, U.S. regulatory/tax rules, and the act‑of‑state doctrine), while Paper B examines public international law instruments and mechanisms (the 1983 Vienna Convention, customary state practice, arbitration commissions, and informal regimes) used to govern succession to debts and assets.

shared_topics.topic: interaction between law and politics and the limits of legal rules in resolving sovereign indebtedness
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights how political and regulatory developments (national treatment, access barriers, domestic legislation and agency action) and pragmatic policymaking shaped restructuring practice, and Paper B analyzes how political and strategic objectives of successor states and creditor states condition the application, development, and limits of international legal rules on succession and debt allocation.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 70lawcontempprob53!!ARTICLE: INSOLVENCY PRINCIPLES AND THE ODIOUS DEBT DOCTRINE: THE MISSING LINK IN THE DEBATE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: INSOLVENCY PRINCIPLES AND THE ODIOUS DEBT DOCTRINE: THE MISSING LINK IN THE DEBATE

shared_topics.topic: legal and contractual frameworks for sovereign debt restructuring
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates sovereign debt relief through the lens of domestic insolvency law (the U.S. Bankruptcy Code) and argues restructuring should prioritize rehabilitation of the sovereign; Paper B maps the actual legal architectures used in the 1980s debt crisis (rescheduling, multiyear restructuring agreements, documentation and IMF/official-creditor frameworks) and analyzes the contractual mechanics that govern restructurings.

shared_topics.topic: alteration, subordination, and equal-treatment rules among creditors in restructurings
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses how bankruptcy permits discharge, subordination, or reprioritization of creditor claims to enable debtor rehabilitation and analogizes those principles to sovereigns; Paper B examines the practical contractual devices (sharing provisions, negative pledges, mandatory prepayment rules) and regulatory changes that enforce or relax equality of treatment among commercial-bank creditors in sovereign restructurings.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal grounds for repudiation or non‑repayment of sovereign debt and their legal consequences
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on the odious debt doctrine as a normative and potentially enforceable ground for successor sovereigns to repudiate prior regime debts and tests it against insolvency principles; Paper B surveys the legal consequences of sovereign default, the limited litigation that has arisen (e.g., act of state defenses), and how legal doctrines and litigation risk affect restructuring outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: effects of legal doctrines and restructuring techniques on creditor behavior and market incentives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that the prospect of odious-debt invocation could discipline lenders ex ante and affect lending to risky regimes; Paper B analyzes how multilayered restructuring techniques (securitization, debt‑to‑equity swaps, regulatory/tax changes) and the developed contractual framework changed banks' exposure, secondary markets, and incentives during the sovereign debt crisis.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2005utahlrev401!!ARTICLE:International Law and State Succession: A Solution to the Iraqi Debt Crisis?*
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:International Law and State Succession: A Solution to the Iraqi Debt Crisis?*

shared_topics.topic: legal frameworks and mechanisms for resolving sovereign debt crises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the contractual and market-based mechanisms (multiyear restructurings, sharing clauses, securitization, debt-to-equity conversions) and the negotiation framework used by debtor states, commercial banks, the IMF and official creditors; Paper B examines the international-law rules and precedents (pacta sunt servanda, rebus sic stantibus, state succession) that determine when and how sovereign debts should be honored, renegotiated, or discharged.

shared_topics.topic: when creditor rights and pari passu/burden‑sharing principles can be altered or set aside
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on documentation features (mandatory prepayment provisions, negative pledges, pro rata sharing) that enforce equal treatment among creditors and on newer arrangements that introduce flexibility; Paper B engages with doctrines (notably 'odious debt' and state succession) that justify partial or total discharge of debts and thus create exceptions to absolute creditor equality and enforceability.

shared_topics.topic: the role of international legal norms and institutions in shaping debt outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A describes the practical role of international institutions (IMF, official creditors) and the de facto legal framework that emerged in 1980s restructurings to structure negotiations and outcomes; Paper B reviews formal international-law instruments, ILC work, and precedents that could supply legal bases for allocating debt responsibility after regime change or succession.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal and enforcement barriers to creditor remedies against states
shared_topics.justification: Paper A considers litigation risk, the rarity of lawsuits, the act of state doctrine, and procedural issues like extraterritorial discovery and bank secrecy that limit enforcement; Paper B assesses legal doctrines surrounding state succession and odious debts that, if accepted, would bar or limit creditors' claims against successor states.

papers.node_id: 51umiamilrev779!!MERGERS AND ACQUISITIONS SYMPOSIUM: ARTICLE: Summary of Acquisition Agreements *
papers.title: MERGERS AND ACQUISITIONS SYMPOSIUM: ARTICLE: Summary of Acquisition Agreements *
papers.authors: Lou R. Kling; Eileen Nugent Simon; Michael Goldman
papers.abstract:
There are basically three different methods for acquiring the business of another corporation under state law: a stock purchase, an asset purchase, or a merger. Although each transaction differs significantly in structure, the same basic contractual provisions can be built into any of these methods. Provisions basic to any acquisition agreement include mechanical provisions, purchase price provisions, representations and warranties, covenants, conditions, indemnification provisions, termination provisions and provisions relating to expense reimbursement and fees, as well as a number of miscellaneous provisions.
Although these basic provisions are present in virtually all acquisition agreements, their relative importance can differ dramatically. This Article compares some of these differences by examining the operation of these provisions in public company acquisition agreements, private company acquisition agreements and leveraged buyout agreements.
In principle, public company acquisitions are no different from acquisitions of subsidiaries, divisions and private companies. In fact, the agreements are generally simpler than for other types of acquisitions. Public company acquisitions, however, do have their own unique problems. Two interrelated factors generally cause the greatest concern. First, shareholder approval for a public company acquisition does not occur until near the end of the acquisition process, long after public announcement of the transaction. Second, public company acquisitions suffer from an increased risk of third party competition. This can arise both prior to the execution of a definitive agreement and thereafter, until target shareholder approval is obtained or sometimes even until closing. A third, unrelated aspect of public company transactions is that, unless an escrow or similar holdback device is established, there is no way for the purchaser to obtain indemnification from public shareholders.
Private company transactions tend to have some of the same characteristics as public company transactions, but with a few significant differences. Private companies do not have the same reporting requirements as public companies, which creates a greater need for enhanced representations and warranties. Additionally, acquiring the principal stockholder's consent not to compete post-closing with the business sold to the acquiror may be significant in a private company acquisition.
A leveraged buyout has three distinct characteristics. First, it is an acquisition of all or a majority (or substantial) equity interest in an entire company or in a subsidiary, division or other portion of a company, by an investor group or entity. Second, the major portion of the purchase price is financed through the incurrence of debt. Finally, the creditbacking up such debt is (primarily) that of the entity or business being acquired.

questions.question: How do the key contractual provisions of acquisition agreements (for example, purchase price mechanics, representations and warranties, covenants, conditions to closing, indemnities, and termination/fee provisions) differ in importance and operation across public-company acquisitions, private-company acquisitions, and leveraged buyouts?
questions.answer: The same basic provisions appear in all acquisition agreements but their weight and operation vary: public-company agreements are generally simpler and, unless an escrow or holdback is used, cannot provide buyer indemnification from public shareholders while facing late shareholder approval and competition risks; private-company deals require enhanced representations and warranties and may include a principal stockholder non-compete; and leveraged buyouts are defined by purchase-price financing largely through debt backed primarily by the acquired business.

questions.question: How do transaction-specific features and risks-such as the timing of seller shareholder approval, exposure to competing bids, informational asymmetries between buyer and seller, and reliance on debt financing-shape the allocation of risk and the drafting of specific clauses in acquisition agreements?
questions.answer: Transaction features shape drafting and risk allocation such that in public deals late shareholder approval and heightened exposure to competing bids create special concerns and, because recovery from public shareholders is unavailable, indemnification requires an escrow/holdback if desired; in private deals limited reporting heightens informational asymmetry and thus the need for enhanced representations and warranties and a principal stockholder’s non-compete; and in leveraged buyouts the heavy reliance on debt financing primarily secured by the acquired business drives the agreement’s focus.

papers.node_id: 75ucinlrev977!!NINETEENTH ANNUAL CORPORATE LAW SYMPOSIUM: DEBT AS A LEVER OF CONTROL: CONTRACTS WITHOUT LAW: SOVEREIGN VERSUS CORPORATE DEBT
papers.title: NINETEENTH ANNUAL CORPORATE LAW SYMPOSIUM: DEBT AS A LEVER OF CONTROL: CONTRACTS WITHOUT LAW: SOVEREIGN VERSUS CORPORATE DEBT
papers.abstract:
The role of debt in corporate governance has been the subject of much law and economics scholarship over the past twenty years or so. The dominant paradigm is that of principal-agent: the lender is a principal and the borrower is an agent (or perhaps several individual agents) who has the discretion to put the lender's funds at risk. The paradigm is predominantly contractual: although social and market pressures may bear on the agent's decisions, the lender disciplines the borrower's use of its funds by a contract that can be enforced in court. The principal-agent model reflects well the similar tensions present in lending to sovereign countries, but the contractual approach must yield to the distinctive feature of international relations: the absence of a third party arbiter with coercive power. Our goal in this article is to outline some of the resulting differences in the design of sovereign and corporate debt contracts.
An important feature of corporate finance is that creditors of a common borrower have both convergent and divergent interests. They converge in seeking to minimize the risk of insolvency, but they divergebecause each creditor competes for the borrower's assets if it becomes insolvent. To the extent that creditor interests converge, the borrower can reduce its cost of capital by delegating monitoring and governance responsibilities, thereby avoiding the cost of free riding or duplicative monitoring. Banks often serve the role of delegated monitors. One might think they could play the same role in the sovereign debt context. Banks in fact performed this service until the early 1980s, when they were joined as delegated monitors by the International Monetary Fund ("the IMF"). In this respect, it is interesting that investors would value the monitoring and control of a not-for-profit, public institution, whose mission is to promote economic development and stability rather than investor returns.
This paper elaborates and integrates the foregoing observations - the informal enforcement of sovereign debt and the delegated monitoring of the IMF - in order to explain the different contracting patterns in sovereign and corporate debt instruments. In particular, the combination of informal enforcement and IMF monitoring explains the covenants and events of default that are found in sovereign debt agreements, and those that are not (despite being commonplace in corporate debt contracts). Part I reviews the principal-agent analysis of corporate debt; Part II discusses the difference in the enforcement of sovereign debt; Part III examines the significance in sovereign debt of the delegation of monitoring activity to the IMF and its implication for the design of debt covenants and events of default.

questions.question: Whether the absence of a coercive third-party arbiter in international lending causes sovereign debt contracts to include different covenants and events of default than corporate debt contracts subject to formal judicial enforcement
questions.answer: Yes: because international lending lacks a coercive third-party arbiter, sovereign debt relies on informal enforcement, producing different covenants and events of default than in court-enforced corporate debt.

questions.question: Whether delegation of monitoring to an external international institution substitutes for contractual monitoring and enforcement and thereby alters the design of sovereign debt contracts (e.g., which covenants and default triggers are used)
questions.answer: Yes: delegated monitoring by the IMF (alongside earlier bank monitoring), together with informal rather than judicial enforcement, is presented as the mechanism that shapes which covenants and default triggers sovereign debt contracts include or omit.

questions.question: Whether differences in creditor coordination problems (convergent vs. competing claims) lead borrowers to delegate monitoring differently in sovereign versus corporate settings, and how that delegation affects cost of capital and contract terms
questions.answer: The abstract does not attribute delegation differences to creditor coordination problems, but it notes that corporate borrowers reduce the cost of capital by delegating monitoring to banks, whereas in sovereign debt monitoring is delegated to banks and the IMF and, together with informal enforcement, explains which covenants and default terms appear.
