papers.node_id: 56amjcompl605!!SPECIAL SYMPOSIUM ISSUE: "BEYOND THE STATE: RETHINKING PRIVATE LAW": ARTICLE: Relations: The Anti-Network: Private Global Governance, Legal Knowledge, and the Legitimacy of the State
papers.title: SPECIAL SYMPOSIUM ISSUE: "BEYOND THE STATE: RETHINKING PRIVATE LAW": ARTICLE: Relations: The Anti-Network: Private Global Governance, Legal Knowledge, and the Legitimacy of the State
papers.abstract:
In the late 1990s, a visitor to a Japanese derivatives trading floor encountered a large open room full of metal desks and computer screens. At most of these desks, traders hunched over their computers or shouted into their telephones. As the traders at their computers entered into a swap with traders at another bank in New York or London, they scribbled the details of the trade onto a form, then tossed it into a basket at the edge of their desk.
But a few desks to one side were stacked high with documents and large quantities of paper. Periodically, the people working behind the stacks of documents collected these forms and returned to their desks. Within eyesight of the traders and the manager of the derivatives team, these "documentation people" "papered the trades" as people said. The employees at these desks produced confirmation agreements and sent these to their counterparts at the other bank.
These confirmation documents adhered to a standard format, such that the documentation person's principal task was simply to complete the form, fax it, receive a similar fax from his or her counterpart at the other bank, and file it away. Occasionally, this person might discover discrepancies - misunderstandings between the two parties over the terms, for example - and then would refer these back to the traders to resolve or contact their counterparts at the other bank to resolve the dispute.
Global private law is now the source of both anxiety and euphoria. So-called global private law regimes - private in the sense that they do not rely primarily on the legitimacy or the coercive power of the state for their authority - now fascinate legal theorists for whom the authority, legitimacy, and power of law has long been tethered to the state.But much of the conversation about global private law proceeds at some distance from the concrete moments, practices, and individuals that constitute global private governance regimes.
In this article, I build upon research in one arena of global private law, the production of legal documentation for the global swap markets, to challenge the way both utopic and dystopic accounts describe private law beyond the state. I argue that these accounts stand on a set of anthropological assumptions or claims - assertions about what this private law actually is, from an insider's point of view, about how it is interpreted and experienced "in the real world" - which for the most part go unexamined, untheorized, and undefended empirically. This matters because they also turn out to be, at the very least, seriously incomplete.
In particular, I want to challenge, or at least complicate, three views of the source of private law's legitimacy that figure prominently in both defenses and critiques of private law: the view that law is an artifact of state power,the view that law enshrines a set of norms,and the view that law is a coherent system of one kind oranother.In contrast, I will suggest that if one approaches these debates from the standpoint of the deceptively naive question, "what is collateral, really, in the derivatives markets?" one begins to grasp a view of law as something very different from a body of norms. Global private law is also, I want to suggest, a set of routinized but highly compartmentalized knowledge practices. I will shorthand this description of global private law as the Anti-Network in order to contrast it to celebrations of global private law as an artifact of global networks of various kinds.Debates about the sources of private law's legitimacy, I will suggest, need to be redirected to contend with a more accurate picture of global private law.
My alternative description of private law beyond the state has implications for the question of how and to what extent global private law threatens the legitimacy of the state. Up to now, it has been taken for granted by most proponents and critics alike that global private law is something analogous to, but ultimately different from state law.That is, it has been assumed that global private law threatens the legitimacy of the state by taking over the functions of the state through other (ostensibly more efficient, more accepted, or more normatively defensible) means. In contrast, I argue that to the extent that global private law poses a threat to the state it is not because private law is somehow functionally analogous to, but qualitatively different from, state law. Rather, if one understands private law beyond the state, as I do, as a set of institutions, actors, doctrines, ideas, material documents - of "knowledge practices"- one begins to see remarkable similarities between the technical workings of global private law and the nature of "state work." From this perspective, the "threat," if any, of global private law inheres instead inthe way it replicates and hence supersedes the state in practical, mundane, routine ways.
In the sections that follow, I consider how a close-up description of some moments in global private law-making, like the one with which I began, might cause us to rethink the three most prominent assumptions about global private law. I then conclude with some implications for how to think about whether and how global private law might be "beyond the state."
. Rethinking Private Law as an Artifact of State Power
In order to evaluate and specify the claims often made about global private law, I turn to empirical observations conducted through participant observation in one arena of private governance, the self-regulation of the global swap markets through the posting of collateral in Tokyo. The privately negotiated derivative markets are intended to be the most private of markets. Unlike the futures and options markets, swaps are not traded over an organized exchange. The parties to a swap make their own rules, tailor their own contracts, and above all, privately bear the full risk that one or another will not perform their obligations rather than placing their confidence in the exchange as an intermediary.Since securities regulation law was designed to regulate on-exchange activity, much swap trading falls between the regulatory cracks.When disputes arise,therefore, often parties' only option is to bring a lawsuit in a domestic court under ordinary common or civil law claims such as breach of contract, or fraud.Since this is often impractical, the effect is that the parties have relatively little recourse to the state to resolve their internal problems. And this is precisely the appeal of these markets, from participants' point of view.
When the documentation people described above were not at work completing and dispatching confirmation forms, they huddled behind piles of binders full of printed forms, dictionaries and pencils in hand, talking on the telephone with colleagues at other banks as they worked through the blanks in the forms. The most common printed form was a standardized "master agreement"that provides the legal framework for all individual swap transactions between any two banks. It defines key practices, rights and obligations, such as the use of confirmation documents, or the procedures for cashing out obligations in the event of the financial failure of one of the parties.
The form had been produced by representatives of important players in the swap markets, working together under the auspices of the International Swaps and Derivatives Association (ISDA). Founded in 1985, ISDA is a private organization of more than 750 over-the-counter derivatives "dealers" - banks and securities firms that are repeat players ("dealers") in the privately negotiated derivatives industry, the market for derivatives that are not traded through an organized exchange.The master agreement is one of ISDA's early and lasting achievements, and the production of this and other standardized agreements is one of the principal functions of the association.
Although the document standardizes many aspects of the practice of swap trading, it also allows for a certain amount of flexibility and adaptation by its users through a "schedule" at the end in which the parties can specify some of the details to their particular relationship, such as how payments are to be made. Hence the task of the documentation people was to tailor the agreement to the needs of the bank and its counterparties by filling in the blanks in the form.
At first blush, it may seem odd to focus on this kind of legal work as an example of global private law. It has become commonplace in sociolegal studies to focus instead on the "creative capacities of lawyers"- in bringing clients together, inventing innovative solutions to business problems, pushing the development of law, and hence shaping the character of society. But the rote and repetitive work of the documentation people, defined by its precision and attention to detail rather than its creativity, and by its distance from legal theory, points to another, too little acknowledged modality of legal work.
All this mundane activity is relevant to the nature of global private law and to the question of the extent to which it operates outside or beyond the state in two senses. First, the ISDA master agreement is the work of a powerful global private organization of the kind that is now at the center of many debates about global private law.Second, within the field of global derivatives trading, collateralization is a legal technology that is paradigmatic of global private law solutions. Although collateral is an artifact of multiple kinds of national law,it is also a device for running an end-game around certain aspects of national law. In the event of bankruptcy, collateral gives swap counterparties a mechanism other than the priority system of national bankruptcy laws with its concerns for the interests of thirdparties through which to resolve disputes.Collateral is a self-help mechanism: in many jurisdictions the collateral holder may simply keep the collateral to satisfy the debtor's obligations, without going to court.Collateral emerges as a solution to a practical problem of transnational governance, therefore. The problem is that the terms of the national bankruptcy laws of many of the countries in which derivatives trading occurs and the way these are interpreted and enforced by national bankruptcy judges do not always suit the global derivatives industry because they do not prioritize their claims ahead of others.
But collateral has many other advantages other than protection against bankruptcy. For example, it becomes a vehicle for the parties to privately steer their relationship through other turbulent waters: the ISDA Master Agreement lists a number of "events" short of bankruptcy that trigger the collateral holder's right to close out its positions and use the collateral to satisfy any residual debts.In this respect, collateral shares certain functional features with other private commercial practices such as the uses of barter in international trade,or the rules commercial banks have developed for letter ofcredit practices.We might say that collateral becomes, in a practical sense, a kind of private constitution for the parties' ongoing relationship.
For some, claims about the global production of private law of this kind become an urgent object of critique. These commentators seek to show that the "technical" quality of global private law is in fact highly politicized.They renew and expand longstanding critiques of the public-private distinction in domestic law to demonstrate that global private law is always dependent upon state legal institutions for enforcement.
It is certainly true, as these critics assert, that collateral is an artifact of multiple kinds of publicly created law.Collateral transactions in the privately traded derivatives markets raise particular problems of interface between multiple national legal systems, including problems of determining what law applies to any particular collateral transaction.The answers to these questions are murky,doctrinally arcane, and just as variable, from jurisdiction to jurisdiction, as is the law of collateral itself.Robert Wai terms these thornydoctrinal problems "touchdown points" in the relationship between global private governance and national law - points at which the efforts of private organizations such as ISDA to achieve "lift-off" from national regimes comes to rest on national law itself.
But this critique of global private governance is certainly not news to the proponents of global private governance institutions like ISDA. The legal experts with whom I worked understood full well that the private law of collateral is always only a partial global solution to their local legal problems.They were intimately aware, for example, that the terms of any collateral agreement must satisfy national requirements for creating a valid and enforceable security interest in order for the lender to be able to use the collateral, or again, that national bankruptcy law must recognize the primacy of the interest of "secured creditors" over other creditors if the collateral agreement is to have force once the debtor has declared bankruptcy. In fact, it was at these junctures that the legal actors I studied labored - these constraints created the legal work for them to do.
For example, where the terms in ISDA's standardized documents conflict with the norms enshrined in national statutory or judge-made law, ISDA actively works to supplant or change the latter so that it conforms to the former. ISDA hires local lawyers to investigate discrepancies between the terms of ISDA documents and national law, and where necessary, to lobby national governments to change national law to either conform to the terms of the Master Agreementor explicitly declare the ISDA documents enforceable.Partly at the urging of ISDA, and with active input from the organization, several transnational bodies are busy creating substantive legal rules concerning collateral that would apply in multiple jurisdictions and supersede national law. ISDA has pressed for the creation of a treaty - perhaps the ultimate example of global state law - that would mandate that national judges respect private parties' right to choose whatever law they wish to have applied to their collateral agreements.In response to lobbying from ISDA,the European Union has adopted a Directive on Financial Collateral Arrangements defining how security interests are to be created in EU Member States, and the rights of holders of collateral.And ISDA has also worked with UNIDROIT, the international body devoted to unifying private law globally,on a Convention on Harmonised Substantive Rules regardingIntermediated Securities to be adopted by individual nations as international law.ISDA members aim not only to create substantive legal rights through private contracts, but to influence the shape of those rights as they find expression in state law.
What Wai views as "touchdown points," then, were for my informants, projects - problems that demanded creative work, political mobilization, technical skill, and considerable devotion. What is interesting about typical artifacts of private global governance such as collateral, when viewed in practice, is not whether they are truly private (and outside the purview of the state), or actually public (and within state control), but rather how the impulse, the fantasy of a private market engenders particular kinds of practical projects, particular registers of engagement between lawyers working for private parties under the umbrella of transnational organizations such as ISDA, national and international law-makers, judges, and regulators.
Moreover, the view that private law is just a pass through to state power overlooks the role of the materiality of ISDA forms in the global private governance regime. The rhetorical force of the argument that judges will wreak chaos on the markets if they fail to honor market practices is perhaps different because of the sheer physical ubiquity of these documents. For example, in the early 1990s, the ISDA Master Agreement's procedures for closing out the agreement in the case of the bankruptcy of one party, and its delineation of the rights of the other party in such a scenario, arguably conflicted with the substantive rules and procedures of many national bankruptcy regimes. However, interviews suggest that the widespread use of the Master Agreement - the physical existence of thousands of such signed documents - transformed the question of what to do about substantive legal rules that industry members found unfavorable, a policy question, into a far more general and technical question of the enforceability of this contract in each national jurisdiction.
The sociological fact that material documents matter admittedly flies in the face of the longstanding assertion that the paper of the contract means nothing in itself, that it is the agreement between the parties, and not the document, that matters.But commentators have begun to pay attention to the consequences of standardized contracts such as ISDA documents for the authority, legitimacy and power of privatized law in a global market.Some even celebrate these standardized contracts as examples of "the changing paradigm of international commercial law" towards "privatized law-making."And indeed, for ISDA staff and members, collateral documents are crucial technologies of private transnational legal infrastructure - devices through which particular technical, institutional, political, legal, and economic arrangements gain solidity and durability.This is not to say that judges do not understand that a privately created document is legally meaningful only to the extent that a state-sanctioned court holds it to be enforceable. But what empirical observation of private law in action demonstrates is that in order for the transaction to "work" all sides (parties and judges alike) must be both aware of the "truth" that state power lies behind all private legal regimes and able to momentarily forget this fact to immerse themselves the practical and technical day to day experience of doing private law.

questions.question: Whether standardized private legal documents and the routine work of documentation personnel in transnational financial markets produce governance effects that replicate or supplant ordinary state legal authority.
questions.answer: Yes; through standardized ISDA documents, collateral-based self-help, and the routine documentation practices that build a private legal infrastructure, these regimes replicate and can effectively supersede state legal authority in practical, everyday ways.

questions.question: Whether the legitimacy of global private law primarily depends on state enforcement, shared normative commitment among market participants, or on routinized, compartmentalized knowledge and material practices.
questions.answer: The paper contends that legitimacy rests less on state enforcement or shared norms and more on routinized, highly compartmentalized knowledge practices and the material ubiquity of standardized documents.

questions.question: How interactions between private standard-setting organizations' documents and national legal systems determine the enforceability and practical reach of private global legal regimes.
questions.answer: Enforceability and scope are determined at national-law “touchdown points” (e.g., security-interest and bankruptcy rules) where ISDA forms must meet local requirements, with ISDA and market actors tailoring, lobbying, and pursuing harmonization so that courts recognize the widely used standards, thereby extending the private regime’s practical reach.

Who creates contractual innovations, why, and what incentives and constraints shape the supply of such innovations?
What public policies or institutional interventions would increase the generation and widespread adoption of socially valuable contractual innovations?
Do commonly used standardized contract clauses operate as analogs to default legal rules, and can a systematic 'standard clause' method be used to predict, construct, or interpret such clauses?
To what extent can national governments effectively impose and enforce controls on cross-border banking transactions and deposits held at foreign branches?
Does standardizing the form and language of legal opinions and contract documents reduce negotiation time, transaction costs, and inefficient or overly broad opinion requests?
Can anthropological and human-centered methods enrich legal scholarship to produce more accurate accounts of contemporary sovereignty and authority?
Can market participants effectively revise or repair degraded boilerplate after adverse judicial interpretations, or do coordination and agency problems prevent timely collective correction?
Do trade associations, reputation systems, and linked-membership mechanisms enable creation and revision of standard-form contracts despite lack of IP protection for contract language?
Do recurring, modular 'contract patterns' systematically structure how attorneys draft agreements and how those agreements interlock and scale into complex transactions and markets?
Is the persistence of imperfect contract forms best explained by path dependence, network effects, and switching costs rather than efficiency?
What institutional or normative responses should courts, legislatures, or standards bodies adopt to manage cross-contract externalities created by single interpretive decisions?
Why and by what mechanisms are contractual innovations and standardized clauses created, disseminated, and adopted across legal markets?
Do cross-border payment transactions and bank intermediation routinely generate conflicts-of-laws problems that produce uncertainty and litigation risk?
How do business lawyers add value in complex transactions-do they act primarily as transaction-cost engineers who structure deals, allocate risk, and influence asset pricing?
How and why do certain contractual innovations diffuse widely while others fail to spread-what roles do reputation, branding, and deliberate dissemination play?
Do standardized private legal documents and documentation personnel in transnational finance produce governance effects that replicate or supplant state legal authority?
How do organizational features of contract production (centralized drafting, mass-customization routines, modular standard forms) affect distribution of power among drafters, users, and non-parties?
Can parties reliably allocate legal risks for cross-border deposits and banking operations by contract, and will such contractual allocations be enforced across jurisdictions?

Why are complex commercial contracts frequently long, redundant, and written in dense legalese - is this primarily due to reliance on prior-transaction forms, form-based production processes, editorial churning, branding incentives, or other causes?
Does globalization and increased transacting-party heterogeneity drive adoption of comprehensive, U.S.-style contract documentation across other jurisdictions?
What trade-offs arise between reducing contract customization through standardized 'good-enough' provisions and parties' ability to secure precisely tailored outcomes?
Should empirical contract research prioritize testing existing theories or seek new interdisciplinary explanations for real-world contracting puzzles?
How do the identity and behavior of market participants and external pressures influence who originates and who standardizes innovations in boilerplate terms?
What speech-act function does entering into a complex business contract serve: creating enforceable promises or setting a framework that enables non-legal governance and cooperation?
Do groups of market participants (committees, task forces, networks, trade associations) overcome coordination problems to facilitate efficient change in entrenched contractual or social norms?

What factors explain the persistence or 'stickiness' of particular disclosure and boilerplate practices-do market norms and network effects keep standard language unchanged despite substantive shifts?
What institutional or normative responses should manage or limit cross-contract externalities created when a single interpretive decision changes the meaning of boilerplate across many contracts?
To what extent are complex agreements organized as modular subsystems (enabling mass customization) versus thickly interconnected integrated systems, and how does that shape transaction design?
Why do persistent, costly, or apparently nonfunctional boilerplate clauses persist in sophisticated contracts?
Why do some inefficient or nonfunctional contract features persist in markets despite competition - is path dependence, network effects, or branding responsible?

How do private standard-setting organizations, form contracts, and transnational documentation practices interact with national legal systems to determine the enforceability, reach, and governance effects of private global legal regimes?
What governance effects do standardized private legal documents and routine documentation work produce-do they replicate, supplement, or supplant state legal authority?
Can a single general theory of contractual innovation account for diverse incentives and dissemination pathways, or is contractual innovation inherently idiosyncratic?

Do legal, institutional, and normative features (statutory backstops, professional practices, standardized forms, repeat-dealing norms) reduce the need for bespoke contract customization and thereby lower transaction costs?
To what extent did public-sector actors influence contractual and market shifts through non-coercive means (advocacy, informational cueing) versus private-market learning and network effects?
What governance tradeoffs arise when crisis responses are structured as private deals rather than regulatory interventions?

How do transaction designers manage infra-transactional complexity in large contracts - by modular designs or by flexible specialization - and what are the implications for drafting, negotiation, and enforcement?

Do law firms and transactional deal teams organize contract production as modular, standardized subsystems that enable mass customization, or as integrated, flexible-specialization routines, and how do these organizational forms affect drafting quality, diffusion, and persistence of boilerplate?
Do market norms, network effects, or legal stickiness explain persistence of dated disclosure or opinion practices despite material changes in contract substance?
When do standardized contracts and boilerplate produce social costs by enshrining language that courts enforce differently from parties' intent or that courts reinterpret during crises?
How do standardized forms, firm templates, intermediaries, and market participants drive convergence or heterogeneity in transactional documentation across deals and jurisdictions?

Should major legal transplants (e.g., U.S. contract documentation) be expected to produce the same investor-protection effects in other jurisdictions, or do they mutate and yield unintended consequences?
Why do courts and markets sometimes mirror legal arguments and interventions developed elsewhere, and does such mimicry undermine international legal coherence or serve pragmatic purposes?
Do market learning and network externalities cause firms to converge on standardized contract terms rather than customize or innovate them?
Do contract drafters typically copy boilerplate blindly across deals or actively tailor and evolve terms, and what organizational routines explain their behavior?
How large and practically significant are downstream effects of standard contract changes-that is, how many contracts and parties are affected and with what consequences?
How do standard-form 'boilerplate' clauses evolve in practice, and do courts' interpretations of such clauses create significant spillover effects across contracts?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 77chikentlrev29!!SYMPOSIUM: THEORY INFORMS BUSINESS PRACTICE:A COMMENT ON LANGUAGE AND NORMS IN COMPLEX BUSINESS CONTRACTING
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: THEORY INFORMS BUSINESS PRACTICE:A COMMENT ON LANGUAGE AND NORMS IN COMPLEX BUSINESS CONTRACTING

shared_topics.topic: the performative/constitutive power of contractual language and documents
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes complex business contracts as performative speech acts that bring legal states of affairs into being, and Paper B shows how ISDA master agreements and confirmations function materially and practically to constitute obligations and shape market realities.

shared_topics.topic: the interface between private contracting and state law (enforceability, 'touchdown points')
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats enforceability in courts as central to what entering a contract does and examines how law shapes contractual relationships, while Paper B traces the dependence of private global contracts on national law and documents the junctures where private regimes must engage or reshape state law.

shared_topics.topic: the role of non-legal mechanisms (reputation, routines, material practices) in making contracts work
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes reputational and other extra-legal forces that give content to contract relationships beyond literal wording, and Paper B documents routinized, compartmentalized labor and material documentation practices that sustain private law in practice.

shared_topics.topic: standardization and blank-form contracts as infrastructure for complex transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses how lengthy, complex contracts and their grammar set the stage for ongoing accommodation among parties, while Paper B empirically examines the ISDA Master Agreement and standardized confirmation forms as instruments that enable and stabilize global swap trading.

shared_topics.topic: limits of language and knowledge and the importance of tacit/embodied expertise in interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A foregrounds limits of literal meaning and knowledge—arguing contracts are best understood within constrained contextual meaning and economic ends—while Paper B highlights the tacit, technical knowledge practices of documentation personnel and legal actors who interpret and operationalize standardized documents.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 85geowashlrev57!!ARTICLE: The Inefficient Evolution of Merger Agreements
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Inefficient Evolution of Merger Agreements

shared_topics.topic: the governance role of standardized transactional documents
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies the ISDA Master Agreement as a standardized legal technology that structures global derivatives relationships and stabilizes private governance; Paper B investigates merger agreements and argues their heterogeneous, precedent-driven drafting obstructs the kind of standardization that would lower transaction costs and increase legal certainty.

shared_topics.topic: routinized, technical documentary work as central to legal practice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A foregrounds the mundane, repetitive work of documentation personnel who 'paper the trades' and produce enforceable forms; Paper B empirically analyzes the everyday drafting process (precedents, edits, 'editorial churning') that generates the operative terms of merger deals.

shared_topics.topic: how precedents, lineage, and material documents shape legal evolution and practice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes the material ubiquity of ISDA forms and how widely used documents transform doctrinal and policy questions into questions of enforceability and practice; Paper B reconstructs family trees of merger agreements to show path-dependent evolution where prior drafts shape current deal terms.

shared_topics.topic: private ordering by repeat players and its interaction with public law or market governance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows how ISDA members and other industry actors use private drafting and lobbying to influence national and transnational law (e.g., EU directives, treaty efforts); Paper B highlights repeat players (law firms, private equity) as central actors whose incentives determine whether private standards emerge or inefficiencies persist and suggests industry-led standardization.

shared_topics.topic: efficiency, incentives, and the costs/risks of current drafting practices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A links routinized private legal practices to practical replication of state-like functions and raises questions about legitimacy and systemic consequences of private ordering; Paper B documents inefficiency and unnecessary editing in merger drafting, linking lawyers' incentives and lack of standard forms to higher costs and legal risk for clients.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 1988uilllrev371!!ARTICLE: ALTERNATIVE TECHNIQUES IN SOVEREIGN DEBT RESTRUCTURING 1988 Center for Transnational Legal Studies
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: ALTERNATIVE TECHNIQUES IN SOVEREIGN DEBT RESTRUCTURING 1988 Center for Transnational Legal Studies

shared_topics.topic: private-market techniques for managing cross-border financial obligations
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze concrete, market-generated instruments and practices (Paper A: debt-management/restructuring techniques used by commercial banks in LDC renegotiations; Paper B: collateralization and ISDA documentation in swap markets) as primary tools for resolving transnational financial obligations and risks.

shared_topics.topic: interaction between private contractual regimes and national/state law
shared_topics.justification: Both discuss how privately produced arrangements depend on, collide with, and seek to shape domestic legal regimes (Paper A limits itself to techniques that operate within existing political, legal, and regulatory constraints; Paper B details 'touchdown points' where ISDA documents must align with or prompt changes in national bankruptcy and secured transactions law).

shared_topics.topic: standardization and routinization of legal/financial practices
shared_topics.justification: Both papers examine the emergence of routinized, widely adopted techniques or documents that turn innovations into 'conventional' practice (Paper A: once-innovative debt-management techniques becoming standard in renegotiations; Paper B: the ISDA Master Agreement and standardized confirmation forms that normalize swap operations).

shared_topics.topic: private financial actors as transnational governance agents
shared_topics.justification: Both treat commercial banks and private market organizations as governance actors who create, enforce, and lobby for rules governing cross-border finance (Paper A focuses on banks' renegotiation practices in sovereign debt; Paper B focuses on ISDA and dealer banks shaping private law and pushing for legal harmonization).

shared_topics.topic: focus on tactical, incremental solutions within existing institutional constraints
shared_topics.justification: Both works emphasize pragmatic, incremental reforms or mechanisms rather than sweeping structural overhauls (Paper A explicitly confines discussion to tactical techniques within current frameworks; Paper B documents how private documentation and technical fixes function as practical governance projects that work around, and sometimes seek to modify, state law).

compared_to.partner_node_id: 31cardozolrev99!!ARTICLE: CANCELING THE DEAL: TWO MODELS OF MATERIAL ADVERSE CHANGE CLAUSES IN BUSINESS COMBINATION AGREEMENTS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CANCELING THE DEAL: TWO MODELS OF MATERIAL ADVERSE CHANGE CLAUSES IN BUSINESS COMBINATION AGREEMENTS

shared_topics.topic: contractual allocation of commercial risk through private legal instruments
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how collateral clauses and ISDA master agreements function as private legal technologies that allocate bankruptcy and counterparty risk outside state procedures, while Paper B studies how Material Adverse Change (MAC) clauses allocate signing-to-closing deal risk in merger agreements and the contractual mechanics parties use to assign those risks.

shared_topics.topic: authority and governance effects of standardized contract forms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on the ISDA Master Agreement as a standardized, widely used form that creates durable private governance practices across jurisdictions, and Paper B documents the ubiquity and heavy negotiation of MAC clause templates in public-company merger agreements and how their standardized (but variable) language governs deal outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: the interface between private contracting and state law/courts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights 'touchdown points' where private ISDA documentation must engage national bankruptcy and enforcement regimes and how private actors lobby to change state law, while Paper B shows how courts (not the parties) are often compelled to supply interpretive standards for MAC clauses because contractual texts are indeterminate, revealing the crucial role of judicial doctrine at the private–public boundary.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal indeterminacy and the limits of textual contract definitions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that the practical authority of private documents cannot be understood solely from doctrinal claims about state power or norms and emphasizes the messy doctrinal interfaces practitioners confront; Paper B demonstrates that MAC clauses frequently lack a principled materiality standard in text, forcing judges to develop ad hoc or econometric models to decide cases.

shared_topics.topic: routine, specialized legal work and the materiality of documents in producing legal outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses participant observation of 'documentation people' to show how repetitive, routinized drafting and the physical ubiquity of ISDA forms produce legal facts and industry norms, and Paper B foregrounds the negotiated drafting practices and empirical prevalence of particular MAC formulations, showing how drafting choices and written clauses materially shape litigation and deal resolution.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 41iowajcorpl393!!ARTICLE: Law Firm Selection and the Value of Transactional Lawyering
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Law Firm Selection and the Value of Transactional Lawyering

shared_topics.topic: the role of standardized contractual forms and templates in enabling transacting parties
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how elite law firms compile and deploy market precedents and standardized deal terms to secure better bargaining outcomes, while Paper B studies the ISDA Master Agreement and confirmation forms as standardized legal documents that structure swap trading and stabilize private transnational markets.

shared_topics.topic: repeat-player informational advantage and private market knowledge in bargaining
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that law firms that are repeat players in particular transaction types accumulate private, real-time information about deal terms that gives clients a bargaining edge; Paper B shows how repeat dealers and ISDA members generate shared, routinized knowledge (and documentation practices) that orient counterparties and reduce uncertainty in derivatives trading.

shared_topics.topic: private actors shaping transnational legal rules and market governance (private governance beyond the state)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contends that elite firms' information aggregation and knowledge management can alter transactional power and market outcomes independently of in-house or state mechanisms, while Paper B documents how ISDA and market participants create private legal infrastructures and actively seek to influence or harmonize state law to support those private rules.

shared_topics.topic: the significance of routinized, material legal work and knowledge management for market functioning
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights associates' work aggregating precedents and firms' knowledge-management practices as central to transactional value, and Paper B foregrounds the ‘documentation people’ and the material ubiquity of printed ISDA forms as mundane, technical labor that produces durable private legal order.

shared_topics.topic: tension between professional confidentiality norms and the pooling/monetization of client transaction information
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explores how professional responsibility norms coexist with firms' practice of pooling client deal information to generate market knowledge that clients effectively buy, and Paper B shows how widespread use and material presence of standardized documents creates shared private knowledge that operates independently of, and sometimes seeks modification of, state-enforced legal rules.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2014uilllrev67!!ARTICLE: SOVEREIGN IMMUNITY AND SOVEREIGN DEBT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: SOVEREIGN IMMUNITY AND SOVEREIGN DEBT

shared_topics.topic: interaction between private contract terms and state law/enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces how sovereign bond contracts incorporated dispute-resolution and waiver-of-immunity clauses in relation to changes in sovereign immunity doctrine (noting the limited practical effect of those legal developments), while Paper B shows how ISDA master agreements and collateral arrangements are drafted and promoted with constant attention to how national law will recognize or frustrate those private terms (including lobbying to change state law).

shared_topics.topic: standardization and evolution of boilerplate contracting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents a sudden, broad shift in boilerplate dispute-resolution language in sovereign bonds (especially after the FSIA) and considers why drafters adopted particular standardized clauses, while Paper B analyzes the ISDA master agreement as a pervasive standardized form and the quotidian work (the "documentation people") that produces, adapts, and stabilizes that boilerplate across global markets.

shared_topics.topic: private governance actors shaping transnational legal order
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates the role of market actors, drafters, and statutory codification in producing contractual norms that structure sovereign lending, and Paper B examines ISDA and related private organizations as transnational governance actors that create technical rules, press for harmonization, and seek to influence state and international law.

shared_topics.topic: empirical challenge to doctrinal assumptions about law and enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses a large dataset of bond issues and market-price evidence to question doctrinal claims about the practical import of sovereign-immunity reform and enforcement rights, while Paper B relies on participant observation and interviews to contest theoretical accounts of global private law and to show how mundane practices and documents mediate between private regimes and state authority.

shared_topics.topic: private (self-help) enforcement mechanisms versus reliance on state adjudication
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses arbitration clauses and the limited practical value of litigation against sovereigns (and how investors sometimes rely on reputational or other non-judicial incentives), while Paper B focuses on collateral and close-out rights as self-help mechanisms that allow derivatives counterparties to resolve disputes or protect claims outside national bankruptcy processes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 6chijintll287!!ARTICLE: SYMPOSIUM: SOVEREIGN DEBT RESTRUCTURING: The Role of the IMF in Sovereign Debt Restructuring
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: SYMPOSIUM: SOVEREIGN DEBT RESTRUCTURING: The Role of the IMF in Sovereign Debt Restructuring

shared_topics.topic: interaction between transnational governance actors and national legal/political systems
shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces how ISDA's private contracts and collateral practices confront 'touchdown points' with national bankruptcy and property laws and actively lobby to reshape those laws; Paper B analyzes how IMF proposals for sovereign debt restructuring must accommodate and are constrained by diverse national political and legal systems.

shared_topics.topic: how institutional features and mundane practices shape international economic outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes routinized, compartmentalized knowledge practices (documentation work, standardized forms) and material documents as mechanisms that produce legal effects in global markets; Paper B argues that the IMF's institutional design and decisionmaking procedures – not just its technocratic staff – materially influence the outcomes of restructuring proposals.

shared_topics.topic: legitimacy and authority of non-state or supranational governance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A problematizes assumptions about the sources of private global law's legitimacy (state power, norms, coherence) and shows legitimacy arising from everyday technical practices and material ubiquity of documents; Paper B highlights the IMF's political foundation beneath a technocratic veneer, showing that questions of authority and legitimacy affect acceptance and feasibility of international arrangements.

shared_topics.topic: limits of high-level reform proposals absent empirical attention to practice and institutions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques utopian/dystopian accounts of global private law for ignoring on-the-ground practices and the empirical complexity of private governance; Paper B warns that many proposals to expand the IMF's role are analytically flawed because they ignore institutional realities and will produce unintended outcomes when confronted with political and legal practice.

shared_topics.topic: challenges of creating and enforcing cross-jurisdictional standards or arrangements
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows ISDA's attempt to produce standardized master agreements and collateral rules and the difficulties of enforcement and harmonization across jurisdictions (leading to lobbying, EU directives, treaties); Paper B discusses proposals to govern international transactions (including debt restructuring) and the compromises and enforcement problems that arise when accommodating multiple national systems within single international arrangements.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 77nyulrev1040!!ARTICLE:RETHINKING CORPORATE BONDS: THE TRADE-OFF BETWEEN INDIVIDUAL AND COLLECTIVE RIGHTS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:RETHINKING CORPORATE BONDS: THE TRADE-OFF BETWEEN INDIVIDUAL AND COLLECTIVE RIGHTS

shared_topics.topic: the interaction between private contractual governance and state law/enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how ISDA-produced collateral agreements operate in practice at 'touchdown points' with national bankruptcy and other state laws and how private bodies lobby to reshape state law; Paper B examines how indenture provisions, judicial interpretation, and statutory backstops determine the practical enforceability of bondholder rights, showing the dependence of private contract regimes on courts and legal rules.

shared_topics.topic: the role of standardized contractual documents as infrastructural technologies of financial markets
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers the ISDA Master Agreement and confirmation forms as ubiquitous, material technologies that stabilize and routinize swap markets; Paper B focuses on bond indentures as the canonical contractual form governing corporate bonds and even provides model provisions to structure market behavior.

shared_topics.topic: the allocation of enforcement and amendment powers between individual investors and collective representatives
shared_topics.justification: Paper B develops a framework on the trade-off between individual enforcement rights and collective mechanisms (majority amendments, trustee enforcement) in indentures; Paper A addresses analogous questions in swaps—who acts to enforce or operationalize rights (documentation teams, counterparties, ISDA, or state courts) and how private organizations and intermediaries mediate collective action and enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: contractual design choices for creditor protection and managing counterparty/default risk
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows how collateral, close-out and netting provisions in ISDA documents are private-law techniques to manage bankruptcy and default risk across jurisdictions; Paper B analyzes how indenture terms, remedy structures, and trustee powers (or their limits) affect bondholders' protection against issuer default and opportunistic amendment.

shared_topics.topic: the institutional division of legal labor and routinized, technical legal practices in finance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes 'documentation people' and routinized knowledge practices as central to how private global law operates in swaps; Paper B highlights the institutional role and incentive structure of the indenture trustee and the procedural barriers that make enforcement a function of routine institutional practices rather than ad hoc litigation by retail holders.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 22upajbusl209!!ARTICLE: PROACTIVE RESOLUTION OF SOVEREIGN AND SUBNATIONAL DEBT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: PROACTIVE RESOLUTION OF SOVEREIGN AND SUBNATIONAL DEBT

shared_topics.topic: the role of collateralization in constraining legal and policy responses to financial distress
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes collateral as a private legal technology in derivatives markets that sidesteps or reshapes national bankruptcy rules and reduces states' ability to protect third-party interests; Paper B highlights the growth of collateralized sovereign debt as reducing maneuvering room in crises, enabling creditor seizures of assets and complicating restructurings.

shared_topics.topic: the interaction and friction between private contractual ordering and national/state law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents how standardized private contracts (ISDA master agreements) generate 'touchdown points' where private ordering depends on, contests, and seeks to change national law; Paper B emphasizes that sovereigns lack formal legal mechanisms analogous to corporate bankruptcy and that contractual features and creditor diversification create legal obstacles to restructuring under national legal regimes.

shared_topics.topic: the importance of transnational legal infrastructure and standard-form instruments in governing cross-border finance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows how organizations (e.g., ISDA), standardized forms, and material documents create durable transnational practices and influence international and domestic law; Paper B addresses how evolving creditor structures, contractual terms (including collateral and creditor priority), and international institutions (IMF, potential fora) shape the practical possibilities for cross-border sovereign and subnational debt resolution.

shared_topics.topic: normative tensions between private creditor entitlements and state/public legitimacy or policy goals
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates whether global private law undermines the state's legitimacy by routinizing private governance that can supersede state functions, while Paper B discusses how honoring creditor claims (and bailout conditions) can constrain governments' ability to provide public services and raise questions about who should bear the cost of debt resolution.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 94iowalrev937!!ARTICLE: VALUES AND VALUE CREATION IN PUBLIC-PRIVATE TRANSACTIONS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: VALUES AND VALUE CREATION IN PUBLIC-PRIVATE TRANSACTIONS

shared_topics.topic: standardized private contracts and documentation as transnational legal infrastructure
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the ISDA Master Agreement and the material ubiquity of confirmation/ collateral documents as infrastructures that produce durable private legal effects across jurisdictions; Paper B shows how deal lawyers draft and structure contractual terms in public-private transactions so that those documents operationalize policy goals and allocate risks across public and private actors.

shared_topics.topic: private actors shaping or leveraging public law and regulation to make private ordering effective
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents ISDA's active efforts to identify 'touchdown points' and lobby for EU directives, treaties, and national law changes so its private forms will be enforceable; Paper B theorizes and documents how deal lawyers 'engineer regulatory costs' and perform 'regulatory translation' to adapt to, work around, or capitalize on the regulatory environment in structuring deals.

shared_topics.topic: tension and interaction between private governance/value-creation and state legitimacy or public policy goals
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates claims that global private law either supplants or depends on the state and asks how private law practices affect the legitimacy and routine functions of the state; Paper B examines how value creation in public-private partnerships must be balanced with non-economic public-policy objectives, highlighting conflicts and alignments between private dealmaking and public legitimacy.

shared_topics.topic: the importance of routinized, technical legal labor (documentation, translation) in producing real-world legal outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights the repetitive, detail-oriented work of 'documentation people' as central to how global private law operates in practice; Paper B identifies the practical, often technical task of regulatory translation by deal lawyers as a form of value-creating labor essential for making complex public-private deals function.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 1988uilllrev371!!ARTICLE: ALTERNATIVE TECHNIQUES IN SOVEREIGN DEBT RESTRUCTURING 1988 Center for Transnational Legal Studies
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: ALTERNATIVE TECHNIQUES IN SOVEREIGN DEBT RESTRUCTURING 1988 Center for Transnational Legal Studies

shared_topics.topic: private transnational governance of cross-border financial obligations by creditor networks
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how commercial banks collectively developed and applied ad hoc debt-management techniques to renegotiate sovereign LDC debt, and Paper B examines how dealer networks (via ISDA) create private governance for derivatives, showing both study creditor-led, cross-border private ordering of financial obligations.

shared_topics.topic: the role of standardized contractual/instrumental techniques in producing durable market practices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces how innovative restructuring techniques became 'conventional' tools in sovereign debt renegotiations, while Paper B shows how standardized documents (the ISDA Master Agreement and collateral forms) routinize and stabilize derivatives market practices.

shared_topics.topic: points of interface between private ordering and national/state law (enforcement, bankruptcy, and legal constraints)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A limits itself to techniques that operate within existing political-legal constraints and notes limits imposed by state institutions, and Paper B investigates 'touchdown points' where private collateral and ISDA terms run up against national bankruptcy and enforcement regimes and prompt legal change.

shared_topics.topic: how incremental, tactical innovations by market participants can ossify or impede broader legal/policy reform
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that past debt-management innovations quickly became orthodox and in some respects obsolete, potentially obstructing new mechanisms, and Paper B shows how the spread and material ubiquity of ISDA documents and collateral practices can transform policy disputes into technical enforceability questions, shaping reform trajectories.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 50umemlrev655!!ARTICLE: Abuses of the Act of State Doctrine
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Abuses of the Act of State Doctrine

shared_topics.topic: boundaries of domestic judicial review over extraterritorial acts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how private transnational instruments (e.g., ISDA master agreements and collateral practices) interact with and sometimes aim to sidestep national courts, while Paper B analyzes the act of state doctrine and statutory exceptions that determine when U.S. courts must defer to or may review a foreign sovereign's acts.

shared_topics.topic: conflicts and interfaces between transnational/private norms and national law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A investigates 'touchdown points' where ISDA-standardized contracts bump up against divergent national bankruptcy and property rules, and Paper B treats the tension between international comity (deference to foreign sovereign acts) and domestic legal principles governing adjudication and remedies.

shared_topics.topic: mechanisms that shield outcomes from ordinary adjudication (doctrines, documents, routines)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows how routinized documentation and collateralization operate as private legal technologies that achieve enforceability outside ordinary state procedures, while Paper B shows how the act of state doctrine can function to preclude judicial fact-finding and thereby insulate foreign sovereign determinations from adjudication.

shared_topics.topic: strategic use of domestic legal and political processes by external actors
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents how ISDA and market participants lobby, draft forms, and engage transnational bodies to shape national and international law in their favor; Paper B critiques how foreign sovereign plaintiffs may invoke the act of state doctrine (and sovereign-immunity choices) to manipulate U.S. procedural posture and avoid presenting proof.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 50umemlrev655!!ARTICLE: Abuses of the Act of State Doctrine
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Abuses of the Act of State Doctrine

shared_topics.topic: interaction between transnational/private legal regimes and domestic state law (the 'touchdown points')
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically analyzes how ISDA's standardized collateral documentation interfaces with national bankruptcy and property rules and must be reconciled at 'touchdown points' where private transnational practices meet state law; Paper B analyzes how the act of state doctrine marks a doctrinal boundary where foreign sovereign acts claim immunity from domestic adjudication, similarly creating a site of interaction between extraterritorial legal claims and domestic legal systems.

shared_topics.topic: judicial deference versus adjudication in cross-border disputes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows how judges and market actors must sometimes 'momentarily forget' state power to let private norms operate and how courts ultimately decide enforceability of private transnational contracts; Paper B examines when U.S. courts should decline to adjudicate (defer to) a foreign sovereign's determinations under the act of state doctrine and critiques inconsistent judicial application of that deference.

shared_topics.topic: the legitimacy and evidentiary force of extra-state legal acts or documents in domestic forums

papers.node_id: 50vandjtransnatll1033!!SYMPOSIUM ARTICLE: Tribunalizing Sovereign Debt: Argentina's Experience with Investor-State Dispute Settlement
papers.title: SYMPOSIUM ARTICLE: Tribunalizing Sovereign Debt: Argentina's Experience with Investor-State Dispute Settlement
papers.abstract:
It is fair to say that the global sovereign debt market is governed by what its participants think the law should be - rather than what it actually is.The role of legal imagination - and constant re-imagination - is stronger in sovereign debt finance than arguably any other part of the global financial system. The absence of a formal bankruptcy regime or binding regulatory oversight is fertile ground for rogue behavior by opportunistic debtors and creditors alike.Nowhere has this been more evident than in Argentina's decades-long dispute with holdout creditors following its historic default in 2001.While Argentina's standoff with its holdout creditors appears to finally be over,its reverberations will be felt for decades.
The search by creditors for the holy grail of enforceability has spurred a range of novel legal strategies. Arguably one of the most important consequences of Argentina's debt crisis is the use of investor-state dispute settlement (ISDS) to adjudicate and enforce sovereign debt obligations. In Abaclat and Others v. The Argentine Republic, an arbitral tribunal at the International Center for the Settlement of Investment Disputes (ICSID) determined that it had the legal authority to hear mass claims by Italian bondholders brought under Argentina's bilateral investment treaty (BIT) with Italy.This landmark decision has been followed by two other ICSID cases against Argentina.
The use of ISDS in Argentina's debt disputes raises two intertwined questions. First, what are appropriate fora for resolving sovereign debt disputes? Sovereign debt is typically refinanced through the exchange of original bonds for new bonds following ad hoc negotiations between sovereign debtors and their creditors.Argentina's unilateral exchange offers in 2005 and 2010 involved limited and narrow negotiations and the presentation of "take-it-or-leave-it" offers to creditors.Refusing to participate in these exchange offers, holdout creditors filed hundreds of lawsuits in New York and other jurisdictions, arguing that they were entitled to full repayment.Given the likelihood of future cases before other ICSID panels and other arbitral tribunals, how should the "tribunalization" of sovereign debt finance be addressed in the event of overlap or conflict with litigation in national courts?In the years following Abaclat, legal scholars have started to grapple with the implications of this source of pluralism in the global sovereign debt market.
, what interests should be taken into account in ISDS cases involving a sovereign debtor? BITs and other international investment agreements (IIAs) have dramatically grown in number and importance in the past couple of decades.At their heart is the private right of action granted to foreign investors to sue host countries for violation of a treaty-based standard of protection.As this Article: shows, Abaclat and its progeny may be viewed as a consequence of Argentina's extraordinary intransigence.However, responses to rogue debtors, such as Argentina, often make bad law.Critics remain skeptical that ISDS is likely to rectify fundamental problems in sovereign debt restructuring. In fact, prescriptions for the widespread or standardized application of ISDS underestimatethe systemic implications of sovereign debt restructuring.Rather than fixing sovereign debt restructuring, the tribunalization of sovereign debt disputes through ISDS undermines the need for flexibility and the importance of politically palatable settlements.
This Article: proceeds as follows. Part II describes the convergence of international investment law and sovereign debt finance. The Article: explains how the unique challenges of enforcing creditor claims against sovereign debtors and the proliferation of ISDS mechanisms gave rise to this new remedy. Part III examines Argentina's debt restructuring cases before ICSID as a case study. Retrospectively, the Article: analyzes Abaclat and its progeny in the context of Argentina's experiences in litigation in national courts. Prospectively, the Article: identifies and addresses current and possible future measures by Argentina in response to sovereign bondholder arbitration. Part IV addresses the systemic implications of ISDS for the exercise of sovereign authority in the context of sovereign debt restructurings.
. The Application of International Investment Law to Sovereign Debt Finance
The use of ISDS is a product of iterative efforts by Argentina and holdout creditors to exploit legal uncertainty and ambiguity in the sovereign debt restructuring process. The following discussion examines the legal and institutional basis for applying international investment law to resolve sovereign debt disputes.
A. The Problem of Rogues and the Challenges of Enforcement in Sovereign Debt
The global sovereign debt market differs from the commercial debt market in several fundamental ways. There is no global court or regulator to enforce debt commitments or monitor restructurings,and there is no bankruptcy law to determine priority of payment to creditors.Due to a lack of enforcement mechanisms, sovereigndebtors have the discretion to default opportunistically.However, most sovereigns do in fact satisfy their debt obligations, sometimes even under significant economic duress.To explain this compliance, many scholars cite the threat of reputational sanctions, political pressure, and internal collateral damage.
Traditionally, sovereign insolvencies are resolved through voluntary negotiated exchanges of existing debt obligations for new debt obligations.Holdout creditors seeking full repayment have chosen to sue sovereigns in foreign courts, typically in New York City and London.Creditors have had little difficulty establishing jurisdiction over sovereign debtors, either by negotiating waivers of sovereign immunity in loan documents ex ante or through the commercial activity exception to foreign sovereign immunity.However, creditors have limited recourse collecting judgments against sovereigns that assert immunity against attachment of assetsor contract out of debt liability.
This ad hoc, decentralized restructuring process has deteriorated dangerously in recent years.Negotiation between sovereigns and their private creditors has drifted towards "litigotiation" - an unstable situation in which litigation and negotiation in different courts against multiple sovereigns blurs with unpredictable results.Fragmentation among creditors that have weak institutional relationships with each other and divergent interests has enabled rogue behavior by sovereign debtors and creditors.Reputational considerations, creditor coordination mechanisms, and cross-conditionality all have weakened as sources of order and authority in the global sovereign debt market.Contentious, costly, and inequitable restructurings - most notoriously, Argentina's - have incited calls for legal reform.
For the past couple of decades, reformers have fallen into two camps: the public law institutionalists and the private law contractualists.Among institutional reform advocates, the International Monetary Fund's proposed Sovereign Debt Restructuring Mechanism (SDRM) exemplified efforts to transplant bankruptcy-like procedures into sovereign debt restructurings.In contrast, contractual reform advocates point to the ability of sovereign debt contracts to impose meaningful restraints on sovereign behavior, in spite of the weakness of coercive external enforcement.First and foremost among the contractual innovations that have taken root are collective action clauses (CACs), which permit a majority or a supermajority of bondholders to change the payment terms of an issue of bonds.Coupled with exit consents, which enable a sovereign debtor to implement modifications to nonpayment termsas a condition to participating in an exchange offer,CACs are a powerful tool against holdout creditors. However, CACs are not a panacea: among various shortcomings, many old sovereign bonds do not include them, and they do not address coordination problems in loans and other non-bond debt.

questions.question: Does resorting to international investor-state arbitration to resolve sovereign debt disputes improve creditor enforcement and recovery compared with litigation in national courts or negotiated restructurings?
questions.answer: No; the abstract argues that turning to ISDS does not fix the fundamental problems of enforcing and resolving sovereign debt and, rather than outperforming courts or negotiated restructurings, risks worsening outcomes by undermining needed flexibility.

questions.question: Does adjudicating sovereign debt disputes through international tribunals undermine the flexibility and political feasibility of sovereign debt restructurings?
questions.answer: Yes; the abstract explicitly states that tribunalizing sovereign debt disputes through ISDS undermines the need for flexibility and the importance of politically palatable settlements.

questions.question: What competing public and private interests should adjudicators take into account when resolving disputes between sovereign debtors and their creditors?
questions.answer: Adjudicators should balance investors’ treaty-based private rights against public interests in sovereign authority, restructuring flexibility, politically acceptable settlements, and the broader systemic implications of sovereign debt restructurings.
