papers.node_id: 52hastingslj795!!SYMPOSIUM CONSUMERS IN THE DIGITAL AGE: PERSPECTIVES ON THE INTERSECTION OF LAW, TECHNOLOGICAL INNOVATION, AND CONSUMER PROTECTION:PERSPECTIVES ON ANTITRUST LAW:A Case for Letting a Firm Take Advantage of "Locked-In" Customers
papers.title: SYMPOSIUM CONSUMERS IN THE DIGITAL AGE: PERSPECTIVES ON THE INTERSECTION OF LAW, TECHNOLOGICAL INNOVATION, AND CONSUMER PROTECTION:PERSPECTIVES ON ANTITRUST LAW:A Case for Letting a Firm Take Advantage of "Locked-In" Customers
papers.authors: Dwight R. Lee; Richard B. Mckenzie
papers.abstract:
Many products are said to exhibit "network effects." This means that the value a consumer realizes from the product increases as the number of consumers using the product increases.Telephones, fax machines, computer operating systems, internet browsing software, and word processing software are several of the more obvious and widely cited examples of goods with network effects (two of which, operating systems and web browsers, have become central to the antitrust prosecution of the Microsoft Corporation).However, it has been pointed out that many other products - for example, some books - also exhibit network effects (readers gain the added benefitsof being able to discuss the book when many others read the same book).
According to network theorists, when incompatibilities exist between different variations of a product, it is possible for a producer of one of the variations to secure a competitive advantage over producers of other variations by being the first one to achieve a critical market share, the net result of which is that the market "tips" toward the dominant producer, causing its market share to expand with consumer demand that, in turn, reflects growing consumer benefits caused by the producer's growing market dominance.With the retreat of other producers from the market, consumers may find themselves "locked in" to the most widely used variation of the product simply because it is widely used, with perhaps superior variations of the product having a difficult time entering the market and attracting consumers. The cost of actually switching to another technology or product (which involves the costs of retraining, and new equipment and software, as well as the establishment of new office routines and, possibly, cultures) reinforces this lock-in.This suggests to some that a firm that is aggressively lowering price and expanding output could be a potential monopolist and a suitable candidate for antitrust action, if its product generates network effects. Indeed, the Justice Department has argued that Microsoft's monopoly stems from network effects, coupled with the protection against market entrants afforded Microsoft by the 70,000 existing Windows applications, the source of the so-called "applications barrier to entry."
While there are efficiencies realized from the widespread use of one variation of the product from what can be called demand-side economies of scale, the concern is that such action can lead not only to a monopoly position, but to a monopoly position for an inferior product.When there is evidence that this is happening, antitrust action is commonly recommended with a remedy of breaking up the monopoly (or potential monopoly), as was done by the Justice Department and judge in the Microsoft case.
The case for antitrust action to counter inefficiencies arising from network effects and lock-in has been vigorously attacked. At the forefront of this attack are Liebowitz and Margolis, who argue on both empirical and theoretical grounds that there is little risk of inferior technologies and products becoming entrenched by lock-ins caused by network effects.For example, Liebowitz and Margolis dispute the inferiority of the QWERTYkeyboard arrangement and of the VHSformat for videorecorders, which are commonly cited examples of the inferior out-competing the superior because of the lock-in effect. Of course, with constant technological improvements there are cases of existing technologies being widely used and benefiting from network effects and significant switching costs, despite being inferior to new technologies. But if the gains from switching are greater than the costs of doing so, incentives exist for entrepreneurs - so-called "network sponsors" - to overcome the built-in resistance to change. Each consumer may face the prisoners' dilemma of being unwilling to switch to the new technology even though all would be better off if all (or most) switched. The entrepreneur-owner of the new technology, however, can internalize this effect by sharing the gains of the efficiency improvements with customers through subsidies in the form of low, possibly negative, prices over some period of time. Not all network effects are necessarily network externalities, with the latter leading to potential market inefficiencies that might require collective correction.
Without such internalization of network effects, it is hard to explain the large number of new products and technologies thatovercame the network/switching cost advantage of previously dominant products and technologies. Examples of how firms overcome lock-in have become common, including cellular phone companies (Pacific Bell) that have offered free or reduced-price phones for new customers, software companies (Microsoft) that have lowered the prices for users of competing applications, banks (Citibank) that have offered credits for customers' initial Internet transactions, and Internet retail sites (MotherNature.com) that have provided advertised discounts on customers' initial purchases.
In 1998, the Justice Department accused Microsoft of engaging in "predatory pricing" tactics with the intent of crushing Netscape, a potential rival for the computer platform market, by giving away Internet Explorer, and by integrating Internet Explorer into Windows at no additional cost.In addition, Microsoft was accused of, at times, charging below-zero prices by offering Internet service providers an upfront fee (what the Justice Department called "bribes") for making Internet Explorer their recommended browser.
Of course, a consumer subsidy to overcome the lock-in effect of an existing product is an investment that sellers expect to generate positive returns through higher prices for their products once consumers get "locked in" again.Obviously such investments are risky, as the new products may not be sufficiently superior to replace existing products, or may have a short reign in the marketplace even if they do. We can think of the high prices temporarily realized from establishing a large and "locked-in" market share as an incentive for technological improvements and as a means by which consumers reimburse suppliers for helping them overcome the prisoners' dilemma. Put another way, without the potential for some degree of "lock-in," network firms might not have sufficient incentive to lower their initial prices for the purpose of creating the network and providing users with the attendant network benefits as the network expands. This suggests caution in attempts to use antitrust remediesto prevent firms from exploiting "locked-in" consumers. Even if a firm is able to exploit network effects and switching costs by locking in consumers indefinitely, breaking up the firm under the banner of increased competition will actually do less to protect consumers than standard models would indicate, and may even harm consumers.
In the next section we develop a model of a firm selling a product that generates network effects, but not network externalities. That is to say, the demand for its product in each period increases as the number of units currently in use increases. Under the assumption that the firm is able to expand until it dominates the market and is able to fully exploit all network effects, we extend the analyses of othersand examine the effect of threatening to break up the firm into separate competing units (or in other ways that impair the ability of the firm to exploit locked-in consumers). If credible, we find that the breakup threat is certain to produce a price reduction that is less than the standard monopoly model would predict, and may even result in a current price increase. Any resulting increase in efficiency is less than the standard model would predict, even when ignoring the very real possibility that the antitrust action reduces network benefits to consumers and retards the introduction of new technologies.

questions.question: Whether threatening or carrying out remedies that break up (or otherwise impair) a firm that benefits from network effects and customer lock-in leads to lower prices and greater efficiency for consumers.
questions.answer: No; the paper finds that credible breakup threats or remedies against network firms produce smaller-than-expected price reductions and efficiency gains and can even raise current prices, so they do not reliably lower prices or increase efficiency for consumers.

questions.question: Whether allowing a firm to exploit "locked-in" customers (for example, by initially subsidizing adoption and later charging higher prices) is necessary to create networks and innovations and thus ultimately benefits consumers.
questions.answer: Yes; the paper argues that the ability to later charge higher prices to locked-in customers provides essential incentives for firms to subsidize initial adoption, build networks, and spur technological improvements, thereby benefiting consumers.

questions.question: What the net effect on consumer welfare is of antitrust interventions that reduce a firm's ability to exploit network effects, given the tradeoff between immediate competitive gains and the loss of network-related benefits and incentives for entry/innovation.
questions.answer: Such interventions yield less consumer protection and efficiency than standard models predict and may even harm consumers by reducing network benefits and retarding the introduction of new technologies.

matched_themes: How do antitrust interventions affect consumer welfare in markets with network effects, weighing short-term competitive gains against the loss of network benefits and innovation incentives?
Why do costly, nonfunctional product (or contractual) features persist in competitive markets, and do these persistence mechanisms extend beyond contracts to other product attributes?
Under what conditions do pro-competitive regulatory reforms (deregulation, liberalization) produce real competition, and when are explicit competition laws and advocacy also necessary?
Why do some inefficient or nonfunctional contract features persist in markets despite competition - is path dependence, network effects, or branding responsible?
Do pro-competitive regulatory reforms and stronger competition policy increase private investment, productivity, and growth-particularly when firms benefit from network effects?
Is allowing firms to exploit initially locked-in customers (subsidize adoption, later raise prices) necessary to create network effects and innovations that ultimately benefit consumers?

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: LAW AND ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT IN LATIN AMERICA: A COMPARATIVE APPROACH TO LEGAL REFORM: INTRODUCTION TO LAW AND ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT IN LATIN AMERICA: A COMPARATIVE APPROACH TO LEGAL REFORM

shared_topics.topic: trade-offs of structural antitrust remedies (e.g., breakups) versus preserving scale- or network-generated consumer benefits
shared_topics.justification: Paper A models how breaking up or handicapping a firm that exploits network-driven lock-in can reduce the very demand-side economies of scale that benefit consumers and may yield less price reduction than standard monopoly theory predicts; Paper B repeatedly debates whether strong, 'hard law' competition interventions are desirable in developing economies—highlighting carve-outs, sectoral tolerance of dominance, and the potential costs of imposing binding remedies on concentrated markets.

shared_topics.topic: barriers to entry, switching costs, and market concentration as sources of persistent dominance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes applications barriers to entry, consumer switching costs, and how network effects can entrench a firm's position (the Microsoft/applications example); Paper B documents high barriers to entry, legacy state-owned firms and concentrated corporate groups in Latin America and treats market concentration as a central obstacle to effective competition and development.

shared_topics.topic: the adequacy and measurement problems of orthodox antitrust models and metrics for assessing dominance and harm
shared_topics.justification: Paper A challenges standard monopoly prescriptions in the presence of network effects and argues conventional antitrust remedies can misjudge consumer welfare; Paper B (notably De Leon's contribution) critiques traditional antitrust assumptions (perfect competition, market definitions, concentration metrics) and emphasizes that orthodox tools may mismeasure effects and lead to flawed policy.

shared_topics.topic: how competition policy interacts with innovation and entrepreneurial incentives (including use of subsidies or aggressive pricing to build networks)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses how entrepreneurs (network sponsors) may subsidize initial consumers or set low/negative prices to overcome coordination problems and create a superior network — an action that can both promote innovation and later allow recoupment; Paper B addresses how competition law and industrial policy should be designed to foster entrepreneurship, market entry, and productive investment, weighing the need to remove barriers while preserving incentives for innovation.

shared_topics.topic: network effects/externalities as drivers of standardization and market tipping

shared_topics.topic: roles of third parties or sponsors in spreading or overcoming established standards
shared_topics.justification: Both papers study intermediary actors who can internalize externalities and influence diffusion — Paper A analyzes underwriters and law firms as vectors for contract term diffusion and internalizing network effects, while Paper B analyzes entrepreneurs and firms using subsidies or pricing strategies to overcome incumbents' lock‑in.

shared_topics.topic: welfare and policy implications of decentralized adoption versus collective or regulatory intervention

shared_topics.topic: trade-off between individual rights and collective benefits when stakeholders share legally entangled interests
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how bondholders' rights are allocated between individual enforcement and collective decisionmaking (via trustees and majority consents) and the welfare and enforcement consequences of that allocation; Paper B examines the tension between protecting individual consumers from exploitation by a dominant firm and preserving collective network benefits that arise when many users adopt the same technology, arguing antitrust remedies can upset that trade-off.

shared_topics.topic: coordination failures and collective-action problems among dispersed parties that impede efficient outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents how dispersed bondholders face barriers to suing or coordinating (reliance on trustees, high voting thresholds), producing enforcement gaps and inefficiencies; Paper B models consumer-level prisoners' dilemmas and switching costs that prevent adoption of superior technologies absent coordinated subsidies or a sponsoring firm, showing how lock-in arises from coordination failure.

shared_topics.topic: limits of market mechanisms and the potential need for legal or contractual intervention
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques how market forces and existing indenture terms fail to correct structural defects in bondholder enforcement and proposes contractual and judicial reforms; Paper B questions whether antitrust remedies (like breakups) will actually improve welfare given network benefits and argues for caution in legal intervention because market-based strategies (subsidies, pricing) can overcome lock-in.

shared_topics.topic: misaligned incentives of representatives or dominant actors who stand between principals and enforcement/welfare
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights the indenture trustee's weak incentives to enforce bondholder rights and how that misalignment harms creditors; Paper B analyzes how a dominant firm that internalizes network benefits may both enable coordination (by subsidizing adoption) and later exploit locked-in consumers, raising concerns about the representative role and incentives of market-makers.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Boilerplate Shock: Sovereign Debt Contracts as Incubators of Systemic Risk

shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how standardization around a single technology produces demand-side network effects that create consumer benefits but also risks of lock-in; Paper B treats standard-form contractual boilerplate as a form of market standardization that generates positive liquidity externalities while also producing systemic (negative) externalities and common-mode failure risk.

shared_topics.topic: legal or contractual features as mechanisms of market lock‑in and entrenchment
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on product incompatibilities, applications barriers, and switching costs (and how antitrust or breakup threats interact with these legal-economic facts) as sources of durable market dominance; Paper B shows how specific contractual clauses (currency and governing-law boilerplate) can legally lock issuers and creditors into outcomes that amplify crises and entrench exposures.

shared_topics.topic: trade‑offs and unintended consequences of legal intervention or rule changes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates how antitrust remedies (e.g., breakup threats) may reduce monopoly exploitation but also diminish network benefits and innovation incentives, possibly harming consumers; Paper B assesses how judicial interpretations and proposed interpretive rules could either mitigate or magnify systemic turmoil, stressing that well‑intentioned legal changes can have perverse market-wide effects.

shared_topics.topic: collective‑action/coordination problems and mechanisms for internalizing externalities
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames consumer switching as a prisoners' dilemma resolvable by an entrepreneur who internalizes network gains via subsidies or pricing strategies, while Paper B diagnoses a coordination failure produced by boilerplate and proposes contract‑design and bargaining rules to better internalize the risks of redenomination and systemic contagion.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: PUERTO RICO'S ODIOUS DEBT: THE ECONOMIC CRISIS OF COLONIALISM

shared_topics.topic: when and how courts or regulators should use legal remedies to undo economic dominance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A models whether antitrust interventions (e.g., breakup or constraints on firm behavior) actually improve consumer welfare in markets with network effects and lock‑in, while Paper B analyzes whether legal remedies (bankruptcy, debt repudiation or equitable defenses) are appropriate responses to creditor dominance over a polity and the potential consequences of such interventions.

shared_topics.topic: private actors leveraging market structure to extract rents from captive populations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines firms exploiting network effects and switching costs to ‘lock in’ consumers and extract supracompetitive returns, and Paper B documents hedge funds and creditors using bond markets and Puerto Rico’s constrained political status to extract high returns at the expense of residents.

shared_topics.topic: tradeoffs between economic efficiency (incentives for innovation or credit) and distributive justice/protection of vulnerable stakeholders
shared_topics.justification: Paper A weighs how potential future monopoly rents may be the price of upfront subsidies and innovation versus present consumer harm from lock‑in and argues remedies may reduce network benefits, while Paper B contrasts creditors’ enforcement of debt claims with the distributive harms to Puerto Rican citizens and asks whether equity justifies debt relief.

shared_topics.topic: the use of economic theory to critique or inform legal doctrines addressing systemic market problems
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops an economic model of network effects to assess antitrust doctrine and the welfare impact of breakups, and Paper B applies doctrinal concepts (odious debt, bankruptcy, equitable defenses) together with political‑economic context to evaluate the legitimacy of debt obligations and policy responses.

shared_topics.topic: collective‑action problems and institutional solutions to holdouts and coordination failures

shared_topics.justification: Paper A cautions that antitrust remedies (like breakups) intended to undo lock‑in can reduce welfare or deter network benefits, and Paper B questions whether the CAC campaign and public promotion of boilerplate actually addressed underlying restructuring problems or instead produced symbolic, reputation, or governance effects with ambiguous welfare consequences.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: TAX LAWYERS AS TAX INSURANCE

shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how firms use subsidies, below-cost pricing, or free products (e.g., free handsets, free browsers) to overcome switching costs and coordination problems and build a locked-in network; Paper B treats tax opinions as a form of partial indemnity that shifts risk from clients to lawyers, functioning like an insurance subsidy that alters parties' willingness to take tax positions.

shared_topics.topic: how legal or regulatory intervention alters private incentives to provide those mechanisms

shared_topics.topic: credibility and incompleteness of contingent commitments (conditional promises/insurance)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines the effects of credible versus non‑credible breakup threats and the fact that firms' consumer subsidies are risky investments (they may or may not secure long‑term lock‑in); Paper B emphasizes that tax opinions create conditional, partial indemnities—carefully drafted and not full guarantees—so the commitment is incomplete and affects allocation of residual risk.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of risk and its impact on market behavior and innovation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that the prospect of future rents from locking in customers motivates firms to invest in networks and lower initial prices, with consequences for entry, innovation, and consumer welfare; Paper B shows that indemnification via tax opinions reallocates tax litigation and penalty risk between clients, lawyers, and sometimes the government, which in turn influences advisers' conservatism, clients' risk‑taking, and the structure of the market for tax services.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A deliberately limits its analysis to tactical techniques for renegotiating bank-held sovereign debt and distinguishes these from sweeping strategic reforms, while Paper B contrasts temporary firm strategies (subsidies/pricing to overcome lock-in) and short-term remedies (threatened breakups) with their longer-run effects on market structure and innovation.

shared_topics.topic: how third parties and downstream markets alter sellers' design and pricing incentives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that secondary purchasers (buyers of contractual interests) influence the original seller's choice of contract terms, and Paper B shows how 'network sponsors', complementary adopters, and downstream user bases lead firms to subsidize or price strategically to build a dominant installed base.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies how M&A 'boilerplate' intended to standardize contracting instead 'speciates' into divergent lineages, and Paper B analyzes how markets may converge on a single product standard (or not) under network effects; each paper interrogates why and how uniformity or heterogeneity of a standard emerges and the consequences thereof.

shared_topics.topic: policy implications and recommended interventions informed by analysis of real‑world practices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A derives implications for improving drafting practice and standardization from its empirical findings about drafting drift, while Paper B draws policy conclusions about the risks and limited benefits of breakup/remedies for firms exploiting lock‑in; both translate analytic results into critiques of existing responses and propose more cautious or targeted reforms.

shared_topics.topic: tradeoffs between legal/policy intervention and private market solutions

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: INDUSTRIAL AND COMPETITION POLICIES IN MEXICO

shared_topics.topic: designing regulatory remedies to control de facto market power arising from industry structure

papers.node_id: 55urichlrev565!!SYMPOSIUM FEATURE: MERGERS, MACS, AND COVID-19
papers.title: SYMPOSIUM FEATURE: MERGERS, MACS, AND COVID-19
papers.abstract:
On May 20, 2020, Forescout Technologies filed a lawsuit seeking a declaratory judgment against Advent International.Forescout and Advent had signed a merger agreement in early February, some three months before.By May, it was becoming apparent toForescout that Advent was suffering buyer's remorse: a deal that looked good prior to the onset of a global pandemic looked less wonderful after the U.S. economy ground to a halt in an effort to battle the spread of COVID-19. Forescout's lawsuit sought a declaratory judgment from the court that COVID-19 did not represent a material adverse event and an order that Advent proceed to closing of the transaction.Ultimately, Forescout and Advent settled the litigation through a renegotiation downwards of the merger price and the transaction moved forward to closing.The Forescout litigation was one of a small number of cases that followed the onset of COVID-19 in the spring of 2020 in which buyers sought to walk away from merger agreements citing a material adverse effect.While the Forescout story is consistent at first glance with the conventional wisdom that parties use material adverse effect/material adverse change ("MAE/MAC") clauses in merger agreements to facilitate renegotiation, the paucity of such efforts following the COVID-19 outbreak should cause us to re-evaluate that conventional wisdom.This Article argues that the ambiguity that often serves the corporation law well has, by now, dissipated with respect to MAE/MAC clauses, and there has been a fundamental change in the role of the MAE/MAC since 2001. The lack of ambiguity surrounding modern MAE/MAC clauses has, as a result, fundamentally changed the role MAE/MAC clauses play in merger agreements. Rather than act as a quasi-force majeure clause, with the seller bearing the burden of adverse shock, modern MAE/MAC clauses allocate exogenous risks to the buyer and endogenous risks to the seller consistent with the role described by Professors Gilson and Schwartz.Consequently, conventional wisdom that describesMAE/MAC clauses as contractual devices that potentially facilitate efficient renegotiations in the face of adverse shocks is overstated.
The sudden onset of COVID-19 in spring 2020 was, and remains, a tsunami-like event. It was totally unexpected and swept across the economy with frightening speed. It also threatens to extend well into the foreseeable future. COVID-19 is precisely the kind of adverse event that the MAE/MAC clause in merger agreements is intended to protect signatories against. The COVID-19 outbreak gives us a unique opportunity to evaluate the role the MAE/MAC clause plays in merger contracting. Most transactions pending at the outset of the COVID-19 outbreak in the U.S. closed notwithstanding the massive disruption brought on by the pandemic. In a small number of transactions, buyers refused to close, citing a MAE/MAC as the reason not to move forward with the merger. In three of those transactions, the parties sought to litigate the question of a MAE/MAC (i.e., Simon v. Taubman,LVMH v. Tiffany,and Forescout Technologies), but ultimately settled their litigation by renegotiating the terms of their merger agreement. In Mirae's acquisition of Anbang's hotel assets, a court refused to declare a MAE/MAC, but permitted the buyer to walk away for breach of a seller's covenant.In another transaction, the parties agreed to terminate the transaction voluntarily (i.e., Victoria's Secret) rather than renegotiate or litigate the issue of whether there had been a MAE/MAC.
The MAE/MAC provision is one of a number of risk-shifting clauses in the merger contract. In most cases, the MAE/MAC does this by assigning the risk of exogenous material adverse events between signing and closing to the buyer and the risk of endogenous material adverse events to the seller.Because the MAE/MAC assigns the risk to the party best able to bear it, one can reasonably conclude that the MAE/MAC is an efficient term. Where there has been a MAE/MAC, the buyer is permitted to terminate the transaction and walk away, or the parties can renegotiate the terms of the agreement in order to facilitate an efficient transaction. Where there has been an adverse event that does not rise to a MAE, the buyer bears the risk of loss. However, because the MAE/MAC provision can act as a fulcrum for potential efficient renegotiations, the conventional wisdom is that the MAE/MAC provision has a subsidiary function as a renegotiation clause in the face of any adverse shock.
By now, it is clear, however, that courts are extremely reticent to permit a buyer to simply point to an adverse event between signing and closing and walk away from a transaction. Notwithstanding courts' reluctance, the conventional wisdom remains that following an adverse event, a buyer may lean on these clauses, and the threat of litigation, to push sellers to renegotiate the terms of merger agreements. This conventional wisdom overestimates the degree of judicial ambiguity surrounding modern MAE/MAC provisions. Where the parties overestimate judicial ambiguity, buyers may be able to take advantage of bargaining dynamics to hold up the seller and shift the cost of adverse shocks, at least in part, to sellers rather than bear them themselves. Renegotiating in the absence of a true MAE/MAC represents an inefficient ex post distribution of transaction surplus.
This Article seeks to illustrate the role MAE/MACs play in the merger agreement and understand how they may affect bargaining dynamics that accompany renegotiations of merger agreements. In particular, this Article adds to the literature on merger contracting by observing that the conventional wisdom with respect to the role played by MAE/MACs misapprehends the role of a modern MAE/MAC provision.
This Article proceeds in the following manner. Part I situates the discussion of the MAE/MAC as a lever for renegotiation by providing an overview of the conventional wisdom with respect to the role of MAE/MAC clauses following the occurrence of an adverse shock. Part II provides an overview of the MAE/MAC clause in merger agreements, including an analysis of the work MAE/MAC clauses are intended to accomplish in the contracting process. Part III provides an overview of the current state of the doctrine with respect to MAE/MAC clauses in Delaware. Part IV discusses the experience of merger parties with renegotiations in the wake of the COVID-19 outbreak. Specifically, this Part asks why there were so few renegotiations following the outbreak and how the conventional wisdom with respect to the role of MAE/MAC in renegotiations misapprehends its role. Finally, Part V summarizes and concludes.

questions.question: Do contractual material-adverse-change/adverse-event clauses in merger agreements function primarily as risk-allocation devices between buyer and seller (assigning exogenous risks to buyers and endogenous risks to sellers) rather than as contractual levers to facilitate renegotiation after adverse shocks?
questions.answer: Yes—modern MAE/MAC clauses primarily allocate risk (exogenous shocks to buyers and endogenous shocks to sellers), and the idea that they chiefly serve as levers for efficient renegotiation is overstated.

questions.question: How do sudden, large, unforeseen systemic shocks (e.g., a pandemic) affect the incidence and outcomes of renegotiation, termination, or enforcement efforts tied to these adverse-change clauses in pending transactions?
questions.answer: During the COVID-19 shock, most pending deals still closed; only a small number of buyers invoked MAE/MAC to avoid closing, litigations were settled via price renegotiations, courts declined to declare a MAE/MAC (one walkaway occurred for covenant breach), and one deal was voluntarily terminated.

questions.question: Has greater judicial clarity about the scope and meaning of adverse-change clauses reduced buyers' ability to use those clauses opportunistically to extract renegotiation concessions from sellers?
questions.answer: Yes—diminished judicial ambiguity and courts’ reticence to let buyers walk have limited buyers’ ability to use MAE/MAC clauses opportunistically to extract renegotiation concessions, rendering the conventional leverage view overstated.

papers.node_id: 71chikentlrev1053!!SYMPOSIUM ON DERIVATIVE FINANCIAL PRODUCTS: RESPONSIBILITY FOR CUSTOMER LOSSES DUE TO FAILURE OF CORRESPONDENT BROKERS AND OTHER DEPOSITORY INSTITUTIONS
papers.title: SYMPOSIUM ON DERIVATIVE FINANCIAL PRODUCTS: RESPONSIBILITY FOR CUSTOMER LOSSES DUE TO FAILURE OF CORRESPONDENT BROKERS AND OTHER DEPOSITORY INSTITUTIONS
papers.abstract:
The default of Barings plc in February 1995focused world attention on the dangers to futures exchangesand brokerage firms posed by nonmarket, or systemic, risk. In particular, the Barings crisis underscored the difficulty in confining such risk to a single exchange, especially in an environment characterized by growing interrelationships between and among futures exchanges worldwide. Nevertheless, the Barings crisis revealed a strong willingness on the part of both regulatory and self-regulatory authorities to work together to coordinate the liquidation and transfer of positions and margin collateral from Barings to other brokers with minimal market disruption.Dire predictions of a chain reaction of defaults spreading to other markets and triggering a global financial meltdown did not materialize.Instead, confidence in futures exchanges substantially remained intact and market activity continued without significant interruption.8131*1054
The success of futures exchanges and their regulators in managing systemic risk, and in averting lasting adverse consequences following the Barings default must, however, be qualified by the key role played by Internationale Nederlanden Groep N.V. ("ING"). Immediately following the collapse, a United Kingdom bankruptcy court ordered a freeze on Barings' assets worldwide, including those used to collateralize positions on futures exchanges, thereby depriving the exchanges of a major source of liquidity provided by an important market participant. ING's agreement to purchase major portions of Barings' assets and liabilities enabled the United Kingdom bankruptcy court to rescind its order, thus forestalling more serious consequences.The intervention of ING, however, effectively precluded the resolution of an important issue raised by the crisis: the question of a broker's responsibility to its customers for the loss of customer funds following the default of another ("correspondent") broker, an exchange clearing organization, or a bank (hereinafter referred to collectively as "depository institutions"). No clear consensus with respect to the resolution of this issue exists and, absent such consensus, there remains a level of uncertainty in a future default situation.
Existing regulatory systems rely on depository institutions to hold funds and other property used to collateralize positions. The potential delay in transferring positions and property used to margin such positions following the failure of depository institutions may impair the short-term liquidity of both brokers and exchanges. To restore liquidity, positions must be remargined; however, issues regarding the source of the additional funds necessary to remargin such positions are complex and subject to distinctly divergent interpretations.
* * * * * This Article will examine the alternative legal theories and arguments likely to be advanced in any dispute involving issues of a broker's responsibility for customer margin property following the default of a depository institution holding such property. To fully appreciate the context of this debate, Part I will summarize the chain of 8131*1055 transactions created in the course of effecting futures and options transactions on both domestic and foreign exchanges. Part I also will summarize the regulations imposed by United States and United Kingdom regulatory authorities applicable at each link in the chain. Despite extensive regulation, customer property is not immune from invasion and Part II will examine these dangers and discuss regulatory efforts aimed at mitigating them.
Included among the threats to customer property described in Part II is the potential default of the customer's broker. The rules applicable in the United States to commodity broker defaults provide that customer property includes the assets of the broker to the extent that the amount of funds segregated on customers' behalf is insufficient to meet all customer losses. At least one factual circumstance may arise, however, that complicates the application of the default rules. To limit the scope of their duties, implied or otherwise, many brokers have inserted clauses into their customer agreements exculpating the broker from liability for losses caused by events beyond the broker's control, such as the default of a depository institution. The general enforceability of such clauses in a default context has never been tested.
Additionally, where a broker possesses sufficient capital reserves to meet its minimum financial requirements and remains in operation following the default of a depository institution, the default rules do not apply and the solvent broker may be able to argue that it bears no liability to its customers to make up any shortfall in such customers' segregated accounts, particularly if it has a valid exculpatory clause in its customer agreement. Customers arguing in favor of imposing liability on the broker may rely on several sources, including the common law treatment of the relationship between brokers and their customers, the legislative history of the segregation provisions of the Commodity Exchange Act (the "Act")and subsequent judicial and administrative pronouncements. Part III will examine each of these sources as well as evaluate the general enforceability of exculpatory clauses and the effect an enforceable exculpatory clause may have on a broker's obligations to its customers.8131*1056
. Customer Margin and Segregation: The "Chain" of Transactions in the United States and the United Kingdom
Before analyzing the arguments surrounding a broker's liability for a customer's margin property following the default of a depository institution, it is necessary first to have an understanding of the complex chain of relationships created in effecting futures transactions both on domestic and foreign futures exchanges. Prior to the Barings collapse, many brokerage firms and banks engaging in the brokerage business marketed their ability to provide "seamless access" to the world's futures exchanges. A single phone call to a domestic account executive was all that was necessary to trade on any foreign or domestic futures exchange, with the attendant margin transaction handled domestically in the home currency and confirmed on the customer's combined statement. While emphasizing the relationship between the customer and the initiating broker with its worldwide reach, the concept of seamless access blurred the existence of an underlying chain of relationships among correspondent brokers, clearing organizations and bank depositories. The Barings collapse focused attention on this network of relationships and compelled a new appreciation of the presence of systemic risk at each link in the chain. In addition, the collapse highlighted major differences among exchanges in the manner of calculating margin, in segregation requirements, and in the level of regulatory oversight,while underscoring the potential problems created by conflicting bankruptcy regimes in different jurisdictions.This Section will describe the movement of customer funds from the customer through various depository institutions to margin futures transactions on both domestic and nondomestic exchanges. The applicable regulations at each stage also will be summarized to provide an understanding of the safeguards imposed by the regulatory system in both the United States and the United Kingdom.

questions.question: Whether a customer's broker is legally obligated to make up shortfalls in customer margin accounts that result from the failure of a correspondent broker, clearing organization, or depository institution holding those customer funds.
questions.answer: There is no clear consensus on whether a customer's broker must make up margin shortfalls caused by the failure of a correspondent broker, clearing organization, or depository institution: while U.S. commodity broker default rules can sweep broker assets into customer property, a solvent broker may argue it has no such liability, particularly if it has an exculpatory clause.

questions.question: Whether and to what extent contractual exculpatory clauses in customer-broker agreements can relieve brokers of liability for customer losses caused by the failure of depository institutions.
questions.answer: Brokers often include exculpatory clauses to disclaim losses from depository institution failures, but their general enforceability in this context has never been tested and remains uncertain.

questions.question: How the chain of correspondent relationships, cross-border custody arrangements, and differing regulatory regimes affect the allocation of losses and the remargining process when depository institutions default.
questions.answer: The cross-border chain of correspondent relationships and differing regulatory regimes introduces systemic risk and can delay transfers, impairing liquidity and requiring remargining, with responsibility for supplying additional funds and allocating resulting shortfalls remaining complex and subject to divergent interpretations due to varying margin, segregation, oversight, and bankruptcy rules.

papers.node_id: 88washlrev1323!!SYMPOSIUM: CONTRACTS IN THE REAL WORLD: ESSAY: CONTRACT AS PATTERN LANGUAGE
papers.title: SYMPOSIUM: CONTRACTS IN THE REAL WORLD: ESSAY: CONTRACT AS PATTERN LANGUAGE
papers.abstract:
Scholars and practitioners routinely talk about the "architecture" of individual contracts.Many observers have also noted the broad-brush similarity between the drafting of legal contracts and computer programming or coding.It is strange, then, that contract law scholarship has overlooked part of the landmark literature linking design in architecture and computer code.In 1977, Christopher Alexander, a professor of architecture at the University of California, Berkeley, drewupon his background in computer science to co-author A Pattern Language.This practical book - together with Alexander's more theoretical companion volume, The Timeless Way of Building,and his other work- provided an influential blueprint for architects, urban planners, and the reading public who sought a more organic, humanistic, and democratic way of designing buildings and cities amidst the failures of modern urban renewal and widespread dissatisfaction with the course of architectural modernism.This article examines how Alexander's pattern language framework explains how attorneys draft contracts,including in response to the types of legal design problems illustrated in Larry Cunningham's book, Contracts in the Real World.Moreover, the pattern language rubric explains how individual legal agreements interlock to create complex transactions, and how transactions interconnect to create markets.Furthermore, this pattern language framework helps account for recent evidence, including from the global financial crisis, of failures in modern contract design, even in cases where sophisticated financial firms and their lawyers were the architects.
Alexander and his collaborators described a series of "patterns" or design solutions for buildings that meet specific environmental needs of individuals. A pattern represents an encapsulated abstract or conceptual solution to a recurring design problem. Patterns thus free architects and designers from having to reinvent the wheel; they can use the solutions that evolved over time as designers in the past grappled with, and crafted answers to, similar problems.In Alexander's work, a pattern describes a particular solution that can be used to plan growth in a particular region, city, or neighborhood, to design homes or other buildings, or to create rooms or spaces within a building. Interlocking individual patterns create larger design patterns, which, in turn, connect to form still larger patterns.Thus, patterns for rooms and structural elements combine to create design patterns for buildings. Arranged together, patterns for buildings form patterns for neighborhoods. Patterns for neighborhoods join to create patterns for cities and regions. Through scaling and rules that define when patterns fit together, Alexander's system created a larger "language" for architectural design.Alexander's architectural ideas inspired computer programmers who borrowed his idea of patterns that solved particular environmental problems and that connected into alarger language to meet their own design needs.The concepts in A Pattern Language shaped a generation of new computer languages and approaches to coding, particularly object-oriented programming.
Alexander's work also provides a unique lens to look at how transactional attorneys draft contracts. However, the pattern language framework does much more than explain the function of contractual boilerplate or the process of assembling particular contracts. It also describes how individual contract patterns form complex transactional patterns, and how, in turn, complex transactional patterns form complex financial markets. For example, transactional attorneys arrange individual patterns for provisions in legal agreements - e.g., the basic provision establishing the loan of money in exchange for interest and principal repayments, representations and warranties, covenants, provisions defining default, and remedies - to form legal agreements, such as mortgages or bond indentures. Patterns for separate contracts connect to create transactions. For example, a mortgage, note, deed of sale, and other agreements operationalize the purchase of real estate. Patterns for simple transactions fit together to create more complex transactions and even markets. For instance, mortgage documents, pooling and servicing agreements, trust documents, and indentures create mortgage-backed securities.Patterns of complex transactions and markets, in turn, create more complex financial systems. To extend the examples above, mortgage-backed securities form part of a web of connected financial instruments and markets, called the "shadow banking system," that connect consumer and commercial borrowers to investors in capital markets.
By contract "patterns," I mean an encapsulated solution within a legal agreement (or set of agreements) to a specific legal problem. Thisproblem might consist of a need to match the particular objectives of both counterparties in a discrete part of a bargain. The solution might also address a certain feature of the legal environment, such as one of the contract doctrines examined so colorfully in Cunningham's book. Lawyers can repeat and adapt a contract pattern each time a version of that problem, whether miniaturized or supersized, appears. Each contract pattern interlocks, nests, and works together with other contract patterns to solve more complex problems and create more intricate and elaborate bargains.
Moreover, interlocking patterns enables scalability. That is, arrangements of individual patterns form larger patterns, which combine with other patterns to form still larger patterns. Just as Alexander's patterns for rooms create patterns for buildings, which create patterns for neighborhoods and then cities, so then patterns of individual contract provisions form legal agreement patterns, which interlock to create patterns for transactions, which, in turn, mesh to create patterns for markets. Larger patterns solve larger problems and can meet more complex demands of a greater range of counterparties. This scalability differentiates contract design from contract boilerplate. It also highlights how contract patterns are different than other examples of preformulated language in the law, such as writs or pleadings in procedural law.
This essay examines how patterns enable the transformation of contractual provisions into contracts, contracts into transactions, and transactions into markets. Although contract design patterns are broader than contract boilerplate (as described in Part II.C. below), some of the extensive legal scholarship on boilerplatehelps explain how contract patterns generate agreements, transactions, and markets. The work of Henry Smith on the modularity of contract boilerplate proves particularly useful in this regard.Contract patterns perform several functions. Contract patterns break complex problems and bargains into components.Attorneys can then repeatedly apply these particularsolutions to similar problems. Patterns also serve as heuristics for attorneys, i.e., devices to estimate quickly whether particular language solves certain bargaining problems, meets client objectives, and will be interpreted by courts in an anticipated manner.
Contract patterns, like Smith's modules, allow teams of lawyers to work on different aspects of a contract or transaction simultaneously. Multiple persons can work on the same agreement, Smith explains, because contract modularity restricts the information transfer of certain "boilerplate" provisions. This means that if one lawyer modifies one module of a contract, other modules can remain relatively unaffected.
Patterns also enable scalability or the transformation of contracts into transactions and transactions into markets.Smith's work on modularity and restricting information transfer comes into play here too. To boil part of his theory down: standardized contract language means that third parties need to incur less cost in valuing either certain contracts or parties to those contracts.We can expand Smith's logic to explain how contract patterns enable standardized contracts to be traded on organized financial markets. In extreme examples, contract patterns allow certain debt contracts to become what economist Gary Gorton calls "informationally insensitive" debt.Certain financial instruments become informationally insensitive when they are (at least in theory) immune to adverse selection by traders with inside information. Investors can value informationally insensitive contracts at low cost. The ease of valuation, in turn, makes these tradeable contracts both highly liquid and endows them with many of the economic features of money.
The pattern language framework explains not only how sophisticated contracts function, but also how they fail. The pattern language framework provides a lens through which we can examine recent contracts law scholarship on the failures of sophisticated contract design, including "sticky" contract provisions in sovereign bond agreements,"Frankenstein" contracts in mortgage-backed securitizations,and the "flash crash" and other episodes of massive losses generated by automated, algorithmic trading on financial exchanges.Just as modularity and contract design patterns foster the development of new financial instruments and markets, so too can their features contribute to the unraveling of these markets. For example, by restricting the information content of contracts, patterns and modularity not only midwifed the creation of liquid markets for those contracts, they also played a role in the catastrophic freezing of these markets. This essay points to the "shadow bank runs" triggered when modularized and standardized asset-backed securities became almost impossible to value during the financial crisis.So failures of contract design can have broader social consequences far beyond the private relationship of the two parties to a bargain. More broadly, the failure of contracts can have systemic effects for entire markets when a particular contract enjoys widespread use or when it is so connected to other critical contracts that cascading failures occur.
Common threads run through these separate contract failures. Thesefailures proliferated as contracting became increasingly rigidified,routinized, modularized,interconnected,and even automated.These same dynamics mean that Alexander's ideas in architecture have more purchase for contract design, given that he wrestled with analogous changes in contemporary architecture.
At first blush, Alexander's description of architectural patterns may appear to have little application to contracts. Indeed, contracts are not buildings, not least because contracts represent social rather than physical constructs (and for all the other reasons explained in Part II.G. below). However, Alexander's pattern language framework also illuminates how modern contract design has failed spectacularly. Alexander's pattern language framework recasts the problems created when interconnected contracts no longer work together, when inflexible contracts do not or cannot adapt to legal or economic shocks, and when automated contracts remove human judgment and generate both agreements and errors at light speed.In addition, Alexander's rubric has much to say for the consumer end of the contracting spectrum. His program speaks to problems of consent, equity, and error as contracts ofadhesion migrate onlineand to a mobile device world.It also provides a framework for thinking about improving contract design as companies, such as LegalZoom, enable consumers to bypass transactional lawyers and draft and botch their own complex agreements.
This essay also briefly considers how Alexander's normative program serves as a starting point for a longer discussion of ways to improve contract design. Alexander's collective work served not merely as an instruction manual - it also represented, in roughly equal measure, hymnal and manifesto.For Alexander and his collaborators, better design of the built environment served not merely to increase its functionality or aesthetics. A Pattern Language and Alexander's other work also aimed to make the design process more democratic, by providing lay people with a clear vocabulary, grammar, and syntax to create their own architectural plans.Alexander also sought to make individual buildings, neighborhoods, cities, and regions more harmonious with one another and with the natural environment.At the same time, his work underscored the need for a pattern language of design to be adaptive to changing social needs and environmental conditions.Finally, A Pattern Language and Alexander's other writings present a thoroughly humanistic vision of architecture, in which design meets basic needs of individuals and families rather than those of abstract, mechanistic institutions or ideologies.
These normative elements and, moreover, the descriptive power of A Pattern Language provide guideposts for how contract design and drafting can move from teaching a legal skill, which is too often relegated to the outskirts of the legal academy, to studying and addressing complex, cascading, and catastrophic failures of contract design in modern markets, if not a more ambitious, normative program. In short, the increasingly automated, routinized, rigid, interconnected, complex, and opaque nature of modern contracts presents practical problems for meeting client needs and averting systemic contract failures. Moving from a descriptive plane, these failures also pose deeper philosophical challenges to values central to contract law, such as individual consent and equity. On a normative plane, rethinking contract design and drafting in terms of a pattern language may make contracts not only more intelligible, but more closely hew to the human needs and values of the individuals ultimately bound.
This short essay follows the following simple plan. Part I provides an overview of Christopher Alexander's writings on architectural design and explains how A Pattern Language created a vocabulary, syntax, and grammar for architects and planners. It also sketches how computer science borrowed pattern language to structure solutions to its own design problems. Part II describes how the design of legal contracts exhibits some of the same logic of a pattern language. It describes how contract patterns work to create contracts, transactions, liquid markets for financial instruments, and entire financial systems. If Part II describes how contract patterns function, then Part III examines how they break down, sometimes catastrophically. This final Part considers how the pattern language framework describes and illuminates recent contract failures and provides some normative guideposts for improving contract design.

questions.question: Whether recurring, modular 'contract patterns' systematically structure how attorneys draft individual agreements and how those agreements interlock and scale up into complex transactions and markets.
questions.answer: Yes; the essay argues that recurring, modular contract “patterns” guide how lawyers draft provisions into agreements, which interlock and scale into complex transactions, markets, and even broader financial systems.

questions.question: Whether the standardization and modularity of contract patterns that enable tradability and liquidity also increase the likelihood of valuation breakdowns and cascading or systemic market failures under stress.
questions.answer: Yes; the abstract contends that the same standardization and modularity that enable low-cost valuation, tradability, and liquidity also restrict information and, under stress, contributed to valuation freezes, shadow bank runs, and cascading systemic market failures.

questions.question: Whether adopting a 'pattern language' approach to contract design can produce practical reforms that make contracts more intelligible, adaptive, and aligned with human needs, thereby reducing drafting errors and systemic risks.
questions.answer: Yes; the paper proposes that adopting Alexander’s pattern-language approach provides normative guideposts for practical reforms that can make contracts more intelligible, adaptive, and human-centered, thereby helping address errors, consent and equity problems, and avert systemic contract failures.

matched_themes: Does the standardization and modularization of contract patterns that facilitate tradability and liquidity also increase the likelihood of valuation breakdowns and systemic market failures under stress?
Who creates contractual innovations, why, and what incentives and constraints shape the supply of such innovations?
Do commonly used standardized contract clauses operate as analogs to default legal rules, and can a systematic 'standard clause' method be used to predict, construct, or interpret such clauses?
Does standardizing the form and language of legal opinions and contract documents reduce negotiation time, transaction costs, and inefficient or overly broad opinion requests?
Does the form-based contract production process cause and sustain drafting imperfections (unnecessary complexity, redundancy, ambiguities) even after repeated use and learning?
Do recurring, modular 'contract patterns' systematically structure how attorneys draft agreements and how those agreements interlock and scale into complex transactions and markets?
Why do contract clauses that appear costly, nonfunctional, or poorly understood persist among sophisticated parties despite competitive pressure?
Is the persistence of imperfect contract forms best explained by path dependence, network effects, and switching costs rather than efficiency?
Why and by what mechanisms are contractual innovations and standardized clauses created, disseminated, and adopted across legal markets?
How do business lawyers add value in complex transactions-do they act primarily as transaction-cost engineers who structure deals, allocate risk, and influence asset pricing?
How do secondary purchasers and secondary markets influence whether contracts become standardized commodities versus remaining customized documents?
Can XML-style structured languages, pattern-language approaches, or document automation meaningfully improve contract drafting, interpretation, and standardization without unduly rigidifying meaning?
How do lawyers create measurable transactional value, and what are the implications for allocation of work among professions and legal education?
How do organizational features of contract production (centralized drafting, mass-customization routines, modular standard forms) affect distribution of power among drafters, users, and non-parties?
Do secondary purchasers and active markets for reselling contractual rights induce sellers to standardize form contracts across industries, and what institutional factors moderate this effect?
Is the degree of contract standardization emerging from atomistic contracting socially optimal, or does decentralized contracting produce too much or too little standardization?

Why are complex commercial contracts frequently long, redundant, and written in dense legalese - is this primarily due to reliance on prior-transaction forms, form-based production processes, editorial churning, branding incentives, or other causes?
What trade-offs arise between reducing contract customization through standardized 'good-enough' provisions and parties' ability to secure precisely tailored outcomes?
Should empirical contract research prioritize testing existing theories or seek new interdisciplinary explanations for real-world contracting puzzles?
Why do costly, nonfunctional product (or contractual) features persist in competitive markets, and do these persistence mechanisms extend beyond contracts to other product attributes?
What speech-act function does entering into a complex business contract serve: creating enforceable promises or setting a framework that enables non-legal governance and cooperation?

What factors explain the persistence or 'stickiness' of particular disclosure and boilerplate practices-do market norms and network effects keep standard language unchanged despite substantive shifts?

Can pattern-language approaches, standardized clause libraries, XML-style structured contract languages, or other 'standard-clause' methods measurably improve contract intelligibility, reduce drafting errors, and serve as effective default rules without unduly rigidifying contracting?
To what extent are complex agreements organized as modular subsystems (enabling mass customization) versus thickly interconnected integrated systems, and how does that shape transaction design?

Does editorial churning, copying, and form-based production of contracts produce 'speciation' and persistent drafting imperfections-redundancy, ambiguity, and nonfunctional features-even after repeated iterations and learning?
Why do persistent, costly, or apparently nonfunctional boilerplate clauses persist in sophisticated contracts?
Why do some inefficient or nonfunctional contract features persist in markets despite competition - is path dependence, network effects, or branding responsible?
What practical reforms-such as a 'pattern language' approach or accountable standard-setting institutions-could make contracts more intelligible, adaptive, and aligned with human needs?
Can a single general theory of contractual innovation account for diverse incentives and dissemination pathways, or is contractual innovation inherently idiosyncratic?

Do legal, institutional, and normative features (statutory backstops, professional practices, standardized forms, repeat-dealing norms) reduce the need for bespoke contract customization and thereby lower transaction costs?

How do transaction designers manage infra-transactional complexity in large contracts - by modular designs or by flexible specialization - and what are the implications for drafting, negotiation, and enforcement?

Do law firms and transactional deal teams organize contract production as modular, standardized subsystems that enable mass customization, or as integrated, flexible-specialization routines, and how do these organizational forms affect drafting quality, diffusion, and persistence of boilerplate?

Do market participants price deal-specific legal terms and collective enforcement features separately from observable financial terms, and under what informational conditions do such prices reflect or obscure these legal differences?
How do standardized forms, firm templates, intermediaries, and market participants drive convergence or heterogeneity in transactional documentation across deals and jurisdictions?
Do market learning and network externalities cause firms to converge on standardized contract terms rather than customize or innovate them?

Can structured interventions-pattern-language design, multi-pass contract-reading protocols, document automation, or AI tools-improve contract intelligibility, drafting quality, and novices' comprehension, and what are their ethical and technical limits?
Is drafting complex contracts as flexible stage-setting (for future accommodation) superior to exhaustive literal specification given limits of knowledge and language?
Do contract drafters typically copy boilerplate blindly across deals or actively tailor and evolve terms, and what organizational routines explain their behavior?
How large and practically significant are downstream effects of standard contract changes-that is, how many contracts and parties are affected and with what consequences?
How do standard-form 'boilerplate' clauses evolve in practice, and do courts' interpretations of such clauses create significant spillover effects across contracts?

shared_topics.topic: allocation of risk between contracting parties through contractual clauses
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how recurring contract 'patterns' (e.g., covenants, default and remedy provisions) function to allocate risks between counterparties across transactions, while Paper B examines how Material Adverse Change (MAC) clauses are negotiated and used specifically to allocate interim deal risk in mergers and acquisitions.

shared_topics.topic: how contractual design and clause selection shape transactional outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that the arrangement and modularity of contract patterns determine whether contracts scale into stable transactions and markets (or fail), and Paper B shows concretely how the presence, wording, and enforcement of MAC clauses determine whether large deals close or are terminated with large economic consequences.

shared_topics.topic: handling unforeseen events and economic shocks through contract language
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages with the problem of contracts being rigid or adaptive to legal and economic shocks and proposes pattern-based design to improve responsiveness, while Paper B focuses on MAC clauses as an explicit contractual mechanism to address deterioration or unforeseen adverse changes between signing and closing.

shared_topics.topic: standardized (boilerplate) versus highly negotiated clause language and its effects
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines the role of standardized, modular contract language in lowering valuation costs, enabling liquidity, and producing both efficiencies and systemic risks, and Paper B contrasts that by highlighting MAC clauses as typically complex, highly-negotiated provisions whose bespoke wording critically affects allocation of risk and likelihood of litigation.

shared_topics.topic: contract interpretation and litigation over clause meaning
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses how contract patterns interact with doctrines and judicial interpretation—contributing to both predictable and catastrophic failures—while Paper B centers on disputes and litigation over whether a given set of facts satisfies a MAC clause, illustrating the interpretive stakes of clause drafting.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 82lawcontempprobi!!ARTICLE: THE BUTTERFLY EFFECT IN BOILERPLATE CONTRACT INTERPRETATION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE BUTTERFLY EFFECT IN BOILERPLATE CONTRACT INTERPRETATION

shared_topics.topic: how interpretation of standardized boilerplate affects non‑parties and other contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops the ‘butterfly effect’ thesis showing that a single judicial interpretation of boilerplate can alter the meaning of identical language across thousands of contracts; Paper B likewise treats recurrent 'contract patterns' (including boilerplate) as replicable units whose meaning and implementation affect many interlocking agreements and thus third parties beyond the bilateral bargain.

shared_topics.topic: the role of modularity/standardization in enabling scalability and market integration
shared_topics.justification: Paper A foregrounds how widely used boilerplate creates standard meanings that propagate across contracts, and Paper B analyzes how modular contract patterns and standardized provisions allow individual agreements to scale into transactions and liquid, tradable markets (e.g., informationally insensitive debt).

shared_topics.topic: systemic risks and cascading failures that arise from interconnected or rigid contract designs
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames concern about far‑reaching consequences of interpreting boilerplate that can ripple through many contracts, while Paper B documents how routinized, modular, and automated contract patterns contributed to market failures (e.g., frozen asset‑backed markets, flash crashes) and explains mechanisms for cascade effects.

shared_topics.topic: the influence of legal doctrine and judicial interpretation on contract design choices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on how courts' interpretive decisions shape the practical meaning of boilerplate going forward, and Paper B emphasizes that lawyers design patterns with an eye to anticipated judicial treatment and legal doctrines, both treating interpretation as a key input into drafting and systemic outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: normative and design responses to problems of boilerplate and patternized contracting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A aims to inform scholars, judges, and legislatures about interpretive challenges posed by boilerplate and possible remedies, while Paper B draws on Alexander's normative pattern‑language program to propose ways to redesign contracts to be more adaptive, intelligible, and aligned with human needs.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 88uchilrev1!!ARTICLE: Stickiness and Incomplete Contracts
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Stickiness and Incomplete Contracts

shared_topics.topic: standardized templates, boilerplate, and modularity in contract drafting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how contract patterns and modular boilerplate enable scalability and the repeated reuse of solutions across agreements and markets; Paper B empirically documents that law-firm templates (sticky boilerplate) determine whether key clauses like forum-selection appear in deals and drive cross-contract uniformity.

shared_topics.topic: how incomplete, rigid, or automated contract design generates costly downstream consequences
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that rigid, modularized, and automated contract patterns can cascade into market failures (e.g., valuation freezes in securitization) and systemic harms; Paper B provides case studies (Sprint/Nextel) and empirical evidence that omitted terms (like forum clauses) produce large transaction costs, litigation complexity, and even acquisitions to resolve disputes.

shared_topics.topic: the central role of lawyers and law firms in shaping contractual form and market outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes how attorneys assemble contract patterns and thereby create transactions and markets (or their failures); Paper B demonstrates empirically that external counsel and law-firm templates overwhelmingly determine whether dispute-resolution clauses are included, affecting the allocation of rights and litigation risk.

shared_topics.topic: limits of the ‘sophisticated parties optimize defaults’ assumption and implications for default rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A questions assumptions that standardization and automation necessarily produce efficient outcomes and highlights how contract design failures undermine core contract law values; Paper B challenges economic theories that treat defaults as irrelevant among sophisticated actors, arguing that defaults matter because parties often do not negotiate around them due to sticky drafting practices.

shared_topics.topic: normative responses: redesigning drafting practices, regulation, and legal education to improve contract design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes using a pattern-language informed normative program to make contracts more intelligible, adaptive, and human-centered; Paper B calls for scholarly, regulatory, and educational attention to template-driven drafting and suggests law schools can teach students to avoid template pitfalls and improve contractual allocations.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACTS AS TECHNOLOGY

shared_topics.topic: mechanisms, incentives, and barriers to the diffusion and adoption of contract innovations

shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes a normative agenda inspired by Alexander—making contracts more intelligible, adaptive, and equitable—while Paper B surveys policy interventions (IP changes, rules on unauthorized practice, public clearinghouses) aimed at promoting beneficial contractual innovation and broader dissemination.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Challenge of Legitimacy in Sovereign Debt Restructuring

shared_topics.topic: design of legal/institutional frameworks to promote legitimacy and resilience
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses Christopher Alexander's pattern language to diagnose how contract drafting choices create scalable contract architectures and proposes design-oriented reforms to make contracts more intelligible and resilient; Paper B analyzes how the institutional design of a potential debt workout mechanism (DWM) must incorporate legitimacy-enhancing features so it will be trusted, used, and resilient in practice.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows how interlocking contract patterns (e.g., mortgage contracts, pooling agreements, securitizations) produced networked financial systems that propagated failures during the financial crisis; Paper B treats sovereign-debt problems as systemically consequential, arguing that fragmented ad hoc practices can produce cascading economic, political, and social disruption and therefore require coherent institutional responses.

shared_topics.topic: tradeoffs of standardization/modularity in law — liquidity and efficiency versus fragility and exclusion
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how modular, standardized contract language reduced transaction costs and enabled liquid markets but also created 'informationally insensitive' assets that froze under stress; Paper B engages the analogous question in institutional design, weighing the benefits of a coherent, standardized DWM (predictability, efficiency) against political resistance, distributional harms, and risks that a one-size-fits-all mechanism would be perceived as illegitimate or inappropriate.

shared_topics.topic: the role of normative values (consent, participation, accountability, and equity) in shaping legal mechanisms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A foregrounds Alexander's humanistic goals — making contract design more intelligible, equitable, and responsive to individual consent — as a normative guide to reform; Paper B centers on participatory legitimacy, accountability, and respect for values as central criteria for designing a DWM that will secure voluntary compliance and fair distributional outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: seeking voluntary compliance as an objective of legal/institutional design
